CONFIDENTIAL. 


——_—_———— 


Correspondence respecting the Rights and Privileges of 
the Latin and Greek Churches in Turkey. 


(EASTERN QUESTION.) 


PART IV.* 


No. 1. 


The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received March 27, 
12°10 P.M.) 


(Telegraphic). | Vienna, March 27, 1854. 

THE ‘Austrian Correspondence” journal of this day publishes a 
telegraphic despatch from Bucharest of the 24th instant, stating that 18,000 
Russians crossed the Danube on the 23rd, near Gedschid. 11 was expected 
that 30,000 would have passed before stinset. 

The Turks retreated without offering opposition. 

General Liiders was moving from Galatz towards Ibraila to support the 
passage of the river. 


SS 
No, 2. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —( Received March 28.) 


(No, 388.) : 
My Lord, Paris, March 27, 1854. 
THE publication of the seeret correspondence on the Eastern question 
between Her Majesty’s Government and the Court of Russia, has had, as far 
as my observation goes, the happiest effect here; and, while recording the 
homage which is paid to the loyalty displayed by Mer Majesty’s Government, 
it gives me no less pleasure to bear testimony to the justice which is done on 
all sides to the ability and judgment displayed by Sir Hamilton Seymour. 
1 may relate, as a curious circumstance counected with this publication, 
that the Cardinal Archbishop of Bordeaux, with whom I had not the honour 


al 


of being acquainted, called upon me, a few days ago, and informed me that 
the object of his visit was to express the admiration which he felt for the British 
nation on reading the seeret correspondence. He had, he said, been previously 
suspicious of the real intention of Fler Majesty’s Government, and he desired to 
express his regret, at the same time that he offered his prayers for the pros- 
perity of the Queen. M. Dronyn de Lhuys has informed me also that a depul- 
ration of merchants from Bordeaux had waited upon him, and had told him 
that their opinion of the war was quite changed since they had read the cor- 
respondence in question, 

My private communications to your Lordship haye long since made you 
aware that, hardly had the Emperor Nicholas failed in his overtures towards 
Great ae than he turned his attention to France, and that, both through 

( 5 


o — 
= é Ce 
py es 


j Lety 


2 


General Castelbajac and through M. de Kisseleff, he endeavoured to establish 
the same understanding, in respect to the Hastern question, with the Emperor 
of the French, that he had failed in cementing with Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, [tis so painful to allude to transactions of this nature, in which good 
faith has been sacrificed to intrigue, that I should certainly have avoided the 
subject altogether ina public despatch had I not wished to place on record 
the honourable conduct of the French Government. Not only have all the 
Russian proposals been met in the most straightforward and dignified manner, 
but in order that Her Majesty's Government might not be led away, by false 
rumours, (0 suppose that seeret negotiations were going on between France 
and Russia, | hace heen constantly informed of every step taken, either at St. 
Petersburgh or Paris, to detach the Emperor of the French from his alliance 
with the Queen. 
L need hardly add how little they have succeeded, 


[ have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY., 


No. 3. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receited March 28.) 


(No. 153.) 


My Lord, Berlin, March 25, 1854. 

IN obedience to your Lordship’s instructions I have this evening read to 
Baron Manteutlel your Lordship’s despatch No, 74% of the 22nd instant, on the 
subject of Count. Groben's late mission to London. 

His Excelleney listened with the greatest attention to the observations 
which your Lordship had made te Count Graben, but he said very little in 
return, though he appeared to admit the validity of the arguments used by your 
Lordship in combating those of the Prussian Envoy, and he was by no means 
surprised at the effect produced on Her Majesty's Government by this mission, 
for, as | have already informed your Lordship, he expected it would be a 
failure, 

He was struck with your Lordship’s remark that England and France had 
been compelled to accept war by the Emperor of Russia, and thatdit was incom- 
prehensile that Prussia should expose itself to so many risks on account of the 
personal character of the Emperor, and that His Imperial Majesty would only 
become the more inflexible by tinding friends to support him, whereas he might 
be disposed to make concessions to reason and truth; but the deepest impression 
made on Baron Manteutfel appeared to be that part of the despatch in which 
you allude to the position of a second or third-rate power which Prussia seemed 
disposed to occupy im the approaching struggle. 

T did not fail to lay particular stress on your total ignorance of the quarter 
from whenee the threatening language attributed to Her Majesty’s Government 
had proceeded, and of the contrast of the tone which had been employed by 
England and France and that which had been adopted on many occasions by 
the Russian Government, 

His Excellency promised to make known to the King the substance of 
these remarks, but he added that he believed Count Groben had faithfully 
reported to His Majesty all your Lordship had said to him, and his Excellency 
appeared to expect that even at this late hour they might have a salutary effect, 
and assist in bringing about a better state of things, 

T have, &e, 
(Signed) BLOOMPITELD. 


* Sce Part IV, p, 349.

No. 4. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receiwed March 28). 


(No. 157. Confidential.) 
My Tord, Berlin, March 25, 1854. 

I HAVE made another and almost fruitless attempt to learn from Baron 
Mantenffel some details of the late communications sibieh have been sent from 
this Court to Vienna. ab LA eee 

His Excellency said that the communications which had been made 
emanated directly from the King, and that they consisted in assurances given 
by his Majesty that he had no object to influence in any way the policy of the 
Austrian Government on the Eastern question, that it was for them to decide 
on the course which it was most advisable to be adopted with a view to their 
own interests, but that Prussia desired to maintain her entire independence, 

Tt is evident that Baron Manteuflel does not approve of these communica- 
tions, which he considers can now only tend to lower Prussia in public estima- 
tion in Germany, and he observed that the King is so resolved to use every 
effort to retard if not to prevent the commencement of hostilities, that his mind 
is perpetually occupied in inventing new projects, and that he said to him the 
other day that matters were now beyond the pale of ordinary diplomatic 
arrangement, and that the only chance of success was to leave them to direct 
negotiation between the Sovereigns, 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 

CNo, 131.) 
My Lord Foreign Office, March 28, 1554.

Lord Clarendon.” Your Lordship will immediately communiente this despatch 
to Count Buol, and you will invite his Excelleney to-earry out the proposals 
suggested by his Excellency and referred to in your Lordship’s despateh 
No. 76 of the Sth instant,* and which 1 informed you in my despatch No, 122, 
of the 16th, were agreed to by Her Majesty’s Government, 


lam, ke. 
(Signed) CLARENDON. 


No, 6. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(No. 133.)

No. 11. 
Mr. Buchanan to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received Mareh 30,) 


(No. 107. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Copenhagen, March 24, 1854. 

IT may not be uninteresting to your Lordship, on the eve of events which 
are about to take place in the North of Europe, to be made acquainted with 
the opinions and feelings of the people of this country, as far as | have been 
able to ascertain them, respecting the approaching war and the parties about 
to be engaged in it. | 

In the first place with regard to the Court, 1 may observe, that the 
opinions of the King are ecient considered to be anti-Russian, and that the 
‘afluence of Madame Danver will most undoubtedly be employed to increase 
any feelings of hostility which ‘His Majesty may entertain towards the Emperor 
of Russia and his Government, 

Unfortunately, however, from the weakness of His Majesty's character, 
his opinions have little or no influence upon those of the Government or of the 
nation, and | am even assured that on matters of domestic policy His Majest tg 
Ministers have not untfrequently received his support by exaggerating his 
apprehensions of the danger of following a course which would be displeasing 
to the Court of St. Petersburg. 

Tt may, therefore, be assumed that His Majesty, whatever may be his 
personal feelings, is not likely to give an anti-Russian aroction to the policy of 
the country; but it may be at the same time hoped that His Majesty would 
willingly avail himself of the services of ministers who would be willing to 
adopt such a policy, especially if circumstances should occur to diminish the 
xamrorated opinions which have lately prevailed in Denmark of the power and 
the resources of Russia. 

The other members of the Royal Family may be all said to entertain, ina 
ercater or less degree, Russian feelings and opinions, 

This remark applies more particularly to the family of the Landgrave of 
Hesse, whose son-in-law, Prince Christian, considers himself to be mainly 
indebted to the Mmperor Nicholas for his present position in Denmark, and 
whose son, Prince Frederick of Hesse, is son-in-law of His Imperial Majesty, 
and a pensioner of Russia. The Princess Anne of Hesse, and wife of the 
latter, a young and amiable princess, has brought with her from the Court of 
Berlin the strongest sympathies for Russia; and although these royal per- 
sonages exercise no ostensible political power, their spinions have an un- 
favourable influence on those of many members of the Retne classes of society. 

The Government is of a Jess decided colour. Some of its members, more 
particularly Count Charles Moltke and M.de Criminil, have a strong Russian 
bias,—the tormer especially so, in consequence of favours received at St. 
Petersburg, and probably also from a sympathy with strong governmental 
opinions, A newspaper, suid to be supported hy his Excellency and the 
reactionary party in Denmark, openly supports Russian views, and its columns 
not unfrequently contain violent articles against England. 

If circumstances should, therefore, ever oblige the present Government to 
take an active part against Russia, it would do so against the wishes and 
inclinations of, [ fear, the majority of its members. At present they profess 
that they are neutrals, not only physically but morally, and they sedantically 
decline to express an opinion on the merits of the question which is about to 
plunge Enrope into war. 

With regard to the nation, from what T have already said your Lordship 
will be prepared to learn that among the higher classes Russia has more well- 
wishers than Great Britain, ‘The social changes eflected in 1848, the abolition 
of the game laws, and other measures affecting the privileges of the aristocracy, 
are ascribed to the tnflnence of English principles and ideas, and it is alt 
from Russian support that any improvement is expected by such persons ina 
state of things which they look upon as little removed from anarchy and 
communism. 

With the mass of the people sehen also, England is not popular; 1807 


6 


is not quite forgotten, and an impression prevails alinost universally that it was 
Russia alone that stood by Denmark in 1848. ‘That while England held back, 
Russia espoused Denmark’s cause, and that, finally, it was to Russia’ menaces 
and influence that Denmark is indebted for the terms which she ultimately 
obtained from Prussia and Germany. PS 

Although the extremes of society would thus appear to be unfriendly to 
England, she is fortunately, however, not entirely without a large and dagen! 
party among the Danish people. T feel assured that I do not err in considering 
the whole of the commercial and better educated portion of the middle classes 
as entirely devoted to English interests, so identical with their own, Every 
man who hopes to see constitutional liberty firmly established m the land, looks 
to England for countenanee and support; every man who is engaged in com- 
mercial pursuits, Knows that, his interests connect him with England None 
and though many persons among this class of society may vee i ity Sine 
ness of 1807, or draw comparisons in favour of Russia, with reference to the 
events of the Schleswig-Holstein war, they would all unanimously protest 
against any attempt on the part of the Government to assume a DOAN 
towards England, and would not hesitate to join lier ranks if they were calle 
upon to decide between the parties in the coming war, ea 

There are, L also believe, men in this party who would rejoice in seeing 
their country engaged in hostilities with Russia, m the hope that thereb Bone 
new arrangement might be secured respecting the relations of Sclilean ie with 
Denmark. Such persons perhaps would not even object, to England and 
France forcing the nation to a decision, Mm order to cover its future responsi- 
bility to Russia; and there is. I believe, little doubt that were a purely Danish 
policy to be adopted by the Western Powers with regard to Schleswig, and 
were the incorporation of that duchy into the kingdom guaranteed s Penmaes 
as the price of Danish support in an European war, the major ity of the people 
would espouse with enthusiasm the cause of the Western Powers. 

In the foregoing pages | have endeavoured, my Lord, to lay before you a 
correct statement of the opinions and feelings of the people of this country, as 
far as they are known to me, on the subject of the war, ‘The Dane. is not of an 
expansive character; our officers must not therefore expect an Snthusnte 
reception, even from our well-wishers. — Beloved we are not; but those M ne 
are anced to give us their support will do so on better and surer grounds 
than an oll grudge against Russia, or an ephemeral jealousy of Russian 
ambition, ‘They will give it to us upon a well-considered and correct estimate 
of their own interests, 

Wehasie; Groh ee ese ae ae 
(Signed) ANDREW BUCHANAN.

The ‘Turks are concentrating upon Karasoul to support the troops in advance.

No. 16. 


Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received March 31.) 


(No. 166.) 


My Lord, Berlin, March 28, 1854, 

THE Austrian General Hesse arrived here last night on a special mission 
from Vienna, but has been indisposed since his arrival, and had not made any 
attempt up to four o'clock this afternoon to see Baron Manteuffel. He is 
charged, I am assured, with direct communications from the Emperor to the 
King of Prussia. His Majesty, though better, is still too unwell to see anybody, 
and some time may yet elapse before he recovers from the accident which he 
met with last week. 

Baron Manteuffel, whom I have just seen, informs me that he has not 
received from Count Armim any positive indications of the object of General 
Hesse’s journey to Berlin, but he nevertheless believes that he is the bearer of 
some propositions for the joint military action of Austria and Prussia in the 
Eastern question, and that he is to suggest how far the co-operation of Prussia 
can be made useful at the present moment. 

His Excellency said, however, that he only guessed what might be coming, 
for he had no positive intelligence as to the plans of Austria, and further that 
he did not think the King would consent to signa military convention if one 
were proposed, 

He told me that the feelings at Vienna were very anti-Russian, and the 
account of the passage of the Danube by the Russians, if true, might decide the 
Austrian Cabinet to take active measures without further delay, 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

My Lord, Paris, March 31, 1854. 
MY private correspondence with your Lordship will have informed you that 
the Emperor was desirous some weeks ago of writing to the Emperor of 
Austria, in the hope of obtaining from His Majesty some explicit declaration as 
to the future policy of Austria in the astern question. A draft of the 
Emperor's letter was submitted for the consideration of Her Majesty's (Grovern- 
ment, and the idea having been discouraged by them as inopportune was 
abandoned by the Emperor. , ; 
His Majesty appears to have spoken subsequently to M. de Hubner of the 
‘atention which he had had, and to have been encouraged by Count Buol to 
ersist in it. His Majesty accordingly addressed a letter last week to the 
Baigneroe of Austria, in which he begged the Emperor, in the most friendly 
manner, to explain what his future policy would be, His Majesty assured the 
Emperor that it was not from motives nither of mistrust or curiosity, that he 
made the request, but that, as France and England were about to send an 
expedition to Turkey, it was most important to them to know the intentions of 
Austria, since their own plans would naturally depend in 4 great measure upon 
the attitude assumed by that Power. His Majesty promised at the same time 
the utmost secrecy should the Emperor of Austria require Te o 
M. de Bourqueney had an audience of the Emperor of Austria, on the 25th 
instant, in order to place this letter in His Majesty’s hands, ‘The Emperor did 
not read it at the time, but he entered into conversation with the French 
Minister. From the short summary of this conversation given by M. de 
Rourqueney in a telegraphic despatch, it would appear that the Emperor renewed 
his assurances that he would abide by the policy of Franee and England, though 
ag usual his assurances went no further, He said that his alan towards 
Russia was difficult and delicate, and that France and England must be indul- 
gent. He seems to have hinted that the passage of the Danube at the distant 
point at which it had taken place, rendered it apparently less hostile towards 
Austria, In general, the Emperor's tone was friendly and courteous when 
speaking of France, very reserved with respect to Prussia, and very bitter when 
alluding to Russia.

Sip J Milbanke to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 1.) 


(No, 21.) | 
My Lord, Munich, Moreh 20, 1854, 

THE messenger Grattan arrived here on the 25th instant, and delivered to 
me your despatches to No. 16 inclusive, ane 

"1 have reason to believe that some new intrigues, in reference to the 
expected declarations at the Diet at Frankfort on the part of Austria and 
Prussia relative to the neutrality of Germany at the present crisis, have heen 
set on foot among the smaller States of the Confederation, though Tam as yet 
but imperfectly acquainted with their object, What [have heard, however, 1s 
that the Wurtemberg Government has lately addressed a“ circular” to those of 
the other second-rate Sates, calling ben them to come to an understanding 45 
to the course which it will be for their common interest to pursue when the 
announcement of the policy of the two great German Powers shall be mide to 
them in the Diet. IT have been informed, though it. is scarcely credible under 
existing circumstances, that one point upon which the South-Western States 
are disposed to insist, i9 the concentration of a federal force on the western 
frontiers of Germany; but such a step, if taken, or even seriously meditated, 


li 


would fall little short of a menace towards France, and might be attended with 
the gravest consequences, inasmuch as it must of necessity be followed by 
corresponding preparations on the French bank of the Rhine. 

T seek in vain for any indication of hostility towards any member of the 
Confederation on the side of France which could in the least justify such an 
open demonstration of mistrust, and if, therefore, there be any foundation for 
the ramour to which I have alluded, I am compelled to trace the notion to the 
renewed efforts of Russia to hamper the action of the two great Powers which 
are now said to be perfectly agreed, Certain it is that the quarter in which the 
initiative has been taken lays the proposal open to suspicion ; for Stutteard has, 
ever since the arrival there of the Grand Duchess Olga, been generally con- 
sidered to be the head-quarters of Russian influence and intrigue in Germany, 

Something or other, which it 1s sought to keep seeret, is unquestionably 
going on, for much activity is observable among the diplomacy of the small 
Courts. From what Iam able to collect the declaration about to be made to 
the Dict by Austria is in substance an expression of her readiness to devote her 
power to the interests of Germany, which she thinks will be best secured by 
abstaining as long as possible from any active participation in the coming 
struggle, These views coincide exactly with those entertained here, and as is 
asserted with those of Prussia also, Such at least is the language reported to 
have been held by the Emperor of Austria during his late visit to Munich, but 
if Lam correctly informed it was generally made to appear that in the event of 
those interests requiring him to turn his arms against his Northern ally he 
would consider that he made a sacrifice of his inclination to his duty to the 
Confederation. 

If, which is, however, as yet by no means clear to me, Austria and Prussia 
are as cordially united as they are represented to be, the present movement 
amongst the smaller States would be easy to be accounted for on the grounds 
which [ have explained in former despatches. Their suspicions that: they are 
not even to be consulted in the arrangement have been aroused by the circum. 
stance that not even a confidential overture has been made to them on the 
subject. ‘This was admitted by M, de Pelkhoven in the course of a conversa- 
tion which | had with him two days ago, and in which he made show of a 
reliance upon the two great Powers, which T do not believe this Government in 
reality feels, for he stated nearly at the same time to one of my colleagues 
that Bavaria was go little satistied with the hesitation and concealment practised 
towards her by the Austrian Cabinet, that she had contemplated requiring some 
previous explanation of the policy which she would shortly be called upon to 
support in the Diet. 

What effect the passage of the Danube by the Russian forees may have 
upon the decisions of Austria remains to be seen: here it is much feared that it 
will foree her into more energetic measures than she has hitherto been disposed 
to take, or than will be at all palatable to the Confederation. 

T have, &ec. 
(Signed) J. R. MILBANKE.

13 


The observation on my part had, in fact, elicited an almost involuntary 
avowal of the great principle of the party to which he himself belongs, of his 
belief in Prussia’s destiny to dominate in Germany, 

He went on, however, to say, that when an announcement was made to 
Lord Bloomfield that Prussia could not accede to the proposed convention, 
M. de Manteuffel expected that the communication would be received by his 
Lordship in a very different spirit from that in which it was accepted. In lieu 
of any strong expression or outbreak which was, it seems, fully expected by 
him, Lord Bloomfield only observed, with perfect coolness, “ Well, then, we 
mist endeavour to obtain our object by some other means,” 

His Excellency then proceeded to give me some details of what those 
other means are likely to be, and said, that if England only songht an assurance 
that Prussia would in no case assume an attitude hostile to us while we were 
prosecuting war with Russia, we might feel perfectly sceure. “In no case,” 
said M. de Bismark, “can we become the allies of Russia, but to incur the 
risks and expenses of a war with that Empire is quite another thing, especially 
when the possible advantages to Prussia, even of a suecesstil issue to such a 
war, are fairly weighed,” 

There being no object for my entering on an argument with M. de 
Bismark, and wishing only to elicit such information on recent transactions, 
and such opinions on coming events as might prove of sufficient interest to 
report to your Lordship, 1 let the subject drop, and adverted to M, de 
Manteuffol’s communication of the 18th of March to the Prussian Chambers. 

I mentioned to his Excelloney the two points whieh had chiefly struck me 
in that document, viz., that while Prussia was set forth as adhering strictly to 
the principles laid down in the Vienna conference; it was at the same time 
sought to establish that she had interests which might nevertheless conipel her 
to take a course different from that taken by some of the Powers with which 
she had acted in those conferences. Tt would seem then to be M. de 
Manteuflel’s argument that the separate interests of a State apparently con- 
curring with others for a common object might at any time override such 
engagements as that State had contracted in coneert with others, 

The next point was the stress laid on Prussian leadership in Germany :— 
Prussia, it was said, would secure to her confederates the blessings of peace.’ 

L hardly need point out to M. de Bismark in what light such a pretension 
would be regarded by Austria; or the risk of assuming such a position, if there 
Was any wish to keep measures with the Imperial Government. 

As regarded my first remark, M, de Bismark said the meaning of the 
sentence to which I referred was not intended to go the whole length I 
imagined, that Prussia had interests of her own so much at variance with 
those of England and France, that without differing from them on the principle 
laid down at Vienna, that Russia had made an unjust aggression on Turkey, 
she might still have diverging views as to the mode in which that aggression 
was to is dealt with, and aleo Interests so apart from those of Austria that no 
one could argue on their being identical. 

As to the offence which might be felt in Austria at Prussia’s offer of 
securing peace to Germany, he did not think it would alter in any degree the 
sentiments with which the two States mutually regarded each other, and for 
his own part he believed that Austria would have been heartily glad to have 
been in a position to give a similar assurance, 

Our interview ended with strong assurances on M. de Bismark’s part that 
in no case was it possible for Prussia to become the ally of Russia, and that it 
was, as he affirmed, the national and not the Russian party which had rejected 
the Convention, but which nevertheless would use every effort to maintain 
good understanding with England, though their national pride and feelings of 
independence had been deeply wounded by the tone of menace adopted towards 
them in quarters where it had not been expected, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) A. MALET.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 4.) 
(No. 169.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 1, 1864. 
THE publication and presentation to Parliament of Sir Hamilton Seymour's 
secret und confidential despatches has had a wonderful influence on public 
opinion here. They are read with great avidity by all those who are desirous of 
learning the truth as connected with the Bee of Russia in the Kast, and I 
believe that I may safely assure your Lordship, that the effect produced by these 
despatches has heen general throughout Germany. I cannot learn that they have 
as yet been seen by the King, and I, consequently, suggested to Baron Man- 
teuffel to-day, that the knowledge of these documents by His Majesty might be 
attended with advantage, his Excellency said that he should speak to the King 
ate these papers, and recommend that they should be read to His 
jesty. 

‘i [ ‘have not failed to draw the attention of the Minister President to the 
declaration published in the “ Gazette” of the 28th ultimo, upon the subject of 
the commerce of neutrals, and have been assured by his Excellency that the 
King and the Prussian Government are highly gratified at the generous 
forbearance of Her Majesty's Government in regard to this important 
question. 

No country will perhaps be more benefited than Prussia by the concessions 
made in favour of neutrals, for her vessels will probably get a large portion of 
the carrying trade in the Baltie, whilst her merchants are already speculating 


largely on the prospect of a vast quantity of Russian produce being shipped in 
Prussian ports. 


T have, &c. 
(Signed ) BLOOMFIELD. 


No. 29. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receiwed April 4.) 
(No. 171.) 
My Lord, 


Berlin, April 1, 1854, 

M. LE MENSEBACH, the Prussian Consul-General in Wallachia, has 
lately written to his Government complaining of indignities to which he has 
been exposed by the Russian military authorities, and of the impossibility of 
obtaining any redress, 

They have been carried to such an extent, that the Prussian Government 
has at last arrived at the conclusion, that their agent should be withdrawn, 
and as the only explanation offered is the existence of martial law in the Princi- 
palities, and as circumstances now preclude all chance of a return toa better 
state of things, Baron de Manteutfel has instructed M, de Mensebach to retire 
from Wallachia, if he should deem it desirable upon a repetition of any 
proceedings similar to those of which he has already had just reason to 
complain, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFTELD.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received April 4.) 
(No. 121.) 


My Lord, Vienna, March 29, 1854. 

TCOMMUNICATED to Count Buol your Lordship’s despatch No. 122," 
which, while alluding to the serious obstacles which have arisen to the = 
ture of the Convention, which had been proposed for adoption by the our 
Powers, yet refers to the satisfaction with which Her Majesty's Government 
had learnt that Count Buol withdraws from none of its stipulations, and is 
perfectly willing lo confirm them. 

Count Buol received this assurance with great satisfaction, as well as your 
Lordship’s els to the feeling he had expressed, that if a document, 
drawn up with the object of cementing more closely the alliance between the 
Four Powers, was only signed by three of those Powers, the impression would 
be most unfavourable. 

To avoid such a result, Count Buol stated that, in his last communications 
to the Prussian Government, he had again urged upon them the importance of 
their being parties to this document ; but if they still objected to become so, he 
had hopes that they would not refuse their assent to the adoption of a 
protocol, in which the engagements contained in the proposed Convention 
might. be inserted. 

In case neither of these recommendations should he adopted by the 
Prussian Government, Count Buol stated that he must still continue to 
entertain the views he has already expressed to your Lordship, of the dis- 
astrous effects which might be produced, particularly in Germany, by the 
adoption of the Convention by only three of the Powers instead 0 the four, 
for which it was originally ineended. 

_ He states that your Fon may rely with confidence upon his decided 
opinion upon this subject, he would therefore anxiously desire that some other 
form might be adopted, by which the same mutual guarantee between the 
Sorapnne would be obtained, and to which he would most willingly 

re. 

In making this appeal to your Lordship, Connt Buol again assured me 
that he had the best hopes that the Prussian Government would not withdraw 
from the principles which were embodied in the convention.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received April 6.) 
(No. 127.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 25, 1854. 

1 AVAILED myself of General Sir John Burgoyne’s return from 
Gallipoli, to put him in personal communication with Omer Pasha, conceiving 
that an officer of his ability and experience would be able ina few days to 
form a correct judgment of the condition and prospects of the ‘Turkish army 
in Bulgaria, and to afford important information as to the character and inten- 
tions of its commander. 

Sir John returned from Varna on the 2lst instant, and having at my 
request committed to paper the result of his observations, | ofler no excuse for 
transmitting to your Lordship herewith in copy two memorandums, which 
contain not only an account of what he saw and heard in the course of his visit 
to Shumla, but also some notes of the opinions which he had formed in 
consequence. 

[ hold the latter to be worthy of the Porte's attention, and therefore make 
a point of communicating them to Reshid Pasha, 

Thave, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Memorandum. 


Constantinople, March 22, 1854, 

I ARRIVED at Shumla on the evening of the 12th of March, and 
waited on Omer Pasha by appointment the next morning. Nothing could 
have been more courteous than his behaviour, and he has been full of 
attentions to myself and the party with me ever since our arrival; one of his 
aides-de-camp almost constantly in attendance to provide for any wants we 
might have; horses for the whole party, mounted orderlies, and dinners sent 
to ns to the bare walls, in which, according to the custom of the country, we 
were lodged, We were not less than an hour with him, without any pressure 
on our part on his time, and he returned the visit the same evening at 8 
p.a., and remained as long, His conversation was cheerful, frank, and, | 
believe, quite honest, as far as he chose to communicate, but not very full as to 
his intentions. He set out for the Danube on the 4th, | was, therefore, only 
just in time to cateh him. He calls his excursion a tour of inspection, adding, 
Heaeven with a smile, that if he foundan opportunity, he might perhaps strike 
some little coup—implying rather the makin some little attempt upon the 
enemy, if circumstances seemed favourable, fhan having any fixed plan of 
advance in much foree; and yet the preparations seemed to be extensive, 
Some regiments have been moved to the front from Schumla, and the force 
from Adrianople (and pevtiaps other parts) are moving forward, One regi- 
ment arrived at Shumla on the 14th, consisting of a very fine body of men, 
armed with percussion muskets; but there appear to be large forces atill 
remaining on the two extreme flanks at Kalafat and the Dobruscha; and from 
a remark made by the Pasha incidentally, | imagine his project is to support 
a principal advance from the centre by a diversion from Kalafat, or, vice versi, 
to draw the Russian forees to the centre, while an attempt is made from 
Kalafat to take possession of the Lesser Wallachia, where the inhabitants are 
said to be particularly indisposed to the Russians, and where a new line along 
the river Aluta is said to be very strong. There is, moreover, manifestly 
some danger in those wide movements, or in these greatly dispersed positions, 
with an enemy concentrated in the midst of them, from whence he can 
attack any one he pleases, with nearly his whole foree. 

Omer Pasha is vigorous in body, and full of information and intelligence, 
He knows all this country thoroughly; he is evidently very sanguine and 
confident; but he holds strong opine and a considerable bias towards points 


a2 


he would wish to be established. I never knew so low an opinion given of the 
value of Russian troops as he entertains, while he is enthusiastic on the merits 
of the Turks. He says the difficulty is to restrain hig soldiers from moving 
forward, while those “f the Russians have to be urged on by their afhicers. 
‘After descanting in this way for some time, | said to him, lightly, “ lt would 
appear that your Highness would have no hesitation on any day to pit a regi- 
ment of Turks against one of equal force of Russians,” to which he answered, 
emphatically, that he would readily attack three Russian regiments with two 
of Turks; and J am persuaded that he fully believes their value to be in that 
proportion. There ‘= no difference of opinion anywhere as to the courage of 
the ‘Turkish soldier; and | can believe another of Omer Pusha’s opinions, that 
he has more natural intelligence than the Russians, whom he describes as mere 
machines, ‘There isa Prussian officer at Shumla in the Turkish service, wlio 
gives a much better account of the Russians. Asa Prussian, however, he will 
naturally approve of a system that is worked precisely like that of his own 


country. He mentions in favour of the Russian officers what might appear, 
but not correctly, to justify the Pasha’s judgment of the demerit of the soldier 
—that the officers were Very forward in coming to the front. in action, to 
encourage the men to advance. Hf these judgments were formed at Oltenitza, 
‘+ must be recollected that the position of the Russians was most trying: on 
a dead flat, of great extent, subjected to a very heavy cross fire of a powerful 
commanding artillery, during an advance to a well-manned entrenchment. 
Of the Russian artillery the Pasha deseribes the practice as bad, while it 1s 
said that the Turkish field-pieces are well served, and, according to the Pasha, 
weil horsed and equipped, and, if-so, the capability of movements, quick and 
continued, is of even more consequence than accuracy of practice. | inquired 
of him about the provision of reserve ammunition. He said that he had in the 
different depots in the earrisons 25 muchas 1,000 rounds for every effective 
field-piece ; but did not cive a clear account how the spare musket AMMINTILLON 
was conveyed. 

Fe acknowledges that cavalry the Russians have a complete superiority, 
bt rather surprised me by considering that the most important of that force 
were the Cossacks, This country, that is everywhere excepting the higher 
ridges of the Balkan consists of vast open plains, the cavalry ought therefore 


ta be of great service, and mn trying contests, whon the infantry becomes loose 
in order, must be very influential. It 1s said, however, that in ordinary cases 

the Turkish infantry put themselves. readily into compact mass’® and repel 

the charges of cavalry—a ereat proof of courage and mutual self-confidence, 

The Prussian officer, and indeed general report, considers the Turkish officer 

ag very inferior; he says that from the corporal upwards they are of descending 

order in merit as they ascend in rank. 

Omer Pasha estimates the Russian forces in the Principalities at 150,000 
men in all; but he says that they have a large number of sick, a great many 
irregulars, Many scattered posts and depdts to protect, so. that he does not 
consider that their effective maneevuring force can be valued at more than 
100,000, which does not appear wnreasonable. It is probable that thus far he 
may have tolerably woud snformation, but he does not seem to know what they 
are doing in the rear, : \though he is inclined to believe that reinforcements to 
any amount are as far back as Kiefl, It is very difficult to obtain information 
from within the Russian outposts at any time, and more particularly with such 
an impediment as the Danube in their front; on the other hand, the Russian 
system of espionage ‘n their favour seems to be carried to a great extent, 
Qmer Pasha not only cautioned us to secrecy In all our projects for the dispo 
sition of our troops OF proceedings, but he evidently in. lis owl manner shows 
a distrust of any of lis proceedings being divulged. He was comparatively 
very open to Ws, hut we coulil observe the difference in his conversation the 
instant any servants or officers came into the room, and L really believe that 
sart of his reserve to Wa May be owing to this caution, nota distrust of our 
honour, but perhaps of our ‘dliseretion, ‘This distrust of even their own fol- 
lowers and of one another seems to be quite common to all the ‘Turks in 
authority. 

Omer Pasha must be sensible of knowing 80 much more than we can of 
the state of affairs here, he is so decided in his opinions, has so well considered 
a proposed course of action, and is now so high position and power, that to

actually joining him, and when he entered upon the subject with me, he more 
than once recommended that we should take post at Varna. He deseribed it, 
as a healthy country, that it would be easy to obtain there any amount of 
supplies, that there were already defences there for a large force or a moderate 
one, that it would threaten in flank or front any Russian advance in Bulgaria, 
and, at the same time, by our command in the Black Sea, would also threaten 
an attack upon the whole Russian north and north-eastern coast, Odessa or the 
Crimea. An attack on the latter is a very favourite project with him; he said 
the inhabitants of the Crimea (Tartars and Mahomedans) were peculiarly 
adverse to the Russians, that, on account of the narrow neck connecting It 
with the main, we could retain it, and that it would act powerfully in 
endangering the possessions of the Russians in Georgia and Cireassia, but did not 
advert much to what we should consider most valualle, the fall of Sebastopol 
and the fleet there. All this is very sensible, but there are several difficulties 
to he considered. 1 told him that Varna, though a fine bay, was quite open to 
some winds and no port, to which he said, that if was well sheltered from the 
prevailing winds, and in summer was always considered an excellent roadstead. 
| then mentioned that the conquest of the Crimea would be most advantageous, 
Init would be most extremely difficult, by a landing from the sea against such 
a force as the Russians no donbt had within reach. He estimated that foree 
at, perhaps, 20,000 men, I told him that our Government believed there were 
there as much more, perhaps 30,000 or 40,000. He mace light of any difficulty 
in his confident manner, and said you had only to land and entrench yourselves 
near the shore, so as to maintain a footing until you put in the necessary 
amount of foree; a very natural idea for a Turk, as it is very much in their 
mode of warfare, but too hazardous to be attempted by us, and especially 
without ascertaining the nature of the country and of the position itself 
previously, and would be considered a wild project. The force of the argu- 
ment relative to the Bay of Varna as a roadstead for the purpose, would be 
decided by the navy after more knowledge of the Black Sea; but there would 
be another considerable objection, It would not be thought right probably to 
eend an army thus early into the Black Sea, with the Bosphorus and 
Dardanelles unsecured in its rear, = 

The presence of a respectable force of British and F rench troops at Varna 
during the summer is well worthy of consideration, lt would, no doubt, 
ercatly embarrass the enemy by its central position, from whence it might be 
directed to the Danube or any part of Bulgaria, or by Aidos into Roumelia 
on the one side, while on the other it would be more ready to make an 
attack upon the Crimea, and all the northern and eastern coasts of the 
Black Sea, than from the Bosphorns, and oblige him to maintain large forces 
in those parts, or risk the suffering of some heavy disasters there, brut will 
probably, he considered, be too forward a movement to be determined upon 
until events shall more completely justify it. Any previous footing, however, 
made at the Dardanelles or Constantinople will be all in the way for such an 
advance into the Black Sea, should cireumstances render it desirable, and will 
no doubt be so esteemed by the enemy. | 

With regard to the capabilities of the Bay of Varna, Colonel Neale, the 
British Consul, states that during the seven years that he has been stationed 
there, he has only known of the loss of six or seven vessels in it, and those ill- 
found Turks and Grecks, although an open bay well frequented for trade. 
It is little more than 4,000 yards wide,—vessels in it would he within range of 
heavy guns on either shore ; within the place there is a barrack for full 3,000 
men, and a line military hospital, é 

Whether in effecting a landing on the enemy’s coast, or in retiring from 
it, the co-operation of a Turkish force would be extremely valuable for covering 
the advance or retreat in entrenchments, for which they are peculiarly well 
adapted, and they would be more particularly desirable in any enterprise in 
the Crimea, or other part, where the inhabitants are Mahomedans, and of 


fricndly disposition towards the allies.

Memorandum. 


Constantinople, March 22, 1854. 

THE prospect of affairs on the frontier of Turkey is extremely discouraging. 

The Russians have not less than 100,000 men in Wallachia for a 
maneuyring army after deducting for sick, inefficient, and various other posts ; 
they are known to be good troops, well appointed and commanded, and under 
every approved principle of organization and arrangement. 

The Turks have, perhaps, about as many, including garrisons of numerous 
fortified places; their really available force to take the field is, therefore, much 
less: in their composition they are far inferior to their enemy; the recent 
improvements in their army have only reached the equipment and exercises of 
their infantry and artillery, Their infantry consisting of fine men, full of courage 
and well armed, serviceably clothed, and, moreover, with a degree of correctness 
and steadiness which does not fail them even in action ; the artillery is well 
served and well horsed ; the cavalry is in small foree and inefficient; the officers 
of all arms, taken in the mass, know nothing of their business, 

Omer Pasha is a man of energy and intelligence, on a par with men of the 
most civilized nations, but, from his extreme over-confidence in his troops and 
himself, and from his arrangements, appears to me to be wanting in judgment 
in some respects. All other pashas or generals that I have seen are evidently 
without any professional knowledge, although, yery probably, of much personal 
courage, ‘The engineering of the Turks is beneath criticism, and there is every 
appearance that their arrangements for depots of provisions, ammunition, &c. 
are quite defective, partly from want of knowledge; thus, as an army, they are 
not to be compared to'their enemy, nor fit for campaigning operations, 

To this inferiority is to be added the injudicious principles of a vague idea 
of defending the line of the Danube, which cannot be deemed practicable. 

A line of river of hundreds of miles in extent affords no more defence than 
the Wall of China; it is merely an obstacle for the passing of which means can 
always be readily obtained. In the civilized Christian countries a river frontier 
may be of importance when fortresses are judiciously established on its banks 
(with tétes-de-pont) at the bridges and passages of the great leading roads of 
communication, because it is by those roads that the movements of armies are 
directed; but in Wallachia and Bulgaria there are no made roads, one part of 
the country is as easily traversed as another, and any part of the banks ean be 
reached. A few towns on the right bank are particularly fortified, but without 
tétes-de-pont, or any lodgment on the left bank, except at Widdin. There can 
be no very great difficulty, therefore, in forcing the passage, when all the 
scattered batteries and defences will fall into the hands of the enemy: more- 
over, the line is between 300 and 400 miles in extent from Kalafat to the 
mouth of the river, and most disadvantageously circumstanced in presenting 
concave line to be defended instead of the most favourable, which is convex ; 
thus the two flanks, Kalafat and the Dobrudscha, particularly the latter, which is 
on the right, are considerably advanced, while the centre is re-entering. 

_ ‘Toall these natural disadvantages must be added a vicious disposition of 
the troops; on each of these two advanced flanks are collected about 25,000 
men, which disposes of one-half of the whole army; the Russians occupying the 
central position, at about an equal distance between the flanks, and more 
aprons to the centre, can concentrate their main force to attack the latter, 
while they merely hold in cheek the flanks: thus it is presumed that they will 
cross somewhere between Silistria and Rustchuk, or between the latter and 
Nicopolis, with 60,000 men, to oppose which the Turks will not have above 
30,000 available, with the presumption that they will not happen to be collected 
in the right place ; a rapid advance will probably then be made on Shumla, 
and possession obtained of it, and perhaps at the same time the rear of the 
Turkish foree in the Dobrudscha may be gained, which will then be seriously 
compromised ; some 10,000 or 15,000 men will be sufficient then to follow the 
retiring corps from Kalafat and the Dobrudscha, who may be expected, from the 
moral effect of their first failure, to get into great disorder, ih be driven back 
in confusion by inferior forces.

26 


Schumla is in « fine strategical site for concentration, either for attack or 
defence, but, under the circumstances here assumed, cannot, it 1s conceived, he 
retained to advantage j it is not a fortress, but merely an intrenched camp, that 
would require 25,000 or 40,000 men to defend, and, even ‘f such a corps could 
be collected there, which is hardly to be expected, it would be improvident to 
have them shut up in it, when the next line, that of the Balkan, would require 
all the forces that can be collected on it. | 

The fall of Shumla will have @ serious effect on the morale of the Turkish 
army and nation on account of a strong prevalent prestige and boast that 
Shumla has never been taken, It ia to be hoped that after all these events 
on the Danube and in Bulgaria, the Russians will have been 80 detained by 
detailed operations, the collecting provisions, bringing up depots, subduing 
fortified posts, and other arrangements as not to be able to prevent the remains 
of the Turkish army from oecupying Varna in strength, and taking Up positions 
for the defence of the passes of the Balkan; it is then that the energetic 
defence of the country may he attempted with a prospect of success, 

The measures that it would seem desirable to adopt to meet these antici- 
pated evils would appear to bes— iets 

1. To put it seriously to the consideration of Omer Pasha, if it is not now 
too late, the probable passage of the Russian main body to an amount 0 
perhaps 60,000 men, aa the want of men on his side to prevent it, with his 
inferior forces, also to submit to his better judgment the policy of retaining 
auch a large force on each of the extreme flanks, while the encmy occupies & 
central position, from whence he can attack the centre or either of them; in 
short, whether he can consider it possible to yrevent being forced by very 
superior numbers, somewhere, im so. very extensive @ line a5 that of the 
Danube. 

© ‘fo submit to that general whether the passes of the Balkan would not 
wresent a more suitable feld of battle for his army, acting on the defensive, 
with such places as Shumla, &e., ocenpied in his front, if he thought proper ; on 
the Balkan the enemy would be at once deprived of one great source Ol 
their superiority, namely, that of their cavalry. Ip ract 

5. ‘That the Turkish forces should defend the line of the Danube lightly, 
and avoid any general or serious action in Bulgaria, but rather retire under 
previously regulated arrangements for an orderly retreat, each soe to its 
destined position on the Balkan, ag soon a8 the enemy shall be firmly estab- 
lished on the right bank of the river, with arrangements for due supply of 
provisions and other necessaries. for the troops in their new position, and the 
least available resources left for the enemy. 

4, 'To provide Varna in due time with a good garrison, and the necessary 
provisions and ammunition to withstand a s1ege. 

5. That the combined fleets, if the admirals approved, should take station 
temporarily, but early, in the Bay of Kavarna, where they would be able to 
co-operate to many (seful purposes with the Turkish right, and would threaten 
all the Russian consts, and where their presence would lead to an expectation 
that they might be f ollowed by the land forces of the allies. 

(. That the position of Boulabar, and one in front of Constantinople, 

between the Sea of Marmora and the Black Sea, be thoroughly entrenched for 
places of last retreat. 
7 "The troops of French and British now under orders for this service to be 
collected at the Dardanelles, and in the neighbourhood of Constantinople, where 
they could act as a nucleus for the last defence of these positions, or AGvan’s up 
the country, or even into the Black Sea, as the coming events shall seem to be 
most proper. 

Tt is presumed that after the present force, which the Russians have in the 
Principalities, and the 6th Corps (supposed, perhaps, 45,000) shall have joined, 
they would have much difficulty, and require & considerable time to bring 
forward more, and that by the above measures, and, if necessary, further 
reinforcements from France and England, such force, or whatever they could 
add, it may be confidently presumed would be quite insuflicient to auceeed in 


their enterprise, 
(Signed) J, F, BURGOYNE.

Consul Neale to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Varna, March 16, 1854. 


I HAVE the honour to acquaint your Lordship that his Highness, Omer 
Pasha, left Shumla on the 18th istant, for the Daiibe accompanied by 
Ismail Pahsa, late second in command at Kalafat, and most of the troops who 
were at Shumla. 

The troops now remaining in Shumla do not exceed between 3,000 and 
4.000 men. With the exception of about 14,000 men stationed at Varna, 
humla and ‘Ternova, the whole of the Turkish army of Bulgaria are now on 
the Danube, or within a day’s march of that river. 

1 am informed, however, that there is a reserve of about 10,000 men at 
Sofia, who are also advancing towards the Danube. 

‘Phe Russian force hitherto assembled in Little Wallachia, with its head- 
quarters at Craiova, is now known to be effecting a retrograde movement, The 
villages round Kalafat are abandoned by the Russian troops, and a ree onnais- 
sanee had been made by some Turkish cavalry nearly to Craiova, 

Tt would certainly appear that the Russian army is about being concen- 
trated round Bucharest, or opposite the centre of the urkish line. A move of 
the Turkish troops out of Kalafat would tend to delay the accomplishment of 
such an object. 

Should there be no forward movement out of Kalafat, IT humbly conceive it 
probable that the Russians would be in a condition to pass the Danube with 
70,000 or 80,000 men, still leaving a force of 20,000 or 30,000 men opposite 
Matchin. [tis probable that his Highness, Omer Pacha, could concentrate 
50,000 or 60,000 to oppose to a Russian invading army; but such a concen- 
tration, I fear, would occupy a week, and the means of transport for the 
necessary provisions and munitions of the army, I am informed, are very 
deficient and inadequate, 

T have, &

(Signed) EDWARD ST. JOHN NEALE.

Consul Neale to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Varna, March 21, 1854, 

NO intelligence of serious importance has reached Varna from the 
Danube since the Generalissimo, Omer Psalia, left Shumla on the 14th 
instant. 

[ have, however, received accounts of heavy cannonading having occurred 
at Silistria and at Turturkai, and on the part of the Russians from the oppo- 
site sido of the river. ‘The Russians would appear to have established several 
batteries, and had twenty-four guns engaged against ‘Turturkai. These 
events are reported to haye taken place between the 12th and 15th instant. 

At this juncture, I beg leave to lay before your Lordship, in the enclosed 
paper, the result of the best and most recent information | can obtain respecting 
the force and distribution of the Turkish army on the Danube. 

This distribution, which | have every reason to believe to be the present 
one, will doubtless be changed, and especially as regards the large body of

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—{ Received April 6,) 
(No. 177. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 3, 1854, 

_ THAD some conversation this morning with Baron Manteutffel respecting 
his negotiations with General Hess, when his Excellency informed me that they 
had not yet come to any definite understanding, though they had entered into 
discussion on the following points, He said that it was proposed that the 
Convention between Prussia and Austria should be made for the whole duration 
of the war between Russia and the Western Powers, that it was intended 
especially for the protection of German interests, and that there was to be a 
mutual guarantee of the whole of the territory belonging to the two States. 
That Austria had proposed that Prussia should place a force near the Austrian 
frontier, and that when the arrangements were made, Austria and Prussia were 
to address a summons to Russia to withdraw her armies from the Turkish 
territory. I told his ee ee [ was glad to hear that such proposals had 
come from Vienna, and that hoped there would be no hesitation m agreeing 
to them, for it was essential that no more time should be lost in determining 
the position of the two German Powers at the commencemont of the war, that 
we had seen the rapidity with which the Russians were advancing, and that as 
they had now taken up a position south of the Danube, inportant duties 
devolved on the allies to arrest their further progress. 

Baron Manteutfel replied that he hoped the King might be brought to 
agree to the arrangements that had been proposed, but he feared His Majesty 
would raise Serious objections, and that he would not easily be brought to 
mobilise his army unless the interests of Germany were actually menaced, and 
that His Majesty did not consider that the moment was come for making the 
sacrifices which this step would entail on the country; that he should, however, 
use his best endeavours and advise the King to adopt the proposed measures 
and that, at all events, I might depend on his doing all in his power to ensure 
the joint action of Austria and Prussia at the present crisis. 

This was the substance of Baron Manteuffel’s conversation, 

I wish I could add that | thought there was a prospect of his Exeellency’s 
hopes being realized, but since my interview this morning I have heard that the 
King has declared that he will not agree to anything that compels him to take 
an active part in the war, and that His Majesty proposes that there shall he a 
clause in the Convention that neither party shall act without previous consulta— 
tion and agreement with the other, which stipulation, proposed by a Sovereign 
of the timid and yacillating character of the King of Prussia, whose disposition 
seems to be all in favour of Russia, though he is afraid openly to avow it, would 
completely tie the hands of Austria, and prevent her from taking the course 
which appears indicated by all her late communications. 

Thus Prussia is again impeding the realisation of an alliance with Austria, 
and it appears that we can count on her for no useful purpose: her object seems 
to be to endeavour to defeat all our projects for joint action against Russia: 
such has been too clearly the drift of her policy during the last six weeks, and 
Earn men eare eae on the King is as evidently declining as that of 

ns erlach and the Court party, from being m menial to the King’ 
feelings, is gradually Sa: 3 Sree aaa eee

(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

My ea oe Rerlin, April 5, 1854, 
SORGE of Mecklenburgh-Strelitz arrived here esterday fro: 
St. Petersburgh, with a letter from the a ea of Russia to the King of 


Prussia, in answer to the one oh (ha F ; 3 : 
fnsperial Majesty. e one of which General Lindheim was the bearer to His 


ot 


Baron Manteuffel has told me that this letter is written in the most friendly 
and affectionate terms, and that it has again roused the King’s hopes that 


The Emperor appears to have stated that the late concessions made by the 
Sultan to his Christian subjects of all denominations did away with the main 
object of the war with Turkey, and that he only required some guarantees for 
the future, and that he did not see why negotiations for peace should not he 
renewed; that, however, he should no longer agree to their being carried on at 
Vienna, and that he thought Berlin would now he the proper place for them. 

The Emperor seems to have added that though he was always ready to 
negotiate, the march of his armies would not be stopped, and that the first ste 
by way of neotiation must be the evacuation of the Black Sea by the British 
and French fleets, alter which his troops would be ordered to retire from the 
Turkish territory. 

| said to Baron Manteuffel that the proposals of the Emperor, as he 
described them to me, were nothing more than a repetition of what had been 
rejected by the Conference at Vienna, and that of course there could be no question 
of their being entertained fora moment, and that 1 presumed the King must 
view them in this light. His Excellency replied that this was the impresssion 
he had himself received on reading the Emperor's letter, but that his Royal 
Master was not of the same opinion, and thought that some such communica- 
tions might be based on the letter. 

I rejoined that I lioped he would not encourage His Majesty in any suppo- 
citions of the kind, for that the object of this mission of Duke George of 
Mecklenburgh-Strelita was none other than to play with the King’s fancies for 
peace-making, and to endeavour to retard the eonelusion of any Convention of 
arrangement that might be under negotiation at Berlin or elsewhere, and that 
he had been encouraged ly the success whieh had attended his former attempts 
to make this new effort, and that it would be deplorable if the King listened to 
these last suggestions, or allowed himself to be biassed by them, or to suppose 
that England, France, or Austria would entertain them,

SOUS ln demande des Royaumes de France et de Grande Bretagne, la 
Conférence s'est réunie pour entendre la lecture des picces qui Gtablissent que 
V'invitation adressée au Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg, d’évacuer les Principautés 
Moldo-Valaques dans un délai fixe, étant resté sans réponse, état de guerre 
déja déclarée entre la Russie et la Sublime Porte existe également de fait entre 
la Russie d'une part, et la Grande Bretagne et la France de l'autre. 

Ce changement opéré dans Vattitude de deux des Puissances représentées 
dans la Conférence de Vienne, en consequence dune démarche tentée directe- 
ment par la France et Angleterre, et appuyée par l’Autriche et la Prusse, 
comme fondée en droit, a été jugée par les Puissances d’Autriche et de Prusse 
comme impliquant la nécessité de constater de nouveau Vunion des quatre 
Gouvernements sur lo terrain des principes posées dans les Protocols des 
5 Décembre, 1863, et 18 Janvier, 1854. En conséquence les Soussignés ont 
Ace moment solennel déclaré que leurs Gouvernements restent unis dans le 
double but de maintenir Vintégrité territoriale de l'Empire Ottoman, dont le 
fait de l'évacuation des Principautés Danubiennes est, et restera, une des 
conditions essentielles, et de consolider dans un intérét si conforme aux sen- 
timents du Sultan, et par tous les moyens compatibles avec son indépendance 
et sa souveraineté, les droits, civils et religieux, des Chrétiens sujets de la 

orbe, : 

L’intégrité territoriale de Empire Ottoman est, et demeure, la condition 
sine qud non de toute transaction destinée A rétablir la paix entre les Puissances 
belligérants, et les Gouvernements représentés par les Soussignés s'engagent 
4 rechercher en commun les garanties les plus propres i rattacher l’existence 
de cet Empire 4 l'équilibre général de Europe, comme ils se déclarent préts 


43 


4 délibérer et a s’entendre sur V’emplot des moyens les plus convenables 
pour atteindre l’objet de leur concert. ! 

Quelqu’événement qui se a net ars s uitede cet accord fondé uniquement 
sur les intéréts généraux de I'Hurope et dont le but est d'amener le retour 
d’une paix solide et durable, les Gouyernements représentés par les Soussignés 
gengagent réciproquement A n’entrer dans aucun arrangement definitif avec 
Ja Cour Impériale de Russie, ou avec toute autre Puissance, qui seratt contrarre 
Aux principes énonces ci-dessus, ef qui nimpliquerait pas la rétablissement de 
la paix générale.

No. 57. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Sir Alecander Malet. 

(No. 4.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, April 8, 1864, 

HER Majesty's Government approve the language held by you to 
M. de Bismark, as reported by you in your despateh No. 11 of the 20th ultimo, 
on the subject of the policy of Prussia in the present crisis, and I have to 
instruct you to state to his Excellency, that Her Majesty's Government are 
entirely without control over the English press, and have regretted the unbe- 
coming terms in which it has oceasionally re-echoed the opinions expressed by 
some of the Continental journals upon that policy. Her Majesty's Government 
know nothing of the indiseretions alluded to by M. de Bismark, and unless such 
indiscretions are officially brought to their knowledge, and they can only be 
responsible for the language they themselves hold, and the instructions they 
give. But itis quite impossible that the Prussian Government should be under 
any mistake upon the subject, because in various despatches which have been 
read to Baron Manteuftel by Lord Bloomfield, and of some of which copies have 
been given to him, Her Majesty's Government have not only disclaimed all 
right as well as disposition to hold a menacing language, but have constantly 
declared, that in seeking to ascertain the course that would be pursued by 
Prussia, they had no desire unduly to press the declaration of it upon the 
Prussian Government, That course seems now to be determined upon, and 
Her Majesty's Government fear that Prussia, when too late, may discover that 
it will extend the theatre, and lengthen the duration of the war, and that it 
will favour the cause of revolution. But Her Majesty's Government must 
protest against its adoption being in any way attributable to the cause alleged 
by M. de Bismark, who may be assured that Her Majesty's Government have 
too much respect for the independence of Prussia, and are too desirous of seeing

No, 62. 
Lord Cowley to the Bart of Clarendon.—(Receiwed April 10.) 


(No. 478, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, April 10, 1854. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS was good enough to read mo this morning 
a despatch, dated the 6th instant, which he had just received from M. de 
Bourqueney, i 

Count Buol appears to have viewed in the same light as do your Lordslnp 
and M. Drouyn de Lhuys the mission of the Dake of Mecklenburgh to Berlin, 
namely, that it had no other object than to endeavour to sow dissension 
between the Maritime Powers and the Powers of Germany. He declared to 
M. de Bourjueney that the time had gone bye when such overtures on the 
part of Russia could be accepted, and that, although the future condition of 
the Sultan’s Christian subjects might with propriety form part of any arrange- 
ment to be concluded, there were other questions of still greater importance to 
be settled with Russia, which the loyalty of Austria could not permit her to 
lose sight of. Count Buol added, that he had reason to believe that the King 
of Prussia was coming round to this way of thinking. 

M. de Bourqueney said, that without pressing Count Buol indiscreetly, 
he should be glad to know whether, if the negotiations with Berlin failed, 
Austria would come of them as free an agent as she had entered them, to 
which question Count Buol eagerly replied in the affirmative. The Count 
then showed M. de Bourqueney, in confidence, a despatch from Count 
Esterhazy, dated St. Petersburgh the 80th ultimo, mentioning the alarm which 
was beginning to be entertained in that capital now that war was so near. 
The attitude of Austria, Count Esterhazy asserted, had contributed much to 
this depression, which caused Count Buol to exclaim with some satisfaction, 
“You see what I told is true, and that the arming of Austria is almost 
equivalent to active co-operation.” 

“How then," said M, de Bourqueney, ‘do you account for the passage 
of the Danube and the occupation of the Drobrudscha?” 

“Oh,” replied Count Buol, none of our military authorities consider the 
present movements of the Russian army as the commencement of a general 
plan of campaign.” E 

I have, &c.

With respect to“ menaces,” none that I am aware of have been used, 
thoueh your Lordship is aware of the imprudent language held by Chevalier

of political intriguers, or the wilful fabrication of language placed in the mouths

bodies of their own country, imploring them to pursue a policy in accordance 
with the Western Powers; but | am confident that during M. de Bismark’s

sometimes forget themselves on like occasions,

to England that, during the war, she would im no case assume an attitude hostile 
to us, is one which I have reason to believe was concerted by him with the 
Russian Minister at this Court, as being entirely in accordance with Russian 
pohiey ; for in this event a similar assurance would probably have been given ta 

ussia, and thus a perfect neutrality would have been seeured by her,

the National party, of having caused the rejection of the Convention, seems to

well known that the politieal party towhich he belongs is styled the “ Nenker™

with Russia,

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved April 11.) 


(No. 189. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 8, 1854. 


| HAD the honour to inform your Lordship on the 6th instant hy telegraph 
that General Hess had forwarded to Vienna the draft of a Treaty, to be signed 
between Austria and Prussia respecting the Eastern question, 

I have this evening had some conversation on the subject of this proposed 
Treaty with Baron Mantenffel, when 1 endeavoured to learn some particulars 
as to its contents, but his Excellency said little else than was reported mm my 
despatch No. 177 of the Srd instant. ; xa 

He told me that it contained mutual guarantees of the territory of the two 
States, that Austria would take that course which she might deem aclvisable 
in her own interests, and that Prussia would not be called on to interfere for 
other than German interests, [ inquired of his Excellency whit engazenients 
would be made with regard to military co-operation, He replied: that the 
Prussian Government could not go to the extent that had been desired by 
General Hess, and that he had declined to enter into a perpettal mutual 
guarantee of territory as proposed by him, and he had therefore proposed that 
the "'reaty should only remain in force for the duration ot the war; that as 10 
the employment of troops it had been so far arranged that Prussia should make 
arrancements lo have three corps-d'armée, upwards of one hundred thousand 
men, placed in the Duchy of Posen, from whence they could be marched 


Sad. 


| 


51 


eastwards if necessary, and that it would only require twenty-six days to 
concentrate them, and that, if not required for hostile purposes, manceuyres 
of those troops would take place in that district. ie 

| asked if this was intended to menace Poland, and if the King would 
consent to any such movement. His answer was that he thought the King 
would agree to it if affairs became serious, of which there was every appear- 
ance at the present moment. ; 

This is all the information on te subject which | was able to extract 
from Baron Manteuffel, and it is so far satisfactory that it tends to prove that 
the Prussian Government, though unwilling to go the whole length desired by 
Austria, are nevertheless disposed to give a feeble support to the alliance, 
whilst Ute step is certainly in the right direction, 

His Excellency added that when the Treaty was concluded it would be 
communicated to the Dict, and that the German Powers would be requested 
to accede to it, but that their agreeing to it, or not would have no influence in 
preventing the fulfilment by Austria and Prussia of the stipnlations which it 
contained, or in any way impede the carrying its provisions into eflect. 

In reply to another question which I put, he said that there was nota 
word in the Convention that implied neutrality, and it appears to me that he 
expeets Prussia will be impelled by the force of circumstances to take an 
active part in the approaching struggle,

Sir John Milbanke to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 11.) 
(No, 25.) 


My Lord, Munich, April 6, 1854, 

I HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Lordship's 
despatches to No, 18 inelusive, and two marked “circular,” of the 29th and 
S0th ultimo, 

My French colleague has been good enough to allow me to peruse a 
despatch from his Government, containing instruetions to urge upon thie 
Bavarian Government the expediency of avoiding any step at the Diet which 
might have a tendency to inerease the difliculties with which the Austrian 
Cabinet has already to struggle in the Eastern question, or to embarrass it in 
the defence of the interests of Germany on the Danube, which the geographical 
position of Austria specially assigns to her. The French Government seems to 
presume, and I entirely concur in that opinion, that the only object of the 
secondary Powers in evineing impaticnce for a declaration of the policy of the 
two great German Powers, is simply to claim their share of influence in the 
deliberations whieh may closely affeet their interests, 

France, the despatch says, will assuredly not contest their right so to do; 
but she expects from their intelligence and patriotism that they will not multiply 
the difficulties which Austria already has to overeome, and which would he greatly 
Hat if she were deprived of the aid and sympathy of her natural and 
lega allies; for, at all events, whether she makes an appeal to the Confederation 
for its military aid or not, it is clear, that previously to employing her own 
forces, she has need to assure herself not only of the adhesion of the Diet to the 
eause she supports by arms, in concert with England and France, but also of 
the effective assistance in all cases in which the the chances of the war might 
foree her to invoke the elauses of the Act of Confederation, 

‘The despateli contains a warning against the dangers which might arise 
from hesitation or differences of opinion, as well within as between themselves, 
adding that the fall of the Ottoman Empire could not take place without bring- 
ing about a territorial dislocation. the effects of which the second-rate States 
of Germany would be the first to feel. After remarking that the loyal conduct 
of the Emperor Louis Napoleon had dispelled many preventions, it proceeds to 
state, thet there is one federal Government to whose intentions the Emperor is 


averse to attach suspicion ; but the despatch gives clearly to be understood, that 


France could never allow the other great Powers to add to their possessions

without claiming an indemnity which is only to be found in Her Or Pelee 
hood, ‘The secondary States have now to choose between bas Heaton o ie 
Cabinet of Berlin and the fixed resolutions of that of Vienna. to eheeume® . 
first, argues M. Drouyn de Lhuys, would be to paralyze the Leer whils ne

(No. 142.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, April 12, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me the despatch addressed by Count 
Nesselrode to Baron de Meyendortff, in reply to the communication which the 
Austrian Government forwarded to the Cabinet of St, Petersburg, supporting 
the summons of the British and French Governments to Russia to evacuate 
the Principalities, 

In alluding to the advice given by the Austrian Government to that of 
Russia, to accede to this summons, and to arrange the differences with the Porte by 
nerotiation, Count Nesselrode observes, that if on a more attentive examimation 
of the letters which were addressed to his Excellency by M, Drouyn de Lhuys 
and myself, the Cabinet of Vienna were not struck by the insulting tone of 
these communications, the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh can only regret that 
Austria has not taken a different view of a demand such as Russia never 
received at any time, even when the conqueror of Europe menaced her with an 
invasion at the head of an army of six hundred thousand men, 

Count Nesselrode proceeds to say, that the most painful effect which was 
produced on the Russian Cabinet, was to see it asserted that it was impossible 
to contest the right and the equity of this demand. Such a point saiit have 
been still matter for consideration, if the relations of Russia with the Porte 
were still (as at the period when the temporary occupation of the Principalitics 
took place) not actually hostile, But the Porte having declared war against 
Russia ; having attacked Russia on her own territories, of which she occupies a 
point up to the present moment, ina word Russia being in open war with the 
*orte both on the Danube and in Asia, the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh must be 
permitted to differ in opinion from that of Vienna on the equity of a demand 
which exacted everything from one of the two belligerent parties, without being 
addressed equally to the other. | 

The Austrian Government, observes Count Nesselrode, considered that the 
submission of Russia to the imperious ultimatum sent to her, would be a proof 
of generous moderation which the world would applaud, and which would detract 
nothing from the glory and moral power of Russia, 

he Emperor of Russia, however, had judged otherwise, and Count Nessel- 
rode had been instructed to notify verbally to the Consuls of England and 
France, that His Imperial Majesty had no reply to make to the letters trans- 
mitted to Count Nesselrode, and that they were at liberty to dispatch the 

messengers who were the bearers of these letters. 
After the silence which Russia had maintained as to the summons 
addressed to her, the ‘Two Powers could of course take such measures as they 


—————_— 
o_o 


a4 


should think advisable, ‘That which it was not in their power to do was to cast 
upon Russia the initiative in hostilities, and arbitrarily to give to the rejection 
of their ultimatum the title of a declaration of war,
