The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland, 
(No. 145.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 12, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despateh which he has 
received from Count Buol, referring to the importance attached by Her 
Majesty’s Government to a knowledge of whether the Maritime Powers can, 
and to what extent, count wpon the active co-operation of Austria in the im- 
pending war. 

Count Buol alludes to the language which you have held to his Excel- 
leney, in which you have dwelt upon the influence which would naturally be 
exercised on the plan of operations under the consideration of the Western 
Powers, by a knowledge of the decision of the Austrian Government on this 
subject, ; 

Count Buol proceeds to observe that the moral attitude assumed hy 
Austria in the Bastern question, and which is identical with that of the other 
Three Powers represented at the Vienna Conference, has not been modified. 
The Austrian Government declared themselves ready to sign a Convention of 
Four, caleulated to render binding the principles recorded in the Protocols of 
the Conference. ‘The Cabinet of Berlin having, however, declined to athx its 
signature to the projected act, the Austrian Government have considered it 
their duty, in the interest of the object in view, to pomt out the inconveniences 
attached to a signature of Three, 

But the Austrian Government have all the more felt the absolute necessity 
of being first of all completely informed of the definitive resolution taken at 
Berlin; and Count Buol is convinced that Her Majesty's Government will 
understand, that before taking a decisive step, of which the inevitable conse- 
quences would be a rupture with Russia, it is of the highest importanee to 
Austria to ascertain whether she ean, in certain contingencies, count upon the 
material support of Prussia and the German Confederation. 

Such is the object of the mission of General Hesse, whose high position in 
the Austrian army is in itself an indication that the military combinations 
which the events of the war may render necessary, have not been kept ont of 
sight. At all events the Austrian Cabinet have made known to the Cabinet of 
Berlin that they will not depart from the principles traced out in the Vienna 
Protocols, and they have expressed their confident expectation that the 
Prussian Government will act in a similar manner, — 

Before the whole result of General Hess's mission is known, the Austrian 
Government cannot, even under the seal of secrecy, give eventual assurances 
which would in fact amount to a formal engagement; and they desire, that 
under these circumstances the Maritime Powers will not prematurely insist 
upon more positive explanations. 

On the other hand, the Austrian Government, appreciating the relative 
positions of the several Powers, will feel no surprise if, in conseqnence of the 
reserve imposed upon Austria by the force of circumstances, the French and 
English Governments are obliged to decide upon their plan of operations with 
reference only to military considerations, 

Inshort, Count Buol observes, it is absolutely necessary that the Austrian 
Government should have a clear knowledge of the attitude which Prussia will 
assume, This knowledge, when obtained, will form one of the most essential 
elements in determining the nature and extent of the military measures to be 
taken by Austria, and which, when determined upon, will be communicated 
without delay to the Governments of Great Britain and France, 

| requested Count Colloredo to thank Count Buol for this frank and explicit 
communication. TL admitted that the views of the Austrian Government were 


55 


reasonable, and that the difficulties of their position were great; but, I said, 
there must be a limit to the deference shewn to Prussia, or the power of 
Austria would be neutralised, and she would expose herself to far greater diffi- 
culties and dangers by permitting Russia to pursue her aggressive policy un- 
checked, than by acting independently of Prussia, supported as Austria would 
then be by the unanimous public opinion of Genes 5

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 
(No. 97.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 12, 1854. 

THE Chevalier Bunsen has communicated to me a despatch whieh has 
been addressed by Baron Manteuflel to the Prussian Representative at 
St. Petersburgh, in reply to the letter from the Emperor of Russia to the King 
of Prussia, of which Prince George of Mecklenburg-Strelitz was the 
bearer. 

In this despatch Baron Manteuflel, after referring to the accident which 
befel the King of Prussia as a reason for preventing His Majesty from 
answering himself the Emperor of Russia's letter, submits for communication 
to His Imperial Majesty and to Count Nesselrode the following considerations. 

The Emperor has declared in his letter that His Imperial Majesty might 
consider himself satisfied as soon as he shall have been officially informed by 
England, France, and Turkey, of the conclusion of a Treaty between the 
Three Powers for the amelioration of the condition of the Sultan’s Christian 
subjects, and that the new concessions accorded to them are more liberal than 
those which on the demand of Russia have been refused to the Christians of 
the Greek Church. 

On this subject two observations suggest themselves: first, that the extent 
of the new concessions destined to assimilate the Christian rayahs to the 
Mussulman subjects of the Porte is not yet fixed; the lirmans by which they 
will be promulgated are not yet published, except one, which has for its object 
the reorganization of tribunals; and it appears evident that such ameliora- 
tions can only be introduced in succession. Moreover, it is not by a “ synal- 
lagmatique” form that the innovations relative to the rights of rayahs have 
been, or will be, stipulated for with the Porte by the Maritime Powers. It is 
principally this form which at the first brunt had been judged of a nature to 
attack the independence and sovereign rights of the Sultan, and the Govern- 
ments which had been the first to avert the danger at the time of the mission 
of Prince Menschikolf would avoid even the appearance on their part of 
exposing the Ottoman Porte to it. If in consequence there has not been, and 
will not be, a Treaty concluded which could be brought to the knowledge of 
the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, this want of an international form docs not 
appear to be prejudicial to the condition of the Christians themselyes, The 
lustory of the Hast and this very complication is a sufficient proof that the 
letter of ‘Treaties does not furnish in such matters the necessary guarantees. 
These are to be found rather in the continual and effectual solicitude of the 
Powers of Europe, and this ellicacy can only increase in proportion to the 
union which manifests itself in the practical efforts of Governments to.ensure 
the execention of laws emanating from the Porte in favour of its Christian 
subjects. It is on these grounds, above all, that Prussia considers an under- 
standing of the Five Powers as procuring the most salutary results, and as 
offering perhaps in itself the chances of arranging on the basis of negotiations 
a difference which unhappily has led to an appeal to arms. 

The Cabinet of St. Pateiarch has ieenay pointed out Berlin as the 
proper seat for eventual negotiations, and although Count Nesselrode has been 
informed confidentially of the reasons which induce the King of Prussia to 
prefer Vienna still as the Emperor of Russia has again expressed his desire 
for the former place, the Prussian Government will communicate with the 
Cabinets of London, Paris, and Vienna, and if the wishes of Russia are 
acceeded to by these Cabinets, the King of Prussia will receive this agreement 


56 


as a fresh motive for making every effort for the amelioration of the condition 
of our Christian brethren in the East. 

I expressed to the Chevalier Bunsen my satisfaction that Baron Manteuflel 
in this despatch should have Gee stated, for the information of the 
Emperor of Russia, the course that hac been pursued by the Four Powers, 
and the reasons which must still guide their policy respecting the Christian 
subjects of the Porte.

(Signed) CLARENDON,

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 12.) 
(No. 136.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 30, 1854. 

I HAVE already informed you by telegraph that the Russians crossed 
the Danube at Galatz on the 28rd instant, in numbers varying from fifteen to 
thirty thousand. 

Inclosed herewith in copy are the reports addressed to me, and also to 
Her Majesty’s Consul at Varna, by Captain Simmons, of the Royal Engincers, 
who went, at my request, to be near Omer Pasha under the present most 
interesting and important circumstances. Together with them I forward a 
copy of Vice-Admiral Dundas'’s accompanying despatch, 

We are not yet sufficiently informed to determine the character of this 
operation. It may have been undertaken with the sole view of occupying the 
Dobrudscha, or with that of engaging the main body of the Turkish army, and 
perhaps even attempting the possession of Shumla, In the former ease Varna 
may possibly come within the range of attack, and the weakness of its garrison 
is a just motive for apprehension, ‘The fleets, however, are close at hand, and 
their presence, exclusive of any actual succour which they might eventually 
afford, may be expected to retard the advance of the Russian army. 

It is much to be desired that reinforcements should be sent from Constan- 
tinople; but the garrison of the capital is so much reduced by the detachments 
of troops to Volo and Prevesa, that until the regiments expected from Alex- 
andria, or some brigades of the allied armies arrive, it would not be prudent 
to reduce it much lower ata moment when the Greeks are about to be sent 
out of the Sultan's dominions, and a dangerous excitement is likely to prevail 
in consequence. 

I have, nevertheless, exhorted the Turkish Ministers to hazard the conse- 
quences of sending a couple of thousand men to Varna; and by way of 
encouragement | have written, in complianee with their wishes, a letter appriz- 
ng the commander of any lroops already arrived at Malta, of the state of 

hings both here and in Bulgaria, expressing at the same time a hope that he 
may find himself at liberty to move the troops in this direction, without further 
delay. | have the honour to inclose a cde of my letter to the officer in 
command, together with a covering despateh, also in copy, addressed to Sir 
William Reid. | venture to reckon upon your Lordship’s indulgent con- 
sideration of the unauthorized step, which a strong sense of duty, under 
circumstances of unusal embarrassment, has impelled me to take. 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Captain Simmons to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
My Lori, Silistria, Mareh 26, 1854, 
| HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that upon my arrival at 
Varna, | immediately proceeded to Shumla, and, Omer Pasha having left 
with ‘he main body of his forces for the neighbourhood of Rustchuk, leaving 
eight battalions (probably about 4,000 effective) at Shumla, [ proceeded to 


57 


Rustchuk, and, finding that he had moved from the Danube, I followed him, 
and joined him this morning at this place. 

No movement has taken place on the part of the Russians since the 
demonstration which was made before Turtukai on the 12th and 13th instant. 
On the 12th, the Russians having previously taken possession of and thrown a 
bridge across to a small island opposite Turtukai, commenced to throw a 
bridge across to a larger island, more in advance towards the right bank of 
the river. The Turks upon the larger island opened a fire upon them, which 
stopped their operations for that day, On the following morning the Russians 
opened a heavy cannonade upon the larger island oceupied by the ‘Turks, and 
recommenced their bridge, the head of which was advanced some distance into 
the stream; but the fire of the Turks being too severe, they ceased their opera- 
tions, and in the night withdrew altogether, removing their bridge. In this 
operation a force of about one brigade (six battalions) of the enemy was 
engaged. 

After my arrival at his Highness’s head-quarters, orders were sent this 
morning to the troops in the Dobrudscha to retire, and concentrate upon 
Karasu: and the troops with his Highness were ordered to halt, and will 
probably fall back upon Shumla, it being his Highness's intention, at all 
hazards, to cover that place. ‘ 

‘Since writing the above, while out with his Highness, inspecting the 
fortifications of this place, an aide-de-eamp arrived from the Dobrudscha, with a 
despatch to the effect that on the 23rd the Russians made a demonstration with 
about 5,000 men, opposite Pothashi, which was repulsed ; but that about the 
same time they crossed at Galatz with a force of 30,000 men, and that the 
troops from Matchin and Toultcha are in retreat. 1 think it probable that the 
strength of the enemy has been exaggerated; but there ean be no doubt that 
they have passed the Danube in considerable foree—probably a division of 
15,000 men may have crossed. As, however, the Russian army in the Princi- 
palilies is in greatest force at Bucharest and in front of it, itis not improbable 
that a more serious attack may be made shortly towards the centre, at 
Rustchuk or Matechin. 

His Highness had determined to fall back upon Shumla, if necessary, 
being fully impressed with the necessity of preserving that place, ‘The troops 
in the Dobrudscha will also, in all probability, in consequence of this movement 
at Galatz, have time to gain that place, or, at any rate, Varna; so that I think 
Shumla will be secured against all accidents. 

In the communication | had with his Highness this morning, lie informed 
me that the Government at Constantinople had promised a month ago to rein- 
force him immediately with 12 battalions of infantry (two of which Chasseurs), 
and a corresponding force of artillery, 

‘Their non-arrival at Shumla has caused him much embarrassment, and 
will, no doubt, have the effect of preventing him from forming those combini- 
tions which he otherwise might have been enabled to make, to check the 
advance of the enemy, 

Your Lordship will, however, perceive that it is of very great consequence 
that in the present state of affairs they should be forwarded without loss of 
time by sea to Varna, as that garrison is weak, not exceeding about 3,000 
men; and it is of the utmost importance that it should be held. If the troops 
in the Dobrudscha retire on Shumla and not on Varna, Varna without reiforee- 
ments will not be in a position to resist many days. 

Nis Highness is abou to dispatch a courier immediately by land to Con- 
stantinople, who will convey this, and ifanything of importance occurs, I will 
not fail to send your Lordship immediate AS oeRanan! if necessary, by Varna, 
lo 20 by the steamer, which, according to the information I received from your 
Lordship, before Jeaving Constantinople, may be expected to be there. A 
dupticate shall, however, be forwarded by land. 

[ have only time to add that the country is now ina very good condition 
for the movement of troops of all kinds, and that the Danube has not yet 
commenced to rise, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) J. A. SIMMONS.

Vice-Admiral Dundas to Lord Stratford de Redelufe, 


My Lord, * Britannia,” in Beicos Bay, March 10, 1864. 
AS the very great difficulty now experienced in obtaining coal in 
quantities sufficient for the ordinary service of the steam squadron under my 
orders would be seriously increased in the event of active and extensive opera- 
tions in the Black Sea, or elsewhere, and as the success of such operations and 
the utility even of the steam vessels would be endangered by a deficioney in 
the supply of coal, it has become aperainrey necessary for me to use every 


66 


endeavour to provide for the possible wants of the squadron, as well as to use 
every precautionary measure of strict economy in the consumption of that most 
important article. , 

As one of those precantionary measures, [have the honour to acquaint 
your Excellency, for your ‘formation, that after the approaching departure of 
the * Caradoc” for Marseilles, with Sir John Burgoyne, it is not my intention 
tosend any of the steam vessels under my orders with despatches for Marseilles, 
or even to Malta, but to forward them by the French packets, English screw 
vessels, and the “Cyclops (a vessel to be employed in provisioning the 
squadron), as opportunities may offer, and | am glad to hear the number of 
French packets helween this and France is to be increased. 

With the same view, it is also my intention, when engaged in the Black 
Sea, that all communications for the squadron shall he conveyed by the 
Austrian boats to Varna or Sinope, 48 cirenmstances may demand, and thereby 
effect a considerable saving in this most valuable munition of war. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) J, W. D. DUNDAS,

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to Vice-Admiral Dundas. 


Bir, British Embassy, Constantinople, March 17, 1854. 

IN acknowledging your despatches No. 63 and No. 67, dated respectively 
the Loth and 16th instant, T understand, as to the former, that besides object- 
ing generally to the reception of Turkish troops on board any vessel under 
‘our command, you have no steamers to spare for the service which | recom- 
mended to your special attention, and that you are of opinion that the Porte 
has plenty of sailing vessels at its command, which, notwithstanding that the 
main object is expedition, you think sufficient for the purpose, 

With respect to your second despatch on the subject, principally of coal, 
I fully appreciate the resolution which you have declared, to vse that “ most 
important article” and valuable “munition of war” will economy, and | have 
the satisfaction to inform you that the Porte is prepared to allord every facility for 
your obtaining supplies from the mines at Heracloa, at the Government price, 
if not gratuitously, and, at all events, in common with both squadrons, which: 
Lam sure will he agreeable to you. 

With reference ta the last two paragraphs of the same despatch, I beg to 
be informed whether, in case of emergency, | am no longer to rely upon you 
for an express conveyance of my despatches, and whether Austrian vessels are 
to be acclaively employed in conveying the communications between Constan- 
tinople and your squadron whenever it may be in the Black Sea. 

1 beg to draw your attention to the importance of establishing some speedy 
means of communication between Varna and this capital, at a period when the 
Russians may hazard an attempt at passing the Danube before the annual 
inundation of that river, towards the middle of April, shall render the passage 
for a time impracticable. .

directed to convey them immediately to him: but 1 beg to suggest, as a still 
ereater economy of tine, that you should direct all vessels coming in from the 
Black Sea under British or foreign colours, to be questioned on their down 
passage near your squadron. 

It may interest you to know that advices received from Bucharest, Vienna, 
and Varna, warranting an expectation that about this time the Russian troops 
will attempt to cross the Danube in force. I grieve to add that those from the

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 13.) 
(No. 197.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 8, 1554. 


1 HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that General Lindheim 
returned yesterday from his mission to St. Petersburgh. | 

Lam not aware that he has brought any data that are likely to encourage 
the King to make further communications on the subject of peace, but the 
General nevertheless says that the Emperor of Russia declares that he 
continues to be animated with most pacific intentions. His impressions as 
to the future military operations are that the Russians will attack Silistria, but 
will not go beyond the Danube and the Dobrudscha. . | 

A “Te Deum” was celebrated at St. Petersburgh for the suecessful Vt 
of the Danube. Neither the Austrian nor the Prussian Missions attended the 
invitation of the Court to this ceremony. 

The marked attention shown by the Emperor to Mr. Seymour, the newly 
arrived Minister of the United States, appears to have been much commented 
on by the diplomatic body, and given rise to various rimours. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

No. 81. 
Mr. Grey to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 13.) 


(No, 76. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Stockholm, April 6, 1854. 

{1 HAD the honour of being received yesterday evening by their Majesties 
the King and Queen of Swedan and Norway, Her Majesty the Queen Dowager, 
and Their Royal Highnesses the Prinee and >rincess Royal, for the presentation 
of Mr. Adams. 

Before Mr. Adams was intoduced, I was received by the King alone, and 
His Majesty desired that I would write to your Lordship, and state the extreme 
satisfaction with which he had read the declaration relative to neutrals, pub- 
lished in the “ Gazette” of the 29th ultimo, which he felt was all that he could 
desire. His Majesty further expressed to me his sense of the friendly course 
pursued by Her Majesty's Goyernment towards Sweden, and said that he fully 
appreciated the manner in which anything which could eause embarrassment 
to Sweden, or throw obstacles in the way of the neutral policy he had adopted, 
had been avoided on the part of England. | 

Immediately before my interview with the King, the French Minister had 
had an audience, in order to present the new French Secretary, M. de I'rézals, 
and he availed himself of that opportunity to read to His Majesty a despatch 

which he had received from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, and which he was instructed 
to read to Baron Stjerneld, without leaving a copy with his Excellency, The 


75 


despatch in question expresses the hope of the French Government that Sweden 
will take an active part in the approaching struggle, and side with England 
and France against Russia. It appeared to M, Lo stein that the news of the 
recognition of the Swedish neutrality by Russia had not officially reached the 
Freneh Government at the time this despatch was written, and, after consilt- 
ing with me, he accordingly determined not to carry out his instructions till 
after the arrival of another post, Nothing farther avis however arrived, 
and the King having somewhat unexpectedly fixed yesterday for our reception, 
M. Lobstein resolved to submit his instructions to His Majesty in person, first 
asking whether he would wish to receive them without their previously having 
been communicated to Baron Stjerneld. ‘The King having expressed his 
willingness to receive the communication, M. Lobstein placed the despatch in 
his hands. His Majesty was considerably moved (fortement éniu) by the natare 
of the communication, but appears to have taken it exceedingly well, and to 
have thanked M, Lobstein for the straightforward and friendly course which 
he had adopted. His Majesty then entered into a conversation of some length. 
and concluded by desiring M. Lobstein to communicate with Baron Stjerneld, 
A. council has been held to-day at the Palace, and as it is an unusual day, it 
ve be presumed that the French Minister’s communication was the cause 
oF it. 

Varions interruptions have prevented my learning more from M. Lobstein 
to-day, and I fear that shall not be able to obtain further details betore the 
departure of the steamer to-morrow morning, nor has M. Lobstein yet had his 
interview with Baron Stjerncid, I may perhaps add, however, that His Royal 
Highness the Crown Prince said to me this evening he thought the step had 
been taken somewhat teo soon, The Prince’s own wishes and feelings appear 
to me to be entirely in favour of the course proposed by France, but he seems - 
to fear that the premature communication of the plan may cause delay in its 
being carried into effect. That it will be ultimately carried into effeet His 
Royal Highness does not appear to doubt. 

In his subsequent interview with me, the King did not in any way touch 
upon the subject, and I thought, on the contrary, that his expressions of 
eratitude to England for not having cansed embarrassinent to Sweden were 
somewhat marked. ‘This may, however, very possibly have been caused by 
my being aware of His Majesty just having received the communication above 
mentioned. I have, &e, 

(Signed) W.G, GREY

WITH reference to my despatch to your Excellency, No. 50 of the

‘atertere with the district of Kotoor, even if it were completely evacuated

The Shah has, moreover, evinced much sympathy and friendly fecling 
for the Porte; and | have to instruct your He callcney, under these circum- 
stances, to point out to Roshid Pasha that the moment is opportune for 
the ‘Turkish Government generously to do an act of justice, and to restore 
Kotoor to Tersia.

No. 84. 
Mr. Grey to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receiwed April 16.) 


(No. 84. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Stockholm, April 8, 1854, 

THE French Minister, M. Lobstein, has this day read to me the 
despatch in whieh he reports to M. Drouyn de Lhuys what passed between 
himself and the King at the interview whieh | alluded to, in my despatch 
No. 76 of the Gth instant, 

M. Lobstein, upon bemg introduced to the King’s apartment, said, 
after a few introductory phrases, that he had a communication of an ex- 
tremely delicate nature to make to the Swedish Government, that he had 
not had an opportunity of making that communication to Baron Stjerneld, 
but, as His Majesty had always treated him with confidence, he thought he 
might venture to submit the despatch to His Majesty himself in the first 
instance. 

The contents of the despatch in question are, doubtless, well known to 
your Lordship; Twill, therefore, content myself with repeating that it 
expresses the hope of the French Government that Sweden would take an 
active part in the present war, and seize the opportunity of recovering those 
territories which she had been deprived of by the House of Holstein, and thus 
add fresh lustre (¢elat) to the present dynasty. 

The King took the despatch and read it from beginning to end without 
making any observation, but shewing signs of considerable emotion, On 
returning the despatch to M. Lobstein, His Majesty said that he had made a 
declararion of neutrality in the face of the world, and of the Swedish nation, 
and that he was bound in honour to maintain that neutrality. England and 
France had announced that hey sought no territorial advantage for themselves 
in prosecuting this war; still less could he engage in it for the purpose of 
retrieving the losses which Sweden had suffered in former times; but His 
Majesty at the same time expressed to M. Lobstein that he only spoke with 
reference to the present state of things; he could not presume to say what the 
course of events would be, nor could he direct them, and His Majesty, giving 
way to this train of ideas, said; “If Sweden should be obliged to take part in 
the war, we can raise a force of about 120,000 men, of whom from 60 to 70,000 
could be employed upon foreign service. 

His Majesty then thanked M. Lobstein for the manner in which he had 
made this communication, and also for the proofs of friendship he had received 
from the French Government in their offers of support, and concluded by 
desiring M. Lobstein to make the communication to Baron Stjerneld. 

'‘Mhis was done by the French Minister yesterday, atter the matter had, no 
dlonbt, been aly considered in Council, And it appears that Baron Stjerneld’s 
reply was entirely tn accordance with that given by His Majesty on the evening 
helore. 

[am bound to add a few observations to your Lordship on the subject, 
though I do so with the utmost deference, The step which L have reported 


above appears to me to have been taken somewhat too soon, and, if the French 
\inister had been consulted upon it, I believe he would have expressed the 
que opinion, What has already been done, however, cannot be recalled, and 


() 


[ have very high authority for adding that, now the ice has been once broken, 
this step ought to be followed by others of the same nature, The King has 
admitted that his refusal to act in the manner suggested by the French Govern- 
ment was given with reference to the Puree moment only, and I venture to 
repeat to your Lordship that there isa feeling growing up very rapidly i the 
country that Sweden ought not to allow the present crisis to pass by without 
taking advantage of it. T have been informed this very day that the editor of 
the evening paper, the “ Aftonblad,” states that he has reason to expect that a 
demonstration in favour of war with Russia is preparing, and [ know that the 
Russian Mission here entertain extreme alarm as to the intentions of Sweden. 
It can hardly be doubted that Russia will scrupulously avoid giving Sweden a 

retext for taking up arms against her, though, when the winter comes, she may 
hold another language, if the war should nof, ere that time, haye been brought 
to a conclusion. It is, on the other hand, an undoubted fact that the people 
venerally, and, I believe, the great majority of the upper classes, would desire 
nothing more than to see Finland remitted to Sweden upon an independent 
footing like Norway, and the Aland Islands restored to her absolutely. But 
unless Finland is independent (and, on other terms I do not believe the Fins 
would wish to renounce their present allegiance) the Aland Islands would, 
perhaps, be untenable for Sweden, as they are in severe winters completely 
joined by the ice to the mainland of Finland, 

Under these circumstances I cannot help believing that if it is desired that 
Sweden should be enlisted in the war against Russia, it would be well not to let 
the question drop, now that it has once heen broached, and T would venture to 
observe that the answer given by the King m the present instance need not 
exclude all hope of another result on a future occasion. 


_ Thave, &e. . 
(Signed) W. G, GREY.

No. 90, 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 18.) 
(No. 138.) 
My Lord, Vienna, April 12, 1854. 


BY my telegraphic despatch to your Lordship of the th instant, you will 
have been aware that Count Arnim had received instructions to agree to the 
Protocol in the form in which it had been drawn up in the Conference of the 
4ih instant. M. de Bourqueney, however, not having received on the 8th 
‘natant from his Government the authorisation to sign that document, the 
Conference was adjourned to the following day, when the French Minister having 
received the necessary instructions, the signature took place. 

L cannot but congratulate your Lordship upon the completion of a docu- 
ment’ by which the Four Powers have united to carry out in concert the great 
principle of the independence and integrity of the Turkish Empire, conjoined 
with the benevolent desire of seconding the views of His Majesty the Sultan, 
towards the amelioration of the condition of the Christian population subject 
to his rule. 

These great principles being those by which the policy of the allied 
Governments will now be directed, it must be a matter of no amall conzratula- 
tion to Her Majesty’s Government, which, through periods of great difficulty, 
have steadily upheld and pursued those principles, to find that a first step has 
thus been taken to seeure the important objects for which they have laboured, 
all the Great Powers being now formally associated for the attainment of a 
common end, by which the future security and interests of Europe can alone 
be preserved, 

I have, &e.

No. 91. 


Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 18.) 
(No. 209.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 15, 1853. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL has gone to his country seat for a few days, but 
is expected back to-morrow. 

The negotiation of the Treaty with Austria has consequently not made as 
much progress as might have been expected, but the military portion of it has 
been undergoing discussions between General Hess and Generals Bonin and 
Reyher, and I am assured that it 4s likely to be concluded next week. Great 
mystery continues to be observed respecting the contents of this document, and 
Baron Manteuffel, when I saw him the night before he left Berlin, told me he 
could not say anything further as to the details of the Treaty, but that he 
could assure me Her Majesty’s Government would not be dissatistied with it.

No. 92. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 
(No, 100.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 18, 1864. 

THE Chevalier Bunsen has communicated to mea despatch which was 
addressed by Baron Manteuffel to General de Rochow on the Sth instant, 
stating, with reference to the last Russian propositions, that although the 
Prussian Government in its desire to avail itself of every chance, however 
feeble, for a reconciliation of the belligerent Powers, did not delay to bring the 
substance of these last overtures to the knowledge of the Cabinets of London, 
Paris, and Vienna, yet they could not conceal from themselves the great 
difficulties which those overtures would meet with, particularly in London and 
at Paris. ‘The information which the Prussian Government have subsequently 
received has conlirmed these apprehensions. 

It could be matter of no surprise to that Government that, after the 
events which have led to the present attitude of Great Britain and France 
towards Russia, the Maritime Powers, before entertaining the negotiations 
proposed by Russia, and even before receiving without suspicion, and in a 
manner likely to lead to practical results, the mediation of Prussia, should ask 
themselves whether the military movements of Russia are in harmony with the 
pacific intentions which she manifests, and whether the Cabinet of St. Peters- 
bureh is prepared to take such engagements. as would ensure the evacuation 
of’ the Principalities within a reasonable time, 

Foy these reasons, and with the desire that the offers of the Emperor of 
Russia may nol remain unproductive of any result, the King of Prussia urges 
in the most solemn manner upon his Imperial Majesty, to rive orders to his 
armies not to advance any farther beyond the Danube. Such an order would 
paralyze the impression which the intelligence of the passage of the Danube by 
the Russian army, arriving simultaneously with the new propositions of the 
Cahinet of St. Petersburg, must have necessarily produced on the several 
Cabinets as well as on public opinion. It would destroy the seeds of mistrust, 
which without this would oppose themselves at the outset to the establishment 
of an understanding. It would furnish to the mediatory efforts of the King of 
Prussia the indispensable basis of a reciprocal confidence, on such a basis the 
ulterior declarations of the Emperor of Russia would meet with an entirely 
different reception from other Governments, and Prussia might hope to reeom- 
mend them with sueceess, The resolution of His Imperial Majesty to with- 
draw his troops from the Turkish provinces within a fixed term, for example, 
the Ist of May, would, in the opinion of the Prussian Government, most 
effectually contribute to this end, and if they were authorised to communicate 
this decision to the other Powers, an arrangement might possibly be effected 
for the gradual and simultaneous withdrawal of the troops of Russia and the 
fleets of England and France. 


19 


These considerations, which M. de Rochow is instructed to bring to the 
knowledge of the Emperor of Russia, are dictated as well by the desire to give 
effect to the last Russian communication, as by an appreciation of the difh- 
culties which must continue to oppose themsclyes to these propositions so long 
as the occupation of the Principalities threatens to be indefinitely prolonged, 
and a permanent injury to be thereby inflicted upon those interests which 
Prussia, in common with Austria, is peremptorily called upon to preserve. 

Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 93. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Sir John Milbanke. 
(No, 21.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, April 18, 1864. 


HER Majesty's Government entirely concur in the views of the French 
Government on the Eastern question, as stated in M. Drouyn de Lhuys’s 
despatch to the French Minister at Munich, the substance of which you have 
reported to me in your despatch No. 23 of the 6th instant, You will hold the 
same language, and will ont no opportunity of representing that the adoption 
by Germany of the yacillating policy of Prussia must protract the duration 
and extend the theatre of the war, that it would be ascribed to fear by Russia, 
and would be regarded as an acknowledgment of that omnipotence in which 
throughout Germany she has laboured to create a belief; that the success of 
Russia in the present struggle must, as an inevitable consequence, lead to 
further aggression westwards, and that the danger which now threatens the 
future independence of Germany, can alone be averted by the united policy, 
and the vigorous and decided action of all the German Powers. 


Tam, &c. . 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Ear! of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 147.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 19, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has communicated to me a tlespatch from 
Count Buol, stating that there is a point in the recent proposals sent from 
St, Petersburgh to Berlin which seems to merit the attention of the Four Powers, 
viz., that as Russia had declared herself ready to make the amelioration of the 
condition of the rayahs the object of a common deliberation, in which the Porte 
must necessarily have taken part, she would appear to have made a first step 
towards abandoning those pretensions to an exclusive protectorate which she had 
hitherto endeavoured to enforce in her relations with the Porte. 

{ told Count Colloredo that these proposals, adapted as they were to the 
peculiar notions of the King of Prussia, and having for their abject to sow 
dissension between Austria and Prussia, and to prevent the signature of the 
Protocol, did not appear worthy of serious consideration. 

If Her Majesty’s Government believed that the Emperor of Russia was 
sincere in his desire that the condition of the rayahs should be ameliorated, we 
might hope, as Count Buol says, that His Imperial Majesty was taking a first 
step towards abandoning his exclusive claims; but as his real object could not be 
doubted, it was impossible that the Four Powers should now be deceived by his 
proposuls, ‘Those Powers, I said, would betray their own most important 
interests, if they did not turn to account the present conjuncture of circumstances 
for securing the future independance of Europe, or if, by simply re-establishing 
the status quo, they gave an immediate triumph to Russia, aia left her free to 
carry out her own policy of aggrandizement at the time and in the manner that 
might best suit her purpose, 


Tam, &e. : 
(Signed) CLARENDON

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Reeetved April 19.) 

(No, 149) 
My Lord, Constuntinople, April 4, 1854. 

WE have no further news of military transactions along the Danube or in 
the Dobrudseha. It would appear that the Russians are preparing either to fortify 
some position on the right bank of the river within that district, or to undertac 
the siege of Silistria, Omer Pasha, on the other hand, continues to concentrate 
his army at Shumla, without any apparent intention of giving battle elsewhere. 
Varna is exposed by this plan of operations to an attack, Its garrison is weak, 
4a outworks extensive, and its store of provisions anything but abundant. 

These circumstances I have repeatedly urged on the attention of the 
Turkish Ministers, and it is settled that 5,000 of the troops, now coming in from 
Egypt, shall be sent to Varna without delay, I had obtained steam conyey- 
ance for a small reinforcement, from the senior officer on this station, and a 
portion of the troops were sent alongside for embarkation, but owing to some 
unaccountable mistake, they were not received on board, and, shortly after, 
the Turkish steam-frigates from Alexandria began to arrive, Provisions are 
also to be sent; and there is question of stationing © part of the Ottoman 
squadron before Varna, with the double view of covering, in part, the land 
approaches to that fortress, and affording to the combined squadrons a greater 
liberty of action elsewhere. 

bain happy to learn from the latest report addressed to me from Shumla 
by Captain Simmons, that the ‘Turkish Generalissimo manifests every disposi- 
tion to act with prudence and self-denial, Copy of the despatch to which T 
refer, is inelosed herewith, and I wish to draw your Lordship’s particular atten- 
tion to that portion of it which touches the question of command, in the event 
of combined operations in Bulgaria. 

As far as I can learn, the best military authorities within reach, French or 
English, approve of a defensive plan of operations for the present, and such is 
also the opinion of those whose judgment is soundest at the Porte. 


81 


Information of a plausible aspect has reached me from Mr. Wyse, to the 
effect that a considerable portion of the Russian army isto be detached from 
the main body, crossing the Danube above Rustehuk, and marching round by 
Sophia, so as to turn the defiles of the Balkan, and to open communications 
with the Christian insurgents in Macedonia and Epirus. 

T have taken a military opinion as to the practicability of such a scheme, 
supposing an amount of Russian foree equal to what our advices warrant 5 anc 
[am led to believe that the plan might be tried with a fair prospect of success, 
+n the event of the insurrection extending, and of the Turks not having any 
considerable army at Adrianople, or in its neighbourhood, No such army ts 
now in existence, the reserves which had been stationed there in consequence 
of my early representations on the subject, having been withdrawn to supply 
the wants of Omer Pasha in Bulgaria, 

The Porte, however, is in possession of the intelligence iransmisted to me 
from Athens, and whenever the auxiliary troops arrive here, | hope that some 
more effectual and comprehensive arrangement may be made. At present the 
garrison of Constantinople does not exceed 14,000 men, exclusive of the 
Eeyptians, who are not to stay here: and to meet any danger arising from 
excitement amongst the Greeks, it las been thought prudent to place several 
ships-of-war in position near the city.

Inclosure in No, 97. 


Captain Simmons to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


My Lord, Shumla, March 20, 1854. 

IN my letter of the anth instant, No. 1, | had the honour to inform your 
Lordship that the Russians had passed the Danube in force at Galatz on the 
2ord instant, 

T have now the honour to inform your Lordship that at the same time 
that the Russians crossed they made demonstrations at Potbashi, Matchin, and 
Toultcha, and that the Ottoman troops in those places, after having opposed 2 
serious resistance, retired, having suffered considerable loss. 

A colonel, however, having been taken prisoner by the Russians, informed 
that his Highness Omer Pasha was concentrating a considerable foree in the 
Dobrudscha to oppose them, which caused the enemy to halt and strengthen lis 
position, probably to make an efficient téte-de-pont to secure the passage at 
Galaty in ease of being forced to retreat, 

This and the destruction of a bridge by the Turkish forces has enabled 
Mustapha Pasha, who commands in the Dobrudscha, to retire in good order, 
bringing with him all his guns, on Karasn, where and at Borarkent, near 
Chernavoda, the Ottoman forces from the Dobrudscha will be collected to the 
number of 28 battalions of infantry, 2,000 irregulars, 3 regiments of regulars, 
and 2600 irregular cavalry with 60 guns. 

All the heavy baggage and reserve ammunition, &e., of this force will be 
retired forthwith’ upon Shamla, and his Highness Omer Pasha has given 
orders tor the troops to follow, and not to risk a combat at Karasu unless he 
ghould find it unavoidable in order to secure his ammunition, &c. 

His Highness Omer Pasha has moved up 1,200 irregular cavalry to Hadji 
Oglou Bazar to the support of Mustapha Pasha. 

The troops at Turtukai, except some irregular cavalry who remain to 
observe the enemy on the opposite side of the Danube, have been directed to 
fall back upon Shands where his Highness is concentrating the main body of 
his forees, and those at Sistova upon ‘Ternova, so that the position of the 
Turkish army under his Highness’s orders will he nearly as follows, that is 
after the troops in the Dubrudseha shall have reached Shumla :— 

At Shumla, Infantry, 60 battalions; Cavalry, 8 regiments; Artillery, 0 
guns, with horses, without including the heavy guns already mounted in the 
batteries and works. 

At Ternova, 4 battalions. 

Y 


82 


At Rustehnk, 7 battalions and 6 guns horsed. 

‘At Silistria, 5 battalions and 800 gunners. 

At Kalafat and Widdin, 32 battalions, 4 regiments, 42 guns horsed, besides 
the garrison at Varna. 

"This place is provisioned for 50,000 men for some months: the details 
shall be forwarded i my next despatch, as 1 have not time. to send them at 
present, the courier being about to leave immediately. 

Silistria isin a very fair condition, and well provisioned. 

In the interview [ had with his Highness Omer Pasha to-day, | was 
authorized to convey to your Lordship his Highness’s views on the subject of 
the war now commencing. j 

His Highness is of opimion that the Russian army being strong in numbers 
and well conditioned, it is necessary that the utmost energy 88 well as mnity 
of action and combination of strength should be displayed in the war now 
opening. 

He thinks therefore that it is absolutely necessary, 1 order to secure 
euceess, that the allied forces should be combined, and act against the encny 
here in Bulgaria, where the attack hag been made, and that the command 0 
the whole allied force should be confided to one person, who should be the 
most capable and experienced of the several commanders, without reference to 
nationatity or any other consideration. 

His Highness will be content to command the Ottoman army under the 
direction of an officer of either nation, whichever may be considered most able, 
his most anxious desire being that the enemy should be beaten; that he is 
even willing to serve in an inferior position, such as chief of the Etat-Major of 
the allied forces, in order to accomplish this great object, for which he is 
ready to lay down his life. 

"This patriotic and noble abnegation of himeelf will no doubt be appre- 
ciated by your Lordship as conferring the greatest honour upon his Highness, 
who does not doubt that a like sentiment will. prevail with each of the com- 
manders of the allied forces. | 

His Highness after haying thus expressed himself, added that judging 
from the careers of the commanders of the English and French forces, he was 
inclined to be of opinion that Lord Raglan, as having more experience than 
wither Marshal St. Arnaud or himself, having taken part in the great wars at 
the commencement of the present century, Was the most fitting person to 
command. 

T have further to inform your Lordship that his Highness is most actively 
engaged in strengthening the position of Shumla, and making arrangements 
for its defence, which T have no doubt will be perfectly secured until the allied 
forces can arrive on the theatre of operation, 

‘Phe concentration of forees under his Highness’s command is proceeding 
with rapidity, and it is his intention to cncamp the troops as they arrive within 
the position of Shumla, but outside the town, 50 8 to provide in the best 
manner for their health. 

Aceording to the information his Highness has received, the Russians 
continue to cross the Danube b the bridge at Galata, and he is of opinion that 
a great part of their force has been withdrawn from Wallachia, and is now in 
course of concentration in the Dobrudscha. 

On this point | would observe to your Lordship that I fear that the intor- 
mation received at the Turkish head-inarters is not of the most perfect and 
reliable nature, and that 1 think it stil doubtful whether the principal invasion 
of Bulgaria may not take place towards the centre, in front of Bucharest. 

Now that the Russians have crossed the Danube, | am inclined to helieve 
that it would not be impossible to establish three or four reliable persons at 
points on the Russian lines of operation, such as Karasu, Chernavoda near 
Silistria, Turtukai, and Rustchuk, who would observe and give immediate 
and accurate information of the numbers which may pass those various points. 

Lhave already spoken to his Highness on this subject, but he appears 
galishied with his present mens of obtaining information. 

I would therefore suggest to your Lordship, whether, considering the pro- 
babilities of English troops having to acta gainst the Russians, it would not be 
advisable for the English Government to authorize the expenditure necessary 
for obtaining this information. Such an expenditure may amount W a cone 


83 


<iderable sum, but in the large operations which must take place, depending 
so much upon the movements of the enemy, 1 venture to hope that this sugges- 
tion will meet with your Lordship’s approval. If duly authorized by your 
Lordship I believe 1 could find persons who if well placed and properl 
instructed could obtain much valuable information respecting the enemy, ie 
probably Her Majesty’s Consul at Varna could, from his knowledge of the 
country, find capable persons more readily. 

T beg to inform your Lordship that in the present cireumstances I have 
considered it my duty to place my professional knowledge at the disposition ot 
his Highness so long as Her Majesty’s Government may allow me to reman at 
his head-quarters. 

In doing this I hope I shall meet with your Lordship’s approval, 

T have, &c.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 19.) 
(No. 152. 


My Lord, Constantinople, April. b, 1854, 

ACCORDING to our latest advices from the seat of the Hellenic insurree- 
tion, the movement languishes in Epirus, and gathers strength m Thessaly, It 
appears that in both provinces the ‘Turkish troops have fought with spirit, and, 
on the whole, with fair success, that the inhabitants are not of themselves pre- 
pared to raise the standard of rebellion, that without the invasion from Greece, 
they would he unable to make any stand against the Turks, and that, whichever 
party gains the ascendant, they are condemned to suffer most grievously both in 
property and in person. 

T have called the Porte's attention to the importance of sending a further 
reinforcement of regulars into Thessaly, and its intention is to detach 3,000 men 
into that province with the least practicable delay. 

For your Lordship's more complete information, I forward herewith either 
copies or extracts of all such despatches, bearing on the progress of the insurree- 
tion, a8 have reached me since the date of my last report on that subject, with 
the exception of those from Prevesa and Corfu, containing intelligence which 
must naturally arrive in England by a more direct route, 

I cannot rest my thoughts for a moment on the embarrassing question to 
which they relate, without entertaining an anxious desire that Her Majesty's 
Government should enter without hesitation on the measures necessary for its 
settlement. Judging from the facts which have been brought tomy knowledge, 
I conceive that nothing short of the most peremptory language, seconded by 
steps of a comminatory, if not coercive character, can restrain the Court of 
Athens and its unprincipled followers, Your Lordship knows best whether 
France is disposed to go the requisite lengths for that purpose; but the interests 
of the great contest, in which both Powers are engaged, appear to preseribe a 
decided course, 

With respect to the proceedings in Thessaly and Epirus, the Porte is domg 
as much as can be expected, under the pressure of other and greater demands 
upon its resources, Tis exertions may possibly succeed in preventing a further 
extension of the mischief, especially ifa strong hand were to be placed on the 
fountain head from which it flows. But there are chances in favour of the 
adventurers who are throwing the country into confusion, and bringin down a 
weight of ruin upon its inhabitants; and these chances will inerease and brighten 
in their imagination with every hour that yields them a continuance of impunity 
anda hope of ultimate success, It comes to me from every quarter that France 
and England are studiously declared by the leaders of the Hellenic enterprise 
to be favourable at heart to its progress; and cerlain expressions of s mpathy, 
proceeding from the European press, have awakened misgivings at the Porte. 
It is highly important that such illusions should be extinguished; and nothing 
would more conduce to that effect than a decided interference at Athens, and a 
military co-operation with the Sultan’s troops in the disturbed provinces. Such 
mensures would contribute no less powerfully to the advantage of the Greeks 
themselves than to the proverreuan of ‘Turkey, and the discomfiture of Russia, 
They would strengthen the title of Europe to demand an improved condition for 
the Sultan's Christian subjects, and they would tend to secure for England and 
France the twofold glory of aneoeaw war and practical humanity, 

mye 


, &e, 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Letter from Volo. 
( Extract.) Volo, March 29, 18541. 

I HAVE just arrived at Volo, but you must excuse my writimg, as my 
eyes are almost destroyed by the effects of the sun and snow. 

I merely wish to rectify some statements which appear in my letter of the 
25th instant. . 

The first is, that Armyro was not burnt, but a village within a short dis- 
tance called Backlavee, but Armyro is now blockaded by near 5,000 Greeks, An 
Austrian cutter just having arrived, with a friend of mine who speaks English, 
and he states that the Greeks have given notice to the Turks to quit in twenty- 
four hours; but before this time can elapse Her Britannic Majesty's ship 
*Hichflyer” and the French steamer “Gomer” will be with them in that place, 
having left here this morning together. 

My letter of the 25th is substantially correct, with one exception of fire, 
but now I give you the names of the principal leaders; viz, Nako Panovia, 
lst; Papa Costa, 2nd; Grezano, Srd; Cara Yorgi, 4th; Kronia, 5th. And 
also further additions daily arriving, and the whole province of Ghoova is now 
in the possessien of the Greeks, 

Also Demika is surrounded by Greeks, and will soon be taken unless the 
Turks are active. 

Agrafa is also in great trouble from the revolutionists, Nureddin Bey 
writes from Curditsa to his son in Volo with great fear, directing him to listen, 
and put himself under the protection of myself and Gazotre. 

Mr, Blunt not yet arrived from Larissa, and will not be here for several 


8. 
All the Christians in Volo have shut up their magazines, and gone to the 
villages, 

‘The Greeks are certainly deceived; reports have been spread amongst 
them that England and France were supporting them, and from this view 
the Grecians at Ipero were going ahead with great glory under this. false 
impression; but when the news came that English troops had arrived at Prevesa, 
it had the contrary effect, and now they are in a dilemma, because they see 
England and France must keep up their contract with Turkey,

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 21.) 
(No. 161.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, April 6, 1864. 

THE Act of Parliament (59 Geo, ITT, cap. 69) inclosed with your Lordship’s 
eivoular of March the 10th, was brought for the first time on that occasion to 
the knowledge of Her Majesty’s Embassy. It so happens that, ROup MaraneIne. 
the frequent applications addressed to me by British subjects desirous 
entering the Sultan’s service, T have never eiven a certificate for that purpose. 
Since the receipt of your Lordship’s circular, [ have given notice of the Act to 
every candidate for employment in the Turkish army ; and the responsibility 
must lie with those who, in contravention of its enactments, may vnter that 
service without a license under the Sign Manual, or by Order in Council or 
Proclamation. 

If your Lordship instructs me to prevent any subject of Her Majesty from 
entering the Sultan’s service without the legal license, I shall, of course do 
what depends upon me to give effect to the instruction. 

I have, &e. . 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

My Lord, “Britannia,” off Baljik, April 6, 18465. 

I HAD the honour to receive, this day, your ‘Excellency’s letter of the 
srd instant, No. 62, with its inclosure, from Her Majesty’s Consul at Smyrna, 
and I acquaint your Excellency that I am unable to detach any more vessels 
from my squadron beyond the Dardanelles, or to station a vessel at Smyrna, 
as requested by Mr, Brant as a precautionary measure, 

Her Majesty's ships and vessels now employed on the coasts of Greece, 
and in the Archipelago, and the ships of war of different nations now at 
Smyrna and the vicinity, will, I imagine, suffice to keep the peace in that 


quarter.

Sir, Constantinople, April 6, 1864, 

INFORMED that two or three men-of-war might he so placed near Varna 
as to command the ground where operations are likely to be carried on by the 
Russian forces against that fortress, | have made it a point of duty to ae 
whether the Porte would be disposed to detach a portion of her naval force for 
the supposed object. Having obtained an affirmative answer from the Captain 
Pasha, I wish to know whether the suggestion falls in with your views, and if 
zo, what number and kind of vessels would be desirable for the urpoxe, In 
the event of your seeing any decided advantage in stationing a Turkish squa- 
dron of large ships off Varna now that the fine season is coming on, and thereby 
leaving the combined fleet more at liberty to operate with efficiency elsewhere. 
1 am inclined to think that the Porte would acquiesce in your opinion, and act 
accordingly. 

You will oblige me by a reply.

Inclosure 6 in No. 105. 
Vice-Admiral Dundas to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, “Britannia,” off Baljik, April 7, 1854. 
AS it will be necessary that a squadron, under Sir Edmund Lyons, should 
visit the coasts of Georgia and Circassia as soon after the declaration of war as 
possible, I have to request your Excellency will inform the Turkish Govern- 
ment that, if a steamer under their flag cannot be spared to accompany the 
combined squadrons under the Rear-Ac miral, officers (either military or civil) 
may be appointed to embark in the French or English steamers, to enter into 
gome arrangements with the Circassians, so that the services of those people 
may be made available against Russia, and if they should require powder, &c., 
we may have an opportunity of assisting them, as well as coming to an under- 
standing on what parts of the coast attacks might be made in concert with them 
during the summer. : 
T have, &e. 
(Signed) J. W. D. DUNDAS.

THE Porte has received a telegraphic message of the 29th ultimo, from

My Lord, Gallipoli, April 6, 1854. 

SINCE | last had the honour of addressing your Excellency, | returned to 
the Dardanelles in company with Lieutenant Wrottesley, of the Royal Enginecrs 
and Deputy-Assistant Commissary-General ‘Thompson, for the purpose of 
examining the accommodation which might be made available hoth for troops 
and stores, and which had been prepared, under my inspection by the "Turkish 
Government. 

Immediately after our arrival, we examined the quarantine establishment 
at Nagara, which we found ina tolerable good state of repair. We have 
therefore recommended on aecount of its healthy position, and many other 
reasons, that the lazaretto whieh will hold 500 patients very comfortably, he 
used as the principal hospital for our troops stationed in this neighbourhood, 
We have also recommended that the lazaretto stores, which are perfeetly safe 
from fire, and will hold several thousand tons of stores, be used as the principal 
depot for the Commissariat department. 

‘ho water communication between Nagara and Gallipoli, will render the 
transport to and from, between ithe two places very easy. 

Neither the Assistant Commissary-General nor the Lieutenant of Engineers 
being, however, authorised to do so, and as it was evident that if I did not 
interfere, the French officers would have soon appropriated for their service 
every available store and house in Gallipoli, | have taken upon myself the 
responsibility of requiring the Turkish Commission to place the whole of the 
Greck quarter of Gallipoli, and all the lazaretto buildings at Nagura at my 
disposal until further orders, 

We were about to inspect the quarters prepared at the Dardanelles, and the 
neighbouring villages for the rece ition of our troops, when [ received informa- 
tion that the steamer “ Golden Fleece ” with the first battalion of the Rifle 
brigade and two companies of Sappers had passed the forts during the night 
for Gallipoli, I therefore lost no time in returning to this town, and placed 
myself at once in communication with Licutenant-General Sir George Brown 
who is in command of the division. :

ON Thursday, 9th of March, two Russian battalions of Infantry, three 
regiments of Cavalry, five or six hundred Cossacks, and some Artillery, advanced 
upon Kalafat from different directions, to within a distance of two gun-shots, 
ag if to attack it. A body of their Cavalry having approached to within gun 
shot, we opened our fire and killed six or seven men. The enemy withdrew 
without attacking, after five hours.

No. 108. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl af Clarendon. —(Recetved April 22.) 
(No. 213. Confidential.): 
My Lord, Berlin, April 20, 1604. 

I HAVE had the honour to receive your Lordship’s despatch No. 83, 
inclosing the copy of one marked No 67, ‘seeret and confidential” of the 
24th ultimo, from Her Majesty's Charge d’Affaires at Stockholm, in which 
Mr. Grey reports a conversation whieh he had held with the Crown Prince of 
Sweden, as to the means that might be employed to induce the King of Prussia 
to depart from his wavering policy. | 

our Lordship has been pleased to desire that | would comnmnicate to 
you any observations | might have to make on this subject, and I should have 
replied sooner to your instructions, were it not for the ueelessness of making any 
calculations as to what the King of Prussia is likely to do, for he may lave one 
opinion to-day and one entirely opposite to-morrow, His wish is evident 
enough, and the events which have taken place at Berlin during the last two 
months, have proved that His Majesty's wishes anything rather than to quarrel 
with the Emperor of Russia. His Majesty desires in reality to be neutral, and 
circumstances alone will force him to hanes his policy : one half of his Govern- 
ment supports this opinion, bnt the other half feels the impossibility for a great 
power like Prussia to be inactive in the approaching struggle. 

The Court are all, [may say, in the interests of Russia, and hence the 
wavering conduct of the hing, who is first impelled in one direction by Baron 
Manteulfel, who desires to see Prussia take that honourable part in the war 
which becomes her position, and no sooner is HisMajesty brows round to his 
views, than a few hours afterwards the Russian party at Court undo all that 
has been effected by the Minister President, and 1 apprehend that the King's 
feclings are successtully worked on, first through his dread of Russia, and next 
through his want of confidence in (he means possessed by England and France 
to effect the objects they desire to attain by tho Wats | 

He believes it, in fact, to be im possible for us to make any serious impres= 
sion on Russia without the aid of Germany, and is persuaded that if Germany 
were to unite cordially with the Western Powers, that Prussia would be the 
country to anffor most from the vindictiveness of the Emperor Nicholas. 

The policy of this country, however, is not exactly neutrality, for the King 
desires to retain for himself the character of mediator and peace-maker, neither 
is it dictated by a sense of what is just or right or dignified, but by a terror of 
a powerful neighbour and of the revenge which will some day be inflicted on 
Prussia, if she departs from her present pusillanimous system, 

As to the means whieh the Crown Prince of Sweden seems to think could 
he sucessfully employed in bringing the King of Prussia to adopt a more 
decided policy, I suspect that His Royal Highness is but imperfectly acquainted 
with the very vacillating character with which we have to deal. 

There ia no doubt but that a promise given by England and France that 
the Kingdom of Poland should not he reconstituted might have a momentary 
effect on his Prussian Majesty and remove the apprehensions of revolution in 
that direction, Whilst on the other hand he might be alarmed if we threatened 
him with the re-establishment of the monarchy if he did net unite with ts; but 
Tam not of opinion that such language at the present moment would have 
any other effect than to drive him towards Russia, or make him more decided 
in his endeavours to maintain a neutral position, 

A threat of blockading the Prussian Baltic Ports would, | also believe, do 


a7 


more harm than good, The King knows full well how easily this could be 
done at the present moment, and the act itself would set public opinion com- 
pletely against us. 

With reference, however, to the question of the possibility of the re- 
establishment of the Polish Monarchy, and to the King’s opinions on this 
subject, | have availed myself of an opportunity which lately offered to allude 
to this question im conversation with Baron Manteuffel, and on my asking how 
His Majesty felt about it, and if, as had been reported to me, he clune seriously 
to the continuation of the present order of things in Poland, his Excellency 
replicd that he did not imagine the King had any settled opinions. on the 
subject, and he elieves that His Majesty cares very ittle about any of his own 
Polish Possessions except the fortresses, Which he of course would require for 
the line of defence of Germany against an attack from the Kast. 

T have, &c.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 22.) 
(No. 217. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 20, 1804. 

| HAD the honour to inform your Lordship to-day by the telegraph that 
the Treaty which has been for some Hime under negotiation between Austria 
and Prussia has been signed, 

Since sending off that despatch I have had a few minutes’ copversation 
with Baron Manteutfel, but was unable to learn from his Excellency anything 
of importance connected with this Convention beyond what | have already 
reported. Tle said that the two Governments engaged to guarantee the terri- 
tory of the other from all aggression pending the duration of the war; that 
Austria would have full liberty to take whatever steps she pleased to force the 
Russians to quit the Danubian Principalities, and that the Two Powers would 
immediately call upon Rugsia to evacuate them, and that if she refused they 
would take into consideration the means which would become necessary under 
euch cireumstances, and that Austria would then, he believed, march into these 
Turkish provinces. 

His Fexcellency added that, by a secret article, the negotiation of which 
had caused the great delay in terminating this affair, Prussia binds herself to 
hold 100,000 men in readiness for the defence, if necessary, of the Austrian 
frontiers. 

General Hess left Berlin for Vienna this evening, and has promised that 
not a moment shall be lost in preparing the Austrian Ratification which the 
Prussian Government desire to have exchanged for theirs as soon as possible, 
in order that a communication on the subject may be made to the German 
States. 

Baron Manteuffel mentioned to me, in confidence, that he had a most 
dvcadful scene at Charlottenburg yesterday when he went to take the King's 
final orders on the Treaty, and that when he considers all the influences which 
were opposed to the completion of this document, he is surprised that he should 
have obtained His Majesty's congent to it. ‘This, however, he said was no 
gooner obtained than he was set upon by the Queen, and attacked in so violent 
a manner by Duke George of Mecklenburg for having recommended the adop- 
tion of this measure, that the King was obliged to interfere and take up 
M. Manteuflel’s defence. 

| mention this cireumstance to show how incalculable are the King’s acts. 
It is only a few days since he refused (o give his consent to one of the articles 
of this Convention to which he now agrees, and now His Majesty appears to 
have been obliged to come forward to defend his Minister against attacks from 
other quarters tor the advice he had given on the subject. 

This last proceeding proves. the difficulty and uncertainty which attend 
all negotiations with the Court of Prussia in consequence of the public manner 
in which these important matters are discussed, and the many | fhuences which 
can be brought to bear against the King. I have, &c. 

(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

No. 110. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 24.) 
(No, 553) 
My Lord, Paris, April 22, 1894. 

COUNT HATZFELDT appears to have made another attempt yesterday 
to induce the French Government to opel further negotiations at St. Peters- 
burgh for the yet pacific solution of the Eastern question, such overtures to be 
founded on the old story of the evacuation of the Principalities by an carly day 
in May, the evacuation to be followed by the retreat 0 the allied squadrons 
from the Black Sea and internal waters of Turkey, and Conferences to be 
wstablished for the purpose of securing the civil emancipation of the Sultan's 
Christian subjects. 

M. Dronyn de Lhuys replied that France had already on two occasions 
addressed the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh in the sense suggested from Berlin, 
once ina most friendly, and another time ina more peremptory form. Neither 
of these overtures had sneeeeded, and France could not now make a third 
attempt, as if ashamed or afraid of the position in which she found herself, 
Besides which, the Prussian proposition offered no guarantee for the future. 
What was there to prevent Russia renewing at any moment the game she was 
playing to-day ? . 

Sebastopol was within thirty-six hours of Constantinople ; Bessarabia and 
Turkey touched. 

What security was there against future Russian aggression when Turkey 
was left alone and unprotected ? 

The Four Powers had recorded at Vienna their reprobation of the conduct 
of the Emperor of Russia. Prussia, by becoming. the mediator for Russia, 
destroyed the effect whieh this unity of opinion might otherwise produce. It 
was the hesitation of the German Powers which had, in his opinion, been the 
‘ndirect cause of the war which they now deprecated, and it depended again 
upon them to determine whether the war should be confined to the East, or be 
spread throughout Europe. 

M. Dronyn de Lhuys then turned the conversation on the Convention 
which had been signed lately hetween Austria and Prussia, and said to Count 
Hatafelt. that he did not wish to betray any indiscreet curiosity—that if this 
Convention related solely to Austrian and Prussian interests he had no right 
to expect that it should be made known to him, but that if it had reference to 
the Eastern question, he must say that a concealment of its provisions was a 
bad return for the confidence which France and England had reposed in the 
German Powers, they having communicated to the Cabinets of Vienna and 
Berlin every engagement which they had taken as soon As such engagement 
had been contracted. 1 have, &c. 

(Signed) COW LEY.

No. 115. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 25.) 


(No. 224. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, April 22, 1854. 

SINCE I had the honour of addressing to your Lordship my despatch 
No, 208 of the 15th instant, Chevalier Bunsen has tendered his resignation. 

Baron Manteuffel has just expressed to me his great regret and annoyance 
on this subject, and has informed me that Chevalier Bunsen lias communicated 
his intention in a manner which has seriously offended the King. 

T asked his Excellency whether there might not be some misapprehension, 
and whether the door might not be left, open for explanations. He re slied that 
the King was so excited when he spoke to His Majesty, that he had thought of 
ordering Chevalier Bungen to come immediately to Berlin, and have him tried 
hefore a tribunal. That Chevalier Bunsen had declared that he should be 
able to justify his conduct by the publication of documents; that it was his 
intention at the same time to take eare that nothing appeared in print which 
would implicate the character of his Royal Master, for whom he must ever 
entertain the highest respect and veneration. 

Baron Mantenflel went on to state that Chevalier Bunsen’s conduct had 
heen extraordinary beyond all explanation, and that he had now written that 
he would cease to carry ont the instructions that might be addressed to him, 
er pessibne which had naturally produced a most unfortunate effect on the 
King. 

i observed that it was impossible so devoted a servant as Chevalier Bunsen 
could have meant any disrespect to his Royal Master, and that the matter 
might calm down in a few days, and something occur which would enable him 
to place the matter ina different shape before the King. Baron Manteullel 
rejoined that he wished it might be so, but to make things worse, he had just 
seen a telegraphic message from London, dated to-day, which had been received 
by a commercial house at Berlin, reporting the resignation of Chevalier Bunsen, 
and that consequently the intelligence would he in the newspapers to-morrow. 

1 endeavoured to impress on Baron Manieuffel the necessity of taking 
meusures to prevent Chevalier Bunsen leaving his post; that at the present 
moment this intelligence would have the worst possible effect, and would be 
looked upon not only in Germany but throughout Europe as an indication of 
a change of policy in the Prussian Government, and to be the result of Russian 
intrigue, and would perhaps be deeply regretted hereafter. 

His Excellency feels all the inconvenience of Chevalier Bunsen's pro- 
ceedings, but sees no means of applying a remedy at this moment and in the 
present temper of the King, who is evidently deeply offended by his Minister's 
conduct, and I may add, that the Sovereign of this country does not admit that 
his servants have any right to resign, and considers such proceedings as acts of 
treachery on their part. { have, &ec. 

(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

= will, no doubt, be interesting to your Lordship, : This disorganized rabble, for they cannot be called soldiers, with the excep- 


LO4 


tion of a few contingents from Asia, which are more disciplined, ought to be 
withdrawn, and it is much to be hoped that the Sultan’s Government will take 
immediate steps to withdraw them before the arrival of the auxiliary forces, 
for if the allies should advance, and this rabble follow in their wake, they will 
assuredly bring discredit upon the allied armies, and upon their cause, 

Upon hearing of the atrocities committed by the Bashi-Bozouks, | took an 
early opportunity of speaking to Omer Pasha upon the subject, and he fully 
concurred with the views above expressed as to their usclessness, with the 
exception of some few, and he feels the diffieulties in which they place him and 
his army, both as to reputation, and the exhaustion of the resources of the 
COUNLEY. 

Upon my observing to him that it appeared to me absolutely necessary 
that an example should be made of those of them against whom any flagrant 
crime could be proved, and that they should be executed, his Highness informed 
me that some of them had heen captured, and would be severely punished by 
beating, 

is punishment is sometimes carried to the extent that death ensues, but 
there appears to be a great objection on the part of the Turkish Government 
and, | am informed, of the Sultan personally, to the punishment of death, 
Omer Pasha does not therefore feel himself authorized to order the execution 
of these miscreants. 

[ would observe that, under these circumstances, 1b appears to me most 
desirable that orders should be issued by the Government at Constantinople to 
the effect that all offenders charged either with rape, murder, or ill-treatment 
of the inhabitants, should be brought before a tribunal, before which, if the 
charge be proved, they should for either of the first two offences, suffer death, 
and, for the latter, such other punishment as the tribunal should award, subject 
to the approval of the ceneralissimo. 

Buch a system would relieve the generalissimo of ‘all suspicion of cruelty 
or personal animosity, and would have a very beneficial effect, 

The publication of the views of the Government upon the subject, would, 
[ have no doubt, tend much to check the evil. 

lt cannot, however, be put a stop to without sending the whole body, with 
the exceptions before alluded to, to their homes. This, again, cannot be done 
with safety, unless they are disarmed, 

His Highness informed me confidentially that it was his intention to do 
this, but as it is a delicate measure to undertake, it will require caution, and 
some little time must elapse before le can venture upon it, 

In the meantime he assures me that he has done all that he can to cure 
the evil, having detached some cavalry to patrol the country for the protection 
of the inhabitants, and having given strict orders upon the subject. Your 
Lordship will observe that this increases unnecessarily the fatigue of the soldiers, 
and tends to render them and their horses less fit to meet the enemy than they 
otherwise would be. . 

In my despatch No, 3 of March 29th, | did not state the strength of the 
battalions of infantry, as [had not then suflicient information to enable me to 
form a very correct estimate. Omer Pasha considers them as averaging 750 
effective. I should be inclined, however, to estimate them rather less; the Line 
battalions at 500 and the Redifs at 700, These latter, however, vary very much, 
and my estimate may possibly not be accurate. For the present I should be 
inclined to consider the average of the whole at 600, but 1 hope shortly to be 
able to give a more accurate estimate, 

At present the troops here are much oceupied in strengthening the fortifi- 
cations, and the opportunities of seeing them together are rare. 

The new fortifications in course of erection, or about to be erected, will add 
very materially to the strength of this position,
