Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 30.) 
(No. 169.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, April 12, 1854. 


ACCORDING to our latest advices from Varna, of the 10th instant, no 
striking change had taken place on the theatre of war. 

The Russians were not advancing in the Dobrudscha, They were under- 
stood to be rather engaged in securing the positions which they had already 
occupied. ans ; 

The Turkish army, still concentrating at Shumla, is described as amounting 
to 40,000 men. It was likely to add 10,000 more to its numbers. The regular 
cavalry was called in from Kalafat. 

That position was still maintained by the Infantry ; but a very considerable 
mortality prevailed among the troops. : 

At Pravadi, which fronts one of the principal passes of the Balkan, between 
Varna and Shumla, four battalions of Infantry and 1,000 Irregular Cavalry are 
atationd, according to the information received by Colonel Neale. 

The money sent from here to pay up the arrears of the army, at least in 
part, had reached Varna in safety. The garrison of that fortress amounts now 
to between 8,000 and $,000 men. Twelve transports had arrived there with 
uns and stores. Measures also were in operation for getting in grain from 
Kustendji, whence most of the inhabitants had fled, dreading the approach of the 
Russians almost as much as the presence of the Turkish Irregulars. 

Much difficulty is said to be experienced in collecting provisions for Shumla, 
where, however, it is believed the supplies of grain and flour are by no means 
deficient. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clurendon.—{ Received April 30.) 

(No. 171.) 
My Lori, Constantinople, April 14, 1804, 

ON the 9th instant I received despatches from Sir Henry Ward and 
Mr. Saunders relative to the state of affairs in Lower Albania. An earlier report 
from the latter had encouraged me to hope that the plan of proceeding ordered 
by the Porte, under my advice, had produced a salutary effect, that the inhabit- 
ants of the disturbed district were gradually returning to their duty towards the 
Sultan, and that the sympathizers from Greece, though not ern from the 
country, were held in check. ‘The subsequent advices from both represent the 
disastrous events which had ensued, the injudicious conduct of the Turkish 
authorities, and the destructive outrages perpetrated by the Irregular troops in 
league with the barbarous mountain tribes from whom they derive their origin. 
They also brought to my knowledge the afflicting consequences of so much 
imprudence in one quarter, and of so much atrocity in another, leading by natural 
sequence to a revival of the insurrection and an increasedl pressure on the 
resources of the Porte. I spare your Lordship a repetition of particulars which 
have, no doubt, been transmitted by the direct channel to Her Majesty's 
Government. | 

Immediately on receiving the intelligence [ went over to Reshid Pasha, 
and I sent at the same time both to the Sultan and to the Grand Vizir, requiring 
of each and of all that a special council should be assembled on the ensuing day, 
and that effective measures should be forthwith taken, not only for redressing 
the special crimes committed in Albania by the Irregulars, or Bashi-Bozouks, 
but for putting a final stop to the excesses of those barbarians in every part of 
the empire, : 

Satisfactory answers were given to this remonstrance. The Sultan issued 
an order agreeably to my demand, and his Ministers, the Grand Vizir and 


Reshid Pasha, undertook that a Council should be summoned without delay. 


107 


Next morning I sent in a paper repeating the substance of my complaint, 
and specifying the measures of redress which I thought indispensable. Of this 
paper a copy is herewith inclosed for your Lordship’s information. . 

The Council was assembled at the time expected, and the measures I pro- 
posed were adopted. Inclosed herewith is M. Pisani’s report, which he sub- 
mitted to Reshid Pasha before he sent it to me, and which, as M. Pisani assures 
me, received His Highness’s unqualified approval. 

It remains for the Porte to give effect to the decisions of the Council im a 
determined and imposing manner, nor shall I be contented with anything short 
of a full measure of redress, and the utter extinction of an evil which can no 
longer be tolerated with any degree of prudence and humanity, . 

Your Lordship may be assured that I had not waited for the affleting 
incidents in Albania to urge thé importance of abating so great an evil as 
that of the Bashi-Bozouks. My remonstranees had been repeated to saticty ; 
but owing to the inherent difficulties of the case, every assurance of redress had 
remained little more than a dead letter. 

T have, &ec. eo 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIEFE.,

Inclosure 1 in No. 124, 
Mentorandumi. 


THE British Ambassador is inexpressibly grieved by the intelligence 
which reached him yesterday from Prevesa and Corfu. He has already stated 
orally to thé Ottoman Secretary of State the circumstances which constitute 
that intelligence, and he now sends extracts of the correspondence containing 
particulars in support of the general statement. In point of policy as well as 
of humanity, the atrocious outrages perpetrated by the Albanian Irregulars 
under Haireddin Bey, and the Turkish tribes in connection with them, are 
calewlated to rouse the strongest feelings of indignation. Whole districts laid 
waste, forty-six Christian villages burned, many of their inhabitants slaughtered, 
their cattle taken away, their women violated, their children led into captivity, 
—such are the barbarous facts ascertained upon the spot by a British naval 
officer, who risked his lite to verify the statements which had been submitted 
to him. These inhuman acts have been committed, not by a foreign enemy, 
but by subjects of the same Sovereign and by neighbours lying previously on 
amicable terms with their victims. They have been committed in defiance of 
the Sultan's Commissioner, and almost in presence of His Majesty's allies, on a 
population threatened by the Greek insurgents on account of the loyal and 
peaceable behaviour which they continued to maintain, and at a time vieu the 
endeavours to raise an insurrection in the country were checked by the tempe- 
rate and concilitory measures which, together with military assistance, had 
been adopted by express orders from the Porte. 

It is well known that the savage eruelties practised by the Bashi-Bozouks 
in Epirus are also practised throughout the empire wherever these creatures 
of infamy are collected and wherever they pass. Facts in proof of this asser- 
tion imve been re eatealy submitted to the Porte, and promises of justice have 
been as frequently given by the same authority, which has not sought to 
conceal the horrors complained of, and which must admit that the Irregulars 
are as dangerous to the Sultan’s armies as to the peaceful rayah subjects 
whom they trample under foot, 

Their measure of wickedness is now full. Justice must have its duc, The 
Sultan's allies have a right to demand it, They cannot send their fleets and 
armies to fight in His Majesty's cause, and give their countenance and support 
to the measures: adopted by the Porte for the restoration of tranquillity in 
disturbed districts, without incurring a deep share of the responsibility attach- 
ing to crimes such as those which are recited above. The Governments and 
people of Christendom must alike feel the indispensable obligation of not being 
made to appear as accomplices in the commission of such atrocities, The 
Porte: must show by its acts, and the honest enforcement of adequate remedial 
measures, that it redeems the pledge which it has given, and exerts its authority 


108 


with good faith and energy as well for the suppression of the evil as for the 
punishment of the offenders and the indemnification of the sufferers. 
The British Ambassador expects that the present day will not come to a 
close without a meeting of the Council, and the adoption of suitable measures 
irected to those objects. ; 
ama mith reanet to the particular calamities inflicted on the rH 
of Paramithia and other adjacent districts, orders must be sent forthwit Bi 
proclaim the Sultan’s reprobation of what has oceurred, to sel2Ze_ ant pone

plunderers or those who have purchased it from them, to provide a sufficient 
indemnity for that portion of the plunder which cannot he reco. ered by an 
assesement on the bribes which received it, and for the prevention of further 
outrages, to establish rural enards, properly selected, under responsible leaders, 
and supported by such of the regular troops as can be spared for the serviee. 
Secondly, with respect to the irregular soldiery im reneral, it is of para- 
mount urgeney that His Majesty the Sultan should proclaim his determination 
to repress their outrages, and place them in that degree of order whieh, is 
necessary for them to co-operate with his regular troops and the forces of his 
allies, giving authority to his generals lo punish summarily by court-martial on 
the spot every act of insurbordination or violence against his peaceable subjects, 
and making their chiefs and the regular ofhicers under whom they are called 
on to act. responsible for any remissness 1n the execution of his commands. 
Justice at the same time requires that those irregulars who ure employed 
in His Majesty's service should be sufficiently and regularly patd. Tt will Me

protecting the towns and villages or other dwelling places near which they 
have to pass. Above all, it is desirable for the Sultan's service that their 
numbers should be reduced, or, if possible, that they should be dispensed with

Inclosure 3 in No, 125, 
Consul Neale to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Marna, April 8, 1554. 

THE pillage and disorder committed by the fugitive Tartars from 
Dobrudsehia, and by the Bashi-Bozouks in the district of Bazardjk, and to the 
northward of Balik, continues to occasion the utmost panic among the inha- 
bitants. In the immediate neighbourhood of Varna, the Tartars have carried 
off cattle, and the road even between this and Baljik is invested with the 
marauders. ‘The inhabitants in many instances have abandoned their villages, 
and a large number of carts arrived here yesterday from Bazardjik, bringing 
the merchandize and effects of the shopkeepers and other inhabitants. About 
forty or fifly Turkish families have also arrived here from the neighbourhood 
of Toultcha from Isakeha and Matehin, as also most of the ‘Turkish authorities 
of those places. 

At Kustendjee the inhabitants have fled, and I hear that two wounded chil- 
dren of three years and fifteen months old were taken off the shore at that place 
on board Her Majesty’s ship“ Firebrand,” by Captain Parker; the fate of their 
parents is as yet unknown, At this place (Kustendjee), lam informed that a 
considerable quantity of wheat is reported to be abandoned in the magazines 
belonging to the Government, The Turkish authorities might probably 
easily adopt measures to ship and save this grain for the public service. 

At Baljik the panic and fear of being assailed at night by the bands of 
Tartars who are traversing the country has been so great, notwithstanding the 
presence of the fleets, that the inhabitants have packed up all their merehan- 
dise and effects, and are prepared to leaye immediately for Varna and Con- 
stantinople, unless some protection were afforded to them. ‘The Pasha and Council 
of Varna, after seriously deliberating upon this state of things, decided upon 
sending two companies of Infantry to Baljik from Varna, and they left this 
yesterday in the French war-steamer “ Cacique.” 

Admiral Dundas informs me that he haa landed some Marines at Baljik, 
for the protection of the watering parties from the fleet; but the Admiral 
observes that he could not interfere with the police of the place, and thought 
that a few Turkish soldiers would be useful in pacifying the inhabitants; and 
in such an event as the sudden appearance of the Russians in that quarter, the 
Admiral says the fleet would take them off. 

Having heard that many of the fugitive Tartars were making their way 
to the Balkan by the road of Pravodi, together with all their plunder in 
eattle, &e., | yesterday addressed a letter to his Highness Omer Pasha 
mentioning this fact, and submitting to his Highness the practicability of 
sending a few squadrons of Cavalry in that direction, to cut off their escape, 
and to retake the plunder with whieh they are laden, T also represented to 
his Highness the serious inconvenience of the present insecure state of the road 
between Varna and Baljik, by which the land communication with the fleets 
was rendered difficult and dangerous; so much so, that the couriers were 
afraid to go on that road. T acquainted the Pasha of Varna with what 1 had

families had arrived at the river Kamehee, about five hours to the southward 
of this, with upwards of 3,000 oxen, the greater part of which they had 
plundered op the road, immediately sent three companies of troops to seize 
them, and it is thought they will sueceed in doing so, 

Profiting by the oa eae committed by the Tartars and Bashi-Bozouks, 
some gipsies attempted to carry off the cattle of the peasants in the immediate 
vicinity of Varna; but they were seized by the Eidearian peasants, and 
brouglit into Varna, where they have undergone severe punishment, Tam

Inclosure 2 in No. 126. 
Remarks upon the Anchorage off Heraclia. 


THE bottom in Heraclia Bay is clay under sand, affording cood holding 
eround, but it is not a safe anchorage against a west and north-west gale, unless 
anchored well-up in the bay, between Cape Baba and. the ancient Mole, so to 
obtain some shelter from those winds. 

The south-west gales seem not to blow home, or to bring a sea that would 
endanger a vessel well found in cables and anchors. ‘The light over Cape Baba 
is visible eight to nine miles distant. , 

(Signed) T, SPRATT. 


oo  — 


Remarks on the Roadstead of Kosloo. 


'THE accompanying survey of the roadstead of Kosloo will sufficiently show 
it to be only a summer anchorage. The traders resort to itin May for the slip. 
ment of coal, anchoring to the north-east of the valley, so to get better shelter 
from the point, the wind being in general to the east of north-east. The bottom 
‘¢ sand under twelve fathoms water, and mud and sand in deeper water, with 
this plan the lead will be a sufficient guide for anchoring, or the extreme West 
Cape kept open of Alepo Point will lead to a good berth at a quarter of a mile 
from the shore, But to expedite the embarkation of coal, a nearer berth may be 
taken. During the month of May the coast 1s sometimes subject to north-north- 
east gales, which on one occasion caused the wreck of eight or nine vessels, 
During June, July, August, and September, the coast is said to be perfectly sate. 
'The locality is best disinguished by the houses near the shore, there being no 
other village or similar settlement on the whole coast between Heraclia and 
Amostros; and the land about it presenting no remarkable object; the 
coast being generally bordered by high bold mountains covered with 
forest, ; 

(Signed) T, SPRATT.

Inclosure 3 in No, 126, 
Commander Spratt to Vice-Admiral Dundas. 


Bir, Constantinople, April 5, 1864. 

1. [HAVE the honour to report my return from the examination of the 
coal mines in the vicinity of Heraclia, and to communicate the following facts 
connected with them. 

® Coal is found in almost every valley opening to the sea, from about five 
miles north-east of Heraclia, as far as Amastros, and at distances of from one- 
quarter to three miles from the shore. 

5. In several of these valleys parties of Croats have for ten or twelve years 
been employed in working the ‘cal seams, cropping out on their sides, and as 
some of the valleys contain as many as seven or eight seams, good and bad, 


these have been indiscriminately worked, until a want of capita and skill have 
obliged them to abandon these localities for others nearer the surface, this coal 
being unskilfully worked from the worst part of the seam, and much exposed 
before shipping, reached Constantinople in a greatly deteriorated condition, as 
well as being of an inferior quality, through mixing the coal from several 
BEAMS, 


oti ee tT 


112 


4, The chief locality for good coal is at the valley of Kosloo, about sixteen 
miles north-east of Heraclia, where the Turkish Government have an establish- 
ment, under the direction of two civil engineers, Messrs, Barkley, who are in 
receipt of a good salary, with an advantage in addition in proportion to the 
quantity of coal obtained, At this time four Englishmen, miners, belong to the 
Aaabliinient as foremen to the native workers, besides which are some Poles 
and Hungarians, and afew Servians and Bosnians, 

f. The natives employed are Turks from the neighbouring villages who are 
foreed to work out their by from fifty to sixty days labour at these mines, They 
are consequently obtained with great difficulty, quit upon every opportunity, and 
labour with no interest, the foreigners employed being the only men paid by 
the Turkish Government, and this only at intervals of three, six, or nme 
ommths. 

G, In this valley of Kosloo there are no less than nine seams of coal, but 
only four are at present worked. The thickest of these seams is eighteen feet, 
and the least about three feet. Some of them would not pay to work, and those 
now worked have only a portion of their coal gool, A tram road leads from all 
these mines to the shore at Kosloo; the extremity being carried oub upon the 
wast point of the bay, so to enable boats to be under eight or nine shutes, and 
receive the coal direct from the trucks. According. to the statement of the 
engineer and director, Mr. Barkley, 00 tons can he shipped per day, weather 
permitting. 

7. Some of these mines penetrate 500 or 400. yards into the mountain. 

® Under these skilful engineering and mining operations, the Director, 
when supplicd with them in sufficient number, is enabled to procure, on an 
average per month, 2,500 tons from the four Kosloa mines. ‘This amount he 
can ensure even with the present means at his command, ani for a period ol 
three years; thus averaging from the Kosloo mines only about 30,000 tons of 
good coal por annum, 
~ 9, At the present moment there is lying adjacent to the railway in the 
Kosloo Valley, about 9,000 tons of coal mn three or four leaps at the pit mouth. 
Twenty-five tons of coal was shipped in Her Majesty's steam-ship “Spittire™ 
from these heaps, taking a portion from each, of what 1s technically termed, 
‘nicked near the pit’s mouth.” 

~ 10, The ecoul of the three heaps have a close resemblance to each other, 
and in the furnace, whether for steaming or ceonomy, have no appreciated 
difference; the whole being very like Neweastle in weight and appearance also. 

I1. The result of the trials of coal from each pit or mine, as given in the 
Engineer's report, after nineteen: hours steaming, on the first grade, with both 
boilers, shows that the Kosloo coal is equal to the very best Newcastle coal, 
having a loss of about seven per cent, only in elnker and ashes, 

12, ‘Ihe chief engineer of “ Spittire’ reports that the coal used from the 
heaps when “ unpicked" would not show a loss more than from eight to ten per 
cent, the whole being in general large and excellent coal. | 

18. ‘Thus, there is lying at Kosloo ready for shipment, 9.000 tons of coal 
equal to good Neweastle, and, if shipped into steamers direct from this valley, 
would suffer little or no diminution of its value; but, as the quality of the coal is 
of a delicate and friable nature, it easily crumbles into amall fragments, and 
would lose much of its value on being often trans-shipped and long exposed to 
the air: which is the condition that a great portion of if reaches Constantinople, 
The conl has been worked on the Kosloo mines at a cost of as little as sIx 
shillings per ton, but, as the mine ts frequently allowed to he idle for want of 
a supply of candles from the Government, and the absenting of the forced 
labourers, the renewing of the operation brings the average cost to ten or 
twelve shillings per ton, Last year the eoal was sold by the ‘Turkish Govern- 
ment at seventeen shillings per ton at Kosloo, and one pound per ton at 
Heraclin, to which place it is trans-shipped at the depot and residence of the 
‘furkish director of the mines, who is also the governor of the place, And as 
in this trans-shipment it is liable to be mixed with the inferior coal also sent 
there from the mines worked by the Croats, it 16. therefore, more likely to be 
of much less value at Heraclia than at Kosloo; but at the latter place it can 
only he shipped in tine weather, or with southerly winds, whilst at the former 

it van be shipped at all times ; it is, therefore, most desirable that the coal 
supplied to our ships from these mines should be shipped direct from the Kosloo 


118 


valley, or selected from the coal heaps stored at Heraclia by one of the 
engineers, Messrs. Barkley, who have offered their services, through me, for 
such a purpose, to prevent the Government being imposed upon with the 
inferior Croat coal, as in the case of the “Triton,” that very coal having been 
previously condemned by these gentlemen when lying at the mouth of the valley 
it was worked from, and by them reported to the Turkish Director at Heraclia 
as unfit for use, But as it is to the interest of this official to send to Constan- 
tinople as much coal as possible, the report of Messrs. Barkley was unheeded, 
and the coal on arrival not finding a sale at Constantinople, was finally handed 
over forthe use of “Triton,” on her application. 

14, The importance of obtaining from these mines a coal to ensure “ full 
speed” when necessary, induces me to dwell upon the above point, and to 
recommend the acceptance of the voluntary services of these centlemen, under 
sanction of the authority, whenever Turkish coal is required by our Government. 

15. At Heraclia there is at present only two parcels of coal, and one of 
about 450 tons and the other nearly 200 tons, The former is coal procured 
hy the Croats, and of an inferior quality ; the small parcel of coal is from a 
seam of coal recently opened by the Turkish Government, under Mr. Barkley, 
at about nine miles from Heraclia and one from the sea; thirteen tons and 4 
half of this coal, and shipped at Heraclia by the“ Spitfire,” and found to be 
equal to that from the Kosloo valley. During the year 1853 about 50,000 tons 
of coal was exported from this district. 

16, There was found lying at Heraclia, and moored in the bay west of the 
town, between 20 and 80 vessels from LOU to Lo0 tone, which are employed 
during the summer in the transport of the coal, Small caiques are so employed 
during the winter as weather permits, and bring coal to Heraclia from all the 
valleys’ mouths, where it is vided. 

17, Country vessels lie moored head and stern here during the whole 
winter, and are said to be perfeetly safe from every gale, although exposed to 
zome fetch trom the south-west,

(Signed) T. SPRATT.

My Lord, “ Britannia,” off Baljik, April 9, 1854. 

IN reply to your Excellency’s letter of the 6th instant No. 54, 1 beg to 
acquaint you that having consulted with Vice-Admiral Hamelin relative to the 
employment of the Turkish ships of war, we are of opinion that a ship of the 
line and a frigate (drawing as little water as possible), and a small steamer, 
should be stationed under the guns at Varna. 

One of the best steamers should accompany the squadron to the coast of 
Georgia, and with another steamer (not of much speed ) attend to the combined 
squadrons, to bring up from Constantinople supplies, despatches, &e. 

A frigate and steamer should rnn along the coast of Anatolia, calling at 
the coal fields, Sinope, Trebizond and Batoum, but not remaining more than 
three days at any one place. 

When the communication is open with the Cireassians, the Turkish navy 
may be employed to operate with er but until then they should not extend 
their eruize beyond the coast of Europe. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) J. W. D. DUNDAS.

Inclosure 14 in No, 126. 


Information obtained from the Master of a Russian Schooner, taken off Sebastopol 
by Her Majesty's Ship © Fury.” 


THE prize and her companion were bound to Kosloo to take in salt, and 
then to proceed to Odessa for provisions. ‘The owner is a Russian, at Odessa; 
the master an Austrian, native of Caltava, 

Four or five days ago live transports sailed from Sebastopol to St. Nicolai 
for provisions. Between Sievarna and Schastopol town-point there are two 
chains, buoyed up by heavy timbers. 

There are four Admiral’s flags. The line-of-battle ships are in two 
divisions :— 

Three three-deckers, three two-deckers, across the harbour. 
Ditto ditto in dockyard. 
All have sails bent, and are ready for sea, There are in all about thirty men- 
of-war, twelve being ships of the line, twelve steamers, and seven of these 
ready for service, the remainder frigates and smaller craft. Two of the 
steamers are said to be very fast. 

The garrison is about 50,000, principally Artillery, and are exercised by 
day and by night with targets placed in the harbour. An attack hy the com- 
bined forces is expected. 

The two captured Turkish steamers are under repair, one at Sebastopol, 
one at St. Nicolai, ; ) 

Two thousand heavy Cavalry have recently arrived, and four divisions are 
expected, 

The large fort of Nicolaieska, mounting from 200 to 300 guns on the three 
tiers, appears the only land defence on the north. 

The town of Sebastopol is surrounded on the south by walls and ditches, 

At Odessa there are about 60,000 troops, and on the quarantine point 
there were lately ten heavy guns; the defences are since increased, 

Osman Pusha, who was taken in Sinope, has quite recovered, and recently 
vone to Odessa, He was attended by four medical men, He receives great 
kindness, was frequently with the Russian Admirals, and on leaving Sebastopol 
in a steamer all the Russian ships manned yards. 

In Sebastopol there is a passage on each side of the chain for merchant 
vessels drawing about ten feet. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) EDWARD TATHAM,

Consul Calvert to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Gallipoli, April 10, 1854. 

LAST night Her Majesty's steam-vessel “Vulcan,” having on board the 
44th regiment, and three Companies of the 50th, arrived here. 

To-day the greatest part of the stores have been put on shore, and to- 
morrow the troops will be landed, and encamped at once between this place 
and Boulair. 

Two French war steamers have also arrived in port, laden with troops, 
but I have not yet ascertained their names, nor the number of men on board, 
for TU have been out all day with Sir George Brown, reconnoitring the country 
near Cavak, with a view to ascertain its capabilities for the encampment ot 
troops. 

My he great deficiency of a supply of fresh water between this place 
and Boulair will render it absolutely necessary that a great part of the large 
bodies of English and French troops now expected to arrive here, be moved 
further on. 

I return early to-morrow morning to the Dardanelles, as [ have been 
informed that the buildings of the Lazaretto of Nagara which had been given 
to me for the service of the British army, have been demanded by the French 
General. 

We allowed our allies to take possession of every available house in 
Gallipoli, without making any remonstrance because we depended upon the 
atores and other buildings at Nagara, which had been made over to me, with 
every Wish therefo re to be conciliatory, I shall not aceede to the demand now 
made upon our resources, without secing good canse for so doing. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) F. W. CALVERT,

Lieutenant-General Sir George Brown to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Gallipoli, April 11, 1854. 

IT js only this morning that the letter addressed by your Lordship to_the 
Commander of Her Majesty’s land forces destined for Turkey on the 29th 
ultimo, has been sent to me from Malta, and I mention the circumstance lest 
you may have been surprised at not having received an earlier answer 
to it. 

The delay which has taken place, you will observe, is of the less con- 
sequence, seeing that acting under the instructions with which I have been 
furnished by the Secretary of State, it would have been im sossible for me to 
have complied with your Lordship’s suggestion, or to have diverted the small 
force placed at my disposal from the specific service, for which it was destined 
without the express sanction of the Government, or the directions of the 
General Officer under whose orders [ have heen placed. 

Immediately on the declaration of war, orders were transmitted to Malta 
to forward as many of the troops assembled there to this place, as they had the 
means of transport for, and accordingly the 44th and 93rd regiment, together 
with part of the 50th, have arrived in the course of yesterday and to-day, and 
have landed and gone into camp in the neighbourhood 

As the amount of force is increased, we shall be more and more cramped 
for store rooms, magazines and hospitals in this poor place, but the greatest 
difficulty it seems to me, will consist in an inadequate supply of water as. the 
geason advances, when | am led to believe, nearly all the small streams on 
whieh the troops now mainly depend for their supply will be dried up. 

The reports, however, from the proposed fortified position, are rather more 
favorable in foapect to the supply of water, and I am induced to believe we 
might now employ a brigade on the works on the left of it without subjecting 
the troops to any great inconvenience on that score, 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) G, BROWN

No. 13. 
Mr. Magenis to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 1.) 


(No, 21, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Stuitgardt, April 27, 1654. 

THAD the honour to acknowledge the receipt, ina previous despatch, of 
your Lordship’s despateh No, 16, Confidential, informing me that Her Majesty’s 
Government had learned that intrigues were going on amongst the smaller States 
of the German Confederation with reference to the expected declarations to be 
made tothe Diet by Austria and Prussia, regarding the neutrality of Germany 
in. the impending war, and that the Wurtemberg Government had recently 
addressed a circular to the other second-rate States of Germany, calling on them 
to come to an understanding as to the course which it will be their common 
interest to pursue when the announcement of the policy of the two great German 
Powers shall he made to them in the Dict; and further that the South-western 
States of Germany are disposed to insist on the concentration of a Federal force 
on the Western frontiers of Germany, and instructing me to report what credit 
is to be attached to these rumours, 

In order to test as fully as possible the truth of the reports. in question, | 
have had conversations with the Representatives of some of the German Powers 
here, and subsequently with M. de Neurath on the subject. and I have now the 
honour to report to your Lordship their result, 

[learned from the former that as far as they were acquainted, no circular 
of the nature alluded to had been addressed by this Government to their Govern- 
ments: and M. de Neurath, in reply to my inquiry whether the Wurtemberg 
Government had come to any concert with the other German Governments as to 
a common reourse to be pursued, replied distinetly not; that as yet they were unac- 
quainted with the pecise stipulations of the offensive and defensive Treaty concluded 
between Austria and Prussia, and until they were, concert was impossible. With 
respect to the desire to concentrate a Federal force on the Western German 
frouticrs, my informants assured me they had no knowledge of such a measure, 
and the Wurtemberg Foreign Minister assured me that at this moment there was 
no question of it; he said that last autumn before the Eastern question had 
assuimed its present development, there was some question of such a measure, 


123 


but that at present. they might, on the contrary, be obliged to advance their 
reserves to support Prussia, in the event of that Power being called on by the 
more active participation of Austria, to cover the Galician or Hungarian frontiers 
of the latter from any attack on the part of Russia. It appears to me very 
improbable that the concentration of a Federal force on the Western frontiers 
should be either desired or pressed for by the minor German States at this 
moment. Such a measure would be attended with considerable expense 
to those States individually, a point on which they are the most: sensitive, and 
would amount to the gratuitous expression of distrust towards France, which 
T have no reason to believe is felt at this moment. ‘There is quite as little pro- 
bability either, as I believe, that such a measure if proposed would be carried 
in the Wet. 

‘That intrigues are carried on by the minor German Courts, and particularly 
by this Court, is, I fear, too tre; but such intrigues can lone produce any 
result when a want of concert exists between Austria and Prussia; when the 
councils of those countries are united, they are harinless. 

A desire to give greater weight to their representations at the Diet by 
revious concert, is also felt, and particularly by the four Royal Members of the 
“onfederation, Bavaria, Saxony, Hanover, and Wurtemberg, and it is said that 
the late visit here of M, de Knesbeck, the Hanoverian Minister at Munich, who 
is also accredited to this Court, was connected with that object, but Tam 
informed that he was not successful in his mission. 

As I ventured to state that the intrigues of the minor German Courts could 
alone have any result when the opinions of the great German Powers were at 
variance, I may add that the late visit of the King of Wurtemberg to Weimar, 
stopping on his road there, at the Courts of Darmstadt and that of the Duke of 
Nassau, was probably undertaken with the view of inducing those three Courts, 
which are all, as well as-His Majesty, immediately connected by marringe with 
the Imperial Family of Russia, to support the supposed Russian bias of the Cabinet 
of Berlin at 2 moment when the Treaty which has since been concluded, was still 
pendinz. 

‘The King of Wurtemberg is said, and [ beheve correetly, to tuke an active 
part in political affairs in Germany, without the knowledge or participation of 
his Ministers. His sympathies, both from personal triendship and trom his 
connection, as well as from appreciation of Russian power, are in favour of that 
country. His Majesty is at the same time supposed to set great weight on 
his popularity and position as 4 German Prince—witness his letter to the 
late Prince Schwarzenberg advocating a representation at the Diet, which 
shortly after appeared in the newspapers, and which, | remember, Prince 
Schwarzenbere assured me had not been made public by him, It is probable 
then that His Majesty would gladly avail himselt of every opportunity to support 
secretly a policy favourable to Russia, and to make a merit with that Power of 
having done so; but it is improbable, as 1 believe, that [ls Majesty would endanger 
his popularity by supporting publicly at the Dict any measure in favour of 
Russia, or which might be regarded by the public opinion in Germany, which is 
certainly not inclined to Russia, as anti-German. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) ARTHUR C, MAGENIS,

No. 132. 


Sir A. Malet to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Reeeived May 1.) 

(No. 21. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Frankfort, April 22, 165-4. 

IN my brief despatch No. 18 of the 13th instant, written after the inter- 
view which | had on that occasion with M. de Bismark, I reserved to an 
opportunity of secure transmission the giving your Lordship some further 
details of my conversation with his ste SiG) 

Speaking of the last Vienna Protocol, M. de Bismark said he looked upon 
himself as the originator of that State paper. 

After the rejection of the proposed Convention, he had seen M, de 


124 


Moustier, the French Minister, and suggested to him that the object which it 
had been sought to obtain by the Convention might, perhaps, be secured in 
some other way. 

The great difficulty was, that the King had an invincible repugnance to 
put his hand to any act which might have for its object a war with Russia. 

M. de Bismark told me that le had then held a long conversation with 
M. de Moustier, as to the points under discussion, and that M, de Moustier 
took notes of these points with a view to embodying them in some such document 
as had since been agreed upon. 

M. de Bismark further said that he had at the same time observed to 
M. de Moustier, that France in the present conjuncture need have no appre- 
hensions on the side of the Rhine, and might safely act on that assurance. 

Prussia did not say that in no case would she make war on Russia; what 
she did say, however, was that she would not be driven to take that decision, 
and would only adopt it in view of her own undoubted interests. 

Speaking of the ‘Treaty, not then signed, with Austria, M. de Bismark 
vemarked that if the Treaty was based on real mutual interests, it would be 
solid, if otherwise it could have no durability, 

Prussia, lie said, had not sufficient confidence in the foresight or prudence 
of Austrian statesmen to enter into engagements which should bind her in all 
auch contingencies as were comprised in a simple offensive and defensive 
allianee. 

M. de Bismark had previously read to me a letter he had received from 
enme one at Berlin, without telling me the writer’s name, which, with reference 
to the proposed ‘Treaty, said that Prussia would reserve the right of with- 
holding a declaration of war against Russia, even though Austria should take 
that step. 

L remarked to M. de Bismark that whenever the Treaty was concluded, 
it would, at any rate, allow a concerted communication to be made to the 
Diet. To this M. de Bismark gave a very hesitating kind of assent, and my 
observation led him to enter ona lengthy detail of Prnssia’s complaints against 
the constitution of the Dict, and the superior influence exercised therein by 
Austria. 

He particularly inveighed against the order of proceedings (Geschafts- 
ordrung), said how unfair it was that no notice should be given to members 
before a sitting, of what was to be the current business of the day; or, what 
was worse, that the President might acquaint friends and supporters, with- 
holding any communication from opponents, who were thus taken by surprise, 
and obliged lo disenss matters upon which they were quite unprepared. 

The President. had also the faculty of putting a stop to proceedings on 
any question under deliberation at any stage before the final vote, and not only 
that, but of preventing the matter being again taken up. 

The President had the entire official patronage of clerkships, &e., * and 
so much,” said M. de Bismark, “do these gentlemen look on themselves as 
Austrians, that | give you my word, I, asa Prussian, am looked on with an 
eye of intolerable suspicion, whenever I show my face in the offices.” 

M. de Bismark told me without reserve, that in view of these and other 
circumstances, too tedious to explain, Prussia would as much as possible slight 
and ignore the Diet, until its constitution was essentially altered.  “ They 
would not,” he said “subject themselves continually to have unpalatable 
measures thrust down their throats by Austrian majorities.” 

Prussia had 17,000,000, Austria but 12,000,000 of German population, &e, 

L asked, ina pause of M. de Bismark’s conversation, how he would have 
this Assembly reformed ? Would an alternation in the Presidency suffice ? 

M. de Bismark replied at once, that this would not be enough. There 
must be such a change as would put these two States on a fooling of equality, 

observed that it would be a matter of difficulty to induce Austria to 
abdicate the position she held traditionally ; but what I most desired to see 
was, that Prussia should adopt such a course of policy as tended to rally the 
majority to her. Tt was, however, I said, tolerably clear, that as long as 
Prussia was herself only semi-constitutional, and the majority of the little 
States, striving to govern as absolutely as possible, this result was hardly to be 
attained: for, whatever might be the influence on public feeling of a liberal 
policy on the part of Prussia, constituted as the small Governments now were, 


125 


such a policy would only drive them all the more infalliably into the arms of 
Austria. | i 

I by no means concealed from M. de Bismark my opinion of the unpopu- 
larity, and consequent insecurity, of nearly all the Governments of the minor 
German States, nor did this opinion meet with any marked expression of dissent 
from his Excellency. 

That his own Government did not, to Ins thinking, enjoy any high share 
of popular favour, he was ab little pains to conceal; but as M. de Bismark’s 
personal and party principles would tend to the substitution of a system even 
less liberal than that which now subsists, it is to be apprehended that if his 
party were in a position ta put their theories in practice, matters could hardly 
be improved in that respect. ) Send 

M. de Bismark complained much of what he called want of principle on 
the part of M. de Mantenffel, and when [ asked him in what respect, he said 
that he had no fixed objects, that he tided over diffienlties, took his chance of 
success by temporising, and earl} took a decision except in the last extremity. 

I said that whoever guided the rems of her Government, I thought it 
greatly to be regretted that Prussia had not taken a more decided line of 
policy against Russia; that such a decision would, in my judgment, have 
rallied to her the sympathies, if not of the Governments, still of a vast majority 
of the German people. 

This opinion did not meet with M. de Bismark’s assent, Germany, he 
thought, wanted peace, and would reap greater benefit from that policy than 
from any other; nor did he appear to attach much importance to a hint which 
I threw out, of internal discontents becoming troublesome. 

IT remarked that if, as it seemed, the actual crisis of affairs presented only 
a choice of evils. War with Russia, under the auspices now held out, pre- 
sented itself to my mind with far fewer appearances of danger, than were to 
he anticipated, either if hostilities were greatly prolonged, or in the less 
probable contingency of Russia coming out of them snecessfully. 

The least evil to be inenrred under a lengthened duration of war would 
be the heavy charges of a wrolonged armed neutrality, to say nothing of the 
discontents of which his Excellency made so light, whereas 1 saw no other 
prospect to Germany, from the possible suecess of Russia, than subserviency 
(to use the mildest term) in their relations with Russia which must ensue. If, 
on the other hand (as could not for a moment be doubted), an achive co-ope- 
ration of the Four Powers speedily anc effectually curbed the ambition of the 
Czar, Europe might in all likelihood repose in tranquillity for another long 
series of years. ji sis 

The position held by M. de Bismark here, as well asm his own conntry, 
where he is almost always called for by the King to give personal advice on 
every emergency, render his opinions worth reporting to your Lordship. 
must even venture to call further attention to his Excellency’s opinions respecting 
organic changes inthe constitution of the Diet, and beg leave to enter into 
some general considerations on the political condition of the German body 
politic, but will reserve what 1 think it my duty to say on these heads to a 
subsequent despatch. | 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) A. MALET.

No, 188. 


The Karl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 
(No, 220.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, May 2, 1804. 

[ HAVE received your Excellency’s despatch No. 171 of the 15th of 

pril, on the subject of the excesses committed by the Turkish Irregulars, and 
I have the satisfaction of conveying to your Excellency the cordial approbation 
of Her Majesty’s Government for the promptitude and decision with which 
your Excellency acted in this matter, and of the memorandum you presented 
to the Porte, in which the atrocitics of the irregular troops are indignantly 
denounced. 

Her Majesty's Government have learnt with satisfaction that your Ex- 
cellency’s remonstrances and your advice were received in a becoming spirit 
by the Sultan and his Ministers ; but you must know too well, from your own 
experience, how little trustworthy are promises of bold and decided action on 
the part of the Porte, not to feel the necessity of vigorously following up the 
steps you have already taken ; and Her Majesty’s Government rely upon your 
Excellency’s vigilance and firmness for putting a stop to crimes that have now 
become systematic, and which, while they deeply injure the Sultan's interest, 
and promote the objects of Russia, must end by disgusting the allies and 
rendering it impossible for them to support a cause sullied by such atrocities.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfeld.

My Lord, Foreign Office, May 2, 1854. 


1 HAVE received and laid before the Queen your Lordship’s despatch No. 
954, of the 26th instant, inclosing the copy of a communication whieh you had 
-oceived from Baron Manteuffel, announcing that His Majesty the King of 
Prussia had been pleased to accept the resignation of the Chovalier Bunsen, 
and had at jointed Count Bernstorif, at present Minister at Naples, to be his 
Prussian Majesty's Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary at the 
Court of Her Macey 
Even if Her Majesty’s Government possessed accurate information 
respecting the causes that have induced the Chevalier Bunsen to resign, they 
would not think it decorous to offer any opinion upon & juestion that has 
arisen between the King of Prussia and his Minister, and of vekiich his Majesty 
# 


129 


and the Prussian Government are alone competent to judge; but Her Majesty's 
Government cannot refrain from an expression of sincere regret that at this 
most critical juncture of the affairs of Europe, the Chevalier Bunsen should be 
withdrawn from a Mission the important duties of which he has fulfilled to the 
entire satisfaction of Her Majesty's Government, and particularly as regards 
the zeal with which he has always iaboured to identify the policy, and to 
strengthen the friendly relations between England and Prussia. 

The retirement of the Chevalier Bunsen at this moment, and the know- 
ledge that he has incurred the displeasure of his Royal Master, must lead to the 
belief. that the relations between the two Governments have undergone a 
change, and a painful impression will accordingly be produced in this country. 

Your Lordship will communicate this despatch to Baron Manteuffel, and 
you will at the same time assure his Excellency that Count Bernstorff will be 
received by Her Majesty's Government with the consideration due to the 
Minister selected by the King of Prussia to represent His Majesty at the Court 
of our Sovereign. 


Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 143. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(No, 224.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, May 5, 1854. 


1 HAVE to state to your Excellency, in reply to your despatch No. 161 
of the 6th ultimo, that the circular despatch of the 10th of March, to which 
you allude, was specially directed against a practice which was accidentally 

rought under my notice, of formal certificates of permission to enlist in foreign 
service, being granted by one at least of Her Majesty’s Ministers abroad, to 
British subjects applying for the same. But such formal permission can onl 
be given by the Crown, and therefore persons seeking to obtain forma 
permission, can only do so by applying to the Crown through the usual 
channel, 

In some forcign services I have reason to know the applicant for employ- 
ment must show that he hasobtained the formal permission of his Government; 
but where that condition does not apply, I apprehend that Her Majesty’s 
Ministers abroad cannot interfere to prevent a British subject from accepting a 
commission, at his own wish, from a foreign Sovereign. Her Majesty’s 
Ministers, indeed, cannot formally permit a British subject to accept a com- 
mission; but 1am not aware that they have any authority to proceed against a 
British subject in a foreign country for doing so; nor is it any part of their 
duty to interfere in the matter, 

& 


Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

The Earl of Westmorlani to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 8.) 


(No. 169.) 
My Lord, Vienna, May 4, 1854. 

COUNT BUOL has informed me that the late Hospodar of Wallachia 
had waited upon him for the purpose of calling wpon the Austrian Government, 
now that the Russian’ troops had evacuated the Lesser Wallachia, to occupy 
that district with detachments from the Austrian army, and he stated that he 
made this application in a sentiment of loyalty to his Sovereign the Sultan, and 
of anxiety for the protection of the inhabitants of the district who might suffer 
from the violence of both belligerents, should the war be carried on in their 
province. , ; 

Yount Buol replied that this proposal was one to which he could give no 
attention whatever; that the Austrian Government would certainly not place 
any part of their forces in a position which would in fact be one of hostility to 
both parties; he therefore declined altogether to enter upon the subject, 
although if both parties applied to his Government to give any protection by 
the occupation of any portion of territory, the question would assume a different 
shape, but that such a state of things appeared so entirely improbable, that he 
could not look upon it as worthy of any consideration. 

I have, &e 


(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

My Lord, Constantinople, April 20, 1854. 

NOTHING of sufficient consequence to make it the object of a special 
report has come to my dle from the theatre of war, since I had last the 
honour of addressing your Lordship. 

it does not appear that the Russians are advancing ; but statements from 
Bucharest allege that Silistria will soon be attacked, and that Marshal Paske- 
witch is expected in the Principalities, Omer Pasha is understood to be still 
engaged in assembling his troops round Shumla, 


eT 0 


152 


The advices from Asia continue to be anything but satisfactory. What- 
ever improvements have been effected by General Guyon and the other Euro- 
pean officers, whatever readiness to follow their counsels may have been shown 
by Zarif Pasha, the wants of the army are unsupplied, and its ranks are so much 
thinned, through disease and desertion, that instead of amounting te 20,000 
men, it is reported not to exeecd the number of 12,000. Nothing has been 
spared to impress upon the Turkish Ministers the importance of applying a 
remedy to these evils without delay, But, unfortunately, the want of money 
has come in aid of the difficulties ‘eeasioned by a winter of unusual severity 
and protraction, and most, if not all, remains to be done in the essential points 
of providing supplies, and augmenting the numerical force.

Inclosure 1 in No. 149. 


Instructions of the Porte to Fuad Effendi. 

(Translation) April 18, 1854, 

| HAVE received your despatches dated the 4th of Rejeb, reporting the 
lawless proceedings of sonic of the Bashi-Bozouks and volunteers employed in 
that neighbourhood against some Christian villages, and the measures taken 
thereupon by your Excellency, and stating that the reports of these occurrences 
were somewhat exaggerated ; that those lawless acts had arisen out of certain 
local occurrences, and that Haraddin Bey, who had been employed for their 
repression, ad acted with great energy and uprizhtness. On the other hand, 
different reports have come to us on this subject, namely, that all sorts of atro- 
vities had been committed in the district of Paramithia by the Albanians 
serving wider Suleyman Aga, by order of the said Haraddin Bey, and that 
that they had even burnt down forty-six flourishing villages, put the inhabitants 
to the sword, and carried off some of them to the mountains; that they had 
plundred all their property ; that Suleyman Aga and the Albanians in Para- 
mithia were the chief actors in these scenes ; that the share alone of Suleyman 
Aga and his men consisted of 3,850 sheep, 400 head of other cattle, and a 
good many horses ; that a certain Noureddin Aga was also concerned in. the 
plunder ; that the other Albanians of Paramithia took for their share of the 
spoils the silver ornaments of the women and their household roods; and that 
Haraddin Bey had not conducted himself as well as he might have done, 

All manner of crimes have been committed by these Bashi-Bozouks and 
volunteers both in Europe and in Asia, and the Porte eaa ne longer suffer the 


133 


subject to be neglected. New regniations have been therefore forwarded 
concerning the employment of these troops, and the punishment of any erimes 
committed by them, and peremptory orders thereon have been sent in ever 
direction. A copy of these reg ations is enclosed herewith, and your Excel- 
leney will cause them to be publicly promulgated in your province, and to act 
+ conformity with their tenor. 

Tt is of the greatest importance that, while this general measure is carried 
into operation, the measures also bearing reference to the occurrences in cywes- 
tion should be also carried into full execution. ‘These Albanians were guilt 
of such crimes after having contracted a written engagement with your feat: 
lency concerning their peaceable demeanour ; they were, Moreover, pully of 
murder and robbery, and of the atrocious crime of carrying away the children 
of the Christians, and ‘tis evident that they must be. treated with a greater 
degree of severity. 

The Sublime Porte has therefore decided that the following measures shall 
be adopted. 

Your Excellency will, in the first place, make formal proclamation of His 
Majesty the Sultan’s displeasure at these shocking occurrences, and of the 
punishment that aw aits the offenders. 

The accused parties, espectally those whose names have been given in, are 
to be immediately arrested, and put upon their trial and punished. In doubt- 
ful cases the parties are to be sent to the capital by steam. 

If the children separated from their parents should have not been already 
given up, they are to be found and restored, 

All plundered property and eattle in the possession of the plunderers, oF 
which may haye been sold to other parties, is to be restored to the owners. 
guitable indemmity is to be paid by the suspected parties for the property not 
forthcoming. 

It is of importance’ that these measures should be fully carried out, and 
we expect that yout Excellency will take suitable steps likewise for preventing 
the recurrence of such atrocities, as well as for giving due course tothe general 
regulations. Although it may have resulted from the inquiries entered into 
that there existed a certain degree of provocation on the spot for the oceur- 
rences in question, this 1s no reason for delaying the punishment of the guilty; 
but as your Excellency also reports that some Christian subjects were associated 
with the Albanians in the attack (on the villages), these Christians and their 
associates, if the statement be correct, must likewise be punished, 

As the delay which has necessarily arisen in the punishment of the guilty 
parties may be ascribed by lawless men to weakness, it is of the utmost impor- 
tance that the punishment in question should be carried out with the greatest 

igour. 
fe Although it has been proved that the Greek brigands have inflicted the 
ereatest evils on the frontier territory, even against their own co-religionists, 

urning more particularly the Turkish villages, and putting men, women and 
children to death with great ernelty and all manner of ignominy, the Sultan's 
subjects will not be guilty of the actions committed by those vile robbers, but 
conduct themselves like men, ‘They must in the present conflict shew their 
patriotizm by doing their best to beat the enemy. 

Your Excellency is instructed to set forth these matters in language intel- 
ligible to all classes. 

he present instructions haye been approved by the Council, and sanc- 
tioned by the Royal Will. Your Excellency will therefore attend to the due 
performance of them.

Sir, Varna, April 5, 1854. 

[had the honour to address your Excellency yesterday by a messenger 
from the Pasha, who went by land to Baljik. 

A French steamer arrived here yesterday morning, bringing the General 
of Division Bosquet, and some officers of the staff. 

The General goes this morning by land to Baljik, to communicate with 
Admiral Hamelin, General Bosquet mentioned to me esterday that he 
purposes going to Shumla, to consult with his Highness Oiner Pasha, as to 
10,000 or 12,000 of the French troops coming to Varna. The General did 
not appear to consider Gallipoli a desirable position, and said that water was 
even scarce there. He thought that the presence of European troops here 
would give a moral as well as material strength to the Turkish army and 
inhabitants, whieh no doubt it would. 

1 understand from Shumla, that his Highness Omer Pasha, will probably 
withdraw the Egyptians, who arrived here as a reinforcement, 25 he considers 
the former garrison sufficient, joined to the assistance which Varna may 
receive from the sea. 

We have no important news from the interior, The inhabitants of 
Bazardji and the surrounding villages continue to arrive from time to 
time. 

By a letter dated 12th from Shumla, U find that the Russians had not 
Se further than Babadagh, but some Cossacks had been seen at 
Harla. 

General Bosquet seems to be of opimion that the designs of the Russian 
General have been defeated by the managuyre of his Highness Omer Pasha, in 
withdrawing his troops, and concentrating at Shumla. He thinks that the 
Russians desired todraw the Turksinto the Dobrudgcha, when they would have 
erossed in force near Rustchuk and Silistria, and marched on Shumla or the 


Balkan. I have, &e.

Sir, Varna, April 15, 1854, 
A GENOESE merchant-vessel, which arrived here yesterday from 
Odessa, has reported as follows — 

The master states that he left Odessa on the 12th instant. That on the 
1ith an English steamer-of-war came into that port, and sent a boat on shore. 
That the authorities demanded for what purpose they had come, when it was 
replied that the steamer had come for the British Consul, when the authorities 
answered that the Consul had left four days before. he master says that the 
boat then returned to the steamer; ie that while returning, an officer on 

2 


135 


horseback galloped up to the battery, and found fault with the officers of the 
port for not having taken the boat, as they must have known it was from af 
enemy’s vessel. Several shot were then fired at the boat and steamer without 
effect. 

The master adds, that the firing of these guns caused half the batteries to 
fall, as the embrasures were compused of sand-bags. 

On the 13th instant, the master states he saw three frigates about twenty- 
fve miles to the southward of Odessa, and making towards Odessa with a 
strong contrary wind. The master supposed they were English or French. 
They showed no colours. 

The Genoese master states that the utmost panic prevails at Odessa. All 
the grain in the town is said to be removing into the interior, Some Genoese 
merchants, having remonstrated against the sudden prohibition to export grain, 
and having imprudently said on the Exchange that the English and Freneh, or 
Omer Pasha, would soon reseind the prohibition, they were ordered out of the 
town in twenty-four hours. 

The master adds, that there are 25,000 troops at Odessa, but only twenty- 
five guns in the batteries, and that the Russians said that if they had eight or 
ten days time, they would be better fortified ; but that if the flects attacked 
them at present, they would be very ill-prepared to resist them. 

he master conversed with some Polish officers. They said there were 
15,000 Poles (of the 25,000 troops) i Odessa, who were in a great state of 
excitement, and very ill-disposed to the Russians, and that there would bea 
revolt the moment the fleets ap seared and fired a shot, The first part of all 
this statement must relate to the © Fury ;' by its correctness OF otherwise 
‘our Excellency will be enabled to judge of the truth of what follows. 
itive thought it my duty to forward an express to your Excellency with this 
information. I have, &c.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received May 8.) 
(No. 257.) 
My Lord, Berlin, May 5, 1854. 


IN pursuance of the instructions contained in your Lordship’s despatch, 
No. 111, upon the subject of Ghevalier Bunsen’s resignation, and the appaint- 
ment of Count Bernstorif to the post of Enyoy in London, I this day read that 
despateh to Baron Manteuffel, and in order that the feelings therein expressed 
might be known to the King and to other persons, T left it with his Excellency, 
and trust thatin go doing I shall have acted according to your Lordship's wishes. 

The only passage of the despateh on which Baron Manteuffel made 4 
remark, 18 that alluding to Chevalier Bunsen having ineurred the King’s 
displeasure. He said that this might have been so momentarily, but that it 
was no longer the case, and that Chevalier Bunsen had expressed himself most 
rhankful for the manner in which his wishes had been met, 

| replied that it was not to be expected that Chevalier Bunsen would do 

otherwise than make known in proper terms his sense of the arrangement 
made by the King’s orders on his retiring from active service; but 1 begged 
leave to observe to him, that the effeet of hig removal from his post must be 
considered as indicating a change in the policy of Prussia, for the King would 
not, under any other circumstances, have been disposed to withdraw from 
office a Minister whose only fault was an excess of zeal in endeavouring to 
eatablish the most cordial relations with England; and that I hoped in the 
interests of Prussia that His Majesty would not have cause to regret the 
change. ; 
But, I said, if proof were wanting of the King’s altered feelings, I need 
only refer to the rumour which was general in Berlin, that His Majesty was 
ahout to dismiss General Bonin from the post of Minister of War, and | asked 
-f this were true. Baron Manteuflel replied that it was so. Well, I rejoined, 
this then shows that any Minister who chooses to hold independent language, 
i accordance with the policy indicated by late public acts—the Vienna 
Protocol and the Convention with Austria,—was sure to incur the Royal 
displeasure, and it proved beyond a doubt that the King was not disposed to 
carry out the stipulations: of these solemn acts, and that I thought we must be 
prepared for further and more important changes in the Government, that 
his Excellency would stand nearly alone in his opinions, that General Bonin 
had been one of his staunchest supporters, and that 1 thought the party who 
now ruled would not rest until all: persons were removed who happen to stand 
in the way of the Russian policy that was being pursued. 

Baron Mantenflel scarcely made any reply to these remarks. He said 
that the King would never go with Russias and that the person whom the 
King intended to place at the War Department was of the same political 
opinions as General Bonin. 

"Ho did not name the fature Minister of War, but is said to be General 
Waldersee. 


I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received May 8.) 

(No, 288.) 
My Lord, Berlin, May 5, 1864, 

BARON MANTEUFFEL has mentioned to me that Baron Budberg 
communicated to him yesterday a despatch from Count Nesselrode, in answer 
to one which had been sent from here, containing the request of the King of 
Prussia, in his desire to act as mediator between the belligerent Powers, that 
the Emperor would state in writing the concessions which His Imperial Majesty 
was disposed to make, and which would give a chance of the negotiations for 


144 


peace being continued, for up to the present moment the Russian proposals 
were so vague that the Western Powers could not entertain them. 

His Excellency said that the Emperor declined to name any precise con- 
ditions on which he was ready to negotiate, and had written in a tone which 
had disappointed the King, 

T observed to his Excellency that 1 hoped the refusal of the Emperor of 
Russia to bring forward any reasonable proposition for peace would open His 
Majesty’s eyes as to the inutility of attempting to negotiate without having @ 
basis to work upon, and to the necessity of altering his vacillating policy, and 
preparing to act in concert with the Western Powers. The Minister: President 
replied that he could assure me that His Majesty was far from approving the 
proceedings of Russia, and that it would be impossible for him to take part 
with her : but at the same time His Majesty could not bring himself to the 
‘dea that the war might not yet be averted from his own frontiers. 

To this I replied, that but for the policy lately pursued by Prussia | 
believed that war would have been altogether avoided, for if the Four Powers 
had but declared that they were resolved to stand together in opposition to the 
encroachments of Russia in the East, and ready to take up arms for that pur- 
pose, if necessary, Russia would have hesitated if she saw Enrope arrayed 
against her; that moreover I felt satisfied that the policy of Prussia would com- 
pletely fail, and that che would be most unwillingly dragged into the war, 
and that nobody would thank her for her tardy decision ; whereas a frank and 
straightforward policy would possibly have ensured the blessings of peace, 
and serve at all events to discourage the Pies oa pretensoins of Russia.

(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 1.) 


(No. G14. Most Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 7, 1854. 

| OBSERVE that, within the last few days, there is considerable ansiety 
+n the minds of the Emperor and of his Ministers, lost Russia should obtain 
some brilliant advantage over the ‘Turks wpon the Danube, and, having thus 
vindicated the honour of her arms, should, in seeming deference to the wishes 
of Austria and Prussia, retire behind the Pruth, and offer to enter into diplo- 
matic conferences for the settlement of the Turkish question. It appears that 
ML. de Serre, who is acting momentarily as French Chargé d’Affaires at Vienna, 
has called the attention of his Government to the possibility of this course being 
taken by Russia —a course by which she would probably suceeed in regaining 
her influence over the Lwo great German Powers and their smaller satellites, 
and turn them from their unwilling and imperfect adhesion to the poliey of 
Great Britain and France. ‘To obtain such a result would be worth some sacri- 
fiee to Russin; and both the Emperor and M. Drouyn de Lhuys think that it 
may be the present plan of the Russians, after striking a blow on the Danube, 
to withdraw within the Bessarabian frontier, and, concentrating all their fore 
towards the cast, make the Asiatic provinces of Turkey their real point of 
attack, It could hardly be doubted that Germany, relieved from the verils of 
war at her very doors, would be inclined to look with complacency at this etal 
of things, nor would there be wanting those who went further, and would 
regard a war undertaken by Russia in Asia as a holy warfare of the Cross 
against the Crescent. 

‘Th was useless attempting to conceal from oneself,” said the Emperor 
(and M. Dronyn de Lhuys holds the same language), “that, under such Cire 
‘cumstances, the position of England and France becomes one of extreme difenlty. 
Alone, they cannot hope to bring Russia, with Austria and Prussia as her 
fiends, even if the latter remain inactive, lo such terms as would justify them 
in making peace, ‘Their object then should be to seck alliances elsewhere, and 
to endeavour to make such a coalition with and among the other States of 

ae 


a 


i 


146 


Europe, as would in some degree counterbalance the danger that must arise 
from the formidable union of Russia and Germany. His Majesty had reason 
to think that Sweden, Sardinia, and perhaps Spain, would not be unwilling to 
join such an alliance, under certain conditions ; and, if this were so, it was, 
in his opinion, well worth a pecuniary sacrifice to obtain, when possible, the 
material assistance of any of these Governments.” 

His Majesty said further, that he wished that Her Majesty’s Government 
would take this view of the question into their most serious consideration. His 
own opinion was, that if Russia came out of this struggle with her wings in= 
clipped, she became mistress of the destinies of Europe. He considered that 
there was no sacrilice too great fo make, in order to preserve the world from 
so great a calamity.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No, 162.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, May 9, 1854. 

GOUNT COLLOREDO yesterday read to me a despatch from Count 
Buol, stating that Prince Stirbey had strongly urged upon him that Wallachia 
should be occupied by Austrian troops. The Principality, Prince Stirbey said, 
having been devastated by the Russians, was now about to be totally ruined by 
the Turks, and that the Wallachians would be deeply grateful for the protection 
ofan Austrian force. 

Count Buol replied, that Austria had complained of the unjust proceedings 
of Russia. and would certainly not follow the example of that Power. 

Austria, moreover, had no pretext for entering the territory of her ally, 
and were she to do so uninvited, she would lay herself open to just SUSPICLON ; 
but Count Buol added, if the temporary occupation of Wallachia by Austrian 
troops would be of any service to the Sultan, and that a request to that eflect 
were directly made. by the Porte, it would be favourably entertained by the 
Austrian Government, 

I thanked Count Colloredo for this communication, and requested him to 
assure Count Buol that the determination manifested on this and other occasions 
by Austria, not to enter upon any portion of the Turkish territory without the 
consent of the Porte, was most satisfactory to Her Rial Government.

hound to consult with the Western Powers as to the means of obtaining this object 
connexion with further measures for attaching the existence and independence 
of the Turkish Empire, to the general equilibrium of Europe. He proceeded 
to point out that the relations of Austrin towards her allies being of such a 
character, the eventual possibility of her armics being called into action to 
secure the objects for which they strove in common, Wis necessarily contem- 
plated, and although he hoped that the employment of her troops might not be 
required, yet, should such be the case, she had a large army collected, or 
collecting on her frontiers towards: Russia, extending from Gallicia and the 
Bukowina through Transylvania and Hungary, and occupying a most favour- 
able position from whieh to vet at a future period. He said it would not be 
thought advantageous under any case to call upon the Austrian armies to move, 
until the Western Powers could communicate the precise military position which 
they occupied, together with their plan of operations. When the Anglo-Frene 
force had moved towards the Danube, then would be the moment for Austria to 
concert operations with them, and they would then be justified hy the stipula- 
tions of the Protocols, to call upon her to do so. Measures might then be 
taken for the defence of the Balkan, or any other plan of operations which 
should appear advisable, might be adopted in common. But im the case that 
the Russian armies did not advance against the Anglo-French forees, and 
remained in the Principalities, Austria would be the first to desire active opera- 
tious, as she was the most interested in obtaining the evacuation of the Princi- 
palities. Count Buol assured me that the Western Powers might rely with the 
most perfect confidence, if her action was required, on the vigorous cooperation 
of Austria at. the proper time, but he deprecated any appeal to her to destroy 
the fine military position which her armies at present oceupied, by pro MOST Ng 
that any part of her military force should move to secondary or faatied y081= 
tions, or move at all before the armies of England and France were actually in 
the field, when they might rely upon their supporting their operations. Count 
Buol concluded by saying that although he foresaw little prospect of obtaiming 
by negotiation the great objects for which the allied Governments were acting 
together, yet he could not entirely discard all hope of it, and he must therefore 
retain that entire liberty of action for his Government, which he considers 
necessary, to enable him to take advantage of any proposal which appeared 
likely to lead to this result, but in every case it must be of a nature to embrace 
all the objects for the attainment of which his Government is pledged by the 
Protocols and declarations to which they have been a party,

My Lord, Berlin, May 18, 1854. 


BARON MAN'TEUFFEL has been to the country for a few days, and 
came back yesterday. Before his departure | had an interview with his 
Excelleney, when he returned to me your Lordship's despatch No. LIL, upon 
the subject of Chevalier Bunsen’s resignation, which 1 had left with him for 
communication to the King. L inquired whether His Majesty had made any 
observations on it, (0 whieh he said that Tis Majesty had declared that his 
feclings towards England were unchanged, and that might be assured that 
Prussia would follow up the policy which she had laid down, and which she 
had been pursuing for the last dix months, 

To this 1 replied, that if this was His Majesty's intention, 1 must naturally 
ask why two Ministers, Chevalier Bunsen and General Bonin, were removed 
from their respective offices because they were both devoted to carrying out a

wers, and had both incurred the Royal 
displeasure for that reason, and I could not but tell him, that until the King 
ave some proof of 8 rmpathy with us, T could not conscientiously inform my 
Government that | elieved Prussia to be following out a policy in harmony 
with her late professions and acts, for that SNS appeared to have a 
Russian tendency. 1 said also that in all directions I veard that Chevalier 
Bunsen and General Bonin had been sacrificed to please the Emperor of 
Russia, and that the removal of these Ministers had been insisted on as a set- 
off ta the Austro-Prussian Treaty, and. had been urged on the King by the 
Court party, whieh seemed to have established the most complete power over 
His Majesty. Baron Manteuffel replied that no communicalon of this nature 
had passed through him, or had come from the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. 

This, | said, might be; but would his Excellency answer for communi- 
cations of this nature not having reached the King through the numerous 
channels by which the Russian Legation was able to approach His Majesty ? 
The visit ot Duke George of Mecklenbureh, | observed, had no other object 
than to obtain some species of satisfaction for the Emperor Nicholas for the 
steps Which had been taken in opposition to his views; and though he was 
unable to prevent the ratification of the Austro-Prussian Treaty, the effects of 
his labours were nevertheless evident in the removal of Chevalier Bunsen and 
General Bonin, and the departure of the Prince of Prussia. 

Here ended our conversation on Monday, and I have this evening had a 
further interview with his Excellency, and resumed the subject. I told lim 
that during his absence M. de Bismark, the Prussian Minister at Frankfort, 
had been holding the most unmistakeable language here, and had stated that 
Prussia would never, under any circumstances, take up arms against Russia. 
Such language, | said, proved either that he spoke at random, or that the 
Treaty hich Prussia and Austria had just concluded, was to be a dead letter. 
Baron Manteulfel seemed greatly surprised that M. de Bismark should haye 
thus spoken, and said that he knew not whenee he could have drawn such 
opinions, that they were groundless, for this day the King had told him, when 
conversing on the position of Russia, that she must not count upon Prussia’s 
indifference, as the moment might not he far off when she might be called on 
to act. 
I replied, that such expressions on the part of the King were no doubt 
satisfactory ; but, I said, it was strange that M. de Bismark should talk in this 
wild way: he ought to be directed to disown his words, and speak in another 
tone. His predilections, | added, were with Russia, and these, perhaps, gave 
an impulse to his conversation, and was, perhaps, inspired hy the language 
and wishes of the Court Party, with which he might be seeking to ingratiate 
himself, 

Baron Manteulfel then said that M, de Bismark was to return to his post 
in a couple of days, and would then have to support the Austro-Prussian 
Treaty before the Diet, where he trusted it would be adopted without serious 
Opposition.

Dolma was to be the Minister President, and M. de Bismark, Minister for 
Foreien Affairs, have fallen to the ground, and to judge from Baron Man- 
tenifel’s manner and tone to me, he seems secure of his office for some time
