Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 14.) 

(No. 272.) 
My Lord, Berlin, May 12, 1864. 

INTELLIGENCE having reached me that M. d’Alvensleben was on the 
point of setting out for Vienna on a special mission, | have asked Baron Man- 
teuifel if it were true that he was to endeavour to impede the execution of the 
Austro-Prussian Treaty. His Excellency replied, that he was sent there to give 
explanations on the subject of this Treaty, not, however, for the purpose of rais- 
ing difficulties on the subject, but rather to prevent them, and that the Kin had 
decided on this mission in order that there might be less necessity for reference 
to Berlin in the event of opposition heing raised by the German Powers to its 
adoption by the Diet. His Excellency said further that he had already answers 
from Hanover and Cassel respecting the communication and that they were 
favourable ; and that he expected that the question would be laid before the 
Dict at Frankfort in about a fortnight. 

1 then inquired if there was any truth in a report which had reached me, 
that there was to be a Conference of the Representatives of several of the 
German Powers at Bamberg, to concert measures of opposition to it; to which 


156 


Baron Manteuffel answered, that this report had likewise reached him, and that 
he thought the meeting not impossible; but again his Excellency declared, that 
he was without apprehension as to the result, and felt convinced, on the contrary, 
that the propositions would be adopted,

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 

(No. 125.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, May 16, 1854, 

HER Majesty's Government approve the language held by you in your 
conversation with Baron Manteuffel, as reported in your Lordship’s BOS 
No. 271 of the 12th instant, and I have to instruct you to inform Baron 
Mantuuflel that you have corréetly represented the opinions of Her Majesty's 
Government as well with reference to the dismissal of Chevalier Bunsen ail 
General Bonin as with respect to the conduct observed towards His Royal 
Highness the Prinee of Prussia. 

" Kor many months past Baron Manteuffel has been made aware, by the 
despatches that have been communicated to him, of the cordial and. sincere 
desire of Her Majesty's Government that the independence of Prussia, and the 
high position she is entitled to hold in Germany, should be nobly sustained 
throughout a crisis which may determine the fiture destinies of Europe; and 
it has on several occasions heen my agreeable duty to congratulate Baron 
Manteuffel, in the name of Her Majesty's Government, wpon the course of 
policy that Prussia was pursuing. His Excellency will therefore not be 
surprised to learn the deep disappoiutment of Her Majesty's Government at 
finding their hopes and expectations frustrated by the ascendeney of a party 
which now conduets the political affairs of Prussia in a manner which, as Her 
Majesty’s Government venture to think, ean neither promote the well under- 
atoal interests of that kingdom, nor of Germany, nor consequently those of 
Kurope. 


187 


On this, as on every other occasion, Her Majesty's Government disclaim 
all pretension to interfere in the internal concerns of Prussia, but having to 
their great satisfaction been intimately associated with Prussia in the important 
transactions at Vienna, having had good reason to think that the policy of the 
two countries was identical, and having now too much reason to believe that ib is 
divergent, Her Majesty’s Government feel entitled to express their opinion that 
the course now suddenly adopted by Prussia must extend and protract the war, 
for she gives to the unjust and aggressive policy of Russia more than an 
indirect support, and proves to the world that the influence which that Power 
claims to exercise over Germany is, in Prussia at least, a sad reality. 

Your Lordship will read this despatch to Baron Manteuffel,

This consideration has operated much in inducing his Highness to concen-

Shumla would he exposed to the greatest danger.

to fortify Shumla, and it is alone due to the field-works which have been thrown 
ap under the direction of Omer Pasha since its commencement that Shumla 
ean be Weld at all against a large army; and, ag it is, a force of 15,000 men 18

cogil judges oF passing events and the strength of places as those who know 
them and are upon the spot, to issue such an order to his Highness, which, if 
carried into exeeution, and if the movement were known to the Russians, 
would, in all probability, cause an attack upon Shumia ; whieh, if successful, as 
+ could have every chance of being, would cause the destruction of the Turkish 
army, and incrense immensely the difficulties of the allied armies. 

Another consideration which, probably, has not had the full weight with 
the Porte which it deserves, is the fact, that such a movement as that con- 
templated by their order would require a re-arrangement of the magazines and 
etores which his Highness has collected in Bulgaria. 

Finally, if the Government dread an advance of the enemy upon Roumelia, 
oy if they dread a rising among the Christian population, they would probably, 


if his Hiehness had carried their order into effect, have done the very thing 


which would bring about sueh an event, for there is no danger to be appre- 
hended fyom the population, except in the ease of a sucecssful advance of the 
enemy. 

His Hichness feels the extreme difficulty in which this order of the Sublime 
Porte has placed him; but, nevertheless, has taken upon himself the responsi- 
bility of not exeeuting it, and he has no doubt that his determination will meet 
with the sanetion of the high military authorities of the allied armies, with 
whom he will have to aet. 

He informs me that General Bosquet of the French army, who arrived here 
on the 18th instant, and left yesterday for Gallipoli, vid Adrianople, entirely 
approved of his arrangements; and also, that he is confirmed in the opinion 
that there is no extensive movement to be apprehended on the part of the 
enemy on the Upper Danube, by the latest information he has received from 
Wallachia, which is to the effect that the Russians were concentrating their 
forees towards the Dobrudacha.

Inclosure 4 in No. 175, 
Substance of the Despatches receiwed from the Vault of Widdin. 


(Translation.) April 25, 1854. 

ON Monday the 17th, at about 9 a.m, six squadrons of regular 
Rnasian Cavalry, eight squadrons of Cossacks, and a battery of Artillery, were 
marched wpon Kalak at, ta a distance without cannon range, with the object of 
carrying our outposts. | 

We sent out a body of regular and irregular Cavalry, with eight guns, 
under the command of the Ferik Halim Pasha, and beat off the enemy, after 
an engagement of three hours, with considerable loss on his part. We pursued 
the Russians for three miles, and took a number of muskets, swords, lances 
anc other arms, with some horses. 

We had fifteen Irregulars killed, and thirty-three wounded.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received May 18.) 


(No, 211.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 5, L854, 

PRINCE NAPOLEON arrived here on Monday the Ist instant, and took 
up his residence in one of the two palaces on the Bosphorus, which His Majesty 
the Sultan had ordered to be prepared, respectively, for the Duke of Cambridge 
and His Imperial Highness. 

On Tuesday he received the diplomatic body in uniform; and on Wed- 
nesday he dined with the French Ambassador, where the Turkish and Foreign 
Ministers, Lord Raglan, and other distinguished individuals, were assembled to 
meet him. 

On the day following, an unusual incident took place. ‘The Sultan himself 
paid a visit in private to the French Prince, the Grand Vizier having preceded 
iis Majesty the day before. 

Prince Napoleon has since presented his compliments in person to the 
wrincipal Ministers of State. He proposed to extend the courtesy to Mehemet 
Ali, the Sultan’s brother-in-law, but the ex-Seraskier requested permission to 
wait himself on the Prince, and the consequence was & long secret interview 
hetween them at His Imperial Highmness’s residence.

Inclosure 6 in No. 175. 


Consul Brant to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Smyrna, April 28, 1854. 


| HAVE the honour to report to your Excellency that an Binnglish vessel 
called the “Sarah,” Captain Cole, which arrived a few days ago from ‘Trieste, 
at Alatyatta (near Cheame), there to load a cargo of fruit, was attacked a few 
hours after anchoring in that port by two piratical boats, containing about forty 
men, who robbed her of everything portable, a quantity of provisions, and even 
the clothes of the crew. ‘They were very eager in their search for money, and, 
being disappointed at not finding any on board, threatened the eaptain’s life, 
but, fortunately, did not maltreat him. . 

___ As the town of Alatyatta is at a considerable distance from the shore the 
pirates were able to get off with their booty before any assistance could be 
procured. ‘ 

Two vessels, one Hanoverian and the other English, have lately been fallen 
‘n with off Andros, abondoned by their crews, who are supposed to have been 
murdered, marks of blood having been discovered on their decks. 

It is to be feared that piracy will increase in the Archipelago in the 
absence of any ships of war to cheek its progress, 

The shipmasters now in this port are afraid to put to sea, and I, therefore, 
bee to submit to your Excellency’s consideration the necessity of a vessel being 
stationed here, if possible, for the protection of our trade, and to afford convoy 
to British vessels passing down the Archipelago. 

T have, &e. 


(Signed j h. D. BRANT.

Inclosure in No. | 76. 


Military Convention between Prussia ond Austria for the maintenance of the 
German Offensive and Defensive Alliance. 
(Translation.) 

IN order to give the necessary guarantee and foree to the Offensive and 
Defensive Alliance entered into hy the States of the Germanic Confederation for 
the duration of the Oriental erists, the two foremost great Powers of Grermany, 
Prussia and Austria, have reciprocally engaged themselves to the following 
measures. 

1, Austria binds herself, in case of need, to place as 4 second army, in 
addition to the 140,000 men already stationed in Hungary, 2s well as on the 
Danube and the Save, another 10,000 men, at periods to be determined upon 
with Prussia, Her troops mobilised in Galicia, Transylvania, and Moravia, and 
therenpon to he assembled in Galicia, either as a whole or in part, will continue 
in the closest communication. with the active forces to be stationed in Prussia. 

>. Prussia binds herself on the other hand to have, within thirty-six days, 
190,000 men concentrated, as Gireumstanees may require, with one-third in 
Fast Prussia, but with two-thirds near Posen ant Tireslaw, and, in case of need, 
and on a momentary agreement to he then taken with Austria, to increase this 
number of troops in three weeks after to 200,000 men. 

5 ‘Phe general regulations established in the Military Convention of the 
Cermanic Confederation are also binding on Prussia and Austria to their full 
extent, 

4. ‘The Prussian Mimstry of War, iia well as the Imperial Austrian Supreme 
Command of the Army, are hound reciprocally to make every communication 
whieh may guarantee the strict maintenance of the above-named active forces, 
Hoth as regards their number, their state of preparation, the periods at which 
they are to be supplied, as also of the particular pomts to which they are to be 
directed, 

5, Superior officers of both armies are to be accredited to their respective 
states from the commencement of Prussia’s mobilisation for a full and constant 
mutual concert of measures, and then, later, to their respective armics. 

G. Asa military rule for the allied armies the principle is laid down that 
the object of the mutual assistance is only the repulse of an attack, 


(Signed) OTTO THEODOR MANTEUFFEL, (L.8.) 
HENRY F. F. ¥. HESS. (L.8:.)

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received May 14.) 


(No. 278. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, May 16, 1854, 

COUNT ALVENSLEBEN has proceeded to Vienna, and is charged with 
an autograph letter from the King to the Emperor of Austria, and with a private 
letter also fram Baron Manteuffel to Count Buol; but he is not provided, as | 
am informed, with any official instructions. 

The mission would appear to be wrapped up in mystery; but I am never- 
theless assured in the most positive manner, that there is no wish on the part of 
this country to prevent the execution of the Austro-Prussian Treaty, as 18 
eoncrally reported, 

Information having, however, reached me from a private souree, that the 
King’s above-mentioned letter contained allusions which might bear a different 
sense, Lusked several questions of Baron Manteutfel on the subject, and learnt 


169 


that the King has been pressing on the Emperor of Austria the propricty of 
postponing for a while the summons to be addressed to the Emperor of Russia 
to evacuate the Principalities, and urging that the terms in which the summons 
to be addressed to His Imperial Majesty chould be drawn wp in a tone which 
would be as little offensive as possible to the Court of St. Petersburgh. I learnt 
also, that the King has ne on the Emperor of Austria the propriety of his 
being crowned King of Hungary, and the advantage that would perhaps result 
from his not following implicity the policy of centralisation recommended by 
Baron Bach, which his Prussian Majesty thinks impossible to be carried 


Thore are rumours of other and important matters beng contamed in this 
letter, but I have not been able to ascertain the truth of them. I may, however, 
report the most important one, which is, that the King: insinuates that the 
military preparations of France are on & seale to excite alarm, that the 
camp at St. Omer may be easily directed against Prussia, and the one at 
Marseilles against Italy, and that, consequently, it was necessary to be careful 
what steps were taken, as Germany might ‘find herself with war on both sules. 
The whole tone of this letter appears intended, notwithstanding the assurance to 
the contrary, to shake the decisions of the Emperor of Austria, to gain time, in 
the hope of preventing the intervention of Germany in the Eastern question 
until it will be too late this year to commence hostilities, and that when autumn 
approaches negotiations can be resumed with a better chance of leading to some 
arrangement. .

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received May V9.) 
(No, 281.) 
My Lord, Berlin, May 10, 1804. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL mentioned to me to-day that he has received 
a despatch from St. Petersburgh of the 11th instant, reporting that Count 
Nesselrode had completely recovered his equanimity and good spirits, that he 
saw 10 use in attempting negotiations for peace at the present moment, but 
that he felt confident that coming events would produce a desire with all partes 
to put an end to the state of warfare now existing. 

[ told Baron Manteutfel that this intelligence was further proof of the 
uselessness of supposing that Russia was, as many persons attempted to show, 
desirous of putting an end to the war; for no reasonable proposition, none that 
would be acceptable to the Western Powers, had ever been brought forward 
and that the far words to Baron Werthern were probably the result of the news 
which must have arrived, of the changes about to take place at Berlin. 
Further, t gaid, time was what Russia wanted, in order to complete her own 
military preparations, and she no doubt hoped that Prussia sont continue in 
her present mood, which was all she required or wished at this moment.

No. 184. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received May 20.) 


(No: 214. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 8, 1804. 

PRINCE NAPOLEON has now been here a week, and I understand 
that he means to prolong his visit beyond the period which he had originally 
named. He has been treated with much hospitality by the Sultan, and with 
the most respectful attention by His Majesty’s Ministers. The Sultan paid 
him the unusual, and, I believe, unprecedented compliment of a personal 
visit, A splendid banquet is to be eiven to him to-day at the Palace, and it is 
rumoured, that the Sultan will himself sit down to table, which he has never 
yet done on similar oceasions, ‘The Prince, on his side, has called in person 
on the leading Ministers, and he visits the common objects of curiosity with all 
the ardour of a young traveller, 1 have had myself, but two opportunities of 
seeing him; once when Twent as a member of the diplomatic body, to pay my 
respects to His Imperial Highness, and, a second time, at the dinner given to 
him by the French Ambassador. On both these occasions I found his manner 
natural, and his conversation anreseryed. ‘The state belonging to his princely 
rank was, however, fully displayed. ‘The Foreign Ministers were expressly 
invited to appear in uniform; the Ambassador himself attended in his richest 
costume, and the Secretary of Embassy performed the duties of gentleman- 
usher. 

ho Prince's manner in receiving me was affable. He held out his hand, 
and placed me on the sofa at his side. He talked of the war and its difficulties, 
of the sacrifices itinvelved, both for England and France, and of the resources, 
particularly in. point of endurance and evasion, possessed by Russia. His 
language at the same time intimated that the game was to be played out, that 


‘France would eventually put no limits to her assistance, and that resnits 


commensurate with the sacrifices were to be sought. 

At dinner | had the honour of sitting next to him. He talked with good 
humour, and vivacity, but nothing of interest or novelty, cither in thought or 
expression. attracted my attention, One sentiment it gave me pleasure to hear 
from the lips of a Prince, who is in the direct line of succession to a powerful 
throne, Alluding to the frequent dynastic changes of the age, he said, that 
the great thing was to do as much good as possible while power lasted, and to 
resign it with a goud grace when no longer tenable. He spoke of thu 
Emperor as worthy of the fullest confidence, and superior in mental qualities 
to all around him, He expressed a strong wish that the idea of forming 
a Polish legion should be carried into effect without delay, and he mentioned 
General Wysocki with interest. 

Some toasts were given after dinner. Ii was remarked that the Prince's 
health was given before that of the Emperor, that the Sultan’s was given 
last, and that no allusion whatever was made to Her Majesty the Queen, 
or to British co-operation, 

I now beg Aeav to draw your Lordship’s attention to a secret report 
addressed to. me by M. Pisani, and inelosed herewith in copy. Though it 
touches on several topics, they all have reference to Prince Napoleon, who, 
in declaring his opinions, would seem to have borne in mind rather his 
quality of Prince than his rank as an officer. 

With Fepiey to General Baraguay d'Hilliers, | will only allow myself 
to state that | am not suprised; and if a portion of his Embassy were in- 
cludes in the censure, there is reason to believe that little injustice would 
ow: done, 


lid 


That the Commanders-in-chief should meet without unnecessary delay, 
is, indeed, most desirable. But I greatly question the expediency of autho- 
rising Omer Pasha to leave his army at the present juneture, and I should 
hear with more satisfaction that Varna had been selected as the place of 
meeting. 

There is no want of truth, unfortunately, in the supposition that Omer 
Pasha and the Seraskier are not on cordial terms. J am assured that there 
‘. no substantial ground of difference between them, and I have myself 
endeavoured to prepare the way for a complete reconciliation, : 

The continued exclusion of the late Seraskicr, Mehmed Ali, from the 
Cabinet is, in my humble judgment, essential to an tolerable administration 
of the public interests at this time ; and as the French Prince did not entirely 
abstain from interfering on his behalf, [ rejoice to learn from M. Pisani’s 
report that His Imperial Highness appeared at least to acquiesce in the sound- 
ness of Riza Pasha’s objections. . 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Inclosure in No, 134, 
Mr, E. Pisant to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Secret and Confidential-) 
My Lord, Pera, May 7, 1854. 

| HAVE the honour to report that Reshid Pasha informed me that ina 
visit, which Riza Pasha paid last night to Prince Napoleon, His Imperial 
Highness spoke very unfavourably of General Baraguay d’'Hilliers, and highly 
disapprayed his conduct in the question lately mooted respecting the Catholic 
subjects of King Otho, His Highness advised the Pasha to urge the Sultan to 
write to the Emperor and demand his recall. But Riza Pasha having observed 
that he thought his Imperial Master would not do so, the Prince suggested 
that if His Majesty the Sultan was not inclined to adopt that step, his Mimisters, 
at least. Reshid Pasha, ought to write to M. Drouyn de Lhuys. He added, 
that Uie Ambassador was not equal to the task he was called upon to fulfil, and 
that the sooner he was recalled the better, 

Subsequently he spoke of the necessity of the Commanders-in-chief meeting 
together, with a view to concert about the plan of operations, and pro vosed 
that as soon as Marshal St. Arnand arrives here, adier Omer Pasha should 
repair to Constantinople, or the commanders of the allied forees should proceed 
to Shunila, 

Reshid Pasha seems to think, for the good of the service, that Omer Pasha 
had better come to Constantinople, as it will be a fair opportunity for him to 
have also an explanation with the Seraskior Pasha, with whom it would appear 
he isnot on very friendly terms. 

Reshid Pasha farther stated, that the Prince acquainted Riza Pasha with 
Mehmed Ali Pasha’s visit, and gave him to understand that he (Melimed Ali) 
svems very anxious to be employed in some capacity or other. The Seraskier 
availed himself of the opportunity to explain to the Prince why Mehmed Ali 
Pasha was dismissed, and added, that although he had nothing personal against 
him, his humble opinion was, that were he to form part of the present 
administration, he would do more harm than good. The Prince duly appre- 
ciated the motives put forward by the Seraskier Pasha, and assured him that 
he had no intention whatever to intercede with the the Sultan in his fivour. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) EB. PISANI.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Eerl of Clarendon.—(Rereived May 20.) 


(No. 216.) rt 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 9, 1854. 

IT is not true that the Sultan had any intention of taking his seat at 
table on the oceasion of the banquet given yesterday by His Majesty to Prince 
Napoleon. He appeared, as usual, in the saloon before dinner, and after 
paying his compliments to the Prince went round the circle of guests invited to 
mect His Imperial Highness. ‘Toasts were given with the dessert, but limited 
in mumber to three, namely, the health of the Emperor of the French, that of 
Sultan Abdul-Medjid, and finally that of Prince Napoleon, his guest. ‘The 
Prince read a short speech expressed in appropriate terms. 

Such is the tenour of the report which I have received. ‘To my great 
regret T was unable to attend the dinner myself. I had made a considerable 
exertion in the morning to exchange the ratifications of our ‘Tripartite Treaty 
at Reshid Pasha'’s house, where the meeting was appointed. On returning 
home | found a decided manifestation of gout, and with it no choice but to 
send an exeuse. Unfortunately Lord Raglan was also indisposed, and equally 
unable to go; 

With the view of preventing any possible misconstruction, 1 wrote to the 
French Ambassador requesting that he would express my regret 0 the Prince. 
His Imperial Highness sent an officer to inquire after my health, and the 
Sultan did me a similar honour hy means of one of his Chamberlains. 

1 mention these circumstances becanse I understand that signs of dissatis- 
faction appeared among the French, owing, as it would seem, to some delay in 
serving the dinner, and to some difficulty in arranging the toasts. 

Qn the last point there had been a disenssion in the morning between 
Reshid Pasha and General Baraguay, who insisted that the Emperor's health 
should be drunk to the exclusion of other Sovereigns, and before that of the 
Sultan, ‘This took place in my presence, and | was urged to give an opinion, 

| endeavoured to evade the appeal by saying that to my mind such matters 
wvore best left to the host; but, constrained to speak out, 1 said that the toasts 
might with perfect prone be confined to the Sultan and the Prince, or, 


sf more were desirable, that the health of the Emperor of the French and that 
of Her Majesty the Queen, followed by a compliment ta the States in friend- 
ship with the Porte, might be proposed with good effect. 

Other matters of disagreement have occurred between the parties. 

First, an individual named Durutt, suspected of being a Russian spy, was 
arrested some days ago. The French Embassy claimed him as under its pro- 
tection, and one of its interpreters, deaf to every representation, took him away 


176 


from the police. An Tonian, named Civinis, the Porte’s principal agent 1m 
arresting the man, was accused of having violated the rights of the French 
embassy, and his dismissal was peremptorily demanded, Reshid Pasha resisted 
the demand, alleging that Civims had acted under an express order from him. 
This was not sufhicient in the eves of the French Ambassador, and a viciim 18 
still required, though Durutti was only In possession of a Roman passport, and 
strongly suspected of being by birth either a Raya or an Hellenic subject. 
Moroover it is not at all clear that the French Embassy has any authority for 
claiming a right to protect Papal subjects in Turkey: 
Secondly, the Porte was known to have adopted the resolution of removing 
Vely Pasha, the Grand Visier’s son, from Paris, of appointing Namik Pasha 
in his place, of transferring, the former Ambassador to the Government of 
Candia, and of bringing Mehemet Pasha, the present Mushir of that island, up 
to Constantinople, where he would resume his Ministerial functions as head 0 
the police, [For some reason or other the French Government wishes to keep 
Vely Pasha at Paris, and the French Ambassador appears to have been yery 
decided in urging this demand on Reshid Pasha. The Ottoman Minster 
declared that the question was not in his hands, and that the proposed change 
proceeded immediately fom the Sultan. At the Imperial Palace yesterday, 
before dinner, Prinee Napoleon repeated the same demand to Reshid Pasha, 
and, on receiving # similar reply, demanded an immediate audience of the 
Sultan, ‘This was granted, and he succeeded in obtaining a kind af promise, 
apparently much against His Majesty’s inclination, and from special deference 
to the Emperor, that Vely Pasha ghould remain Ambassador al Paris, 
Inclosed herewith, in copy, is a report addressed to me by M, Pisani. Lt 
will serve toinform your Lordship of any particulars which Lmay have omitted 
through inadvertence. 
Much disgust has been occasioned by these and preceding transactions, 
It ig thought no less ungenerous than impelitie that a foreign Power, which, in 
concert with others, has laid the Sultan under a weight of gratitude, shou 
take advantage of his obligation to dictate concessions irrelevant of the pending 
question, and ealeulated to display the soe which it professes to uphold.

Mr. E. Pisani to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


My Lord, Pera, May 9, 1804. 

| HAVE the honour to report that General Baraguay d’Hilliers remon- 
strated with Reshid Pasha on. the subject of the arrest of Signor Durutti, and 
wanted his Highness to dismiss immediately Mr. Civinis, whom he said had 
caused him to be apprehended and sent to the police, The Pasha refused to 
comply with the Aetnerailore demand, and observed that Mr, Civinis having 
acted in pursuance of ‘structions from the Porte, was not to be blamed in any 
way, ‘Then Reshid Pasha asked him how fit happened that Signor Durutti 
being a French subject as stated, had not peace his passport to the police. 
The General replied that he was not exactly a French subject, but that he was 
in possession of a Roman passport, which entitled him to the protection of the 
Embassy. He proceeded to complain that the Porte was paying little attention 
to the French Government, nnd was endeavouring to disparage the Embassy on 
every accasion, . 

He afterwards complained of the recall of Veli Pasha, and said that the 
Emperor will be much displeased when he is apprised of this decision. Reshid 
Pasha explained to the French Ambassador how the matter stands, and gave 
him to understand that he had nothing to say to it, and that it was the Sultan's 
own pleasure that he should be recalled, General Baraguay spoke in such an 
authoritative and dictatorial manner, that Reshid Pasha is unwilling to keep 
on his intercourse any longer, and has made up his mind to tender his resigna- 
tion, Beeause, said, he, the General becomes every day more and more unbear- 
able, and he foresees that some unpleasant scene will happen one of these days, 
which will lead to some serious question between the two Governments, and in 


Vi7 


order to avoid being the eause of such scandal, he has resolved upon retiring 
from office. 

‘At the dinner which took place yesterday at the palace of Beyler Bey, 
Prince Napoleon spoke to Reshid Pasha respecting Veli Pasha’s reeall, and 
expressed regret, and repeated what the Ambassador said inthe morning. His 
Highness gave to the Prince the same reply he had given to General Baraguay. 
Upon which the Prince asked to sce the Sultan, and was introduced to His 
Majesty by Kiamil Bey. After a few minutes interview, the Sultan promised 
to confirm Veli Pasha in his post, out of deference for the Emperor. As soon 
as the Prince left the Sultan, His Majesty summoned Reshid Pasha to his 
presence, and told him what had passed, and without positively saying so, he 
cave him to understand that the Prince complained of him. 

I have, &e.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received May 22.) 


(No. 188.) 
My Lord, Vienna, May 1, 1854. 

BARON BOURQUENEY having received an official intimation from 
his Government, to communicate to the Conference the Convention which had 
lately been signed between the English and French Governments, and to invite 
the Governments of Austria and Prussia equally to place before it the Con- 
vention which they had entered into, and as I had received your Lordship’s 
directions to support this proposal, we jointly made the request 10 Count Buol 
ue he should assemble the Conference, and the meeting was fixed for this 
AA 

"At our assembly, I stated, in conjunction with Baron Bourqueney, the 
objects for which we had desired this meeting, and f placed in the hands of 
Count Buola copy of the Convention concluded between Her Majesty and 
the Emperor of the French, relative to the military aid to be riven to the 
Porte. 

‘ont Arnim stated that this document ad only been unofficially sub- 
mitted to his Government by the French Minister at Berlin, and had not heen 
communicated atall by the English Alinister, so that up to the present time the 
Prussian Cabinet had not officially been ‘aformed of the existence of this docu- 
ment, he was therefore without instructions with regard to its reception in Con- 
ference, but being now ‘avited to receive it, he would refer to his Government 
for orders upon. the subject. Under these circumstances the Conference was 
adjourned until Count Arnim should be furnished with the instructions he 
required, 

L stated, together with Baron Bonrqaeney ae the object of our Govern- 
ments was to place on the Proctocol of the Conference the engagements which 
they had taken towards carrying oul the views which the Four Governments 
had, by the Protocol of the 9th ultima, recognised as those by which their 
policy should be directed, and that by thus enregistering these, together with 
the measures which the other two Governments, parties to that Proctocol, had 
itaken nconcert, to form a complete record. of the series of engagements by 
which the Four Governments had sought to forward their common objects. 

Count Arnim mentioned incidentally that he had been instructed by his 
Government to inquire of Baron Bourqueney and myself whether, since the 
last Protocol had been signed, in whieh the desire of the Four Powers to obtain 
an amelioration of the position of the Christian inhabitants of Turkey had been 
expressed, our Governments had obtained any assurances upon that subject, 
which we were enabled to communicate, 

Count Buol stated, and Baron Bourqueney and myself concurred in the 
remark, that this was not properly a subject t he brought forward in Con- 
ference, that cach of the Governments which we represented tad taken the 
same engagement upon this subject, and they might therefore separately 
make a statement of what each had obtained: but that at present he thought 
“sufficient to say, that this object was anxiously pursued ie all the Powers, 
and that ameliorations had already heen ranted by the Turkish Government, 
whieh, there was every reason to expect, might be further extended, 

I have, &e,

No. 192. 
Mr. Buchanan to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 22.) 


(No. 155. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Copenhagen, May 17, 1864. 

THE Austrian Minister and the Prussian Charge (Affaires waited upon 
M, de Bluhme the day before yesterday, and presented to his Fixcellency 
identic Notes eommunicating to the Danish Government the Austro-Prussian 
Convention of the 20th April last, and inviting them to accede to it for 
the Duchies of Holstein and Lunenburgh. 

[ have not yet seen either the Convention or the Notes, M. de Bluhme 
having assured me that he has been requested to vonsider the communica- 
tion which has been made to him as secret, and my Prussian colleague nol 
having yet fulfilled his promise to make me acquainted with the contents 
of the Convention confidentially, as soon as he had communicated it to the 
Minister for Foreign Affairs, 

From what I have learned, however, from Count Hartig and Baron 
Rechenberg, it would appear that the terms of the Notes whieh have been 
addressed to M. de Bluhme are not entirely identie with those which have 
been presented to the Governments of purely German States, and that, 
instead of the King of Denmark being formally invited to accede to the 
Convention, His Majesty is rather requested to consider whether it might 
not be expedient that he should do so. 

Count Hartig also observed, in speaking upon this pomt, that some 
facilities might possibly be accorded to Denmark in the execution of the 
Convention, as more importance Was attached to the moral effect of her 
accession to it than to any assistance which she could he called upon to 
afford to the Confederation in the event of hostilities with Tussia, 

M. de Bluhme, | am. told, shewed in the course of the conversation which 
followed the delivery of the Notes, that he had little or mo previous information 
respecting the nature of the communication which had been made to him, and 
that he, therefore, declined expressing any opinion with respect to it until he 
should have time to consult his colleagues, and to reflect on the consequences 
of the engagements which he was invited to undertake. 

He made, however, some observations respecting the exceptional position 
of Denmark, and the diffieulties and dangers which she might incur by fulfilling 
a duty to the German Confederation which its other members might perform 
without inconvenience, | . 

I have, &c. 
(Signeil) ANDREW BUCHANAN.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received May 22.) 
(No, 286.) 


My Lord, Bertin, May 19, 1854. 

IN pursuance of your Lordship’s instructions | have read to Baron Man- 
tenifel your despatch No. 125 of the 16th instant, respecting the late removal 
of persons from certain high offices, and the alteration in the policy of Prussia 
which these changes indicate. 

His Excellency seemed vreatly annoyed at this communication, am when 
[ had finished reading it said that these changes of persons did not mean a 
change in the policy of the Prussian Government, observing emphutically, that 
if the King had aliered his opinions, or did not intend to carry out the Conven- 


tion lutely signed, or ack up to the Protocols and arrangements of the Vienna 
Conferences, he should not be found where he was. 
oA 


qand | 


NOONO) "33140 OY¥O53# a 


182. 


He said that it was not true that the King was implicitly euided oy the 
persons about the Court, for that he was not in the habit of being led by any- 
body; neither could he admit that we had any right to remark on quarrels that 
the King might have with lis hrother, or on the removal of General Bonin or 
anybody else from the Government, as long as there was no departure from 
international engagements entered into, nor was it fair that Her Majesty's 
Government should suppose that the King’s policy had undergone any serious 
modification. La: 

{ replied that in England we were in the habit of judging of the probable 
manner of carrying out measures by the choice made of the men selected for 
that purpose, whose opinions were more OF less known, and that-at a moment 
of such vast European importance, when we were at war witha great and power- 
ful country, we viewed these changes with pain, as indicating: & modification of 
the policy which we had hoped to find the Prussian Government willing to 
carry out. 

“THe then said that it was totally unusual for one Government to make to 
another observations such as L had read to him, and that he was sure that the 
British Government would never be disposed to listen to remarks of a like 
nature from him. 

[ replied that his Excellency must permit me to say that we disclaimed all 
pretension to interfere in the internal concerns of Prussia, bur that having acte 
confidentially together at Vienna, we were cricved to think that the policy of 
England and Prussia might no longer be identical. 

Tho Minister President here said that perhaps they never had been iden- 
tical, for we wished to go much further than the King did, but that T might be 
satisfied that His Majesty would act up to his engagements; that the policy of 
Prossia was not the policy of this or that Minister who might be selected for 
the direction of atfairs, but the policy of the King, and that as for the opinions 
of his colleagues in the Cabinet, they ere not much consulted as to what 
passed in the Foreign Department. He then said that I had some time ago 
complained that General Bonin had. been replaced at the War Office hy Count 
Waluersee, who was Russian in his political feelings, and he could inform me 
that Count Waldersee had just declared to him, that he would have nothing to 
do with politics, that he should do his best to maintain the army ina state of 
efficiency, and that it should be ready to move whenever the King gave lus 
orders to that etfect. 

'The whole drift. of this conversation was unsatisfactory. Before it closed 
Baron Manteutfel attempted to show that the persons about the King, and of 
whose influence we complained, did not possess the power that was supposed, 
and he evidently desired it to be understood that the King was all in all, and 
that his Ministers were mere tools, from whom implicit obedience was expected, 
but it may be observed, that as the party in power are less likely to raise 
opposition to his Royal Will than those of the liberal side, the hopes of any 
modification are very distant. 

T have, &c., |

Agents accredited to the German Gaur instructing them to comminnicate

‘nto between Austria and Prussia, and to request in the event of their responding

to subgeribe to the declaration which the Austrian and Prussian Ministers have

The Austrian Cabinet states in this document that they have constantly

matter, and that ules have not ceased to take into consideration the general 
wish of affording to the Confederation an opportunity of expressing their opinion 
on the line of poliey which Germany should pursue in the present phasis of 
political affairs. 

Your Lordship will pereeive that in. explaining the decision which the 
Austrian Cabinet bas taken with respect to the form of their communication to 
the Diet, it is gently hinted in the circular that the Convention with Prussia 
was contracted independently of Federal obligations, while it likewise admits 
that the Confederation, in virtue of the international character which it derives 
from ita fundamental laws, is in no way precluded from acceding to it ag a 
united political body. 

It is therefore proposed by the Austrian Cabinet that a resolution shall be 
passed by the Diet, approving of the conduct of Austria and Prussia, which 
will obyiate any delay or difficulties which might arise in the Diet itself to 
impede the prompt and unanimous acceptution of the Treaty,

lately been ratified between Austrin and Prussia, 

f told Count Colloredo that as the whole of the negotiations connected 
with this Treaty had heen kept a profound secret, | was im ignorance of the 
terms in which it was origmally proposed to the Cabinet of Berlm, but 1 pre- 
sumed they could not have been those which were finally agreed to, and that 
Austria had probably made great concessions in order to procure the adhesion 
of Prussia. 

The only points, I said, which could be considered of any importance in 
the Treaty, or as bearing upon the war, or the alliance of the Two German 
Powers with England and France, were to be found in the Additional Article, 
in which two casus belli were Ustablished, viz, the imeorporation of the Prinei- 
palities, and the attack or passage of the Balkan by Ktussia: but that the first 
ease was null, and might have been altogether omitted, as Russia might occupy 
the Prineipalities for an indefinite period, and their formal oceupation was 
unnecessary to her, and therefore improbable, On the other hand, if an attack 
or passage of the Balkan were attempted, and that Austria and Prussia imme- 
diately thereupon declared and made war against Russia, it would afford

wir,

Mr, Bligh to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received May 25.) 
(No, 10.) 
My Lord, Hanover, May 25, 1864. 


| WAS surprised upon my return hither to find so strong a feeling in 
favour of Russia, as regards the war, to be prevailing amongst that class of 
society with whieh | had principally to do, and such i total ignorance of the 
real circumstances which have brought on the war, as prove that, unless 
wilfully blind to facts and reason, the Mussian manifestoes, proclimations, notes, 
ail despatches must have been the studyof those with whom Thad to converse 
ou the subjeet ; whilst the plain evidence of falsehood and chicanery on the 
one side, and of truth and straightforwardnéss on tie other, which is afforded 
py the published official documents that emanated from those who have been 
eniploved in these matters by Her Majesty, had been totally ignored, 

| have been in no hurry to report this to your Lordship, being desirous 
af previously ascertaining to what extent this feeling went as regards the 
subjects of the Hanoverian Crown, and I have now the satisfaction of being 
able safely to assure your Lordship that it is contined to the nobility, which 


189 


fortunately as relates to this question of general poince) interest, but to be 
lamented by those who may desire to see established in this country a stable 
constitutional form of government, with asalutary balance between the Crown 
and the people, is exceedingly unpopular on account of its exeessive exelusive- 
ness and pretensions, and on account of its ignorance, which prevent its 
marching with the intelligence of the age; and on account of its prejudices, 
which forbid it to forget its lost privileges, is a class without even the weight 
whieh its territorial possessions ought to give to it. 

The reasons for this feeling 1 believe to be the following:—The bitter 
remembrance of French ocenpation and tyranny which keeps alive a fear that 
similar evils will come again from that quarter, unless kept in check by 
Russian power, ‘The seclusion of sentiment as regards us, caused by our 
ancient policy antagonism to France having been exehanged for mitimate 
alliance with that Power. The apprehension that the success of such an 
alliance against Russia would entail the triumph of liberal ideas, if not of 
revolution, The vagne hope that Russia will be able to quell the innovating 
spirit of the age, and thus indirectly help the nobility to recover their lost 
privileges, Such are the reasons, if worthy of the term, which excite the 
aspirations of a class in this country in favour of Russia. As however the 
people in general undoubtedly side with us, | merely mention what I have 
observed, without troubling your Lordship with the arguments with which I 
endeavour to combat such reasoning, and try to convince those who propound 
it that the time is fully come for all to join in resisting the domination of the 
Cossack, 

One other class, which in faet however belongs in great measure to the 
nobility, is inclined to Russie, namely, the younger officers of the army, which 
perhaps may be accounted for by the prestige which attaches to a Government 
and Sovereign so essentially military as is that of Russia and its Czar, But 
[ am glad to say that those officers who served in the German Legion, with 
very few exceptions (and those contemptible ones), retain a warm attachment 
for England, and are devoted to her cause. 

The Court is supposed to be favourable to Russia, but great reserve is 
maintained there on the subject, and the King at present abstains altogether 
from speaking to any foreign Minister about politics, 

I have, &c._ 
(Signed) J.D. BLIGH.

(No. 31.) 
My Lord, Dresden, May 23, 1854, 

M. DE BEUST leaves Dresden this evening for Bamberg, where there 
will be held a meeting of Representatives of most of the secondary Powers of 
Germany, whose object will be to discuss and determine on the line they are 
to pursue regarding the late Treaty between Austria and Prussia, His 
Excellency told me at once that he utterly disapproved of the proposal made 
by the two great German Powers to the lesser ones, that they should all 
become parties to the Treaty without its being previously communicated to the 
Germanic Diet, whose authority would be thus de facto paralysed, and that he 
would ¢ertainly oppose it, As yet nothing has transpired here concerning the 
Secret Articles of this Treaty, but the sensation it has created leaves no donbt 
of their importance. For some time past the most confidential intercourse 
exists between the Governments of Saxony and Bavaria, and the two Ministers 
are working to creaty a third party in the Frankfort Diet, to be a counterpoise 
1o Austria and Prussia,

MY very ill timed indisposition, thougli not of a serious character, has

The two Commanders-in-ehief, However, met here in my presence on the

oecasion to his Grace the Duke of Neweastle What ibis right for me to bring 
immediately to your Lordship's knowledge mity be stated in a few words, 

‘Miree points of leading importance more particularly drew my attention. 
One was the urgency of a meeting hetween the two Commanders and Omer 
Pasha; the second, an idea previously thrown out by Marshal St Arnaud, 
that his command would extend over the Turkish army > the third, a modifica- 
Hon of his idea, to the efleet of incorporating «a considerable part of that army 
with the French forces under his command. : 

lt appeared to me in every sense desirable that the proposed meeting 
should take place with the least possible delay, and that, previous to that 
mecting, the other questions should be held in suspense, as matters (0 be 
decided after full consultation between the three Commanders-in-chiet. To

attention to that chinse of 1 which establishes the principle 1 clear terms, 

Whatever may lave been his previous impressions OF views, the Marshal 
asserted no claim to any exclusive command beyond that of lis own Troops, 
and in explaining Ins idea of interposing, with the Porte’s permission, a Turkish

he obtained for that purpose from Constantinople, or any other part of the 
empire. Tle agreed with Lord Raglan that the efficiency of Omer Pasha’s

1 have ascertained that nothing: in eontradiction with this view has been

Sebastopol, 

L will not conclude this despateh without mentioning thal some conversi- 
tion took place with respect to the armies on the Asiatic frontier. I thought

at Kars, and to the very serious prejudice which would infallibly result to the

frontier, without contesting either the one or the other of these points. ‘The two 
Commanders-in-chief agreed m opinion as to the difheulty, not to-say imprac- 
ticability, of detaching ay offectual aid from the auxiliary armics in’ that 
direction. 

lf such be a correct view of the case, how vastly is the importance 
‘nereassl of engaging the Porte to take eflectual measures for placing its 
Asiatic armies on a less precarious footing, and how greatly is it to be desired 
that the military experience and tried ability of the generals may be able to 
put the Yurkish Government in a wily to apply its resources willy bettcr cllvet 
to the prosecution of the war on that side.

Code of Regulations far the Organisation of the Irregular Troops and Volunteers 
attached to the Imperial Armies. 


(Translation.) 


OWING to the want of a cood system of organisation of the irregular 
troops serving with the Imperial army, and elsewhere; the absence of a strict 
discipline under the existing constitution of those troops, and of a suitable code 
of punishments for the erimes committed by them, they have not, In general, 
heen efficiently or successfully employed, or properly administered, during the 
war, and under uther eireumstances likewise, Some of those troops, moreover, 
while on the march, and at places where hey were quartered, haye been eeuilty 
of oppression and violence towards the inhabitants of the country, against the 
Imperial pleasure 5 and, although as a body, they are animated with the desire 
of serving their Government, and thus earning a title to the Royal benevolence 
and rewards, some of them, 1s above stated, acted against expectation in 4 
different manner, and this owing simply to the want of a proper organisation, 


. as already set forth. 


The following regulations for the organisation of those troops have been 
therefore sanctioned for general application by His Majesty’s approval, and they 
are consequently to be earried into exccution. 

The proper effieiency of these troops when on service depends upon the 
removal of the confusion and want of order that prevails, and the introduction, 
as far as possible, of order and discipline; the first point to be attended to is, 
the formation and regulation of these troops on military principles; the appoint 
ment of proper officers and non-commissioned officers, and the introduction of 
strict discipline in the administration and command. The mounted troops, 
therefore, serving under the command of one chief at the Imperial camp, or 
elsewhere, shall be divided into companies of 120 or 150 men. Youzbashis 
will be appointed to each company from among the men who are distinguished 
for military experience, courage, and good conduct. A lirst and second Mulazim, 
four Tehaoushes, and ten Oubashis, among whom the privates will be distributed, 
will be likewise attached to each company, When the corps commanded by a 
Chief constitutes from four to eight companies, it shall be considered an Alay, 
and the commander a Mirali, When the troops unde" the command of a 
Chieftain constitute less than four companies, they shall be drafted into other 
regiments, if proper and possible. If this arrangement does not suit, those 
companies shall be employed separately, as they cannot be considered in the 
light of an Alay,

No. 206. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 28;) 


(No, 232, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 16, 1854. 


ON the 13th instant, when Marshal St, Arnaud met Lord Raglan here, he 
informed his Lordship, in my presence, that he had found the performance of 
his duties as Commander-in-chief of the French auxiliary army 50 much 
impeded hy the state of misunderstanding which, unhappily, existed between 
the French Ambassador on one side and the Turkish Ministers for War and 
Foreign Affairs on the other, that he had found himself under the painful 
necessity of sending off an express to Paris with information to this effect, and 
a request that the Government would interfere to remove an impediment so 
injurious to the progress of those important matters which he was called upon 
to direct. . 

His Excellency added that, in order to do what depended upon him for an 
earlier acceleration of business, he had waited upon the Sultan in company with 
the above-mentioned Ministers, and entered, with their concurrence, on such 
explanations as he judged to be necessary for that purpose. 

He expressed an earnest desire to move in harmony with the British 
authorities, and, at the same time, gave strong indications of his resolution not 
to submit to any unnecessary obstructions.

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDOLIFFE,

Consul Neale to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Varna, May 11, 1854. 


T HAVE the honour to report to your Lordship, that by intelligence which 
I received yesterday from Silistria, | find that a body of Russian Cavalry (about 
5,000 itisstated) had advanced from the Dobrudscha as far as Jonikoe, a village 
fre hours distant from Silistria; some Cossacks also occupied the village of 
Kanly, two hours still further to the southward than Jenikoe. The most 
advanced position towards the enemy of the Turkish Cavalry was at Kynardji. 
The main body of the Turkish Cavalry was at Bazardjik. 

The Russian force opposite Silstria at Karalash was calculated not to 
execed 10,000 men, ‘The number of Russian troops in the Dobrudscha has 
not been ascertained with any certainty, and has been variously stated to 
amount to, from 40,000 to 60,000 men, Eighteen Russian gun-borts were 
stationed at and near Karalash and opposite Silistria, and Russian steamers 
were daily disembarking tents, stores, and munitions, on the left bank of the 
Danube, about five hours lower down than Bilistria. 

Kor the last eight or ten days, Silistria had not heen bombarded from the 
Russian batteries on the opposite shore, but everything appeared to indicate 
the intention of the Russians to besiege Silistria. 

Lam informed that a regiment of ‘Turkish Cavalry had advanced on the 
2nd instant, out of Kalaflat under the commatd of “Seander Bey,’ and 
encountered a superior body of Russian Cavalry at Radovan, half way between 
Kalafat and Craiova, The Russians are officially reported to have been repulsed 
with loss, ‘The Russians are stated to have left a small force to cover their 
hospitals at Craiova. 

About the same period a party of about 300 Bashi-Bozouks passed the 
Danube, at Nicopolis, and haying been eventually attacked by a superior 
Russian force were entirely destroyed.

Captain Simmons to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Shumla, May 6, 1854. 


[HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that his Highness Omer 
Pasha informed me this afternoon that he had received intelligence that on the 
eh of April a skirmish had taken place between a regiment of ‘Turkish 
Cavalry and several squadrons of Cossacks, who were superior in number, 
between Radovan and Craiova, in which the ‘Turks appear to have been suc- 
cessful, for they are reported to have captured sixty horses, and to have mare 
twelve men prisoners. 

On the 2nd May a reconnaissance was made from Nicopolis into the 
Wallachian territory by 277 Albanians, supported by two companies of regulars. 

‘They took possession of a Russian entrenchment, which was only oceupied 
by a picket, 

The party were then reealled, but the Albanians are stated to have refused, 
having sworn to die rather than fall back. 

They were attacked, first by Cavalry, and afterwards (wo separate 
attacks by Infantry, are stated to have been made. ‘he result was that, the 
Whole of the Albanians, with the exception of one man who was saved and got 
across the river, and fifteen wounded, who fell into the enemy's hands, were 
killed. 

‘The loss on the part of the Russians is stated to have been very great. 

No farther movement of the enemy in the direction of Silistria or the 
Hobrudscha has been reported, ‘Their advanced posts have not been pushed 
to the southward of the Karasu. T have, &c.

Inclosure 1 in No. 208. 


Extract from a Private Letter to Vice-Consul Stevens. 


THE state of affairs at Kars is now hopeless beyond description. ‘The 
roree has dwindled to some 12,000 men, starved, dejected, and com- 
manded by little better than hopeless imbecility. ‘The only means of keeping 
the force together is an immediate advance, but that is simply impossible in a 
hostile territority denuded of everything that can feed or shelter man or beast, 
with a starving country as your base of operations, with no point (appul, no 
stores, no money, no courage and no military skill, ‘There is but the alternative 
of sending a properly equipped foree (European) or of letting the Russians 
march just where they please. Guyon is indefatigable, but his hands are tied, 
and what can the Mushir do with only 10 millions of piastres supplied, 
and actually 200 millions are necessary ta accomplish an advance, the only 
thing that can save the army from dissolution, 

We passed a cortége escorting some paper money to the army on one 
mountain. ‘They are armed chiefly with tchibouques, and set im true Turkish 
‘ndolence upon their high soft saddles, One man with a revolver pistol could 
have posseased himself of the whole affair in twenty seconds, and effectually 


quieted all informants.

Inclosure 2 in No. 208. 
Consul Brant to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Extract) Erzeroom, April 80, 1864. 
THE Mushir Mustafa Yaut’ Pasha isa good but a weak man, that he adopts 
the advice of the last person he has conversed with, is totally ignorant of 


military matters, and from this he throws everything into confusion, His 
Excellency often says that he has no power to do what the General thinks 
indispensable, and he, (General Guyon, seems ta have come to the conviction 
that the army must be defeated and that he ought to resign, as he risks his 
character without a hope of success, Siill he seems reluctant to take such a 
step, because he fears matters will become worse, for not a man in the army 
appears to care whether it will be beaten or vietorious, and he adds that he 
should dic of a broken heart were he to lose a chance of beating the Russians. 

A contract was offered to. the Mushir to supply 1,000 horses from Persia, 
his Exeellency declined it on the plea that the price was high, and that he was 
promised supplies, none have been sent, and the army is in great want of them; 
such apathy and want of foresight cannot but entatl rnin on the cause. 

General Guyon was more hopeful when things appeared to Me WOFSE ; he 
seems now to despair by perceiving | suppose that after such exertions he 


cannot make the army eflective. 

Iam convineed that if he quit his post the army will be lost, and that with 
such a force the invasion of Georgin 1s out of the question, ‘The present 
feeling of the army is des jonding, and the soldiers wil only regain their con- 


fidence on being reinforced by European troops.

Inclosure 4 in No, 208. 


Vice-Consul Stevens to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe 


My Lord, Trebizond, May 5, 1854. 

NEWS arrived here last evening that the Russians having removed their 
earrison from Sokoom Kaleh to Redout Kaleh, the Circassians marched in and 
took possession of the former place on the 24th ultimo, without any fighting. 
The Sultan's standard was hoisted, and a Provisional Government. formed 
under Hamit Bey, a relative, I believe, of Schanil’s. 

Two or three Europeans and some native traders belonging to this place 
were allowed to quit, and arrived here yesterday, several of whom lost their 
merchandize, which the Circassians seized, 

From one of the Europeans [ learn that Russia has abandoned Anapa 
after burning it down, Tt would seem Redout Kaleh is the only place which 
remains in Russian hands, but preparations were making to abandon it; many 
of its inhabitants had already removed to the interior, — 

I presume it would not be a diffientt matter for the Circassians to form a 
junction with Selim Pasha’s army, from which some good might result if a 
march towards Tiflis is in contemplation.

My Lord, Constantinople, May 15, 1854. 

THE Austrian Internuncio having called here yesterday, | took occasion 
to inform him that [ was instructed to support the acceptance of his overture 
to the Porte respecting the entrance of an ‘Austrian auxiliary foree into Turkey 
for the repression of insurrectionary movements proceeding from Greece or 
Montenegro, and that 1 had acted agreeably to my instructions by recom- 
mending the Porte to accept the proposals of his Government. 

An exchange of notes will accompany the Porte’s acceptance, and I col- 
lected from what the Internuncio said that a Convention, perhaps, would 
eventually follow. 

Inclosed herewith, in strict confidence, for your Lordship's perusal, is the 
project of a Note proposed by Reshid Pasha, with the view of drawing out an 
answer of corresponding purport from Baron de Bruck. 

Notwithstanding the Porte’s compliance with his Excellency’s overture, | 
am persuaded that the Turkish Ministers would be better pleased if no necessity 
for the entrance of an Austrian army were possibly to take place. ; 

| may observe, in conclusion, that the Internuncio’s language tended con- 
siderably to confirm those prospects of a more complete co-operation on the 
pe of Austria, which part of the correspondence forwarded to me by your 

jordship enables me to entertain, |

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved May 29.) 


(No. 203.) 
My Lord, Vienna, May 24, 1854, 

WITH reference to my despatch to your Lordship, No. 188, I have 
now to report that the Conference, which was adjourned on the 16th instant, 
was yesterday assembled by Count Buol, and upon our meeting, Count Arnim 
etated that he had received the instructions from his Government which he 
had asked for, and by which he was authorised to communicate a copy of 
the Austro-Prussian ‘Treaty to the Conference, and to agree to the terms of 
the Protocol by which this Treaty, 5 well as the one between England and 
France, was accepted by the Conference, and was recognised as tending to 
carry out the objects of the engagements which had been taken by the Four 
Powers in the Protocol of the 9th of Apnil. 

In consequence of this communication, Count Buol read the substance 
of the Protocol which he proposed for the adoption of the Conference, which, 
having been approved, was drawn Up necording to the form in which it was 
to be signed, and the meeting was adjourned till that evening, when the 
copies of the /lifferent documents haying been prepared, the Protocol was 
signed by the Representatives of the Four Powers. 

[ have the honour of inclosing the copies of these documents. 

The Austro-Prussian Treaty is communicated without the Additional 
Article, which is stated to belong to it, but which your Lordship is acquainted 
with, and which refers to eventual military engagements and details, 

[ have not transmitted a copy of the ‘Treaty between England and 
France, which I communicated to the Conference, and which remains depo- 
sited with the other documents preserved in the custody of Count Buol, as 
your Lordship will not require a copy of that instrument. 

I cannot but congratulate your Lordship upon this further step towards 
securing the co-operation of the great Powers of Hurope for the attainment 
of the important objects which they have engaged themselves to carry out, 


&e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

(No, 205.) 
My Lord, Vienna, May 24, 1894. 

IN a recent conversation with Count Alvensleben, General Hess urged 
upon him the necessity of preparations which he thought the Prussian Govern- 
ment should be making to fulfil the military obligations of the Treaty between 
Austria and Prussia, — 

Ceneral Hess stated that the Austrian Government was placing in all 
haste three corps-d’armée upon &@ war footing, in addition to those which 
already were so, and that as soon as the men had joimed their ranks, they 
would be moved tirto Galicia, 

He added that the note which the Two Governments had agreed to transmit 
to St. Petersburgh, calling upon the Emperor to evacuate the Principalities, 
was immediately to be forwarded to Berlin for approval, and directly afterwards 
would be sent to St. Petersburgh, and as it was possible that the answer might 
be such ag to call for the adoption of the military measures contemplated in the 
Treaty, it appeared necessary that the Prussian army should not be backward 
in its preparations, 

Count Alvensleben stated that before he left Berlin, some dispositions had 
already been taken by the Minister of War for the purchase of horses for the 
Artillery, that being the only arm of the Prussian army which required time to 
prepare it for active service, He said that as it would require only twenty-six 
days to place the Infantry and Cavalry on a war footing, there would certainly 
he time enough for effecting this object efore the march of an army could be 
necessary, and that it was a great object with the Prussian fovernment to 
avoid the expense which such a measure must entail, until a real necessity for 
it should oceur. I have, &e.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received May 30.) 
(No. 657.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 29, 1854. 
THE French Government has received advices from Servia, which 
show that the Servian Government is arming to a considerable extent. 


205 


M. Drouyn.de Lhuys has an idea that these armaments are caused by the position 
assumed by Austria on the Servian frontier, and he has written to M. de 
Bourqueney to shew the danger whieh Austria will incur should she have any 
idea of violating the Servian territory. 

T am not sure that this measure of the French Minister is a wise one, for 
if he alarms Austria by exciting apprehensions of the foree of which Servia can 
dispose, he will give her fresh reason for remaiming simply upon the defensive 
within her own frontier. 

[ asked M. Drouyn de Lhuys whether there was not cause to fear that 
the armaments reported to them from Servia were excited and paid for by 
Russia, and whether they might not eventually be turned against the Porte. 
He admitted that such might be the case.

Lord Cowley to the Eurl of Clarendon.—( Received May 30,) 


(No. 663. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 20, 1854, 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has given me, confidentially, the substance 
of a conversation which he held a few days ago with the Austrian Minister, 
M. de Hiibner, and which is not without interest at the present moment, 

I should observe, that since M. de Hubner’s return from his Jate visit 
to Vienna, he appears to me to be far less sanguine of the immediate cooper- 
ation of his Government with the Western Powers than he was previously to 
his departure from hence; and though he maintains that Austria will remain 
faithful to all the engagements which she lias contracted in the Protocols signed 
at Vienna, he does not conceal his apprehensions that the retreat of the Russians 
from the Danubian Provinces may, in the eyes of his Government, cancel those 
engagements. 

~On comparing notes with M. Dronyn de Lhuys, 1 did not find that 
the Austrian Minister’s language had made the same impression upon his 
Excellency that ib had made upon me ; and it was only a day or two ago that 
he admitted that he had had a conversation with M. de Hiibner, which was 
far from satisfactory, and in the course of which he had spoken his mind to 
the Austrian Envoy with considerable freedom. 

Among the reasons which M. de Hiibner appears to have given for the 
backwardness of his Government was this, that the Emperor Francis Joseph 
was apprehensive that the Maritime Powers wished to enfeeble Russia, and to 
reduce her to the state of a second-rate Power. ‘To this Austria could not 
lend assistance. M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that the Emperor was quite 
mistaken; that what France and England desired was, to prevent Russia 
dictating the law to the whole world; that France had as much need of Russia 
to preserve the balance of power in Europe, as Austria had, and that if Austria 
counted upon Russia to hold France in cheek, he could assert, that France would 
be as sorry to see Russia ma josition which would prevent her from cooperating 
with France to keep Central Europe in order,“ What, then,” cai M. de 
Hiibner (promising secrecy, if necessary), “are your plans?” “7 cannot 
tell you what our plans are,” said M. Drouyn de Lhuys; “but 1 will iell 
you what my personal impressions are. Russia is too strong in the Black Sea, 
and must be weakened there. Bhe 14 too strong in the Baltie, and must be 
weakened there, too, In both places, she bids defiance by sea to the united 
flects of what have been considered the two vreatest. Maritime Powers in 
Europe. ‘This, in itself, is 4 contradiction to the balance of power, and must he 
aliered.” While saying this, M. Drouyn de Lhuys seems to have intimated 
various ways by which this result: might be attained, . 

M. de Hiibner did not dissent from the correctnces of M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys’ views, but he said that his Government feared that more was intended, 
and that there was a hope of raising in the centre of Europe a barrier against 
the encronchments of Russia, alluding plainly to the restoration of the Kingdom 


204 


of Poland, to which he gave it to be understood his Government would never 
consent. 

«© You are mistaken,” replied M, Drouyn de Limys; “ France no doubt 
has sympathies for the Poles, whieh she will never gainsay, and being at war 
with Russia, she ig not sorry that a Polish Legion should be formed in the 
Fast to aid the cause which she is defending. But the reconstruction of the 
Kingdom of Poland, however much she may abstractedly desire it, is politically 
by no means of the same importance [0 her, that, in her opinion, it is to 
Germany, Russia is too far yemoved from France to render her encroach- 
iments dangerous to France, She has a vast amount af way to make before 
she ean reach the French frontier, [t is Germany that requires such a barrier 
between her and Russia as the reconstruction of Poland would furnish. But 
if Germany does not see the advantage of it, it is not for France to stir the 
question.” | 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys then argued on the impolicy of Austria contenting 
herself with the simple evacuation of the Danubian Provinces by the Russians, 
Supposing the evacuation to take place on the summons about to be sent to 
St. Petersburgh by the Austrian Government, did the latter suppose that the 
Russians would not feel the humiliation to which they were subjected, and that 
they would not take the earliest opportunity to avenge themselves on those 
wha had been the immediate cause of this humiliation, namely, the Austrian 
Government; but if the Austrian Government left the Western Powers in the 
lurch, by contentin themselves with the evacuation of the Provinces, did they 
suppose that those Powers would come to the assistance of Austria if attacked 
by Russia? He maintained, therefore, that the true poliey of Austria was to 
act at once and decidedly, and to determine, not to consider, the Eastern 
question as settled, wotil 1 became materially impossible for the Russians to 
make the conquest of Turkey,“ But if you are apprehensive of what may be 
the views and intentions of England and France, ° continued M, Dronyn de 
Lhuys to M. de Hubner, © why do you not propose a Convention tous? Let 
ns, at least, know what it is you desire, and if we can sign a Convention 
together, it is likely that many of the smaller States would wish to join in it, 
Sardinia most sobably among others, and you would thus have indircetly 
during the war a guarantee for the safety of your Italian dominions.” 

ML. Drouyn de Lhnys thinks that his reasoning made considerable impres- 
sion on M. de Hiibner, and that the latter will write to his Government recom- 
mending that something of the kind should be done. At the same time, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys means to send to M. de Bourqueney confidentially the 
substance of thig conversation, and instruct him to follow it up whenever a 
favourable opportunity presents itself, 

When recounting all this to me, M, Drouyn de Lhnys said that he con- 
tinued to receive accounts from Sardinia, whieh showed that a little pressing 
would induce the Sardinian Government. to declare themselves for the Western 
Powers, but that he had written to the Due de Guiche to be cautious in his 
proceedings, ‘The proper time was not arrived, he thought, for putting 
Sardinia forward, A declaration on her part would come with greater effect 
hereafter, either as a relief to Austria, should the latter eventually co-operate 
actively with the Western Powers, or as a menace to her, should her policy 
unfortunately indicate a different tendency. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

No, 216. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Eurl of Clurendon.—( Received May 30.) 
(No, 238.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 17, 1854, 
IT appears that General Baraguay d’Hilliers has been recalled. The 
day before yesterday he wrote to the Sultan's Seeretary, requesting an audience 
af leave, which was granted by His Majesty. He went in fall uniform, un- 
attended by any one but the chief interpreter of his Embassy. No Minister was 


present, and the Porte was not informed of the visit. ‘The Ambassador excused 


205 


this irregularity, on the plea of his almost immediate departure, and the conse- 
quent pressure on his time. He informed the Sultan that he preferred a 
military to a diplomatic position, and that, on returning to France, he was to 
have the command of the Baltic camp. 

| take this opportunity to remark, that in my humble judgement, the 
Sultan would have done better to decline this direct application for an 
andience of leave, which was, in trath, an abuse of privilege, and a slight on 
the Ministers of the Porte. 1am the first Ambassador in favour of whom the 
Sultan has openly admitted a right of private audience, and [ have made a 
point of using the privilege with much reserve, as well out of respect. for His 
Majesty, as to maintain my influence unimpaired. No such considerations 
appear to have ocenrred to my French colleague; and, favoured by the pecu- 
liar cireumstances of the juncture, he has thrown down every barrier, and 
rendered access to the Sultan a matter of mere convenience to himself. Tam 
mistaken if Marshal St. Arnaud is not inclined to pursue the same course, 
The natural results may be foreseen. ‘The Sultan will, hereafter, either return 
fo the old forms of etiquette, or find himself obliged to receive in private all 
Forcign Ministers without distinction, according to their individual pleasure. 
It is, no doubt, mast desirable that the Ottoman Court, as well as the Ottoman 
Government and people, should be brought into easier intercourse with 
foreigners, not only of high diplomatic rank, but of every respectable deserip- 
tion, and the present course of events may produce a salutary effect by facil. 
tating that process. But to those who have the advancement of this Empire at 
heart, and who have had opportunities of studying the character of its Govern: 
ment and people, the advantage of conducting such matters without exageera- 
tion or levity must be apparent, Proceedings of a different stamp originate 
rathor in personal motives, than in views of public interest; and while they 
tend to compromise the dignity of the Throne, they render the whole scheme of 
improvement an object of disgust to the country at large. 

[ have, &e 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

which he justly enjoys. While hesitating whether or not to persevere in the

tive office having been conferred upon him in India, and this cirenmstance, as

He will now present himself under circumstances far more favourable to 
the accomplishment of his purpose, and | shall endeavour to carry out your 
Lordship’s instructions on his behalf, with a confident hope that the Porte will 
not be insensible to the many advantages which may result from his employ- 
ment in the manner proposed, 


Samo difficulties, inherent in the very nature of the undertaking, remain, 
however, to be overcome, and before Colone) Beatson arrives, and is again put 
‘ato personal communication with the Seraskier, who succeeded to Mehemet 
Ali, I cannot hope to ensure the success of my exertions, even with the

the combined fleets off Sebastopol, 1 learn from: his Excellency Vice-Admiral 
Dundas, by a letter dated the 13th instant, that the Wench ‘and English 
squadrons would, weather permitting, be at Baljik for water about the 21st 
instant. 

The Ottoman fleet appeared off Varna a week ago. Moushaver Pasha 
( Admiral Slade) came into Varna in one of the steamers, and after commiuni- 
eating with the authorities here, proceeded in the steamer to communicate with 
the Admirals in command of the combined squadrons off Sebastopol. 

Moushaver Pasha returned here on the 14th instant, and having again 
visited the Pasha, left yesterday to snp Turkish squadron, which had been 

3 


210 


unable to reach the rendezvons at Kavarna Bay owing to contrary winds and 
foggy weather. 

I believe the whole of the Turkish squadron has not yet reached Kavarna 
Bay ; and several of the ships are still lying to the southward of Varna. 

On the 13th instant a line of battle ship got aground during the night in 
a small sandy bay between Varna and Balik. A Turkish steamer coming to 
her assistance, she was got off in a few hours. 

1 understand it is the intention of the ‘Turkish Admiral to anchor in 
Kavarna Bay until the arrival of the combined squadrons at Baljik. 

On the evening of the 14th instant Her Majesty steam sloop “ Fury” 
arrived here from off the Sulina mouth of the Danube and Kustenjee. ‘The 
“Pury brought with her an Ionian brig laden with oil and other stores.

entering the Sulina mouth, and that upon examining her papers she was found 
to have a permit to proceed to Bourghas, and from thenee to the Tonian 
Islands, issued by your Excellency. 

The vessel having heen recently purchased was required to proceed to the 
fonian Islands to obtain the necessary documents,
