My Lord, Varna, May 16, 1854. 

THEE only new feature in the reports which I have received from the 
interior respecting the movements of the Turkish army since I had last the 
honour of addressing your Excellency is, that Selim Pasha, with about 8,000 
or 10,000 of the Egyptian troops, had marched from Shumla to Silistria, and 
that some additional troops had also been ordered from Shumla towards 
Bazardjik. 

The Russian forces in the Dobrudscha is stated, upon the authority of 
several Turkish officers arrived within the las week from the Danube, to consist 
of Gencral Liders’ corps, consisting of 48 battalions, or, al 700 per battalion, 
99600 Infantry, and about 10,000 Cavalry, including the Cossacks ; in all 
about 42,600, exclusive of the usual proportion of Artillery. 

The Russian advanced guard of Cavalry from the foree in the Dobrudscha 
was within four hours of the south-cast of Silistria, I understand that native 
travellers going from this district to Silistria take the road of Shumla, as it is 
considered unsafe to go the direct road. Stores and ammunition sent from 
Shumla to Silistria are now accompanied by strong escort of one or two 
battalions. 

A very considerable quantity of guns, shot and shell, gun cartridges, 
muskets, and other military stores, have heen received recently in Varna from 
Constantinople, but the means of conveyance to Shumla, for which place most 
of these stores are destined, are most dificult to be procured, still some portions 
are sent forward daily.

Inclosure | in No, 222, 
General Lord de Ros to General Lord Raglan. 


My Lord, May 17, 1804. 

IN compliance with your orders, I proceeded on the 10th instant to 
Varna in the “ Banshee,” and landing early on. the llth at that place, rode 
post to Devna, and reached Shumla on the evening of the 12th, Next morning 
[ had a private interview with Omer Pasha, and began by stating your wWisth 
to know his present views and intentions as to the war. 

He said he conceived there was but one course for him to pursue; and 
that he had already taken, and was still taking every measure for the concen- 
tration of his foree at Shumla, with the exception of the Danube garrisons, 
and some regiments of Cavalry which were posted at some villages 1n advaiice, 
hoth for gaining information oF the enemy's movements, and for relieving’ the 
stores of provision in Shumla by the absence of so many horses and men, 
Some squadrons were also posted for communication between Shula and 
Varna. 

Tt was, he said, 2 matter of the ulmost importance to the ‘Turkish arniy 
that the Freneh and English should immediately make some movement demon- 
etrative of aspeedy resolution to support him, He did not desire any prema- 
ture advance of the armies, but the sending up of even 1,000 men to Varna 
by the English, and a small advanced guard of the French to Adrianople, 
would have a most useful effect in encouragement of iis troops, and in checking 
the operations of the Russians towards Silistria, trom which place his list intelli- 
once represented them to be but five marches distant on the south bank of the 
Danube. . ak Rec 

On my observing that the siege of Silistria was in all likelihood their 
immediate mtention, he said he did not feel so sure of that, becanse the rise 
of the Danube these last few days was an impediment to attack on the river 
side, while their knowledge of the concentration of the Turkish force at Shumla, 
only sixty miles distant, would make them hesitate to commence the siege on 
the land side until they had brought up a very large foree to cover their 
besieging army. Now, 8 the troops in Silistria amounted to full 15,000, the 
Russians must have 35,000 for the siege, and double that number for the 
covering army. He estimated their whole force al 140,000, and his own 


Shumla at 50,000; but I think he has not above 45,000 This is exclusive of 


about 4,000 or 5,000 Cavalry in his front, already alluded to. He said his 
authority as Civil Governor of Roumelia, Bulgaria, and Bosnia, enabled him to 


213 


command great supplies for the allied armies in the event of their advance, 
every town and village being assessed in proportion, and no reluetance in the 
‘habitants to contend with ; because the prices fixed by the ‘Turkish Govern- 
ments were a fair and real remuneration to them. He spoke of his having 
already 4,000 carts drawn by two bullocks each, and of 25,000 bullocks “avail- 
able at once as meat for the armies. Orders had been given to certain factories, 
where beasts were killed in great numbers merely for their fat, to desist from 
that proceeding; this being the more important, because in this climate lean 
meat is considered productive of dysentery. 

In reference to this point, he expressed a strong desire that the allied 
fleets should entirely abstain from purchase of vither corn or heef in Roumelia 
or Bulgaria; it raised difficulty as to regulation of prices, and they could, he 
was sure, obtain equally abundant supplies from the coasts of Asia Minor. 

As your Lordship fad desired me to ascertain from Omer Pasha whether 
you or Lord Stratford could in any way assist him with his own Government, 
hw said it would be a very great relief to him if the Sultan would send him a 
public officer to take charge of the whole finance of the army, with which he 
was often much harassed when his attention was needed for other matters. He 
dwelt also very strongly on the great evil of his not having any power of trying 
criminals for life, observing on the horrible alternative left him in aggravated 
eases, such as the recent murder of a boy of ten years old in his father’s sight 
by two followers of the army, of’ sentencing to 500 blows of the stick, which 
the eriminal is seldom known to survive many days. He said, with much 
truth, that such hideous punishments often produced compassion for the 
sufferer, however enormous his guilt, rather than that approval of a just 
example, which so often enhanced its force and moral effect upon the 
soldiers, 

Omer Pasha is not fond of writing, and, indeed, with all he has upon his 
hands, it would be impossible for him to write more than regards his own 
army; and he said he was very anxious to have a “conlidential corresponding 
offiver” from the British army to carry on all his communications with your 
Lordship; remarking, at the same time, on the very great assistance Captain 
Simmons had rendered him both by his correspondence and his thorough 
knowledge of his profession as an ongineer. I asked if I should propose 
Captain Simmons for this purpose, to be permanently attached to Is lead- 
quarters, to which he replied, that nothing would be more agreeable to him if 
+ eould be done, but that it would be still more so if Captain Simmons could 
have two more under him for the “travail de bureau,” thus leaving him more 
time for giving his useful attention to the numerous posts and field-works 
becoming every day more necessary, both at Varna and Pravady. 

Here L feel it is but justice to call your Lordships attention to the very 
great service which I could plainly pereeive Captain Simmons has rendered 
to the Turks by the advice he has given, as Well as by the ability he has 
shown in strengthening the works at Shumla and Pravady, and pointing out 
where the old ones can be improved. 

Omer Pasha receives so much advice, and some of it, as he himself told 
me, so absurd and unealled for, from oflicious adventurers, that it requires 
much discretion to press any matter npon him; and this diseretion, | think, 
Captain Simmons has very judiciously exercised, and with the hest possible 
result of gaining his entire confidence, without exciting any jealousy in those 
about him. At the same time he has acquired a knowledge of that difficult 
country, which may one day prove invaluable to the allies, as well as to 
the ‘Turks. 

Omer Pasha expressed a great wish for a supply of good swords of our 
ordinary pattern for his Cavalry. Jn the exaggerated reforms of Sultan 
Mahmoud, the Turkish Cavalry were deprived of their old sabres and sup- 
plied with a short, weak, and ilenade sword, which lessens the confidence 
of the soldier, I believe that some of our old Light Dragoon swords in store 
at the Tower would be immediately available, 

It would be very desirable that officers going uy to Shumla should have 
some sort of credential to distinguish them from {he persons who are con- 
stantly appearing there as “ Eng ish officers,’ and who are troublesome to 
Omer Pasha, who, in his anxiety to show-attention to our army, finds great 
difficulty in distinguishing who are saicare from reporters and other intrusive 

3 


214 


visitors. It need hardly be added, that there is danger of information reaching 
the Russians through the English newspapers, which would be extremely 
inconvenient. 

In reference to the possibility of forming a corps officered by British or 
French and German officers, Omer Pasha scems to think it might be brought 
about: but that much discretion must be used in the commencement of a 
system so novel to the Turks. He proposes, he told me, to begin with one 
model squadron, and, if he finds no insuperable difficulties, to increase the 
corps by degrees to a regiment; and, once introduced, he anticipated much 
advantage from the example of order, method, and discipline to the army in 
eeneral. 

As had seen at Shumla a person named OReilly, whom | remembered 
an excellent drill at the Maidstone Depdt, | mentioned the fact to Omer Pasha, 
with the assurance that he could not find a man more caleulated for the task, 
while O’Reilly’s present position as supernumerary major of Cavalry, made 
him nearly useless. He seemed to approve the suggestion, but said that 
O'Reilly must first study the Turkish language a little, which is perfectly 
reasonable, and will, | am sure, be diligently followed up by O'Reilly, who is 
an active man, and already knows a little Turkish. 

From what [ saw of the Bulgarian peasantry, 1 cannot but think an 
excellent corps of Cavalry or Infantry might be raised among them by English 
or French officers, and as they are all Christians, no religious obstacles would 
interfere. 

In returning by Varna, I took notice of several facilities for landing 
troops, easily to be accomplished, and | have communicated on this point with 
Admiral Boxer. 

I have, &e. 
(Bigned) DE ROS.

Inclosure 2 in No. 222. 
Memorandum. 


THE meeting at Varna is the first step towards active operations against 
Russia by land. It is the more important as alfording a fit opportunity for 
reviewing the whole situation, and bringing the foree of collective opinion to 
bear on the counsels of the Porte, 

The numerical strength, the efficiency in other respects, the composition 
and distribution of the Turkish army in ulgaria, may then be ascertained, 
together with its command of supplies, its positions for defence, its means 
of recruitment, and its capacity for moving without danger to its communi- 
cations. 

The Commanders-in-chief will also have to consider in what manner the 
auxiliary armies may best co-operate with the native forces, ‘The question of 
command, as well as the plan of campaign will necessarily come into view. 

The theatre of war may be confined to Bulgaria and the Dobrndscha. 

The Russians may possibly obtain an ascendancy there, and risk the 
passage of the Balkan. 

Phe allies may cross the Danube, and attack (licir army in the Princi- 
palities. 

The part to be played by Austria will enter, more or less, into every 
calculation, 

Attention will, no doubt, be paid to the means whieh can be employed for 
improving (he Turkish forces, and rendering them, altogether, more disposable 
and reliable. 

Their officers of the middle and higher grades are said to be generally 
deficient. ‘Their Cavalry is notoriously ill-armed; and the Infantry is far 
from being supplied with muskets of the best kind. ‘There is also the Irregular 
foree, the Bashi-Bozouks, horse and foot—without discipline, without pay, 
without courage, doing in every way more harm than good, and equally 
difficult to retain with advantage, or ta disinias without danger. By what 
additional measures, whether of severe repression, of organization, or ot 


915 


judicious distribution, can they be humanized into soldiers, and made available 
cither separately or otherwise ? 

The aid derivable from the services of foreign officers may also be worthy 
of attention. 

Employed on the Staff, commissioned in the Line, as partisans, instructors, 
or intermediaries, they may, perhaps, in large proportion be turned to account. 
Could not those of a more enterprising character, having experience of irre- 
gular warfare, he employed in reducing bodies of irregular soldiery into some 
kind of order and disposable usefulness. For purposes of this kind the names 
of Colonel Beatson, Sir Stephen Lakeman, and others, naturally present 
themselves. 

Lastly, we have the Poles, with other emigrants on one side, and sundry 
portions of the local Christian population on the other, se ttled like the Cossacks,* 
or indigenous like the Bulgarians. ; 

The means of utilizing these several resources, involve political as well as 
military considerations. With respect to the Poles it would be difficult to 
sug@est anything now. Their claims for our sympathy are very strong. Col- 
lected in good earnest, and formed tor service in such manner as to give full 
scope to their national feelings and military ardour, they might be useful even 
in point of numerical force, and still more so by their moral influence as well on 
Poland, as on the Russian armies, But can they be united? Can adequate 
funds be supplied for their efficient organization and employment? Can they 
be brought forward as they desire, without giving umbrage to Austria, and 
engaging the allies prematurely‘ The solution of this problem 1s very 
desirable, 

Other refugees, if formed into a corps, might, perhaps, be neutralized, as 
to political impressions, by mixture with natives, and employment in Asia, 

Lesser Wallachia, Cireassia, Daghesta ; of these three points of interest it 
may be remarked, that with respect to the second the Admirals haye that matter 
in hand. It remains, however, to be considered, whether the army of Batoum 
might not, since the Russians haye withdrawn and left the natives free to act 
in concert with the ships, be made more useful by reinforcing the army of Kars, 
which is in 80 eplorabl pa state.| 

It is highly desirable that communications should be opened with Schamyl, 
and that a clearer notion should be formed as to his inclination and means of 
cooperating with the Circassians and Turks. It is understood in the present 
state of our information, that he is too far off to assist the army of Kars, though 
he micht detach a force in support of the Circassians, 

With respect to Wallachia, the Porte is prepared to raise the population 
‘i favour of its views, and a man of property, influence, aud military capacity, 
is ready to carry out its intentions, But such a movement has its shectionable 
side with reference to Austria, and the troops at Kalafat might be wanted for 
concentration in Bulgaria, 

The army at Kars, if the latest accounts be true, only in part is exposed 
to much danger, If there is no prospect of its being assisted by the allies, the 
question is the urgency of adopting other expedients for its immediate restora- 
tion to a state of efficiency. Money, gupplics, ammunition, artillery, recruits, 
have been sent, but in very limited quantities, and under unfavourable 
circumstances. ‘The opinion of the Commanders-in-chief might determine the 
Porte to adopt more etlicient measures. The counsels of General Guyon ought 
to be more implicitly followed, and such arrangements should be made as would 
revive the hopes, and retone the energies of the Turkish soldiery. 

‘Turning towards other quarters, and taking in suecession the vulnerable 
points of Servia, Montenegro, Bosnia, and Albania, down to the frontiers of 
Greeve in Thessaly and Epirus, there is, on the whole, a more cheering prospect, 

Servia is no longer menaced by Russia. The vicinity of the Austrian army 
is viewed with less apprehension by the Servians, Austria is disposed, under 
suitable guards and limitations, to enter within the Turkish frontier, controlling

My Lori, Foreign Office, May 31, 1854. 

HER MAJESTY’S Government observe with disappointment and regret 
that the Austro-Prussian Treaty has been communicated to the Conference 
without the Additional Article which alone had reference to the war, or was of 
any value or importance to England and France. 

The Treaty, as it now stands recorded, might, in faet, be considered to 
apply, eventually, as much against England and France as agaist Russia, and 
it is difficult to comprehend in what manner it serves to secure the maintenance 
of the principles recorded in the series of Protocols of the Conference of 
View, 

It isa Treaty of Alliance, offensive and defensive, which the two great 
German Powers have entered into for German objects exelusively, and Fler 
Majesty’s Government cannot, therefore, consider themselves in any way hound 
by the engagements which Austria and Prussia have entered into for these 
objects. 

Tam, &e, 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Sir A. Malet to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received June 2.) 


(No. 58, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Frankfort, May 50, 1854. 

ALTHOUGH in Germany the attitude ‘s one of attempted quictude and 
expectation, it would be quite wrong to suppose that public attention is not 
deeply excited by England’s acts and projects, 

Our alliance with France becomes a subject of progressively increasing 
wonderment as it assumes appearances of ereater extent and durability, and 
all Germany is alive with expectation in seeing England giving a direction to 
European policy in concert with, instead of opposition to, her great continental 
neighbour. 

~The prevailing ‘nelinations of the minor Governments, influenced by 
inordinate fears of Russia, and the occult influence of that Power, exercised in 
various ways, as well as from dislike of incurring the risks and costs of a state 
of war, are unquestionably to observe neutrality. 

I feel, however, equally convinced that anything which would give them 
a semblance of independence, would modify even these dispositions, so deeply 
are they galled by their state of subordination. 

The question occurs how best. may this feeling be utilised and turned to 
account, and two courses of action suggest themselves, which T will endeavour 
to the best of my humble ability to submit to your Lordship’s judgment, 

Phe first of these would be by such action as it might be possible for Her 
Majesty's Government to exercise upon the separate States of the Confedera- 
tion, or upon the Diet itself, 

The composition and idiosyneracy of this bady are too well known to your 
Lordship to make it necessary for me to enlarge upon them. J must, however, 
observe that there exists within this Assembly a sentiment of dissatisfaction at 
their impotence for all useful ends, and a wish to enter on a larger sphere of 
activity, and that any assistance (om tain such objects, come from what quarter 
it might, would mect with eager welcome in not wninfluential quarters. 

i have, for instance, had pointed oul to me by members af the Diet itself 
the clauses of Article XXXV and Article L of the final Act of the Ministerial 
Conferences of Vienna, of May, 1820, establishing political rights in the Dict, 
such as that of contracting ‘Treaties and other attributes of independent 
sovereignty, Which they have never es onerre 

It is the clear opinion of several Members of the Diet with whom I have 
spoken on the subject, that these rights might be called into practical use, but 
your Lordship 1s well aware of the difficulties which would beset any attempts 


219 


to exer a dormant right, unless one or other of the great Powers sanc- 
tioned it. 

Prussia has systematically opposed any useful action of the Diet, especially 
oe the recent reconstitution of that body after the political storms of 
}545-9. 

Austria has been more deferential in forms, but has not in reality varied 
from the old Metternich policy of using this political body as a sort of black- 
hole into which she thrusts troublesome political questions, or as a Star 
Chamber to bear the odium of unpopniar enaetments. 

It is therefore hardly to be expected that Austria or Prussia would concur 
in attempt to arouse the Diet into political activity, unless they had themselves 
a point to gain in so employing it, 

Their influence would besides always succeed In so dividing the votes of 
the secondary and minor States, that, notwithstanding the Articles of the final 
Act previously cited, important measures could scarcely be expected to be 
carried unless by a vigorous interference of the Western Powers in exercising 
rights hitherto allowed to fall into abeyance. ‘This mode, therefore, of acting 
upon the Germanic Confederation would be slow in its operation, and uneertain 
‘nits result: and though it might be worth attention under other circumstances, 
is hardly to be resorted to in a crisis requiting promptitde in decision and 
vigour of action, 

The other mode of proceeding, which I venture to state as possible and 
likely to be effectual, is devhape ealoulated to startle some minds, but not, | 
think, those of Germans, or of persons familiar with German political views 
and ways of thinking, it consists In finding means to satisfy the desire of Prussia 
for territorial extension. 

The wish for this change is by no means confined to Prussia herself, but ts 
familiar to all Germany,.and would, | am persuaded, be acceptable to a far 
greater extent than is venerally supposed elsewhere. 

The great questions attaching to such a change, the assent of France and 
Austria, | do not venture to do more than touch upon, in the persuasion that 
if the object to be attained, namely, that of engaging Prussia to take part in 
our hostilities against Russia, is worth the sacrifice, means will be found of 
conciliating all exigencies and reconciling conflicting Interests. 

| must, however, seck to guard myself In your Lordship’s mind against 
being thonght to have put forward and recommended a measure not accordant 
with notions of volitical morality, by strongly urging my persuasion that, with 
the exception of Holstein, [do not know any state of Germany which could be 
coveted by Prussia that would not be infinitely benefited by the change, and 
my belief that such a re-adjustment of the balance of power (equitable regard 
being had for vested rights), would not only be without danger, but highly 
advantageous to the future tranquillity and prosperity of Europe, guarded as 
it must necessarily be by ‘Treaties and mutual engagements of the most 
stringent kind. 

It cannot escape your Lordship’s perspicacity that Russia, perfectly aware 
of all that Prussia requires, is perhaps at this moment bidding higher for her 
neutrality than we are inclined to do for her active couperation, and it may (1 
anxiously hope) be thought worth while to consider the feasibility of some 
policy which may convert mto useful allies those who, under other influences, 
must be unserviceable friends, if not dangerous enemies. 

It is by no means irrelevant fo what yrecedes, to mention that the President 
of the Diet, Baron Prohesch, is constantly harping upon the doubtfal attitude 
of Prussia, even since the signature and ratification of the Berlin ‘Treaty, and 
on the influence thereby exercised on Austria, in holding her back from the 
course she would otherwise pursue, a point the importance of which will 
certainly not be lost sight of at St. Petersburgh. . 

| have, &c. 
(Signed) A. MALET.

My Lord, Stutigardt, May 24, 1804. 

A CONFERENCE of the Representatives of many of the German States 
to whom the ‘Treaty of Alliance between Austria and Prussia has been 
separately communicated, ‘< to be held at Bamberg in Bavaria, to-morrow, the 
25th instant. 

The object of their meeting is to conceth a common answer to be returned 
by their Representatives at Frankfort, to the communication of that Treaty to 
the Diet, and to the invitation which the Representatives of Austria and Prussia 
are to make to-day to that body to accede to it. Lunderstand that the four 
Royal Courts, the two Hesses, Baden, the two Mecklenburgs, and Nassau will 
be represented at the Conference of Bamburg. M. de Neurath leaves Shut- 
eardt to-day for Bamberg, and it is probable that the Ministers for Woreign 
Affairs of Baden and Hesse Darmstadt, who are expected here, will accom- 
pany him. . 

M. de Neurath thinks he will be absent till the 29th instant, and as he 
may not have returned here before the departure of the next messenger for 
London, | called upon him yesterday, and had 2 conversation with him.on the 
subject of his mission. 

| vemarked that I supposed the States to be represented ut Bamberg 
meant to accede to the Austrian and Prussian invitation, to whieh he observed 
Hat he was not at all certain that such was their intention; he added that what 
they all desired was the re-establishment of peace; or, If war continued, that 
they should be as slighty implicated in it as possihle. 1 then observed [ could 
fully understand both of these wishes, but that if Germany appeared cordially 
united with Austria and Prussia, the Treaty offensive and defensive whieh the 
latter Powers had concluded must have much greater weight in the counsels 
of Russia, and that as to any chance of their being implicated in active warfare 
by their accession to the Treaty, it appeared to me 80 improbable and remote 
that | thought it ought not to weigh in their decision, By their present en- 
wagements as members of the German Confederation, they were bound to 
defend any part of those two States belonging to the Confederation which 
might in consequence of a rupture with Russia be attacked by the latter; and 
| put it to him, whether it was probable that they would ever be required to 
defend those portions which did not belong to the Confederation. He at once 
anawered that he thought they might; he added that Austria was so embar- 
rassed in her finances, he feared she would put her allies forward, not to save 
her army, for she was rich in men, but to economize her finances. 

M. de Neurath told me that both the Courts of Saxony and Bavaria were 
deeply hurt, and he frankly added that the King of Wurtemburg was equally 
amoyed at the reserve and seereey which they had met with from Austria 
respecting the Treaty in question - [ much doubt, however, whether greater 
frankness would haye at all modified their opinions, though it might have 
flattered their self love. ‘The minor States of Germany have such an awe of 
Russian power that they are only too willing to seize on every occasion of 
making a merit of supporting in any underhand way the interests of that State, 
and | hear from guod authority that most of the Representatives of those 
Powers at Vienna express without reserve very Russian views. 

| inguived from my Austrian colleague whether he thought Russia was 
sinenve in her desire to obtain the accession of the other Gernm States to the 
Treaty whieh she had concluded with A austria, M. de Handel, in reply, 
aserree me that both trom the despatches from Berlin which Count Secken- 
Jovif had communicated to him, and from the conduct of the latter here, he 
id vo reason to doubt her sincerity, and | must add that Count Seckendoril’s 
Laneiage on all oceasioas to me has been very much opposed to Russian views. 

It appears to me probable from all I hear that the joint answer to be 
concerted at Bamberg will be an accession in some modified form to the Austro- 
Prussian Treaty, coupled perhaps with the desire or secret stipulation that 


221 


the forces of the minor States shall not be put forward, except for the defence 
of the Confederation. ‘They will, I think, continue to play in secret the 
Russian game, and to make a merit with that Power for so doing. 

M. de Neurath told me that he thought the Bavarian Government would 
endeavour to introduce the subject of Greete at Bamberg, though he did not 
think that such a chord would find any echo. |

My Lord, Paris, June 2, 1854, 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS was good enough to give me yesterday, 
confidentially, the substance of a despatch of some importance, dated the 29th 
ultimo, which he had just received from M, de Bourqueney. | 

M. de Bourqueney had had a conversation with M. de Buol respecting the 
present state of the Eastern question, and the measures to be employed by 
Austria. 

Count Buol stated, that the summons to be sent to St, Petersburgh by the 
Austrian Government, for the evacuation by Russia of th Danubian Princi- 

alities, was ready, and would be sent as soon as the Emperor's sanction to it 

ad been obtained; that Prussia had not required any delay in its transmission, 
as had been supposed, but had merely expressed the hope that its form and 
tenour might be as courteous as cireumstances would permit, and that the 
Austrian Government had never, of course, had the intention of departing from 
this, its general rule of conduct; that Count Alvensleben had shown him the 
document which was to be sent by the Prussian Government to St. Petersburgh, 
in support of the Austrian summons, and that he was satisfied with it; that he 
had, in return, communicated to Count Alvensleben the substance—not the 
text—of the summons; that no observations had been made by the latter, nor 
would they be attended to, if made, 

M, de Bourqueney then asked M. de Buol whether he had reflected on the 
course which Austria should pursue, if the answer to this summons was neither 
complete silence, nor a refusal, but evasive. He could not but fear that this 
would be the plan followed by Russia ; that she would endeavour to gain time, 
and, by negotiations, prevent Austria from taking any active pe in the present 
campaign, ‘The Emperor of Russia had never abandoned the hope of destroying 
the unanimity of purpose which existed among the Four Powers; and, if he 
could stave olf until the winter all ane cooperation against him on the part of

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Karl of Clarendon.-—(Recetved June f.) 


(No. 255.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 25, 1854. 

MARSHAL ST. ARNAUD and Lord Raglan returned from Shumla and 
Varna the day before yesterday. T have not seen either of them since their 
return, Lord Raglin has been detained in camp by indisposition, and a similar 
cause has prevented iny going to wait upon his Lordship, though I hope to make 
the attempt to-day, after the departure of the messenger. 

T learn, meanwhile, that strenuous efforts are making by the two Com- 
manders-in-chief to convey ft considerable force into Bulgaria, by way of Varna, 
with the utmost practieable dispatch. Sir George Brown's division has received 
orders to embark for that destination without any unnecessary delay. At Lord 
Raglan’s request, | have applied to the Porte for orders to procure whatever the 
troops are likely to want from the Turkish authorities in point of supplies and 
means of conveyance. I have also given letters in the same sense to the Com- 
missaries dispatched with that view to Shumla and Varna. 

Lam informed by Mr, Alison that the British and French Generals were 
pleased with what they saw of the Turkish troops; that Omer Pasha will be able 
to concentrate: between 60,000 and 70,000 men, after withdrawing 10,000 from 
Kalafat, and 6,000 from the Danube. 

The Russians are engaged in besieging Silistria. ‘They appear to have about 
70,000 men on the sout tern bank of the river. The earrison of Silistria 1s stated 
at 16,000. Ef the place is duly provisioned, of which there is. a doubt—I hope & 
eyoundless doubt—it may be expected, as Tam told, to resist for three or four 
weeks. 

Inctosed herewith are translations of two yeports transmitted from Omer 
Pasha to the Turkish Government, and communicated by the latter to me, 

L have thought it my duty to state these leading points to your Lordship. 
But fuller accounts will no doubt be forwarded by to-day’s messenger from Lord 
Raglan to his Grace the Duke of Newcastle. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Inclosure 1 in No. 232, 
The President of the Council at Silistria to Omer Pasha. 


(‘lranstation,) May 19, 1854. 
ON Tuesday last 1 informed your Fxcelleney that the Russians had thrown 
a bridge over at Killik Bournan, and had established their camp there, pushing 
forward their troops to within cannon range. The fortifications on the hill above 
the Bilanlik battery on the ground commanding Silistria being weak, another 


226 


six-gun battery had been constructed and occupied by Colonel Mustapha Bey with 
three Egyptian regiments. ‘The Russians on Wednesday last marched some 
Infantry and Cavalry with eight guns against that battery, and we sent out the 
Irregular Cavalry with three guns to meet them, under the command of Mirliva 
Hassan Pasha and the aforesaid Colonel. The reserve, consisting of the Regular 
Cavalry and one battalion of Infantry, was also moved forward, and the action com- 
menced on both sides. ‘Ihe enemy was defeated by the valour of our regular and 
irregular troops, and lost upwards of 200 men, We had five men and six horses 
killed. Great praise is due to all hands, but especially to Mustapha Bey and 
the commander of the Damascus Irregular Cavalry for their gallant attack. 

On ‘Thursday the Russians moved thei troops forward to the distance of 
cannon range from their camps, and we also met that movement by drawing up 
our forces at an equal distance from the aforesaid battery, but both parties retired 
without any action taking place. 

To-day, Friday, we are also both prepared for action, but it is now | P.M. 
and no movement has taken place, 

Last night the enemy commenced fortitying his first parallel, and to-day 
they have constructed a battery and zigzag approaches. It is evidently the 
intention of the Russians to invest the place, but we trust in God that thei 
object will be frustrated by your Highness’ advance with the army, and a great 
battle which will result im the infidels’ being thrust back into the Danube, to 
their utter destruction. 

During the last three days the Russians have been pouring shot and shell 
into Silistria from the fortifications on the opposite bank and on the island, 
night and day. We have not suffered much, thank God, neither by fire nor 
from their shot, which fell principally upon the hospital and barracks, suffering 
severely, ‘Three of the sick were killed by one shot, and we have removed them 
to the easemates under the Medjidiyé battery. A number of other buildings 
in the fortress have been destroyed, and neither the troops nor the inhabitants 
have a moment’s rest or sleep. . 

From the midst of the fire we look forward to the speedy arrival of your 
Highness with the army. 


Inclosure 2 in No. 282, 
Mousse Pusha to Omer Pashe. 


(Translation.) Silistria, May 21, 1854. 

YESTERDAY, Saturday, the Russians marched some troops against the 
outworks and were duly opposed on the part of our troops. In the action which 
ensued we lost a few killed and wounded, while the Russians, defeated by the 
bravery of our troops, had 150 men killed and a great many wounded. They 
attacked the fortifications again to-day, Sunday. During the action two Russian 
horsemen, Cireassians, came over to our troops, and were interrogated by me. 
They are both “ Mulazims’’ (Lnsigns), and are called Osman and fassan. 
Inspired by religious zeal, they deserted to give information of the Russian 
movements. The Russians have, they state, come against Silistria with three 
corps d’armée ; the Emperor's son is with them. They have made a vow either 
to take Silistria to-day by assault or to sacrifice their army. ‘They have the 
appearance at present of attacking the works round Silistria; but as they are 
prevented from advancing by the fire of the batteries, their troops are stationed 
without cannon ranges. Our troops are properly distributed amongst the 
batteries and are prepared to defend them, There is no knowing what will 
happen next; but, as we are in great distress, we beg, as I have before done. 
that we may be speedily suceoured.

No, 233. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 6.) 


(No. 256. Confidential.) 
My Lord, tonstantinople, May 25, 1554, 

HERE is much reason to apprehend that Riza Pasha, the Seraskier, 
instead of making his visit to Varna an occasion of reconciling himself with the 
Turkish Generalissimo and acquiring his confidence, acted so as to increase the 
estrangement between them, and to cause additional dissatisfaction to his 
Highness, Such was the impression made upon Mr. Alison, and also upon 
Lord Raglan. 

Apprehensive of some such consequence | had discouraged the idea of the 
Seraskier’s going on to Shumla, unless Omer Pasha proposed or appeared to like 
it, and the European Generals thought proper to ie of the party. It would 
seem that Marshal de St. Arnaud, though agreeing beforehand with the 
Seraskier's intention of pushing on to Shumla, recognized the importance of 
upholding Omer Pasha, and not affording him cause of discontent. 

On returning to Constantinople, the Seraskier went straight to the Sultan 
and proposed that His Majesty should give audience to the French Marshal on 
the following day in the presence of several of lis Ministers. Reshid Pasha, on 
receiving notice of this arrangement, sent word of it to me, and expressed his 
opinion that Lord Raglan ought to have the opportunity of bemg present at the 
came audience.  apprized his Lordship of this suggestion, and I stated both to 
him and to Reshid Pasha my impressions as to the impropriety of such irregular 
and unilateral proceedings, not over respectful to the Sultan, and likely to be 
attended eventually with much inconvenience and risk of understanding to all 
parties. 

The audience took place without Lord Raglan, who was Indeed toa unwell 
at the time to attend. 

1 have since been informed by Reshid Pasha that Marshal St, Arnaud’s 
communications to the Sultan were confined to a statement of what he had 
observed in the Turkish camp, and of what he intended to do in conjunction 
with Omer Pasha, with the addition of an enurnest recommendation that 
measures should be forthwith adopted in order to obtain an adequate supply of 
money for the prosecution of the war. ; 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

(No. 257.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 25, 1854, 
THE Austrian Internuncio called here yesterday, and with much courtesy 
of expression informed me that he was authorized to put the Porte in possession 
of the late Convention signed und ratified between the Courts of Vienna anil 
Berlin. ‘The communication was, in substance at least, to comprise the Addi- 
tional Article, which he appeared to identify with what has been elsewhere 
termed the Secret Articles of the Convention. ‘The Prussian overture for pouce 
had, he told me, been rejected by the Russian Government. The Cabinet of 
Vienna was now proceeding to make a formal demand. at St. Petersburgh for 
the evacuation of the Principalities. If Russia withheld her consent, Austria 
would be free to enter upon that territory, and meanwhile, a5 ! understood him 
to say, an Austrian army would take position in ‘Transylvania. if Russia were 
to attack the Austrian territory in consequence of the former movement, 
Prussia was engaged to send troops for its defence, and the same obligation 


228 


would take effect in case that Russia should either annex the Prinicipalities, or 
advance beyond the Balkan. poe - 
| thanked Baron Bruck for s0 encouraging @ communication, and 
endeavoured to ascertain whether he could afford me any explanation of the late 
change of Ministry at Berlin consistent with the policy im icated by that Con- 
vention of which he had so obligingly given me an outline. His answer implied 
that he was equally at a loss with pe te explain the apparent contradiction.

Inclosure:1 in No. 235. 


Admiral Slade to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, “ Techrifieh,” Kavarna, May 19, 1854. 

ASSUMING that you have been aware of the departure of the Ottoman 
squadron from the Bosphorus, 1 will now acquaint you with its subsequent 
movements. | 

Achmet Pashi’s orders were to proceed straight to the combined fleet, 
even before Sebastopol 5 and, after consulting with the Admirals, and combining 
operations with them, to proceed to the coast of Cireassia, land there the 
Cireassians and warlike stores embarked in the fleet, and take Soukoum-Kaleh, 
for which, and other objects, a regiment would be spared from the Batoom 
division. 

On the Sth instant, we sent a steamer to Varna, and there found a letter 
from Admiral Dundas to Achmet Pasha, telling him that he had heard from the 
Captain Pasha of the Turkish squadron coming to join, and co-operate with him, 
but that nevertheless, it was his and Admiral Hamelin’s o inion, that it would 
he desirable first to cruise on the coast of Roumelia and of Bulgaria until the 
the return of Sir Edamund Lyons from Cireassia, and the arrival of the combined 
leets at Varna, which would be on or about the 20th instant. ) 

The delay was not approved of in the fleet, especially by the Circassian 
Pashas: and | was deputed to find the Admirals, read Achmet Pasha's orders to 
them, and explain the cirenmstances of the fleet, Proceeding accordingly in @ 
steamer, feaving (he squadron off Cape Kellagria as a rendezvous, | found the 
combined fleets on the U1th instant, twenty-five miles off Sebastopol. Waiting 
on the Admirals in their respective ships, | communicated Achmet Pusha’s orders 
to them; also memorandum to show the nature of the service intended for his 
aquadron. . 

| beg to inelose the memorundum for your Lordship’s perusal, to show you 
that all arguments have been used to obviate delay in carrying out the objects for 
whieh we have come to sea, ‘To me it 1s a matter of regret that the expedition 


225 


now on the coast, had not been delayed a few days from us. It is thought that 
the information it will bring, will prove valuable to us, but! doubt if any that 
may be picked up in a hasty first visit can add to the information which the Porte 
has collected on the subject lately, and possesses traditionally, Both Admirals, 
separately, expressed their discontent to me, at the ‘Turkish squadron having 
come out with the intention of dog more than eruize on the coast of Europe, 
as they had recommended. 1 observed that it might do good service on the 
eastern, but would perhaps be in the way on the western shores of the Black 
Sea, ‘The scarcity of supplies raises a particular objection to agglomerating more 
force than is necessary on one point. With the slender ration of the Turkish 
suilor, we require 200 sheep daily ; wedo not obtain half that number, and it may 
be, in a few ave none will be forthcoming: only 300 head of cattle, three days’ 
supply, have, [ hear, been collected at Varna for the English fleet, and fresh meat 
is needed there, for the scurvy has appeared in one or two of the ships, so Admiral 
Dundas told me. That malady, is, I hear, among the Turkish troops on the 
Danube, and there is a amall cneampment, near Varna, of men thus atfected, 
brought from Matchin. We have had lately about 50 cases in the Turkish fleet 
in the Bosphorus, which of course went to the hospital, Damp, monotony, and 
nostalgia, have been the predisposing causes wilh us. 

The Admirals told me they could not confer with me separately on the 
matter 1 had come about; but promised to meet in one or other of the Rahs 
adding there would not be much delay, as they would make sail for Baltchik on 
the 15th instant, if some absent steamers returned from the Bay of Odessa as 
expected, 

1 found Admiral Hamelin and his Staff-Captain very sore with me on 
account of my letter to your Excellency of the 14th December last, which | 
learnt then had been transmitted to the Admiral by the French Minister of 
Marine. 

The Admirals altered their minds about a conference, and did not mect 
while | was in company. 

On taking my leave on the 15th instant, Admiral Dundas gave meva: letter 
for Achmet Pasha, which only contained a recommendation to him to abide by 
the advice given in his previous letter, and a caut ion not to send him a verbal 
message in future, He desired me alse to mention his wish for the Turkish fleet 
to go to Kavarna on the Lith instant, to wait the arrival of the combined fleet ; 
but we intend to weigh in the morning and remain under weigh until it 
makes its appearance, grieving all the time to see valuable time slipping away. 
The objection of the Admirals to see the Turkish flect employed elsewhere than 
‘1 the Roumelian and Bulgarian const is anomalous, for they seem resolved that 
‘t shall neither sail or remain at anchor with them. This exclusion would 
assuredly affect the morate of the Turkish fleet, and constitutes a reason for its 
being employed elsewhere, apart from the consideration that European ships, 
wanting the affinities of language, customs, and religion, and being strange to 
the scene, cannot effect the good on the coast of Circassin that ‘Turkish ships 
ca. Admiral Hamelin has told me that he does not wish to have another 
Sinope reproached him, and if we go to the eastward the allies must watch 
Sebastopol. 

T have observed in reply that no parallel exists between the circumstances 
of last November and the circumstances of the present time, whether in regard 
to the composition of the Turkish fleet at sea, or in regard to the position of the 
allies, ‘The ‘Turkish fleet would render a good service if it should be the bait 
to draw out the Russian flect. In the meanwhile no objection is seen to our 
lying in the outer berth of the Bay of Kavarna while they occupy the inner one, 
twelve miles distant. ‘The wish of the Admirals has been for the Turkish fleet to 
remain in the Bosphorus altogether; they, in conjunction with their Rear-Admirals, 
had drawn upa letter to their respective Ambassadors recommending that. Iwas 
then at Baltchik ; they were kind enough to read it to me; I protested against 
stich a recommendation being made, and overruled it, “The passage was erased, 
and a recommendation for its eruizing on the coast of Europe pending eventuali- 
ties substituted. Lhad no oceusion to make more thana cursory remark on that, as 
they were already aware of a proposition of mine to the Captain Pasha for its 
employment elsewhere, It is short-sighted policy, in my humble opinion, to 
repress or depress the ‘Turkish fleet, for 1t ts ina position to turn the seale in the 
Euxine, assuming certain possible contingencies. The Turkish officers and 

aN 


230 


seamen are very inexperienced, and another season in the Bosphorus would have 
been of serious detriment to them. The elements are their chief foe ; and it was 
this feeling which made poor Osman Pasha remain at anchor. He had been 
heard to say that he would rather meet the Russians than another gale of wind. 
Believe me, &e, 
(Signed) A. SLADE. 


P.S.—I will keep your Excellency informed of the movements of the 
Turkish fleet as opportunity occurs.

Memorandum, 


THE weakness of the Turkish army in Asia has excited serious apprehen- 
sion, viewing the consequences that would probably ensue from its defeat. In 
that case the Russian army of Georgia would occupy Erzeroom in the course of 
the ensuing summer: and decided by that exhibition of force, Persia, now 
waiting en events, would declare herself avainst the Porte, and in all likehhood 
march on Bagdad, the conquest of which would prove very acceptable to the 
whole Persian nation, and would be considered more than an equivalent for the 
provinces wrested from Persia by Russia during the last half-century. Hereditary 
association and relizious fervour both influence the Persians with respect to 
Bagdad, and the Power which will hold that prize out to them must be readily 
listened to. Such an event might necessitate the sending of an Anglo-Indian 
army to the Euphrates, for the extension of Persian power under Tussian 
protection interests England as much as the decline of Ottoman power under 
Russian pressure. 

The Sublime Porte has considered that it may find the means’ of checking 
the assumed advance of the Russian army of Georgia across its Asiatic frontier, 
in the hostility of the Cireassian and Daghistan tribes. Hitherto, during the 
present war, those tribes have rendered no service to the Sublime Porte, and 
have offered no more hindrance to Russia than they have done at any period 
during twenty years: their attitude has been defensive, whereas the object. is to 
render it offensive, thereby acting on Russia by creating the apprehension of, or 
by making, a powerful diversion on the flank or rear of her army in Asia. For 
this purpose it is necessary to unite cordially the tribes under Sheik Schamyl's 
direct rule and the tribes ruled vicariously by him, and to supply them with aid 
in the guise af soldiers and munitions of war, and if possible with money. 

With orders to proceed to the coast of Cireassia, after consultation with the 
allied Adinirals, the Turkish squadron has left the Bosphorus. Sefer Pasha and 
Behtchet Pasha are embarked in the squndron, with about 150 Cireassians, their 
countrymen, and with several European military officers. They bear the 
<ultan’s firman empowering them to act in his name, and are carrying mishams 
of merit and of rank to give to influential individuals, ‘They are sanguine in the 
hape of being able to create union between Sheik Schamyl's people and the 
Circassians, and induce offensive operations on an extensive scale; they have 
the feeling that unless the Circassian tribes operate in concert, the Russian 
advance in Asia will be certain. 

There is embarked with the fleet a battery of ficld-pieces, with all appurte- 
nances complete, including two Artillery officers, and 800 rounds of ammunition 
for each gun; also 400 barrels of cunpowder, 500 cases of muskets, 40,000 
pistols, 20 cases of cuthisses, 10,000 moulds of lead, 1,000 axes, 7 cases of flints, 
SA soup kettles, 20,000 okes of salt, besides tents and bales of cotton goods. 
Some Circassian merchants have also cinbarked with wares, to reopen the trade 
suspended for many years. 

' Concurrently an order has been sent to Selim Pasha for the embarkation of 
«regiment at Batoom for conveyance to Cireassia in the fleet. 

It is anticipated that with 4,000 regular troops, Sotie Europeun officers, & 

battery of guos, and the other named munitions af war, the Circassian lorces 


21 


will be able to act offensively on the enemy’s territory; at the same time 
Soukoum-Kaleh, alter being reduced, will be garrisoned, its works strengthened, 
+n order to its part becoming of due value to Turkey. 

The Circassian Pashas in the Turkish squadron, and the superior officers of 
the squadron, trust that the allied Admirals will see with pleasure the departure 
of the squadron from the coast of Roumelia to the coast of Circassia without 
delay. ‘Time 18 precious ; the season for operations is rapidly advancing ; and if 
the Circassians shall not he able to act soon, it is doubtful af they will be in a 
position to render valid service in the war. Defensive hostility will prove of ne 
avail as regards the point at issue; they must take the offensive, and to do that 
effectually they require the exeiting causes of union 1m rewards and prise, ancl 
the encouragement and aid which the Ottoman squadron 1s bringing them, not 
mentioning the effect which the presence of that squadron on their coast 1s 
calculated to produce. . 

The Porte has been in communication with the Circassians on the subject, 
and the latter are daily expecting the squadron with the promised aid, as the 
signal for their gathering, If it does not soon make its appearance doubts may 
arise in their minds of the Porte’s earnestness. . 

(Signed) A. SLADE.

Mr. Grey to the Earl of Clorendon.—( Received June 6.) 


(No, 129. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Stockholm, May 28, 1504. 

1 LEARN this day from authority upen which I have implicit reliance, that 
‘ystructions have lately been sent to the Swedish Minister at Vienna, General 
Mansbach, to inquire from the Austrian Government what course they proposed 
to pursue in the present state of affairs, and, as far as he was able, to ascertain 
the real intentions of Austria, General Mansbach was further instructed to 
accompany these inquiries with the most flattering expressions with regard to 
Austria on the part of Sweden, Count Buol is said to have received the 
Swedish Minister's compliments with evident pleasure, and in reply to his 
inquiries, to have said, * Your Government will shortly receive 0 communication, 
whieli will be made to them by General Langeman, at Stockholm.” 

According to my informant this communication is anxiously expected by 
the King; and, as far as Tam able to form an opinion, it appears that His 
Majesty supposes that the Austeian Government will suggest to Sweden the 
possibility of the two Powers acting in concert against Hussia, the one in the 
south, and the other in the north. 

1 was further told that a Seeret Article of the Convention between Austria 
and Prussia was the ground upon which the King founded his expectations, f will 
not say, his hopes. ‘Chis Article 1s said to be to the following effect :— 

That u prolonged oceupation (une cecupation prolongée) af the Danubian 
Principalities by Russia would, inthe eves of Prussia, justify an active intervention 
on the part of Austria; and if euch intervention was the immediate cause of a 
war, Prussia would deem it her duty to take the side of Austria, | 

Your Lordship will doubtless know whether any such Seeret Article exists 
or not; but I have reason to believe that if such 18 the case, any communi- 
cation from the Austrian Government to Sweden in the sense I have reported, 
will be most favourably received. 

I have, &e,

LORD STRATFORD écrit de Constantinople le 31 Mai, 1854: 


“Lord Raglan wishes your Lordship to be informed that the movement of 
the allied armics upon Varna has commenced; that a div'sion of the British 
foree has already arrived there, and a part of a division of the French army will 
arrive there to-day or to-morrow; that the siege of Silistria is proceeding with 
great activity, and that, under the circumstances, it would be of the greatest 
benefit if the Austrian corps could be moved to Widdin by water, or even lower 
down the Danube, at the earliest moment possible.”

No. 259. 
Sir J Millanke to the Earl af Clarendon.—(CReceived June 7.) 
io. 36.) 


My Lord, Munich, June 2, 1854. 
ah a i a a ‘ Ld LI 
THE Bamberg Conference has terminated in a far more satisfactory manner 
than the language held by M. von der Pfordten to myself and my Freneli 


colleague had led us to expect. 


lt seems that finding, before the deliberations commenced, how little 


233 


chance he had of obtaining any support to his projected conditions in respect to 
Greece, he made a virtue of necessity, and opened the proceedings in a speech 
in which he dwelt upon the propriety of the closest union among the German 
Powers in the present crisis, and recommended their immediate accession to 
the Austro-Prussian Treaty signed at Berlin on the 20th of April. 

The only semblance of a condition, if such it can be termed, was, as far as 
Lean learn, that the adhesion of the smaller States should be given collec- 
tively through the Diet, in such a manner as to exhibit their determination to 
uphold and maintain the coalition, the groundwork of which was laid at the 
Darmstadt Conferences some time ago, against any encroachments which might 
be attempted against their independence by the two great German Powers. 

It is somewhat singular that precisely those small States—for instance, the 
Grand Duchy of Hesse, the Kingdom of Wurtemburg, and the Duchy of 
Nassau—whose reigning houses are closely connected with the Imperial family 
of Russia, are said to have been the most pressing and eager for an immediate 
and unconditional adhesion to the policy of the two Great Powers. If such be 
the case, as I am informed from very good authority, Lean only account for it 
on the ground of the apprehension felt by their respective Governments as 
ta the effects which a contrary course would have produced on public opinion. 

M, von der Pfordten has returned from Bamberg to this capital, but [ have 
not yet had an opportunity of conversing with him on these subjects. 

T have, eS 


(Signed) R, MILBANKE.

My Lord, Paris, June 7, 1854, 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received this morning from M. de Bourqueney 
a despatch dated the 3rd instant, in which that Minister informs him that he 
had been invited, together with the Earl of Westmorland, to a conference by 
Count Buol, at which the latter had communicated to them the despateh about 
to be sent to St. Petersburgh to engage Russia to evacuate the Principalities. 

M. de Bourqueney intimates that the tone of this despatch is much milder 
than he thinks the circumstances of the case require. Russia 1s requested to 
fix an early and positive period for the retreat of her armies beyond the Pruth, 
ind to engage at once not to advance beyond the Danube. 

This despatch is accompanied by another not inte nded for Count Nesselrode's 
knowledge, in which Count Esterhazy is charged not to enter into any discussion 
respecting the operations of the maritime Powers. 

Afier this communication some discussion appears to have ensued between

M, de Bourqueney and Count Buol as to the terms on which a final peace 
might be concluded: but the wording of M. de Bourqueney’s despatch on this 
point is so vague that it is impossible without further elucidation to understand

I was sorry to observe that M. de Buol stated, that although all diligence 
had been employed, both by the civil and military authorities, the Austrian

BARON MANTEUFFEL told me to-day that the summons to evacuate 
the Principalities had left Vienna for St. Petersburgh on the 4th instant, and 
that the Austrian Government demanded a clear and an immediate answer to 
their communication. 

I inquired if the King of Prussia approved of the terms in which the 
summons was drawn up. His Excellency veplied that His Majesty rezretted 
that the Austrian Government had not alluded to the retiring of the fleets 
of the Western Powers from the Black and Baltie Seas as necessarily taking 
place simultaneously with the evacuation of the Principalities; and he gave me 
‘most to understand that the King had suggested the insertion of something 
to this effect; however, Baron Manteuffel informed me notwithstanding this 
objection that His Majesty would support the summons at St. Petersburgh, and 
that a messenger should this night be dispatched with orders on the subject to 
the Prussian Chargé d’ Affaires at the Imperial Court.

| HAVE the honour to inclose to your Lordship herewith an analysis of 4 
memoir drawn up by M. von der Pfordten, and submitted to the Conference 


of the German States lately held at Bamberg. I am informed that the 
collective declaration agreed upon by the Plenipotentiaries assembled there and 
transmitted to their respective Courts for ratification is founded on the opinions 
and embraces all the points expressed in the inclosed document. 

This memoir indisputably bears proof of the exclusive pretensions which 
the group of States in Central and Southern Germany (and previously known 
as the “ Darmstadt Coalition”) assume to itself, Lt is evidently their wish and 
ambition, under the influence and intrigues of Bavaria and Saxony, to create 
in Germany an intermediate or third Power, and thus to obstruct and impede 
the policy of the two Great German States. Lam likewise informed that the 
replies which have been received from the different States who met at Bamberg, 
to the invitation of accession to the Austro-Prussian Convention addressed by 
Prussia, are identic in language and embody likewise the opinions expressed in 
this Bavarian memoir. 

Tam told that they further contain the wish that all the communications 
which have taken or may hereafter take place on the Oriental Question 
should be laid before the Diet at Frankfort. It would thus seem to be their 
abject to establish a permanent Committee of the Diet who shall discuss these 
questions, and to give to that federal body the character of a separate anit 
independent power. 

[ have been informed that they likewise intend to propose that the whole 
af the Austrian and Prussian armies shall be at the disposal of the Diet, ns a 
counterpoise to the guarantee to Austria and Prassia of their non-German 
possessions, 

Baron Manteuftel, in speaking to me this evening of the Bamberg 
Conference, remarked with some bitterness that sAustria had on a previous 
occasion instigated this coalition against Prussia, and that in the present 
‘istance she had found her policy to recoil against herself, 

‘These States have been much annoyed at the communication of the 
Austro-Prussian Convention to the Vienna Conference previous to its being laid

yielding its important interests to factious intriguers,

No. 246. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 10.) 


(No. 222. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, June 7, 1854. 

WITH the view of carrying out your Lordship’s instructions, as contained 
in your confidential despatch No, 192 of the 31st ultimo, directing me to hold 
similar language to that whieh is detailed in the despatch of Lord Cowley, 
No. 663, as having been held to the Austrian Representative ut Paris by 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, | read the substance of that dcatient to Count Buol. 
Previously, however, to my doing 50, I consulted with M. de Bourqueney, who 
had informed me of his having received a despatch from his Government, which 
he was ordered to communicate to Count Buol, and which was generally of a 
similar import to the conversation to which the despateh I had received referred. 
M. de Bourqueney stated that there was a passage in the despatch addressed to 
him which alluded to the Sardinian Government, which he thought at the present 
moment it would be unadvisable to bring forward, and he had by telegraph 
inquired of his Government whether they would authorise his omitting it, and 
he had reecived their sanction to do so; he therefore requested me, if there was 
any such allusion in the memorandum of M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ conversation, 
that I would equally abstain from alluding to it, nt in deference to his desire 1 
azreed to do so, 

Upon the general questions which might arise ifa negotiation was entered 
‘ato with Russia for the reestablishment of peace, Count Buol entirely agreed 
with the statement made by M. Drouyn de Lhuys, that France had as much need 
of Russia to preserve the balance of power in Europe as Austria had, and that it 
might be as essential to her to haye the assistance of Russia to keep Central 
Europe in order, as it would be to Austria, under certain circumstances, to hold 
France in check; but Count Buol believed that neither of these eventualities 
were likely toarise. He then stated that there could be no doubt that Russia, 
by her invasion of the Principalities, had taken advantage of her preponderating 
position towards ‘Turkey, which Austria had never failed to remonstrate against, 
und he thought that Russia ought no longer to retain the sole Protectorate of 
those Provinces, but that means should be taken to secure their present relations 
with ‘Turkey under the guarantee of the European Powers. Count Buol also 
thought that stipulations should be entered into by which the mouths of the 
Danube might be rendered entirely free, with a view to which he considered thuat 
i portion of territory which was tow belonging to Russia, should be ceded for 
that purpose, 

With respect to the Treaty of 1841, by which foreign ships of war were 
interdieted from passing through the Dardanelles or the Bosphorus, Count Buol 
thought that the Sultan should be consulted as to its abrogation or its modification 
that it certainly might be a question with that Sovereign low far it would suit 
his objects to have foreign ships of war passing under the windows of his palace 


without restrictions; but he in no way objected to take the whole matter into 


207 


eonsideration, with the view of coming to a proper arrangement with regard 
to it. 

Count Buol expressed, however, his belief that the events of war might at 
any time bring about a material change in the views of the allied Powers as to 
ihe stipulations by which the restoration of peace might be accompanied. Any 
great, success, such as the taking of Sebastopol, might render the arrangements 
at present contemplated inapplicable to the altered position of the contending 
parties, in the same way that successes on the part of Russia might render 
those at present to be required of her more difficult of attainment. There could 
he no doubt that the evacuation of the Principalities by the Russian troops, with 
the understanding amongst the allied Powers that the status quo with regard to 
them was not to be reestablished, would be a considerable advantage to have 
obtained ; but while the operations of war continued, no questions short of those 
for which the war had been undertaken and for the attainment of which the allies 
of Turkey had bound themselves by the engagements which they had contracted 
amonest themselves, could with any certainty be decided upon. 

While I was reading that part of M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ conversation, ais 
reported by Lord Cowley, which relates to Poland, and in which he states that 
it was not for France to stir that question, ’ Count Buol remarked that it was 
similar in tendency to what was stated in M. Dronyn de Lhuys’ despatch, which 
M. de Bourqueney had read to him; and that Minister told me that Count Buol 
had been so much satistied by that passage that he had requested to be furnished 
with a copy of it, which M. de Bourqueney had complied with. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

Mr, Bligh to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received June 10.) 


(No. 19.) 
My Lord, Hanover, June 7, 1854. 

HE word to that effect having been given from M unich, the Austrian and 
Prussian Ministers have received trom the Hanoverian Government, as the result 
of the Bamberg Conferences, formal answers to the communication made to this 
as to all other Governments of Germany, of the Austro-Prussian ‘Treaty of 
April 20, and 1 understand from M, de Lenthe, that the Hanoverian answer 1s 
‘dentical with that of all the Governments which were represented at Bamberg. 

‘As far as 1 can ascertain, no accredited agent of the Governments which 
took part in the Conferences in question, was better disposed than M. de Lenthe 
to give a pure and simple adhesion to the Treaty, the adoption of which would 
have strengthened the position of Austria, and obviated prejudicial delays as to 
the course of action under certain eventualities which may ensue, from the 
reservations which the Governments represented at Bamberg express their 
intention of attaching to their adhesion to the ‘Treaty, if it should be submitted 
io the Diet for that purpose. 

Their intention of reserving to themselves the right of deciding as to the 
application of certain provisions of the Separate Article of the Treaty which have 
reference to offensive action, may only have been put forward for the assertion 
of their independent rights, and may, and probably will, not prevent their acting 
in common with the Great German Powers under the specified eventualities ; 
but anything like hesitation as to community of purpose is, of course, much to 
be deprecated at the present moment, whilst Prussia is so vacillating and whilst 
Russia is striving to foment discord in the Confederation. Something, however, 
would appear to have been gained! by the unanimity which prevailed in a right 
direction at Bamberg, when, from the strong desire of Bavaria to mix up Greek 
polities with the question, and the Russian predilections of some, at least, of the 
Courts, disunion favourable to their cause wis expected by Russian agents, 
among others by Baron Budberg, according to observations of his when he was 
lately here, which were reported to me. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) J.D. BLIGH,

My Lord, Vienna, June 7, 1854. 


_WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatch No. 191 of the 31st ultimo, 

stating the regret and i aU eta felt that the Austro-Prussian Treaty had 
heen communicated to the Conference without the Additional Article, which alone 
had reference to the war, or was ofany value or importance to En eland and France, 
I think it right to explain that as I had not heen furnished with any instructions 
from your Lordship, except that in reply to a confidential communication to 
you of the 3rd of May, in which I stated that M. de Bourqueney ‘ had on that 
day proposed to Count Buol to take into consideration the propriety of assem- 
bling the Conference, in order that the English and French Treaty of the Lath 
of April might be officially communicated and placed on the Protocal of the 
Conference, and that the new Treaty or Convention between Austria and Prussia 
might be equally communicated in the same way ;” your Lordship had answered 
in your letter of the 9th of May, that * you considered it would be quite right to 
summons the Conference to place on record the two Conventions, namely, that 
of France and England and that of Austria and Prussia, but that there should 
also be a memorandum to denote the agreement between the Four Powers, aud 
their united purpose for a common object.” 1, consequently, considered myself 
as cooperating with M, de Bourqueney in supporting this measure, with whom 
the idea had originated, and who had been furnished with the instructions of his 
Government with the view of carrying it out. 
__ When M, de Bourqueney received these instructions, he called upon me to 
join him in inyiting Count Buol to assemble the Conference, and J stated that, 
as [ was aware your Lordship would approve of such a measure, 1 should not 
hesitate to give my sanction to it; and it was therefore upon our united 
application that the Conference was assembled, and upon its second meeting, as 
reported to your Lordship in my despatch No, 203, the Prussian Minister stated 
his having received the directions of his Government to concur in communi- 
eating the Austro-Prussian ‘Treaty to the Conference, and in taking part in the 
Protocol which had been drawn up by Count Buol and M. de Bourqueney, and 
submitted to his Government for their approval, When the Treaty was pre- 
sented to the Conference, T remarked upon thie absence of the Additional Article, 
but it was stated by Count Arnim, and it was concurred in by Count Buol and 
M, de Bourqueney, that as this Article referred to the military operations which 
might arise out of the stipulations of the Treaty, and as it had already been 
communicated to the Governments of England and France, it was not considered 
necessary to annex it to the present Protocol, particularly as there was no 
document of a similar nature attached to the English Treaty, 

Under these circumstances, and more especially as 1 considered myself 
as acting in support of the French Minister who was proceeding under the 
formal instructions of his Government, F abstained from any further discussion 
upon the subject, and 1 tool part in the signature of the Protocol under the 
impressions which are reported in my despatch No, 203 of the 24th ultimo, and 
with the remark which 1 made confidentially to your Lordship, that I had taken 
upon myself to assent to this Protocol, and to put my name to it without any 
official instructions, and without submitting the document to your Lordship, as 
hy the tenour of your letter of the 9th of May, I felt confident you would 
approve my doing so. ‘ haa |

ment you express at the non-presentation of the Additional Article of the 
Austro-Prussian ‘Treaty. 

His Excellency remarked that the presentation of this document had never

reaty to the Conference had originated, and for the reasons stated at that

My Lord, Paris, June 10, 1854. 

HAVING been informed that M. de Hibner had made a communication to 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, of the despatches addressed by the Austrian Government 
to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, with a view of obtaining the evacuation of 
the Danubian Prineipalities, | inquired this afternoon of M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
what impression these documents had made BoD him. 

He replied, that if the communication which had been wade to him had 
been confined to the first of the series of papers addressed by Count Buol to 
Count Esterhazy, he should not have been dissatisfied, but he thought the 
reserved despatch likely to produce lamentable consequences. He had stated 
as much to M. de Hitbner, though unable then to confirm his own opinion by 
that of the Emperor, as he had sinee been empowered to do. He described his 
reasoning to M. de Hiibuer, a8 follows : 

That if Russia accepted the Austnan summons to retire behind the Pruth 
without making any conditions, as required by the ‘Austrian summons, it woul: 
only be done as a lure to keep Austria quiet, to gain time, and to sow dissension 
among the four Powers. Russia had refused more advantageous terms on more 
than one oceasion; was it likely that she would bond_fide accept now, that which 
she had with so much arrogance refused before? 

With regard to the suggestions contained in the reserved despatch to 
Count Esterhazy. as to the way in which Russia might proceed, if ahe wished tu 
offer any propositions in consequence of the demand made by Austra ;

to be found between the patent and the reserved despatch, In the former Count
