No. 254. 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 205.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, June 13, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has communicated to me a despatch addressed by 
Count Buol on the 3rd instant to the Austrian Minister at St. Petersburgh, 
stating that in the existing crisis the Emperor of Austria hus resolved to make 
a fresh appeal to the Emperor Nicholas on the urgent necessity of devising some 
means for putting an end toa state of things in every Spee so threatening ; 
that it was impossible to doubt that the occupation by the Russian forces of the 
two Danubian Prineipalities, was one of the chief causes of the alarming propor- 
tions which the existing contest had assumed, and that it was that measure 
which more than any other had caused the failure of all the attempts which 
have been made to effect a pacific solution. 

The silence observed by Russia with reference to the summons addressed 
to her by the Western Powers to evacuate the Provinces, brought her into 
collision with those Powers, and extended to such a degree the sphere of the 
contest, as to render it impossible to form any estimate of the disastrous conse- 
quences which may result from it, 

It is impossible that the Emperor Nicholas should be ignorant of the extent 
to which the political, commercial, and industrial interests of the Austrian 
Empire, and with them those of Germany at large, have suffered from this 
prolonged occupation, and it is equally clear that all these evils must increase 1 
proportion to the expansion given to the limits of the theatre of war. 

On these grounds the Emperor of Austria has felt himself compelled, out 
of regard for the interests of his people, to enter by the Protocol of the 9th of 
April into engagements from which he cannot recede. 

The Emperor Nicholas, weighing in his wisdom those considerations, will 
appreciate the importance attachéd by the Emperor of Austria not only to the 
Russian armies not pushing any further their operations on the other side of 
the Danube, but also to obtaining from His Imperial Majesty positive assurances 
as to the period, it is to be hoped not far distant, when the occupation of the 
Principalities will be brought to an end. 

The Emperor Nicholas is doubtless desirous of peace, and therefore he will 
seck the means of putting an end to a-state of things which daily threatens 
Austria and Germany with still further calamities. Hoe will be unwilling either 
by an indefinite prolongation of that oceupation, or by attaching to the evacui- 
tion of the Provinces conditions which it would not rest with Austria to 
fulfil, to impose upon the Emperor of Austria the imperious obligation of seek- 
ing for himself the means of protecting the interests which the present state of 
things so seriously compromises, | > ies 

The despateh concludes by instructing the Austrian Minister at St. Peters- 
burgh to press for an early and precise answer, which by calming the anxiety 
of Austvia for her own interests, might at the same timetafford an opening for 
putting an end to the horrors of war, 

Count Colloredo also read to me a contidential despatch addressed by 
Count Buol to Count Esterhazy for his guidance, but which was not to be 
communicated to Count Nesselrode, recommending that the Emperor of Russia 
should be satisfied with the resolution of the three Powers in favour ef the 
Christian subjects of the Sultan, as recorded in the Vienna Protocol of the 9th 
of April; that His Imperial Majesty should no longer require any formal deela- 
ration on the part of the Porte, which the Sultan could not in fact give, and 
which the Western Powers could not permit; und that in return for any 
concession the Emperor might make to Austria, he should not require the with- 
drawal of the allied fleets from the Black Sea, as England and France would 
hot agree to such a demand, 

Count Buel then proceeds to suggest that the Russian forces might quit 
the Principalities, and retire behind the Pruth, on condition that neither the 
Turkish nor allied armies advanced north of the Danube ; that negotiations for 
peace might then be resumed in a Congress, and the terms of an armistice 

ok 


246 


agreed to, when some arrangement would probably be made respecting the fleets 
in the Black Sea. 

I expressed to Count Colloredo my great regret that Count Esterhazy had 
been instructed to make these suggestions, as they would probably be used to 
further the main object of Russian policy at this moment, which was to detach 
Austria from England and France, and that Austria might find herself much 
embarrassed by the acceptance of the proposals originating with herself. which 
could not put an end to the war between the belligerent Powers, and would 
give Austria no guarantee as to the peace which they may ultimately conclude, 

The Porte, | said, at the recommendation of the four Powers, had consented 
to an armistice, and to conditions upon which a peace honourable to Russia 
might have been made; but as they had been contemptuously rejected by the 
‘Emperor, and war had been declared against Russia by England and France, the 
former. state of things was altogether changed : the two great maritime Powers 
had become principals in the contest, and the honour and the interest of both 
required that they should not lay down their arms until the peace of Europe was 
secured on a solid and lasting foundation by an effectual check upon the 
agressive policy of Russia. It was uscless, therefore, to propose, negotiations 
unless we had reason to know beforehand that they would secure the object we 
had in view, which object, 1 begged to observe, Austria was more interested 
than England and France in attaining, for to no Power in Europe would a return 
to tha status quo be more injurious than to Austria. By her measures of sell- 
defence she had already earned for herself the enmity of Russia; andi old Treaties 
were renewed, and no restrictions were placed upon Russia, and if the enormous 
army of Russia was still kept on foot, and large additions were made to hey 
navy, whereby an inereased facility of transporting troops would be acquired, 
Europe might have cause bitterly to regret that the present favourable con- 
juncture of circumstances had not been turned to proper account, but Austria 
would probably be the Power first to feel the consequences of such neglect. 

Lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLAKENDON. 


No. 255. 


The Karl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 
(No, 335.) 
My Lord, Foreign Gifiee, June 13, 1854. 

HER Majesty’s Government learn with regret the changes in the Turkish 
Ministry, reported in your Excellency’s despatch No. 269 of the 80th of May, 
and that the Sultan's service is sacrificed to intrigues and personal convenience 
ata moment when all the strength and stability which union and well-direeted 
zeal can impart are indispensable. 

| take this opportunity of stating to your Exeelleney that from various 
quarters information las reached Her Majesty’s Government of the bitter 
hostility of the Seraskier against Omer Pasha, which is manifested by depriving 
him of the necessary supplies, by retaming im store at Constantinople the clothing 
and munitions required by the army of Omer Pasha, and by intrigues against 
him among his own officers at Shumla. , . 

This cannot be endured; the matter is of such grave importance, the 
consequences of Omer Pasha’s resignation or defeat may be so disastrous to the 
allied armies, and our right to interfere is consequently so indisputable, that your 
Excellency will take the measures which you my judge most advisable for 
insisting either that the unworthy conduct of the Seraskier shall undergo a 
complete change, or that m successor shall be found for him who will prefer the 
Sultan's cause to the gratification of his own passions or the furtherance of some 
personal intrigue. 

Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 256. 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No, 206.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, June 13, 154. 


COUNT COLLOREDO has shown me the draft of a Convention which 
the Austrian Government has proposed to the Porte, and which has for its object 
to regulate the terms on which the Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia 
may be occupied by Austrian troops in the event of war between Austria and 
Russia. 

The preamble states, that recogmising the existence of the Ottoman Empire 
in its present limits as necessary for the maintenance of the balance of power in 
Europe, and the evacuation of the Danubian Principalities is one of the essential 
conditions of the integrity of that Empire, the Emperor of Austria is prepared 
to concur by the means at his disposal in the measures calculated to ensure the 
object of the understanding established between Austria and the Courts repre- 
sented in the Conference of Vienna; which offer being accepted by the Sultan, 
the ‘Treaty goes on to define the manner in which the cooperation shall be 
effected. 

The Emperor of Austria engages to exhaust all means of negotiation and all 
other means in order to effect the evacuation of the Danubian Principalities, and, 
if necessary, to employ a sufficient number of troops for that purpose, in which 
ease, however, the Austrian General would have the sole direction of the 
operations of the Austman army, though making the ‘Turkish Commander 
acquainted with his operations. 

‘The Emperor of Austria engages as fur as possible to reestablish in the 
Principalitics the legal state of things, as derived from the privileges granted by 
the Porte in regard to their administration, but the locul authorities on being 
vestored will not be authorized to control the Imperial army ; and His Imperial 
Majesty engages not to enter into any Treaty with Russia which shall not have 
for its basis the sovereign rights of the Sultan and the integrity of his Empire. 

The Austrian troops will evacuate the Principalities as soon as the object of 
the Convention shall have been effected by the conclusion of a ‘Treaty of Peace 
between the Porte and Russia. 

The local authorities are to give their aid for facilitating the movements and 
providing for the subsistence of the Austrian army, and strict discipline in every 
respect is to be maintained hy the Austrian troops. 

Iam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

WITH reference to your Lordship's despateh No. 926 of the 7th instant,

The Austrian Government, however, appears to have been aware that it

improper.

No, 258. 


Mr. Grey to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received June 14.) 


(No. 1386. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Stockholm, June 6, 1854. 


M. LOBSTRIN, the French Minister at this Court, had on the 29th ultimo 
the honour of an audience of the King, in order to present letters of condolence 
from the Emperor of the French upon the death of His Royal Highness the 
Duke of Sodermania. 

M. Lobstein profited by this opportunity to renew with His Majesty the 
subject upon which he had already spoken, namely, the cooperation of Sweden 
with the Western Powers against Russia. He held out the hopes to His 
Majesty of subsidies, and the assistance of Frimce in reconquering the 
dominions which were formeriy under the Swedish Crown, provided the King 
would take the field with an army of from 50,000 to 60,000 men, his fleet, and 
his gun-boats, M. Lobstein further said that no guarantee for the future could 
be given, but that Sweden must take her share in the wood and evil fortune 
attendant on the war. 

The King appeared to be prepared for this communication, but did not 
receive it as warmly as was expected, though at the same time he by no means 
eave a final refusal, His Majesty said that the course which Austria pursued 
must be his guide, and further he remarked that as it appeared that En land 
and France intended to push matters to extremities, whereas Austria Noreed 
to desire to restore the status qua ante bellum, he wished to know whether 
Austria would agree to all that was proposed by the Western Powers, before he 
took any decisive step. 

| have very good reason for believing that His Majesty's desire ig to take 
part in the war against Russia, and Tum equally sure that if the cooperation 
of Austria is secured, there will be little difficulty in obtaining that of Sweden. 
But I should conceal the truth from your Lordship if I were not to state my firm 
conviction that in order to obtain the cooperation of Sweden it will be necessary 
to press her, and that the King will be grateful for the application of that pressure. 
I do not venture to state this view to your Lordship solely on my own opinion, 
or without having consulted the experience of other persons who have every 
means of knowing, not only the feelings of the King himself, but also those of 
the country at large, With regard to the latter, there can be no doubt as to the 
tendency of their sympathies. They are all against Russia, and no opportunity 
is lust of showing that such is the case. Even the Ministerial paper, from 
whieh | inclosed so violent an article in favour of the neutrality of Sweden in 
iy despatch No. 89, appears to be coming round, and the argument which it 
now puts forward is that “the moment” is not yet come for Sweden to abandon 
that course of policy which she has adopted, 

I am bound, however, to observe to your Lordship that the general opinion 
here is, that if Sweden is to declare aguinst Russia, it must be done at once, 
and without loss of time. The summer and autumn in the north are short, and 
if matters are not speedily decided, even the most eager partisans of England 
and France in this country will advocate delay and the maintenance of the 
neutrality till next spring. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) W, G, GREY.

My Lord, Berlin, June 13, 1854. 
WITH reference to my despatch No. 29 of the 7th instant, inclosing the 
analysis of a memoir drawn up by M. von der Pfordten, and submitted to the 


Conference at Bamberg, | have now the honour to inelose a translation of the 
identie notes which have been addressed by the Ministers of these States to the 


249 


Representatives of Austria and Prussia residing at their Courts, in answer to 
the communication of the Treaty of Berlin of the 20th of April, and the 
invitation to aceede to it. 

Your Lordship will also find annexed the translation of a draft of resolution 
which these States intended to propose to the Diet at Frankfort. 

At the late meeting at Tetschen, Count Buol and Baron Manteuffel agreed 
onthe reply which should be returned to this communication, and I understand 
from Baron Manteuffel that the only delay in forwarding it is that they have 
not yet settled the date to be affixed to the document. 

His Excellency said that in consequence of the difference of opinions 
prevailing at this moment amongst the German Governments, collective action 
could scarcely be expected; that each State would be invited to give its opinion 
separately; and that the matter would not be brought before the Diet until 
Prussia and Austria were sure of two-thirds of the votes, which there was no 
doubt of their obtaining, for that several of the Powers were already beginning to 
hesitate, and some had already given in their adhesion. 

Your Lordship will perceive in the inclosed note of the States represented 
at the Bamberg Conference that under the plea of protecting the interests of 
Germany, of securing the freedom of navigation of the Danube, obtaining a 
general guarantee for the liberties of the Christian populations in Turkey, and 
for the maintenance of the Kingdom of Greece, the German dynasty of which 
country must ever awaken the sympathies of Germany, there is an attempt to 
establish a basis for future negotiations, and a right of active interference to 
which Austria and Prussia can never be disposed to agree. 

Lhave, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

My Lard, Berlin, June 13, 1854. 

TO judge from Baron Manteuffel’s account of the late interview of the 
Emperor of Austria and the King of Prussia, at Tetschen, the principal political 
matter discussed seems to have been the proceedings of the Bamberg Conference 
and the policy of the small German Stites, rather than the general bearing of 
the Eastern question; but his Excellency has assured me that the meeting at 
‘Tetschen cannot fail to do good, for the firmness of the Emperor of Austra, 
and his calm and_reasonable, but very determined, language had made a deep 
impression on the King. ‘The Emperor appears to have said to His Prussian 
Majesty that the days of phrases were past, and that we must now prepare for 
other things. His Imperial Majesty did not, however, enter into any details 
with the King as to military cooperation, and has left to his Ministers the task of 
carrying out the stipulations of the ‘Treaty of the 20th of April; and these 
negotiations are now being pursued here under the direction of General 
Meyerhofer, who has laid the Austrian plans before Baron Manteuffel and 
expleined the dislocation of the different troops, 

There is some little stir in the Prussian War Department, but there is the 
greatest anxiety to avoid giving offence to Russia; little or nothing is said an

(No, 284.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, June 2, 1854. 

| HAD an interview last night with the principal members of the Turkish 
Council, ‘Phe Grand Vizier and heads of the chief departments were present, 
with the exception of Fethi Ahmet Pasha, Master ol the Ordnance, who was 
anwell, and of Namick Pasha, Minister of Comnierce, who was not mvyited, It 
was on my requisition that the meeting took place, The French Charge 
d’Attnires obliged ine by attending it. 


207 


The object of the Conference was common to us both. We had reason to 
complain of the slow and imperfect manner in which our applications on behalf of 
the auxiliary armies were carried into effect. Tt was necessary that a strong 
impression should be made on the Turkish Ministry, and [ thought that by 
summoning the whole Cubinet, or at least all its principal members, to an inter- 
view with both Representatives, the object would be attained. 

It was at Chekib Pasha’s country-house that we met, and, in conformity 
with the inconvenient usages of the Ramazan, our meeting took place at night, 
and occupied nearly the whole of it, 

I will not put your Lordship’s patience to too severe a trial by entering into 
the particulars of our long conversation, It may suffice for every essential 
purpose to state that I urged the importance of union in the Councils of the 
Ministry, the duty, and indeed the necessity, of supporting Omer Pasha, their 
sole reliable commander, to the full extent of the rovernment’s resources, of 
rendering his army as efficient as those resources would allow, and of giving 
every available facility and assistance to the auxiliary forces. This last indis- 
pensable point was pressed on the attention of the Turkish Ministers by 
M. Benedetti and myself with all the earnestness which its importance required 
at our hands, 

We concurred, moreover, in advising that a considerable reinforcement of 
Artillery should be sent to Omer Pasha, that sufficient means for paying up the 
arrears of the army should be forthwith placed at his disposal, that clothes and 
shoes for the soldiers should also be forwarded in greater quantities, that a 
portion of Turkish troops and Artillery should be attached to each of the alhed 
armies in Bulgaria, that the troops at Batoom should be transferred to Shumla, 
with the exception of 1,000 or 2,000 for maintaining the lines of the place, that 
further supplies of all kinds should be dispatched without delay to the army at 
Kars, that the services of General Yusuf, Colonel Beatson and others should 
be accepted for training the irregular bands, and that a wider door should be 
opened for employing such foreign officers as were prepared and qualified to take 
command in the Sultan's army. 

We further availed ourselves of the opportunity to insist upon the urgency 
of endeavouring to obtain, by means of a loan, the funds required for prosecuting 
the war with vigour; and, alluding to the late meursion of Montenegrins into the 
Herzegovina, we advised that immediate measures should be taken to restore 
tranquillity, and that, in case of need, the assistance of Austria should be solicited 
with the degree of confidence warranted and claimed by the present attitude of 
that Power, 

We did not separate without reminding the Turkish Ministers of the 
advantage which they would not fail to derive from European science, applied to 
the establishment of a telegraphic wire, or semaphore, between Constantinople 
and Shumla, and to the construction of a flying bridge over the Bosphorus, a 
plan of which had already been submitted to the proper department. 

The Turkish Ministers were finally reminded that, together with such things 
as were indispensable for making head against the common enemy, objects of a 
deeper and lasting importance claimed their most serious attention. The time, I 
remarked, was fully come when the Porte night with much advantage, dignity 
wud opportuneness, complete its system of improvement, and realise the 
enlightened policy so frequently proclaimed by its Government. Whatever 
was now done by the Porte in that sense, either with respect to its Rayah popu- 
lation, or for the encouragement of trade and industry with the aid of forei 

science, would tell with peculiar force not only on its own populution, but on the 
nations in allianee with Turkey, and even on their common enemy. Its Christian 
subjects, who had resisted every excitement to rebellion, and who, notwithstanding 
their fidelity, had suffered so cruelly from the Sultan’s irregular troops, had increased 
their claim to relief from unjust and degrading laws. No better return could be 
made to the Christian allies, whose fleets and armies were employed for the 
protection of ‘Turkey, than a sincere adoption of mesures calculated to secure 
their fellow-Christians in this country from injustice and oppression. Few 
things would tend more effectively to deprive Russia of every shadow of excuse 

for her unwarrantable aggression, and consequently to facilitate the restoration of 
peace, than a prompt abolition of those partial laws, or rather a complete removal 
of those flagrant abuses, under which, though im some respects relieved, the 
Rayah population in Turkey continued to groan,

The Ottoman Ministers, after ascertaining that our communications were 
terminated, retired, with our consent, to another apartment, where they con- 
sulted together as to the answers which it might be proper and competent for 
them to make. Returning after a short interval, they assured us that the 
Government was perfectly united ; that they fully agreed in the importance of 
supporting Omer Pasha; that they would continue to send him all neeessary 
supplies ; that they had no complaints to make of him ina military sense ; that 
1 finaneial officer had been dispatched, as his Highness desired, to control the 
expenditure of the army, which had fallen into some entanglement ; that measures 
were in operation for securing supplies and means of transport to the auxiliary 
armies; that a commission invested with the requisite authority for that 
purpose was appointed to fix itself at Varna; that seventy-five pieces of cannon, 
completely mounted, had been drawn from Sophia by Omer Pasha; that a 
regiment of four battalions, with its proportion of Cavalry and Artillery, was 
annexed to the two auxiliary armies; that more Artillery could not be forwarded 
without the assent of the Ordnance Department; that the Turkish troops 
attached to the two armies might, however, be increased hereafter; that the 
army at Batoom might be trans erred to Bulgaria if the allied Generals thought 
it best; and that the army at Kars amounted, with the new Rediff, to 35,000 
men, and about 10,000 Irregulars: 

_ On the subject of finanee the Turkish Ministers announced their intention 
of sending two merchants of high respectability, Mr. Black, an Englishman, and 
M, Durand, a Frenchman, with all convenient expedition to Paris and London 
for the purpose of negotiating a loan to the amount of 3,500,000 on the best 
terms they could obtain, after consulting the respective Governments, and 
obtaining the formal sanction of the Turkish Representatives in those capitals to 
their agreement. 

With respect to the incursion from Montenegro, they would give instruc- 
tions to Korshid Pasha, the Governor of Bosnia, in the sense proposed, and 
authorize him, in ease of need, to apply for military aid to the Austrian General 
in command on the neighbouring frontier. 

They declared, moreover, their readiness to accept the services of any 
British of French officer willing and qualified to serve in. the Sultan's army, and 
also of General Yusuf and Colonel Beatson for training the irregular bands or 
Bashi-Bazouks, with the concurrence of Omer Pasha, to whom those officers 
were referred. 

Lastly, they professed their willingness to entertain the plans submitted to 
them for constructing telegraphs and a flying bridge. 

So far all was satisfactory, if reliance could be placed on assurances 
accompanied or to be followed up with corresponding measures. 

What remained was the question of reform, as applicable in part to the 
Rayahs, and in part to foreigners desirous of employing capital, industry, or 
science, in the Sultan’s dominions. 

Qn these very Important matters there was little appearance. of conviction 
or cordialty. ‘The Ottoman Ministers spoke in general terms of their inclination 
to meet our wishes in so far as certain inherent difficulties would permit. They 
offered no objections; but their manner was cold and their expressions 
reserved. | 

Conceiving that a good opportunity would be lost if the Representatives of 
France and England appeared by their silence to aoquiesce in so discouraging 
a reply, I did not hesitate to express my surprise at the coldness with which our 
bonevolent and useful suggestions liad been received, ‘The discussion which 
naturally ensued was carried on with no small degree of warmth, and some 
vecasional asperity, especially when reference to the atrocious and hitherto 
unpunished and unrepressed erueltics of the Bashi-Bozouks, induced the Grand 
Vizier to palliate their conduct by citing outrages of equal abomination cominitted 
by the brigands from Greece. 

I disclaimed every thought of dictation on matters which belonged of right 
to the Sovereign; but I complained without reserve af those contradictions 
which were allowed to subsist hetween the professions of the Porte and its 
measures, between the tenour of its ordinances and the manner of their 
enforcement, 1 appealed in particular to those among the Ministers who 
recognized the abuses complained of and the importance, as well as the justice, 
of redressing them. In acknowledging the merits of that firman which had 


259 


recently placed the evidence of Rayahs on an equality with that of -Massulimans 
in criminal procedure, I lamented the slowness with which it had been 
promulgated and the still existing reluctance to follow it up with other 
indispensable measures, such as the abolition of the haratch — that odious, 
degrading rangom-tax—and the regulation of property on principles corre- 

sponding with the Sultan's proclamations and well-known personal disposition. 
In this part of the Conference, as well as in those which asec lam 
happy to acknowledge the frank and judicious cooperation of M. Benedetti; and 
although we did not sueceed in obtaining any additional assurances of a positive 
nature, it is not easy to believe that our arguments, founded as they were in 
truth and inspired by friendly sentiments, were entirely thrown away, or that 
the concurrent recommendation of France und England, speaking through us, 
could leave no trace on minds open at least to the impressions of danger and 
rudence, if not, as largely a8 we could wish, to the suggestions of humanity, 

justice, and sound administrative policy.

carrying out the duties of so important a charge.

(No. 347) 
My Lol, Berlin, June 16, 1854. 

BARON MEUSEBACH, who lias lately returned from the Danubian 
Principalities, called upon me yesterday, and | endeavoured to learn his impres- 
sions as to the present amount and position of the Russian forces which have 
invaded Turkey, and are now acting near the Danube. 

My first object was to hear what he believed of the rumour which has 
been eurrent for some days, that Prince Paskiewitch had determined on remoy~ 
ng his head-quarters to Jassy, and he scemed to think it might be so, and that 
the plan of the campaign might be changed in consequence of the threatening 
attitude of Austria ; but he observed that the Prussian Government had not yet 
received sufficiently well-founded intelligence to form any positive opinions on 
the subject, and that it was not impossible but that the journey of Prince 
Paskiewitch was in consequence of an attack of fever from which he was 
suffering; that, however, up to the present moment there was no reason to 
believe that anything had occurred which could be considered as the precursor 
of a retreat from the Danube. 

Buron Meusebach afterwards gave me the following account of the present 
effective foree of the Russians on the Danube and in the Dobrudscha, which he 
considers to amount in round numbers to something over 100,000 men. 

He said their toree in the Prineipalities consisted of 137 battalions, or 
108,000 Infantry; 156 squadrons: of Cavalry, at 140 each; 21,800 horses; 


261 


between 6,000 and 6,000 Cossacks ; 408 pieces of Fort Artillery ; 60 pieces of 
Horse Artillery; and 24 pieces of Siege Artillery. 


This, he said, was the force acting near and within reach of the Danube, 


and that the army of reserve statione beyond the Prath was composed chietly 
of recruits, and amounted to about 350,000 men. 


Baron Meusebach said that the Russian flotilla on the Danube consisted of 
two steamers, the “ Pruth,” and the “Ordinaretz,” each armed with four 


36-pounder carronades. At Silistria there were six gun-boats armed with three 


54-pounder carronades each, and four faleonets, and that there were ten or 
twelve more boats, of the same size, and similarly armed, lower down the 
Danube. 

With regard to the condition and morale of the Russian troops, Baron 
Meusebach was disinclined to say much on this our first interview, but I shall 
hope to obtain further details from him, and shall not fail to report them to 
your Lordship without loss of time; but he seems to have no great opinion 
of the Russian soldier, except as to his patience and powers of endurance. He 
said that at the commencement of the campaign their losses from sickness had 
been comparatively trifling, but that men and horses were suffering greatly at 
this moment.

IHAVE received your Exeellency’s despatch No. 284 of the 2nd instant, 
reporting what passed in a Conference which you and the French Charge 
d'Affaires held with the principal members of the Sultan's Government, on the 
night of the Ist of June; and fT have to inform your Lxeelleney that Her 
Majesty's Government entirely approve your proceedings on that occasion, and 
the able manner in which you urged upon the Turkish Ministers the several 
points which, as you will learn hy my recent despatches, have latterly engaged 
the anxious attention of Her Majesty's Government, 

it is hardly necessary to point out to your Excellency that the promises you 
have received ave no guarantee for their performance, and that unceasing vigilance 
will be required in order to secure due attention to the service of the Sultan and 
his allies, 

If the ‘Turkish Ministers were animated by a proper spirit they would be 
aware that reforms ond relaxations in favour of the Rayahs would be well 
received by Christian Europe, and viewed as the best return that the Porte could

The Harl of Clarendon to Sir J. Millanke. 
iNo. 41.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, June 21, 1854, 

HER Majesty's Government have read with extreme surprise the document 
drawn up by M. von de Pfordten and presented to the Conference at Bamberg, 
in which the hostility of Bavaria to England and France ts recorded in terms not 
to be mistaken or forgotten. 

Her Majesty’s Government have no claim and no desire to interfere with 
the undoubted right of the German Powers to deliberate and decide upon their 
own affairs, nor do they complain, however much they may regret, that those 
Powers should constitute themselves the advocates of Russian policy; but Her 
Majesty's Government do complain, and they resent the manner in which the 
Bamberg Conference has been invited by the Bavarian Minister to interfere in 
matters of which it was not competent to judge, and to preseribe conditions to 
Ragland and France respecting the war in which they have been compelled to 
engage by the unjust and aggressive policy of Russia. 

This war may become general; it may be of long duration ; it ma entail a 
ereat European crisis; during the war there is little doubt that Austria will be 
closely united with England and France, and at its conclusion it may become the 
duty of those Powers to take measures for rendering the opposition they now 
meet with from the German Courts harmless hereafter, 

It is for M. von der Pfordten to consider whether the course he is now 
pursuing will promote the future interests of Bayaria, or tend to consolidate the 
Bavarinn dynasty on the throne of Greece. 

Lam, &, 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

THE Prince of Warsaw has suddenly issued, 
inhabitants of Bulgaria, which seems to have been 
the investinent of Silistria. 

This summons was printed in Bulgarian only, and not in Russian also, as 
the usage has been hitherto. 1 have the honour to inclose to your Execllency 
« French translation. The person who gave this to me had the printed Bulgarian 
text before him, and he had thus an opportunity of making this version, which 
is more literal than elegant. 

It is pain from this that the present war 1s represented as one of religion, 
and that Russia wishes for the cooperation of the orthodox Bulgarians, in order 
to effect their speedy liberation from the hereditary foe to the Christians, 

_ ‘The same motive was alleged by Prince Paskiewitch, when he asked the 
Conseil Administratif’ here, the day before yesterday, to place the Wallachian 
soldicry at his disposal. ‘This demand met with a strong resistance, not indeed 
in the Conseil Administratif, but in the body of the officers, and among the men 
eenerally, ‘The former talked of resignation, the latter of desertion, In order 
to prevent mutiny, like that of the border-watch of Grirgevo and ‘Turan Mogu- 
relli, where the people, notwithstanding that every filth raan had heen subjected 
to military punishment for refusing to serve, immediately threw away their arms 
and went over to the ‘Turks, Baron Budberg has made known this day to the 
Great Vornick that the Field-Marshal does not insist upon the soldiers stiniclings 
before the enemy with the Russian troops beyond the Danube, but only that 
they do garrison duty. i 

_ As for other rhatters, I learn from Constantine Csokau, who, us a farmer 
of the Customs’ duce here, is in close connection with Bulgarians, that no 
symptoms of a popular rising in favour of the Russians have hitherto been 
perceptible. Much as they wish to be free from the Turkish voke, they would

prefer any other Christian liberator to the Russians, whose harsh conduet, which 
they have suffered from in previous invasions, is yet fresh in their memory. 
The Bulgarians residing in Wallachia as eolonists—of whom there are about 
300,000 or 400,000—also find that by the jong sojourn of the armies in 
Wallachia, they too are reduced to heggary, and they do not cease to warn their 
brethren on the other side against a similar fate. 

As the means of conveyance are rare in Bulgaria, carriages from this side 
have been compelled to go over there. Many drivers left their vehicles, and of 
a greater number the carriages are broken, and the eattle dead. ‘These unhappy 
people were seen with packs on their backs, in which they were bringing back 
the little iron«work of their broken carriages, begwing their way from the 
Danube, 

Such scenes, unhappily, increase from day to day, and are the more 
distressing inasmuch as it is known that the poorest of them all find their 
families as completely deprived of all as they are themselves. The inhabitants 
of Little Wallachia are therefore considered lucky; the Turks, they say, force 
nobody from his house; take nothing without paying ready money for it; do 
not prevent ficld-labour; and drive neither man nor beast to foreign lands, 
where they meet all the perils of war, without troubling themselves for their 
maintenance, or return home again, 

The reproach is made against the Russians that they, notwithstanding all 
the great sacrifices made for them, all the complaisance and politeness shown to 
them, even to the verge of servility, yet complain that attempts are made to 
cheat and deceive them ; and that whenever any one makes a complaint, however 
well founded, or ventures on disapproval, he is threatened at once with arrest, 
corporal punishment, and exile, Neither rank nor age protects the most 
honourable Boyard from open neglects, insults, suspicion, and unfounded 
reproachies, 

The general feeling is, therefore, one of irritation, and wholly hostile to the 
Russians, which is dangerous for the army even, 50 that a fear is manifested of 
confessing the evacuation of the Principalities. For although Baron Budberg, 
eight days ago, solemnly aasured the whole of the Boyards, “that Little 
Wallachia would be evacuated for a short time only, and Great Wallachia not 
at all,” yet it is plainly seen that an wnostentatious retirement is commenced, 
which every one is now able to see already. 

It is seen, for instance, that General Liprandi has dispatched all the 
provisions from Slatina to Fokschani, keeping back only just so much as he 
wanted for twelve days’ subsistence ; and further, that the Commissariat here 
goes to dassy; that the sick and wounded are also conveyed there; that the 
provisions recently called for are to be delivered in at Buseo and Foksehant ; that 
the districts lying on this side of Bucharest have but little provision; and that 
the divisions still remaining here could not be provided without the utmost 
exertion, and for a short time only. 

Everything required for the army before Silistria must be brought from 
Wallachia, for very little comes from Moldavia and Bessarabia, barely sufficient 
for the troops engaged in the Dobrudscha, Prince Paskiewitch collects troops 
and provisions, where le wishes to strike a blow, in such masses that one is 
tempted to assume that he doubts the courage of the army, or that his renius 
consists in vanquishing only by means of numerical superiority. 

There ave now, in fact, 90,000 bayonets beyond the Danube, in the district 
of Silistria, which, according to Kussian reports, has only 17,000 or 18,000 men 
in garrison altogether; and notwithstandit.s this, he has put a stop to the siege 
until he can be strengthened by fresh succours, and even by Staurolores [fighters 
for the faith 2), or perhaps the Wallachian militia, 7 

But if, alter the capture of Silistria, the troops should be obliged to march 
weatward along the Danube, there is nothing left for him to feed them with but 
the provisions which are brought on waggons, with ineredible labour, to 
Kalarash and Oltenitza; and this will inevitably occasion fresh tortures on the 
peasantry, and the characteristi¢ frauds of the Russian management of matters.

men of the insurrectionary party had entered Little Wallachia with the Turkish 
troops, and their efforts were to instil socialistic ideas into the country people ; 
aleo that this circumstance had given the greatest umbrage to the Boyards. 

In that report I reserved for another inquiry whether, and to what extent, 
the ‘Turkish Commanders protect these principles, and the apostles who 
propagate them. 

in the course of the last week very alarming accounts have come unfortu- 
nately from Little Wallachia. The landholders apprehend, if not a peasant-war, 
at logst a definite and determined refusal of the compulsory and other services of 
their peasants. The farmers and managers have fled from some districts of 
Little Wallachia, in fear of ill-usage from the peasantry, ‘They stated that neither 
payments in kind nor money payments could be obtained from them by other 
than forcible means, They had not only declared the fields and meadows 
assigned to them by the recent landlord and peasant regulations to be their own 
unburthened property, but they said that the payments in kind and money, 
promised by way of compensation to the landlords, had been unjustly imposed 
upon them, and they were determined to liberate themselves from burdens 
unjustly imposed, 

The question as to the support or aid afforded by the Ottoman Com- 
manders to this insurrection has every appearanco of being answered in the 
affirmative, for the proclamations dnd notices are circulated, together with the 
* Journal of Kvajova,” under their eyes. 

____ In regard to the tendency of this journal, I have the honour to remark that 
itis very injurious, because it appeals to passions which, when once roused, it may 
be difficult to appease, 

In order to tranquillize the rich, and all those who have anything to lose, it

No, 283. 


Reply to the Bamberg Answer to the Invitation to the German Courts to adhere 
to the Austro-Prussian Treaty,—(Communicated to the Earl of Clarendon by 
Count Colloredo, June 24.) 


( Translation.) Vienna, June 16, 1854, 


YOUR , through the despatch of the instant, has 
transmitted a note, in which the Government has given its answer 
to our invitation to joi the offensive and defensive alliance concluded on the 
20th April last between Austria and Prussia. 

We have made no delay in carefully considering the statements made in that 
note, and in deliberating upon it, together with the Prussian Cabinet; more 
especially as a similar view of the state of things lies at the bottom of the recent 
deliberations of the other German Governments. After having had the gratifi- 
cation of assuring ourselves that our views were in accordance with those of 
Prussia, J am directed by His Majesty the Emperor, &e. to communicate to your 

the following observations, in order that they may be brought to 
the knowledge of the Government, ; 

His Majesty has been most sincerely gratified to perceive not only that his 
German Confederates have been satisfied with the Convention made between 
Austrian and Prussia, in which their accordance upon so serious a complication 
has found its expression, but also that they approve of that point of view which 
makes the interests and obligations of Germany available beyond the limits the 
Confederation. ; 

In this conviction the Government has expressed to us its 
wish that an address should be made to the Federal Assembly, inviting the 
accession of the whole body, and Austria and Prussia have already unmis- 
tukeably made known their readiness to do this eventually. But both the High 
Courts agree in the opinion that, by Article XI of the Act of Federation, indi- 
vidual German Courts have the right to vecede to the alliance tendered to them; 
and the two Cabinets, in consequence, proceeded forthwith to make such tender, 
partly that they might thus be enabled toanticipate the result of a later propo- 
sition to the whole Confederation, and partly, if such proposition shoulil not 
ultimately be made, that they might act in accordance with such States as 
decided upon acceding, as has 1 fact been done by several Governments. 

The Government will thus understand that there is no 
practical difficulty inthis formal side of the question, and the only thing to be 
done appears to be this—to secure a sufficient agreement of opinion upon the 
question itself, i order to draw up a federative resolution. 

In reference to this, the first observation to be made 1s, that according to 
the view of the Government, the invitation to evacuate the Princi- 
palities, as provided im the Additional Article, was to be completed by the 
proposal to put a stop simultaneously to the land and sea operations, and 
therefore by a withdrawal on the part of the other Powers. The 
Government will certainly have no doubt that a withdrawal from the theatre of 
war hy all parties would ein accordance with the wishes and efforts of the twe 
German Powers, and has really been kept in view by them, as fur as it appeared 
practicable at the time, as will be seen from the accompanying copies of 
despatches sent to St. Petersburgh, in the tenour of the resolution of the 
Additional Article; one from Austria, and the other, in sid of the same, from 
Prussia. 

We hold fast by the hope that His Majesty the Emperor of Russia will, i 
his wisdom, appreciate the uddress of his ancient allies, which is the expression 
of their deep convictions, and that he will put them, by his reply, ina condition 
to effect a pacific understanding between the belligerent Powers and it is hardly 


271 


necessary to observe, looking to the object of the Courts of Vienna and Berlin, 
that his reply will not only undergo their conscientious examination, but that 
they will then make it their duty to treat in confiding unison with those German 
Governments also who shall have acceded to the alliance, and eventually with 
the Federal Assembly, in so far as it shall have declared its adhesion, 

In reference to the supposition expressed by the Government 
+ connection herewith, that the Confederation in the farther negotiations will be 
represented in due form as a party to the alliance, the two Courts willingly 
respond to this supposition, the realisation of which certainly does not depend 
on them only, so far as possible under the circumstances; they will, at all events, 
strictly fulfil the precept of Article XLUX of the Vienna Resolution. 

The Imperial Cabinet would cherish the hope that the Government will feel 
itself induced, by the above-given explanations, to evince at once, by an unreserved 
and complete adhesion to the offensive and defensive alliance concluded between 
Austria and Prussia, its often-shown confidence in these two Powers, and its 
readiness to make sacrifices for the patriotic interests which it recognizes. ‘The 

Government in its note accurately depicts the objects it, wishes 
Germany to attain ; and it enumerates among them, the entire freedom of the 
trade and navigation of the Danube, and an effectual protection to the Christian 
populations living under Turkish rule, to be secured by all parties. The 
Government will certainly not shut itselt trom the conviction that the

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon,—( Received June 26.) 


(No. 353.) 
My Lord, Berlin, June 23, 1854. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL has gone to meet the hing at Bromberg, and is 
to return this night to Berlin with His Majesty. 

I saw his Excellency yesterday before his departure, and endeavoured to 
learn if anything had occurred at the meeting at Gumbinnen of the King with 
the Russian General Griinwald, who had been sent to compliment His Majesty 
on the frontier, which would throw any light on the decision likely to be taken 
at St. Petersburgh on the late communications of the Austrian and Prussian 
Governments, but it did not appear that any positive information on the subject 
had reached Baron Manteuffel. 

_ He told me that he believed General Grimwald had made no communication 
of a political tendeney, and the only intelligence of any importance was the 
first impression made on the Emperor of Russia by the Austrian despatches, 
which, as reported by Count Minster (who had also come from St. Petersburgh 
to see the King), was that the greatest irritation had heen produced, and that it 
was not thought that His Imperial Majesty was disposed to make any con- 
cessions, However it is not expected that the answer of the Imperial Cabinet 
will be prepared until after the arrival of Colonel! Manteuffel, and we are 
therefore not likely to know anything further for a week, 

L asked Baron Manteuftel if the Austrian Minister at St. Petersburgh had, 
as he gave meé to understand a (ew days ago, really communicated to Count 
Nesselrade the reserved despatch of Count Buol of the 3rd instant as well as 
the ostensible one, and he replied that he could not state that he was positively 
informed of its having been read to the Russian Chancellor, or that a copy of it 
had been sent to him from any quarter, but that he had every reason to believe 
tht he was aware of its contents, which if not communicated by Count 
Esterhay might have been reported by Baron Meyendortf. 

[ replied that it seemed strange that this reserved despatch should have 
been so made known, as Her Majesty’s Government had understood that it had 
heen drawn up solely for the use and guidance of Count Esterhazy, and that we 
must naturally desire that it would not become the basis for negotiations, as in 
any arrangement of peice it must be essential that England should be satistied 
for nothing would be vained to Europe if we did not approve of what was done, 
und further that there were certainly to be found in this reserved despatch many 
points of which Hussia might take advantage. 

, Baron Munteuffel rejoined that he had very little ex rectation that the 
Emperor of Russia would yield to these fresh appeals from Berlin and Vienna, 
but that nevertheless he would not attempt to prejudice a question which must 
be decided in a few days, ) |

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 27.) 


(No, 799.) 
My Lord, Paris, June 26, 1854. 

| HAVE read with much interest ao despatch from M. de Bourqueney 
dated the 2lst instant. Passing in review the different phases which the 
Russian answer might bear, M. de Bourqueney says that, if evasive, as feared by 
Count Buol, he had that Minister's assurances that it would not stay the march 
of Austria. If the evacuation of the Principalities was accepted, and Russia 
showed at the same time a disposition to treat for peace, Count Buol said that 
it would be for England and France to lay down the terms for peace. 

M, de Bourqueney adds that, although he has never discussed with Count 
Buol what those terms were to be, he has taken creat pains never to conceal 
from him the conditions on which France sould insist, and that no objection had 
ever been raised to them by Count Buol. M. Drouyn de Lhuys again enume- 
rated these conditions to me: Free navigation of the Black Sea; free navigation 
of the Danube; guarantees against Russian encroachments for the future ; and 
indemnity for the expenses of the war. 

These were the principles on which France would insist, subject to discus- 
sion as to details, 

M. de Bourqueney refers to the activity displayed in the War Department, 
and does not doubt that by the end of July, Austria will be ready either to meet 
an attack, or to march into the Principalities.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No. 221.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, June 27, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol, 
giving an account of a conversation which he had held with your Lordship, in 
consequence of your having mentioned to him that a doubt had arisen im my 
mind whether possibly, from the enrolment ina common Act of the Conventions 
coneluded between France and England on the ene hand, and between Austria 
and Prussia on the other, the inference might not be deduced that France and 
England participated in the mutual guarantee of the existing state of territorial 
possession stipulated between Austria and Prussia by Article I of the Treaty of 
April 20th, , 

Count Buol states that he had not hesitated to reply to your Lordship that, 
according to his opinion, to admit this view of the matter would be singularly to 
pervert the meaning and signification of the Protocol of May 26rd. 

_ It is true, he adds, that by the mutual communication of the two separate 
Conventions, the Four Powers have established that these Conventions tend, in 
the respective situations, to assure the maintenance of the principles sanctioned 
by the former Protocols of the Vienna Conferences; but by declaring tits 
opinion in conformity with the engagement taken by the ‘our Powers to 
consult as to the means most adapted for realising the object of their coneert, 
France and England have in no manner become Contracting Parties to the 
Treaty of April 20th, any more than the Treaty of the 10th of the same month 
has become obligatory upon Austria and Prussia. 

___ 1 thanked Count Colloredo for the communication, and expressed my gatis- 
faction at finding that Count Buol’s opinion coincided entirely with my own upon 

46 


this question, which had not been mooted because Her Majesty’s Government 
felt any doubt about it, but simply m order that we might be able to give a 
complete contradiction to rumours in at opposite sense that had been cireu- 
lated. 


Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

My Lord, Constantinople, June 15, 1854. 

THE military Convention between Austria and the Porte was signed by 
Baron de Bruek and Reshid Pasha the night before last, and | inclose a copy of 
it herewith. 

I understand that two alterations in the original draft were proposed by 
ube Turkish Plenipotentiary. Baron de Bruck accepted the one and rejected 
the other. 

The one he accepted is that clause in Article IIL, which is composed of 
these words, now inserted: “d'un commun accord avee le Gouvernement 
Ottoman.” That which his Excellency rejected relates to the commencement 
of Article V. Reshid Pasha proposed to word the passage so that the con- 
clusion of peace, instead of being described as the object of the Convention, 
should have appeared as detached from that object, though equally marking the 
time at which the arrangements for withdrawing the Austrian army from the 
Principalities should be made. It 1s not easy to perceive why the one Plenipo- 
tentiary should have proposed, or the other rejected, a modification of so little 
apparent consequence.

| HAVE not yet succeeded in obtaining the necessary instructions for 
Omer Pasha to carry into effect the organization of a body of txreilay Cavalry, 
or Bashi-Bozouks, under the command of Colonel Beatson. The general pro- 
position is, however accepted, and what remains to be effected concerns the 
leading details of the measure. 

Colonel Beatson has already forwarded a proposal for paying the men to 
be placed under his command, with the assistance of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, He forwards by this opportunity a proposal for supplying them with 
earbines obtained from the same source, 

That the men, in order to be serviceable, must have arms and pay is 
evident, and | greatly fear that the Porte is ut present unable to furnish them 
efficiently with either. How far it may suit Her Majesty's Government to 
supply the deficiency it is not for me to determine. But I am free to declare 
ny conviction, that real advantage, in point of military service and of humanity, 
may be derived from the proposed enrolment, but that no advantage can be 
secured there(rom in either respect unless Colonel Beatson be made the channel 
through which the wild fagacen to be brought into order are made to loak to 


Zid 


him, not only for control and punishment, but also for their means of living 
independent of plunder. 

Iam informed that the French are prepared to act upon that principle with 
respect to the Bashic-Bozouks destined to be placed under the command of 
General Yussuf, It appears probable that each individual enrolled will have 
a franc and a ration per diem, together with arms, comprising a sword, a lance, 
and a carbine. 

[ cannot conclude this despatch without doing justice to Colonel Beatson’s 
anxiety to enter without delay upon the field of his arduous duties. 

The delay which is experienced arises solely from the habitual tardiness of 
the Turkish Ministers in transacting business during the month of Ramazan, 
and ata time of unusual pressure and official occupation.

No. 294. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 28.) 


(No. 317. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, June Lo, 1854, 

IN a preceding despatch No, 306, dated June 10th, lapprised your Lordship 
of my intention to request Admiral Dundas to explain more particularly the 
meaning which he intended I should attach to the closing paragraph of his 
despatch to me of the 5th instant, already forwarded to your Lordship in copy. 

Having had occasion to refer to our correspondence, I perceive his intention 
with sufficient clearness to relieve me from the necessity of referring to him for 
explanation ; but as lie has complained more than once of the Porte’s inattention 
to his advice respecting the entrance of the ‘Turkish squadron into the Black 
Sea, L beg to submit herewith to your Lordship an abstract of what has passed 
between the Admiral and myself on that subject. 

As the whole correspondence has been sent home, [ run no risk of misleading 
your Lordship by a partial view of the case, 

It appears that Admiral Dundas did not originally object to the entrance of 
the Turkish squadron into the Black Sea, but merely to its advancing beyond # 
certain locality in the first instance. He manifests, indeed, in one of lis 
despatches, a willingness to see the squadron extend its cruise to the coast of 
Circassia, after the intended operations should be completed there. | 

It may be further remarked that the Turkish squadron left the Bosphorus 
with the declared intention of seeking the allied fleets, and following the advice

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 3.) 


(No, 244.) 
My Lord, Vienna, June 28, 1854, 

| REPORTED to your Lordship, in my telegraphic despatch of the 26th 
instant, the retreat of the Russian forces from the siege of Silistria, which took 
place on the 22nd instant, as well as the determination of the Imperial 
Government, which has been announced to me by Count Buol, to order a 
division of the Austrian troops at present assembled under General Coronini in 
the neighbourhood of Semlin and in the south of Hungary, to proceed to 
Wallachia to occupy, in pursuance of the stipulations of the Convention lately 
agreed to between the Austrian and Turkish Governments at Constantinople, 
the portions of that Principality which have been evacuated by the Russian 
forces, and to replace therein, under the sanction of His Majesty the Sultan, the 
legitimate authorities. 

Count Buol stated that the order for this movement of the Austrian troops 
had been given immediately upon the receipt of the intelligence of the 
evacuation of the Principalities by the Russian army, as it was not thought 
advisable to wait the answer to the requisition to that effect which had been 
transmitted to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. The Imperial Government 
considered it more consonant to the position they had taken upon this subject 
towards Russia, toadopt the measure it had decided upon, irrelatively to any 
communication they might receive from St. Petersburgh. 

The Ist division of the Austrian troops (25,000 men) will proceed imme- 
diately to Giurgevo, and thence to Bucharest + the 2nd division wil follow as s00n 
as it is ready to move. These troops have been selected with the view of not 
interfering with the concentration of the Austrian forces whieh is taking place on 
the frontier of ‘Transylvania and Galicia, and which are in a position to observe 
the Russian forees which are collecting in considerable numbers in the Princi- 
pality of Moldavia and on the Russian frontier of Gallicia. 

Count Buol, in directing Baron Bruck to bring under the consideration of 
the Cabinet of the Sultan the measure which, in compliance with the Convention 
upon this subject, has now been adopted by the Austrian Government, and in 
converting with the Turkish Ministers the Various dispositions which they may 
think it advisable should be adopted to insure the good government of the Princt- 
pality, has instructed him to offer as t recommendation that the Hospodar Prince 
Stirbey should be replaced in his authority; and Prince Stirbey has written a 
letter to his Sovercign congratulating him upon the signal success which has 
attended his arms, and has requested His Majesty's permission to return to his 
post and to resume his functions. 

In communicating these decisions, Count Buol stated that, in adopting the 
present measure, a5 relating to Wallachia, it was the firm intention of the 
‘Austrian Government to resist any attempt on the part of the Russian troops to 
reoccupy that Principality; and that if the Austrian troops entered Moldavia, 
they would uphold the same determination, and that if the Porte consented to 
the return of the Hospodars for the government of those provinces, it would not 


285 


be considered in any other light than as a measure taken in accordance with the 
Jesire of the Porte, and not dependent upon any previous stipulations. 

Count Buol contemplated the possible advance of the Turkish and allied 
forces through the Prineipalities towards the Russian frontier. 

General Baron Hess, the newly appointed Commander-in-chiet of the 
Austrian armies Nos. 3 and 4, has dispatched an officer of his staff, Ligutenant- 
Colonel Kalich, to the head-quarters of Omer Pasha, for the purpose of 
announcing to him, and of concerting with him, the march of the Austrian 
troops under General Coronini; and Count Buol, on the part of the Emperor, 
requested me to furnish this officer with a letter of introduction to Lord Raglan, 
in order that he might confer with him as to the movements of the respective 
troops, and I have complied with this request, and herewith inclose a copy of 
my letter, ‘The same desire was expressed to Baron Bourqueney for an intro- 
duction for Lieutenant-Colonel Kalich to Marshal St. Arnaud, with which he 
las complied. 

In closing this despatch | cannot but congratulate your Lordship upon the 
signal suecess which has thus been obtained for the cause of Turkey and of her 
allies, by the total failure of the whole policy of dictation which, by the occupa- 
tion of the Principalities, the Russian Government had adopted towards the 
Porte, and by which they have involved Europe in the present war, during 
which they have themselves sustained so many reverses A the armies of the 
Sultan. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

Inclosure in No. 299. 
Prussian Answer to Bamberg Conference. 


(Translation.) 


YOUR has in the report of the ultimo, with which you have 
favoured us, transmitted the note in which the Government has 
replied to our invitation to become a party to the offensive and defensive alliance 
concluded between Prussia and Austria on the 20th April last. 

Our promptitude has been the greater to examine attentively the ex V0s1tiOn 
contained in this note, and to conter thereon with the Imperial Austrian Cabinet 
as the replies of several other German Governments are founded on a similar 
view (Auffassung) of the situation of things. 

After having had the satisfaction to convince ourselves of the coincidence of 
our views with those of Austria, Tam commanded hy His Majesty the king to 
communicate to your the following remarks in order that they may 
be brought to the knowledge of the Government. Conese 

Tt has afforded to His Majesty the King the sincerest satisfaction not only 
to see the conclusion of the Treaty expressive of the good understanding between 
drussia and Austria in such a serious complication, greeted with joy by their 
allies, but also to see that they duly estimate the point of view in which German 
interests and obligations are to be considered likewise beyond the frontiers of the 
Confederation. If, under this conviction, the Government, on the one 
hand, has expressed to us the wish that the adhesion of the entire Confederation 
should be eflected by means of an invitation to be addressed to the German Diet 
Prussia and Austria, on the other hand, have likewise both expressed in the 
cleavest terms their eventual readiness to accede thereto, 

The Courts of Prussia and of Austria are both, however, of opinion, that 
aecording to Article XI of the Confederation Act, the separate German Govern: 
ments have algo the right to be parties to the alliance oflered to them, and the 
two Cabinets have therefore first applied to them partly to be able to preominate 
the result of a later proposal to the Confederation, partly for the contingeney if 
no proposal was made to act in concert with those States that may have 
declared their adhesion, which has already taken place on the part ot several 
Governments. : 

The Government will perceive from the above, that-on this formal 
side of the question there appears to exist no practical dittculty, and the chiet 
point seems to be to ensure a suflicient unanimity in case of a resolution being 
being brought before the Confederation. * 

In this respect it is worth mentioning that, according to the view of the 

Government, the summons contained in the Supplemental Article 
to evacuate the Principalities should be accompanied by the condition of the 
simultancous cessation of hostilities by land and by sea, and the reciprocal 
retreat of the other Powers. : 

The Government will certainly be convinced that the eventuality 


287 


of a general withdrawal from the seat of war would correspond with the views 
and the exertions of the two German Powers, and therefore, in so far as it 
appeared admissable at the time, was kept in view by them when the two 
despatches, of which copies are inclosed, were sent according to the terms of the 
Supplementary Article to St, Petersburgh, the one by Austria, and the other in 
support of the same by Prussia. 

We adhere firmly to the hope that His Majesty the Emperor of Russia will 
in his wisdom duly appreciate the language of his ancient allies, the result of a 
deep conviction, and that he will by a satisfactory reply place them in a position 
to prepare the way for a peaceful understanding between the belligerent Powers ; 
and it is searcely necessary to remark, that this reply, as regards the object ith 
view, will not only be submitted to the most conscientious scrutiny by the 
Cabinets. of Vienna and Berlin, but that they will also make it their duty 
immediately to enter into confidential communications with those German 
Governments that may have joined their alliance, and eventually with the 
German Diet, in case it may have declared its adhesion to the alliance. 

With regard to the conditions expressed by the Government in 
connection herewith, that the Diet shall be represented in due form im the 
further negotiations that concern it as a party to the alliance, the two Courts 
will use their best endeavours, as far as circumstances will admit, to realise this 
expectation, which, however, they alone have in fact not power to do, and will, at 
all events, see to the strict execution of the terms of Article XLEX of the Vienna 
“ Schluss Acts.” 

The Royal Cabinet indulges the hope that the explanations above riven will 
‘nduce the Government to confirm, by unreservedly and completely according to 
the offensive and defensive alliance between Prussia and Austria, its oft expressed 
confidence in these two Powers, and its devotion to the national interests ts 
recognised by itself. 

The Government points out in its note the objects that it wishes 
Germany to gain, among which it specifies the complete freedom of trade and of 
navigation on the Danube, and an effectual protection guaranteed on all sides to 
the Christian population living under the ‘Turkish sway. 

The Government will certainly be open to the conviction that 
the sooner, the more unanimously and the stronger the members of the German 
Confederation bind themselves together for the promotion of these objects, the 
surer are the prospects of Germany of obtaining them. 

That the Government should at the same time have testified its 
lively interest in the preservation of the Kingdom of Greece, in the state 
guaranteed by Treaty, is the more gratifving to His Majesty the King our most 
eracious Master, as His Majesty participates sincerely in this interest and cannot 
divest himself of the solicitude for the preservation of the territorial proportions 
of the Hast. 

‘[t will afford us peculiar satisfuetion to be assured by a prompt reply from the 

Government to the present communication that its representative in 
the German Diet will find himself empowered to vote without reservation for 
the participation of the Confederation in the ‘Treaty, as it would cause us the 
deepest regret to abandon the hope of seeing the work of union completed by u 
resolution of the Diet and the influence due to the thus formed powerful whole 
secured, 

Ghould we be obliged, however, to give up this hope, then the proposal for 
the alliance would naturally not be made in the Diet, and Prussia and Austria 
would find themselves in the situation to come to 8 further understanding only 
with those separate Governments which have already stepped forward as parties 
to their alliance, or which may still join the same. 

Your is empowered to communicate a copy of this document 
to 

I take, &e. 

Berlin, June 16, 1854.

the remaining members of the Confederation, Should such a case eceur, |

To your Lordship, the tortuous efforts of these petty States to exercise a

and indirectly hampered by the ambitious activity of some of the stutesmen to

affairs.

Sir J. Milbanke to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 3.) 


(No,.42.) 
My Lord, Munich, June 28, 1854, 

MY despatch No. 40 of the 24th instant was already written when T became 
aware of the publication, im ertenso, ef the note whieh emanated from the 
Bamberg Conference, the translation of a-summary of which, as it appeared in 
the German press, was therein inclosed. Since then I have also received your 
Lordship’s despatches bearing upon the proceedings of the smaller German 
States which took part in the Conference; and, in conformity with the instruc- 
tions contained in your Lordship’s despatch No, 42 of the 2\st instant, | have 
communicated to the Bavarian Minister for Foreign Affairs the substance of that 
marked No, 24, addressed by your Lordship, under the same date, to Her 
Majesty's Minister at Dresden. 

After perusal of that despatch, M, von der Pfordten inquired if I wished 
for an answer upon it; to which I replied that it depended entirely on him 
whether he chose to make any observations on it or not. His Excellency then 
observed that he could not admit, either that the Conference at Bamberg had 
heen ill-advised, or injurious to the interests of Germany’; and, above all, he 


denied that the German Powers had made, or intended to make, any sacrifice of 


their interests to Russian intrigues; adding, that had the despatch been intended 
for him, [ presume, in his capacity of Bavarian Minister, he should have 
considered its language in the light ofan insult (" injure” was the term he made 
use of). . 

He then proceeded to vindicate the right of the German States to express 
their opinion on their own internal affairs ; of the best mode of managing which, 
he maintained they were the most competent judges, and in which they would 
not admit any foreign interferenee. The exereise of this right, which I told 
him no one disputed for a moment, so long as it was not converted into an 
officious meddling with great questions of [uropean policy, which, as im the 
present case, involyed other interests hesides those purely German, had been, 
his Excellency said, the principal object for which the Bamberg Conferenee had 
heen summoned: and the raadlinces shown by the two Great Powers to comply 
with the wishes of the States represented at it, were a sufficient proof of the 
cood understanding and union prevailing among all the German States. 

These observations led to a long and desultory conversation, or rather, 
arcument, upon the value of the concessions made by Austria and Prussia, 
which, M. von der Pfordten was. at some pains to convinee me, amounted to 
all that had been required. ‘To this, however, with the knowledge L possessed 
of the answers returned to the Bamberg Resolutions by the two Great Powers, 
it was impossible fov me to assent, and | pointed out in particular the preten- 
sions put forward in his memorandum about Greeee, and the summons to 
withdraw their forces from the scene of action, which he appeared to wish to be 
simultancously addressed to both belligeres: parties. 

The first of these remarks was passed over in silence ; but his Excellency 
sought, ly a comparison of dates, to establish the impossibility of a compliance 
with the second, although the course suggested was approved in principle. 
Vpon this point, however, he explained that some misapprehension prevailed, 
inusmuch as he had only contended that it would be unjust to call upon Russia 
to make a retrograde movement, except upon the previous understanding that, 
from the moment when it began, the other Powers should desist from further 
hostilities, and take preparations for following her example. On the whole, his 
Excellency profesced himself to be highly pleased with the manner in which the 
results of the Bamberg Conference had been responded to by Austria and 
Prussia. Tle dwelt. | thought, with peculiar satisfaction on the prospect held 
out, that the Diet would be consulted upon, and allowed to Pareictiase in, the 
negotiations aud deliberations to which the expected answer of the Emperor of 
Russia to the Austrian summons, sent to St. Petersburgh on the Grd instant, 
iwust give rise under the provisions of the Additional Article of the ‘Treaty 
dened at Berlin on the 20th of April, Should these assurances, which 


ronless appear to me rather yague, be curried out to their full extent, the 


293 


smaller States will have achieved a triumph; and should the Emperor of Russia, 
as we are led to believe he will, comply with the desires of the two Great 
German Powers, and withdraw his forees beyond the Pruth, they will imme- 
diately, under the pressure of Russian influence, be again most actively at work 
to detach Germany from all connection with the views of England and France 
as to the conditions upon which peace ought to be concluded. That upon this 
point serious differences of opinion will manifest themselves, is, | fear, beyond 
all doubt; and I could not dissent from a remark made by M. von der Pfordten, 
that the evacuation of the Principalities was only a first step towards a solution 
of existing difficulties, but by no means to be looked upon as necessarily leading 
to an early or final arrangement of the Eastern question, although he does not 
seem to hope that it may contribute to hasten the assembly of an European 
Congress for that object. 

Before terminatine our interview [ took occasion to notice to M. von der 
Pfordten the just cause of complaint furnished by the hostile and mistrustful 
insinuations contained in his memorandum relative to the ulterior designs of the 
allied Powers. His Excellency’s reply was, that, even with the knowledge of 
the effect produced by the course he had pursued, if he were again called upon 
to pronounce himself upon these questions, he should give utterance to the 
same sentiments and in the same words. 

Not being informed as to the exact position in which the British and French 
Governments stand in respect to the Austrian Cabinet, | am unable to judge in 
how far the latter may be swayed by the tendencies of the smaller States; but J 
must repeat that if they are permitted to exercise that decisive influence over 
the future conduct of the two Great German Powers, which they are in great 
hopes they are on the poimt of acquiring, any negotiations which may be 
commenced, will, in my opinion, be troubled by their intrigues; and, if termi- 
nated at all without a further appeal to aris, will, in all probability, present but 
incomplete results. 

1 have heard from another source that on the arrival of the Emperor of 
Russia's answer, a joint note from the Diet to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh is 
in contemplation, but I have been unable to obtain any positive information as 
ta details, and 1 presume it would only be sent in support of the summons from 
the two Great German Powers in the event of a refusal on the part of His 
Imperial Majesty to comply with ther demands,
