My Lord, Foreign Office, July 3, 1854. 

I HAVE received your Excellency’s despatch No. 324 of the 1 9th of June, 
reporting that the Divan had refused to appoint General Guyon to the 
command of the Turkish army in Asia. 

The state of the Sultan's army at Kars has been under the serious con- 
sideration of Her Majesty's Government. ‘That army has from the first moment 
of its formation been delivered over to the command of men whom the Emperor 
of Russia could most desire to see in the places they have so unworthily filled, 
They have vied with each other in rapacity, cowardice, and ignorance 50 
notorious as to leave little room for doubt that they owed their appointments 
either to some treacherous design against the Sultan’s cause, or to the intrigue 
and corruption which poison the whole system of administration in Turkey. 

The only man who has displayed energy under the most adverse cincum- 
stances, and who in fact has sive the army from total dissolution, is General 
Guyon, and Her Majesty's Government therefore recommended that the chief 
command should be to confided him, not, as L informed your Exeelleney in my 
despatch No, 348 of the Jet of June, from any particular predilection for that 
officer, but because he was on the spot and had already rendered good services, 
and because he had earned for himself the confidence of the army. 

Her Majesty's Government would have been equally pleased if any other 
General possessing the requisite qualifications had been appointed in the place of 
the ignorant officer in command, 

Her Majesty’s Government learn with surprise and displeasure, by the 
report of Mr. Chabert to your ?xcelleney of the 19th of June, that the Turkish 
Ministers, relying upon the opinion of persons acquainted with the strategical 
merits of General Guyon, consider that he has not the capacity required for 
commanding the Sultan's army in Asia; but those Turkish Ministers neither 
admit that the army is ill commanded, nor do they indicate any intention at 
appointing & proper officer to that most important and responsible post. 

The Asiatic territory of the Sultan is now about to become the chief theatre 
of the war, and it is not to be endured that the Turkish army upon which the 
eooperation of which the allies must depend, should be lett in its present 
demoralized and and useless condition, of that the constant representations of 
Ler Mujesty’s Government should he perseveringly disregarded; and 1 have. 
therefore, by the unanimous desire of the Cabinet, to instruct your Excellency 
to spare no efforts with the Turkish Government, and if necessary to nddress 
your remonstrances to the Sultan himeclf, in order to secure that the army at 
Kars shall be placed under’ the command of an efficient and experienced 
General, and that immediate measures shall be taken for supplying its wants 
and improving its organization. 

Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

I did not gee M. de Beust until yesterday, and said at once that I had 
received a despatch which I was ‘nstrueted to communicate to him, but that 
knowing he understood English, it would be easier for him if he read it than if I 
read it to him. He took your Lordship's despatch, and read it twice over with 
the greatest attention, but with more agitation than I have often seen him 
evince, for generally speaking his sel{-possession is very remarkable. His first 
remark was, “Je crois que je serai dans le cas de répondre A tout ceci, et trés 
nettement ; mais qu’avez vous done éevit 

1 could not help smiling, but said the principal point of my despateh had 
been, that Austria and Prussia were resolved to act with those who became 
parties to the Treaty, and without those who declined, and that he knew this 
was correct. 

He said that at all events he must defend his principle, which was, that as 
this was a purely Federal question, the other Governments could not admit the 
right of Austria and Prussia to present. or offer them the Treaty otherwise than 
throueh the Diet, and through which they were ready to accept it. 

(i know that on Monday last, the 26th, he received a telegraphic message 
nen Munich, advising him to keep quiet, and to make no more stir in this 
affair.) 

He said that for some time back he was accused of being under Russian 
influence, but that when afew years ago he was not, and had opposed the 
ambitious plans of Prussia, supported by Russia, against other German States, hie 
defied any one to find in the Saxon or Russian archives such a lesson as wis 
contained in the despatch I had placed ‘1 his hands; and as to his being a 
friend to revolution, he appealed to me whether he had not giyen the strongest 
proofs of the contrary. 

| answered that | knew him to hate democracy as much as I did, but that 
all might be mistaken in measures, and that at a moment when, with the excep: 
tion of u very few individuals, all Germany—I meant the intelligent classes— 
were unanimous in their hatred of Russia and of the heavy hand she wanted to 
Jay upon its States, he surely should be on his guard as to taking a line, in all 
things, great as well as small, as would compromise his talents; for that now, 
when the Turks—not the English nor French—had resisted and beaten the 
Russians, he must see that neither he nor any other Minister could restore a 
prestige of their invincibility as completely destroyed. | 

He said, Mais, mon Dieu, je ne suis pas Russe.” and T answered, “ Then 
the enemies as well as friends of Russia are equally unjust in their opinion 
of you.” 

He said that he had never but the one object in view, to secure the 
independence of his country as long as possible, 

[ answered that no one wished for the independence of Saxony more than 
[, but that it would be better assured by remaining Germans, not Russians, and 
that your Lordship had put the question in its proper light by stating that this 
was the worst moment for showing disunion to the world. 

He said they were cight Powers of the same opinion; that the answer they 
had received from Austria and Prussia was, “tout e¢ quill y avait de plus 
convenable ;" and that the would all accept the Treaty throveh the Diet. 

T remarked that this last was in fact what the two great Powers wished to 
aseertain before they presented their Treaty at Frankfort, for they understood 
the anomaly of having first concluded it, and then im a manner beginning it 
again there; that they had offered it to their acceptance individually on the 
same footing as they themselves had made it as independent Powers, which 
position their Bamberg Conference seemed to decline or at least to hesitate as 
to accepting its responsibility, and that 1 thought on reflection that it would 
have been better left alone.

Proclamation, 
(Translation.) 
THE Commander-in-chief of the 3rd and 4th Armies, Baron de Hess, hus 
issued the following order to the army, which will find a loud echo in the heart 
not only of every soldier, but of every Austrian. 


Order to the Army. 


His Majesty the Emperor has, by an Imperial Decree of the 21st of June, 
graciously pleased to intrust me with the command on the eastern frontier of 
lis impire: 

While L shall seek to deserve this confidence of my Emperor and Master by 
the most unlimited submission to His Majesty’s person and service, and while, 
led by the experience of nearly fifty years spent in an active soldier's life, 1 trust 
it the same time with full confidence to the old invincible spirit which has always 
inspired our army, that spirit of discipline, of order, of bravery, and of self- 
sacrifice which so honouribly distinguishes the Austrian soldier and officer, as 
well as to the intelligence and courageous steadfastness in their duties of all 
superior leaders; but, above all, to the excellent direction of their troops on 
the part of those Generals who command the armies and corps d’armées, whom 
I see with unbounded confidence at the head of them: and I am convinced 
that they, as long and valued companions in arms and battles, will certainly in 
every position stand as true and efficient by my side. 

(Signed HESS,

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received this morning a despatch from 
M. de Bourqueney, dated the 30th ultimo, containing the details of a conver- 
sation of some importance which that Minister had just held with Count Buol. 

The latter had received despatches from Count Esterhazy of the 22nd 
ultimo. Colonel Manteuffel had arrived at St, Petersburgh, and had been 
cordially received by the Emperor, His Majesty's language, however, on the 
subject of the summons was cold, and gave no indication of what his answer 
would be. 

Still, Count Buol suid that he would not await its arrival in order to inform 
the Representatives of France and England of what the attitude of Austria 
would be, under the only three contingencies which could happen: 

1. If the Russian troops retired behind the Pruth, without the Emperor's 
expressing a desire to treat for peace, the object of the Convention signed 
hetween Austria and Prussia would have been attained, and the ‘Treaty would 
consequently become a dead letter. But, in the Protocols simned by the four 
Powers, the necessity of assuring the future integrity and independence of the 
Ottoman Empire had been nid down. 'This must still be provided for, and 
nist form the subject of further discussion between the four Powers, 

9. ‘The answer might be ao direct refusal. In this case, Austria would 
proceed to oecupy not only Wallachia, but Moldavia also, and her troops would 
attack any Russian troops that might endeavour to prevent the occupation, 

3. Russia might evacuate the Principalities, expressing at the same time 
a desire to treat for peace. Should this be the course followed, Austria would 
communicate that desire to the belligerent parties, and invite them to acquaiut 
her with the conditions on whieh they would be willing to make peace, Count 
Buol did not think that there was any likelihood of a divergence of opinion

The Barl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 236.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, July 6, 1504. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to mea despatch from Count Buol, stating 
that the accounts which daily reach him from Wa lachia leave little doubt that 
the Russian troops have received orders to evacuate Greater Wallachia. 

_ ‘The troops, as they retire, carry with them the judicial and administrative 
officers, and also the local treasure-chests and archives. The prospect of the 
total anarchy with which these measures threaten the country has thrown the 
sopulation of Bucharest into consternation, and pressing entreaties reach Vienna 
rom that capital for the intervention of Austria, in order to preserve the people 
from the misfortunes to which they would be exposed, if they were abandoned to 
their fate. ; 

The Emperor is accordingly disposed to send a force into Wallachia, 
although the answer of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh to the Austrian com- 
munications of the 8rd of June has not yet arrived. 

In taking the military measures requisite to carry out this intention, the 
Austrian Government believes that it is serving the common interest, because 
‘t las no other object in view than fo maintain order in countries suddenly 
deprived of the protection of all authority, to preserve them from a fresh 
invasion, and to reorganize there as soon 25 possible a regular administration, 
in concert with the Suzerain Power. 

I told Count Colloredo that I had no objection to make on the part of Her 
Majesty's Government to the course which Austria was about to pursue, and 
which might be now necessary, in consequence of the evacuation of Wallachia 
by the Russians, and the state of anarchy in which they had left the province ; 
but | could not admit that the entry there of Austrian troops was in accordance 
with the Convention lately signed between Austria and the Porte, unless it was 
the preliminary step to ulterior measures. 

The Emperor of Austria, according to that Convention, stipulates by means 
of negotiation to obtain the evacuation of the Prineipalities, and to employ, if 
required, the necessary number of troops for that purpose ; and, if the entry inte 
Wallachia is preparatory to driving the Russians out of Moldavia, it would 
appear to be a well-judged operation, and likely to prove embarrassing to Russia: 
but if, the Russians having quitted Wallachia ot thet own accord or under the 
pressure of necessity, Austria is to occupy that province, while Russia keeps 
quiet possession of Moldavia, I must observe that the Convention did not 
authorize such a proceeding. 

I assured Count Colloredo that I was induced to offer these remarks solely 
from a desire that no future misunderstanding should arise respecting the 
grounds on which a portion of the Sultan's territory was occupied by Austrian 
troops. ) 

Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Marl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(NO, 238.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, July 7, 1854, 

COUNT COLLOREDO read to me yesterday a despatch addressed by 
Count Buol to the Austrian Minister at Paris, with reference to a despatch from 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys to Baron Bourquency, communicating the views of the 
French Government as to the conditions upon which a solid and durable peace 
night be concluded. 

The Cabinet of the Tuilleries, Count Buol observes, will not consent to a 
general armistice, implying a suspension of hostilities by sea, unless it has 
previously the assurance that Russia will accept the conditions of peace which 
the French Cabinet deems indispensable, 

Nevertheless, in the event of Russia determining to evacuate the Princi- 
palities, and declaring herself at the same time ready to open negotiations for 
peace, the belligerent Powers might, i the opinion of the Austrian Government, 
without any inconvenience, consent in the first place to an armistice by land in 
Turkey in Europe. 

Upon the opening of negotiations, and after the basis of peace had been 
agreed upon, the armistice might become general by land and by sea. 

In discussing the conditions of a solid peace, the French Government was 
disposed to admit that, if Russia were ready to make peace at the present 
moment, the re-establishment of the territorial status quo ante might be assented 
to, but that the political status quo ante was impossible. 

Count Buol then proceeds to examine, one by one, the guarantees of future 
peace, which Europe would have a right to demand, 

1, Opening of the mouths of the Danube, 

In the opinion of the Austrian Government this might be regulated by 
means of a Convention, to which Russia would naturally be a party, and which 
should pluce under the control of Europe the cessation of all hindrances to the 
commerce and nayigation of the Danube. 


S01 


2. ‘The protectorate of the Danubian Principalities to be entrusted to some 
other Power than Russia. 

It appears to the Austrian Government that this object would be attained 
by substituting the safeguard of Europe for that of the Power which has notori- 
ously abused the exclusive influence which she had appropriated to herself. 

Austria, in her quality of bordering Power, might be charged with the new 
orgamisation of the Moldo-Wallachian Provinces that has now become necessary, 
The Convention between Austria and the Porte, of the 14th of June, contains 
the germs of the mission which might thus be eanfided to Austria. 

3. The cessation of the religious protectorate of Russia in Turkey. 

The Austrian Government is of opinion that the pretension of Russia to 
exercise an exclusive protection of the schismatic Greek Christians in Turkey, 
would be deprived of all pretext from the moment that there shall be secured to 
the Christian subjects of the Porte, to whatever creed they may belong, perfect 
equality of rights and independence in the administration of their spiritual 
affairs according to the particular laws of each communion, and which should be 
watched over by all the Christian Powers. 

4, The opening of the Black Sea, and the establishment on some part of its 
coast of a military port and naval station for the maritime Powers. 

Count Buol thinks that this implies a cession of territory which would be 
at variance with the principles hitherto laid down regarding Turkey, At all 
events the Austrian Government cannot doubt that no territorial cession ought 
to be imposed upon the Porte, and that such a sacrifice ought to be entirely 
spontaneous on its part. 

Count Buol observes that according to the confidential communications 
which have passed between Count Colloredo and myself, the British Govern- 
ment does not appear to have any intention of acquiring a port in the Black 
Sea, or of establishing there a permanent naval station. The guarantees aimed 
at by the British Government would appear to consist rather in stipulations by 
which Russia, in common with all other maritime Powers, should be forbidden 
to have more than a certain number of ships of war in the Black Sea. 

An arrangement of this nature would appear to the Austrian Government 
a more efficient guarantee for the future against attack upon the integnity and 
independence of Turkey, but it necessarily involves a revision of the Treaty of 
1841. 

5. As to the question of the expenses of the war, the Austrian Government 
expects an opposition on the part of Russia too insurmountable for them to be 
able to engage to support a demand of this nature. 

After thanking Count Colloredo for this communication, and assuring him 
of the value and importance attached by Her Majesty’s Government to the 
friendly interchange of opinions with the Cabinet of Vienna, I said it was 
satisfactory to find that upon several essential points the two Governments were 
agreed. 

| observed that the complete freedom of navigation on the Danube was now 
an European interest; that it must henceforth be euarded by the Great Powers 
of Europe; and that Russia must never again be allowed to obstruct that 
navigulion as she had hitherto done. 

It was’equally out of the question, I said, that Russia should retain any 
right of interference in the Principalities, which, as Count Buol proposed, should 
he placed under the safeguard of Europe ; but with respect to the new organisa- 
tion to be given to the Moido-Wallachian provinces, | remarked that great care 
rust be taken—first, to uphold the legitimate authority of the Sultan in that 
portion of his dominions; and next, that one military occupation should not be 
substituted for another, which might be equally opposed to the independence of 
the Ottoman Empire. 

Count Colloredo observed that the proposal went no further than that 
Austria should be charged with superintending the work of reconstruction ; and 
[ replied that if Austria would consider herscll'us acting on behalf of the other 
Powers, and that nothing was to be done without their previous SUNCLION, 
satisfactory arrangements might probably be made. 

With respect to the pretensions of Russia to exercise an exchisive protec- 
torate over the Greek subjects of the Porte, there could not now be two 
opinions ; but the rights and privileges of all Christians throughout the Turkish 
dominions must be secured and placed under the safeguard of the Five Powers.

With respect to the opening. of the Black Sea, and the establishment there

produced here by these communications than that I am assured that they have 
given satisfaction to the King of Prussia, and that His Majesty sees in them a 
conciliatory spirit which will make the cooperation of Germany with Austria 
unnecessary, and which will ultimately lead to the restoration of peace. 

He hopes no doubt that circumstances will soon arise which will absolve 
him from his liabilities to be ealled on to participate in the war, and I believe 
that there is no subterfuge that he will not have recourse to to extricate himself 
from his engagements with Austria and with the Western Powers. 

I have, &e.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 11.) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, July 10, 1854. 

THE Austrian Government have decided to forward the answer which they 
have received from St. Petersburgh for the consideration of the French and English 
Governments. If this answer had not contained the stipulation of a cessation 
of arms for the required evacuation of the Principalities Count Buol would not 
have forwarded it to the Governments; but as ‘t acknowledges and accepts as i 
basis on which to treat the three propositions ion which the engagements 
between the allies are founded, he has considered Fienself bound to submit the 
proposals, so. that the allied Governments may exercise their judgment with 
regard to them. In transmitting this decision to Gt Petersburgh, Count Buol 
has stated to the Russian Government that he maintains all his original 
demands. 

No relaxation whatever will take plaice in the military preparations of 
Austria, and the same preparations are ex jected from Prussia for the mam- 
tenance of the stipulations of the Treaty with Austria. 

Count Buol will forward to-morrow | or the next day by messenger to 
London an explanation of the views of his Government, together with copies: 
of the documents relating to present transactions.

-eturned this morning from the coasts of Circassia and Georgia. Captain Dacres 
reported to me that Soukhoum Kaleh is only held by about 100 Irregular

has hitherto contributed very much to the security of those places; but without 
proper garrisons they cannot be maintained, and it will become a serious 
question whether, under such circumstances, the guns, &e., should not be

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received July 11.) 


(No. 355.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, June 25, 1854. 


IT must be admitted that the Turkish Ministers and the Turkish officers 
are, for the most part, anything but what we could desire at the present 
juncture. In quieter times their deficiencies were evident enough; and much 
have 1 laboured, sometimes with and sometimes without instructions, to remedy 
evils of which the consequences were So CiSY to foresee, and so greatly to be 
apprehended. The time is now come when the neglect of friendly admonitions 
and the loss of opportunitics are severely felt, and rendered the more apparent 
as their effects stand out in contrast with the superior qualities and more effec- 
tive modes of operation exhibited by the Sultan's Christian auxiliaries. Even 
the strongest motives of action, — impending danger, unusual competition, 
and necessity that takes no refusal,—produce comparatively but little effect on 
those who exercise authority in the Turkish Empire. All such stimulants are 
in a great measure neutralized by confirmed personal habits and inveterate vices 
of administration, fatal alike to efficiency and to improvement, We have not 
to reproach the Ministers with a want of ability or ill-will, so much as with 
ignorance and apathy, mistrust of each other, and dread of responsibility, 
Those other just causes of complaint whieh prevail in the provinces and aries, 
are unfortunately rooted in the remains of a system effete for every rood 
purpose, and almost for every good quality, except cournse, itself tainted deeply 
with fanaticism, and sometimes degenerating into recklessness and cruelty. 

Under these circumstances, | fear we must be content, in wading aemaliiat 
the stream, to thank Heaven that we are not hurried off our legs, and to secure 
for our use such portions of what we require as. either flont loosely on the 
surface, or may be detached by repeated efforts from the bottom. It has been 
well said, that we are not fighting for the ‘Turks, but for T urkey ; and the 
pregnant truth contaimed in these words may serve not only to sustain Ws 
amidst the hazards and sacrifices of war, but also to guide us hereafter through 
the labyrinths of negotiation. Up to the present time, in spite of difficulties anil 
delays on the one side and soine disasters on the other, Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment, in concert with France and Turkey, have advanced steadily towards their 
object; and while the allies unite more closely, and display more actively their 
means of attack, the common enemy becomes more visibly insulated in position, 
with a vast expenditure, no inconsiderable losses, und vonsequently a diminished 
power of raising fresh supplies out of the mass of his resources, 

As sequel to these remarks I venture to remind your Lordship, with 
respect to the movement of Ler Majesty’s. forces, that after all, the principal 
objects required of the Porte have either sen obtained, or are ROW In) progress, 
notwithstanding the whole series of delays, wncertumtics, and obstructions. 
Lord Raglan’s army is actually on the scene of action in almost complete force, 
and, whatever may still be wanting to complete it, is relerable, | believe, ti 
causes independent of the Porte. 

The army, while it was here, occupied the best barracks possessed by the 
‘Turkish Government, All due facilities were afforded tor the xecommodation ot 
the several military departments, no tesa than for those of the fleet. Every 
euitable attention and complimentary distinction was shown to Llis Royul 
Hizhness the Duke of Cambridge. The hospitals indicated by Lord Raglan 
have been appointed for the reception of our sick and wounded. Four battalions 
of the Sultan's regular troops, with more than three field-batteries, and $x 
squadrons of Cavalty, have been attached to, Her Majesty's army, aud are 
preparing to join. The services of Colonel Beatson and of the officers appoliited 
to net under him are accepted by the Porte, and orders are given to Omer Pasha 
for their employment in diseiplining a corps of Irregular Cavalry, intended to 
amount to 4,000 men. Ollers of service from other Iritish olficers desirous ot 
fihting under the Snltan’s standard arc aecepted, so tar as their individual 
qualifications extend. Omer Pasha, who ts necessarily responsible to the Parte, 
has lately entrusted Colonel Cannon with the command of & ‘Turkish brigade, 


all 


and the duty of introducing succours into Silistria, He has uniformly received 
British officers with kindness and confidence, nor has he given slight proof of 
his willingness to listen to the sliggestions of so young, though intelligent, 4n 
adviser as Captain Simmons of the Royal Engineers. 


It is but just to bear in mind that the Porte and its Commander-in-chiel, 


while called upon to meet the advances of England with corresponding testimonies 
of goodwill and confidence, had also to provide for similar requirements on the 
part of its French ally; nor can 1 in fairness omit to mention the various 
instances in which, during the last few months, the Sultan anid his Ministers 
have acted agreeably vo m counsels, though having occasionally to overcome 
preconceived opinions, and to encounter serious aggressions with limited and 


imperfect means. It may be added im the same spirit, that when 1 have met 


with much opposition or evasion, there has been no lack of real difficulty in the 
nature of the case. | allude more particularly to the financial embarrassments, 


to the injudicious selection of public functionaries and officers, to the outrages 
committed by the Bashi-Bozouks, to the deficiency of supplies for the army, to 
the various questions of coal mines, telegraphs, and railways. In all these 


matters, the Government ‘s most assuredly to blame. for want of foresight and 


energy, for want of knowledge and want of confidence i those who can supply 
their deficiencies ; but the mischief 15 of old standing, and its ramifications form 
a barrier outside the Government, which must be taken: into the calculation, 
and which it sometimes exceeds the power of any administration to penetrate 
without a subterfuge or @ compromise. cs 

Perseverance, respecting its efforts, and watchful of opportunitics, can alone 
make head against this host of difficulties, named, or unnamed ; but western 
knowledge and western energy, now brought into immediate contact with the 
Government and people of these countries, and cooperating with the pressure al 
necessity, can hardly ful to work out a great, though gradual, change. Two, 
if not three large friendly armies, are Now occupying portions af the Sultan's 
Empire. Are they likely to leave it as they find it? Is it conceivable that their 
presence, their example, their intercourse with the inhabitants, will pass wily 
like a dream, and leave no permanent impression | 

If the Crusaders on their return from Syria enriched Iurope with the 
spoils of a civilization superior to their own, can We doubt that the enlightened 
armies of Christendom, now ewarming into ‘Turkey, will infuse into its barbarous 
population a part at least of thab knowledge and spirit ol improvement which 
raise them equally above the Christians of a former and the Mahomedans ol the

My dear Lord, Constantinople, June 29, 1854. 

ALTHOUGH no official aceount of the ineident has yet reached me, there 
can be no doubt that the ‘Turkish army near Batoum, under Selim Pasha, has 
undergone a signal defeat. Her Majesty’s Consul at Trebizond has sent me all 
the information he had been able to collect upon the subject, and | forward 
herewith a copy of his letter, to which he has given a private form. 

Reshid Pasha, who acknowledges that an officer had arrived at the Porte 
with news of the battle, assures me that Selim Pasha had no instructions for 
making a forward movement. My recommendation, before the season for military 
operations began, was that a defensive system should be maintained along the 
Asiatic frontier, in so far as the armies of Batoum and Kars were concerned. 

For your Lordship’s further information, | transmit in copy a letter which, 
though dated the 25th ultimo. has only just reached me. It contains some 
particulars relating to Selim Pasha's army and the attack on Redoubt Kaleh, 
which are by no means destitute of interest, The author is an emigrant 
Cavalry officer in the Turkish service. 

T have, &e.

My Lord, Treizond, June 22, 1354. 

THREE days ago some boats from Batoum brought intelligence of another 
battle having been fought on Thursday, the 15th instant, near Choorooksoo. 
There are numerous versions of the affair in circulation here, but the following 
details are those meriting the greatest confidence. 

On the day mentioned Selim Pasha, with five battalions of his beat Regulars 
(Arabistan Nizams and Imperial Guards), was at Ladova, a village situated 
midway between Arzoghetta and Choorooksoo— having, it appears, quitted 
Arzoghetta, discovered to be untenable in theeventof the Russians attacking— 
when a considerable foree (the exact number 1s not inentioned, but which, it is 
presumed, consisted of not less than 10.000 Russian troops and Georgians) arrived 
by a circuitous route and attacked the Rediffsand Bashi-Bozouks. which were in 
the rear of the village, ready to march to Choorooksoo; an umber of these [rregulars 
fell, upon which the rest fled to the hills. It is said 2,000 were killed before 
giving way. ‘The Russians having thus cleared the road to the village, entered 
it, and attacked the Regulars, who foucht well, but some 3,000 were killed, 
wounded, and taken prisoners. ‘The other 2,000 then retreated to Choorooksoo. 
In the midst of the engagement two field-batteries, consisting together of fourteen 
cuns, were ordered by Selim Pasha to quit their station at the entrance of the 
village, on the Turkish side, and to come to his assistance by a round-about way, 
These reached the spot where they were required, but through some stupid error, 
ao ammunition came with them, and not only proved useless, but finally fell inte 
Russian possession without opposition, 1 am not able to state what losses the 
Russians suffered; but they must have been considerable. Selitn Pasha was 
slightly wounded in the wrist, and Hugei Ahmed Pasha, Commander af the 
Lrregulars, had two horses killed under him, und was himself seriously wounded 
in tue shoulder. 

Selim Pasha is at present encamped at Choorooksoo, with the weeek of his 
army, consisting of about 7000 men, and is trying to rally his: lrregulars anid 
Militia. ‘This unfortunate affair has thrown a gloom all over ‘Trebizond. 

lt is evident the Russians evacuated altogether to entice Selim Pasha to it, 
and thus bring him clear of the dense forests, which, while be remained at 
Choorooksoo, rendered the operations of the [ussins dilficult and dangerous

(Pelegraphic,) Vienna, July 12, 1854. 

COUNT BUOL has just informed Buron Bourqueney and myself that 
after scrious deliberation he thought it would be more regular, and of greater 
weight, to convoke the Conference and lay before it Prince Gortchakoft's 
despatch, than to transmit it directly to the belligerent Powers. ‘The Repre- 
sentatives of England and France would, he supposed, declare themselves to be 
without the necessary instructions to accept that document, and would apply to 
their Governments for them. ‘The motives which might provoke a refusal on 
the part of the allied Governments to accept it, or the guarantees on which they 
might insist as the condition of their accepting it, would be communicated by 
their Representatives to the Conference, which would take formal notice of their 
unswers, The Protocol to be drawn up on this occasion, would afford the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh the opportunity of giving explanations which would 
test the sincerity of its proposals. 

This mode of proceeding, Count Buol thinks, has the advantage of concen- 
trating the negotiations on the spot where the dangers of disunion make them.

My Lord, Trebizond, June 26, 1854. 


1 HAD the honour to address you & private letter on the 22nd instant, 
containing the details, such as we had received them, of a battle which was fought 
at a village near Choorooksoo on the 15th instant. The arrival to-day of the 
Ottoman steam-frigate “ Siik-Shadi? enables me to give your Lordship the 
exact details which have been communicated to me by a Colonel atta hed ta 
Selim Pasha’s statl, who 1s proceeding to Constantinople with the Commander- 
in-chief’s despatches, and confirmed by the secons officer of the above-men- 
tioned frigate. 

The battle took place on the morning of the 16th instant (Friday), and not 
Thursday the 15th, us was stated, ‘The Russian force, which attacked in three 
columns, consisted of 25.000 Infantry, 1,500 Mounted Cossacks, and 10,000 
Georgians, with 4 guns. Selim Pasha’s strength was about 6,000 Regulars, and 
12,000 Irregulars and Militia, supported by two battalions of 6 field-pieces each, 
‘The greatest portion of the Turkish Irregulars and Militia gave way in the very 
commencement of the action, and fled 9, the mountains. ‘The Regulars fought 

4 7 


en ie LT | 


1 oe 


a22 


bravely, as did the Artillery ; in fact, the former only ceased their fire when their 
ammunition Was expended. The latter also fell short of shot, and continued to 
fire for a while with blank cartridge; but the Russians soon found it out, threw 
all the Mounted Cossacks on the guns, and captured them. Selim Pasha lost 400 
Regulars, and 1,800 Irregulars and Militia are unaccounted for, but chiefly sup- 
osed to have been slain ; Moreover, 1,500 Regulars and Irregulars w ounded, which 
the Turkish frigate arrived to-day conveyed from Choorooksoo to Batoom, whence 
they will be transported to Khoppa, where # hospital 18 beitig organised for the 
summer months, and to which place all the medical officers have been already 
removed. Both Selim Pasha and Hagsi Ahmed Pasha are said to have 
displayed. the utmost courage and sing froid, ‘The overwhelming force of 
the Russians on this oceasion compelled Selim Pasha to leave m its possession 
all his tents and camp baggage, mules and horses. ‘The loss of the Russians 
was positively very great; as many 0% 6.000 killed and 3,000 wounded. 
Tt took them two days to. bury their dead, and carry away their wounded. 
T am assured General Andronikott, the Commander-in-chiel, retired from the 
field with two wounds. ‘The Russians made afew prisoners, amongst whom, & 
Colonel of Artillery and three Subalterns. 

Portion of the Russian force retired to Kiska, leaving the residue, some 
20,000 men, 1m Arzoghetta, 

Selim Pasha, with about 9,000 men, 15 at Choorooksoo. tHe 18 trying to

tents. The poor troops are on bread and water for want of better; butas the 
Ramazan is over, Lam in hopes our Pasha will resume his former activity, and 
send down supplies forthwith.

by the first steam-packet direct for Constantinople.

terms, that | would beg to submit for your Excellency consideration that there 
representation should be brought under the early notice of the Porte. 

Captain Dacres, who has recently been there, informed me that the 
"Turkish had sent there a considerable equipment of field artillery, 


323 
39,000 stand of fire-arms, an immense quantity of prepared ammunition, 
and at least twenty tons of lead; and these valuable stores he believes to be at 
the mercy of any detachment of Russian troops which may think fit to move 
down upon the place. 

The Circassians, Captain Dacres considers to be quite unfit to form part 
of the garrison. They have no idea of working or firing 2 cannon ; and notwith- 
standing that the large store of warlike supplies 18 within their reach, no one 
of them has evinced a disposition to possess the arms, or to do anything 1 
cooperation with the Turks. 

The wandering mode of warfare to which the Circassians are accustomed is 
the only one that suits them, or to which they are willing to subject them- 
selves. 

Captain Dacres algo represented, that the garrison of Redoute-Kaleh is in 
reat want of an officer of Engineers to suggest, and superintend the execution 
of, any works that may he necessary:

Inclosure 3 in No. 390. 
Captain Jones to Vice-Admiral Dundas. 


( Extract.) Redoute-Kaleh, June 10, 1854. 
I‘ seems to me that the Turks have no troops to spare; they can hardly 


manage to keep this place, and even here have not, in reality, half the number 
that they pretend to have ; the same applies to St. Nicolat and Chooraoksoo. 
The Circassians, Abassians, and the country people do not generally show 
any desire to occupy the seaports permanently ; they come down to Soukoum- 
Kaleh for a few days, amuse themselves walking about and riding out, and in 
taking their guns to pieces and putting them together again, but as to working 
at the fortifications or putting the jines in a state of defence, they will not do it, 
there is no keeping them at work. I mention this with the view of coming to 
some decision as to what 15 to be done with the Circassian forts, for at present | 
cannot help thinking that they are in a most unsatisfactory state. 

In many of these forts there are from twenty-four to thirty guns, merely spiked 
and easily cleared; there are large quantities of shot, and empty shells which have 
heen fitted with wooden fusees, (Asa specimen of the nature of the guns, 1 send 
you the return from Soukoum-Kateh.) 

It is evident us the forts remain, and, so far as the Turks or mutives are 
concerned, are likely to remain, the Russians may return by land whenever it 
auits them, to Gelendjik on the north, and Soukoum-Kaleh on the south; this is, 
af course, supposing that, we have no naval force on the spot: the intermediate 
forts may probably be guarded hy the natives, 

Then, Sir, looking forward to the probability of a cruizing squadron on this 
coust during the winter, would it not be desirable to put Gelendjik and Soukoum- 
Kaleh in a state of defence, both by sea and land, as safe and secure rallying 
points against all contingencies. ; 

Soukoum-Kaleh I should think would be a healthy pluce, without much work, 
but Gelendjik is a muddy swamp, and would require a good deal of labour to 
makethe ground dry and habite le for winter. Materials are abundant, that is 
to sav, seu-beach, and sand, and planks, and building stone. 

There ave lots of good guns in the eleven abandoned intermediate places 
between Soukoum-Kaleh and it, but all are without carriages. 

Report states that the Russians have eleven sailing-boats on the river, each 
mounting a small gun; that they are at a place called Orline, twelve hours 
distant by lind, but that they are on the southern branch of the [hassi. In 
the coasting chart this ranch is not sufficiently marked. It is as large, nearly, 
ae the other; it turns off at right angles about 1,000 yards from the mouth, and 
ata mile and a-half south approaches to within 200 yards of the beach, thence 
goes away east right up the country. 

The Russian map docs not notice this branch at all. 

[have urged Ibrahim Bey to use every mean’ he can devise to find out 
whether these boats exist or not, for, in the absence of a ship, this position 
depends so materially on the fact of whether he is subject to attack by a descent 
on the river; such an attack might carry the place, 

The weather up to the end of last week has heen everything we could desire, 
excepting not quite wind enough for sailing-ships ; on the night of the 7th or 
ath. however, we had a strong breeze cast-aouth-cast right off shore, the air hot 
and dry; barometer having fallen to 29° 59°, 1t moderated gradually, going round 

to south and west, and became very humid; a good deal of surfon the bar, and 
landing dangerous. 

‘To-day we have had heavy rains, with the wind fresh in putts, and very 
variable, a awell coming in from the south-west, but nothing to prevent passing 
the bar if requisite.

IN the course of the night, Selim Pasha and garrison from Asourjet 
arrived and this morning (June i4th) I had a long interview with him. 

[ may mention as an mstance of want of candour, and 1n illustration of the 
amount of dependence to be placed on information even from the fountain-head, 
that Selim Pasha never told me of the defeat he had met, and avoided acknow- 
ledging that he jad been worsted in. his attack on Soupson Ghour, but the 
facts elivited from other quarters clearly showed that he had been defeated with 
considerable loss, stated to be from 500 to 2000 killed, st 

It appears the Georgians had deceived him, by fering to join against the 
Russians, and that he sent o considerable force out under {alil Pasha in 
command of the Regulars, and Hassan and Hamet Beys m command of the 
ashi-Bozouks ; that when near Soupson they were caught in an ambush and 
defeated, losing two guns, the Georgians joining ogainst them in the woods, 
Selim Pasha merely said that he had retreated from Asourjet because he 
found it too straggling a place to defend, and requiring 50 muny points to he 
enarded, and that he was going to make lis present position strong and secure ; 
he showed great anxiety for me to express my approbation of the movement, 

I fully approved of the object, and a ‘e-1 had any doubt t should even 


ee ee i 


g26 


move further back so as to improve the facilities of communication with 
St. Nicolai and Choorooksoo. : 

We then went on the subject of Redoute-Kaleh and Soukoum-Kaleh. He is 
fully alive to the importance of these places, but said it was impossible for him to 
send a man until reinforced himself, and that all he could do at present would 
be to send two more guns to Redoute-Kaleh ; that he had already written to 
Constantinople urging the necessity of more regular troops. 

| offered to take him along the coast, but he said he could not leave the 


eamp until he had seen the defences complete, and that in six or seven days he: 


hoped to have everything finished, and would then be at liberty. He said that 
he had written to Ibrahim Bey, to exert himself to get Redoute-Kaleh in a proper 
state of defence, and desiring him to seck the advice of the English officers, and 
do everything they told him.

HIS Majesty the Emperor of Russia desires you at the earliest opportunity 
to express to the Wallachians the displeasure which His Imperial Majesty 
cannot but feel at the extraordinary attitude assumed by them, and more 
especially by the Bovards, towards the Russian troops who entered the Prmn- 
cipalities, with the object of freeme them for ever from the insupportable yoke 
of ‘Turkey. ee ne 

The Emperor does not consider it right that under existing ciroumstances 
His Imperial Majesty's co-religionists should remain under other than @ Christian 
Government, 

Although the Wallachians do not understand this, because they are too 
much under the influence of the Western sclismatics, nevertheless, the Emperor 
eannat leave unfulfilled the task which i confided to him by Heaven, as chief 
of the faithful Christians; namely, to deliver for ever the members of the true 
Creek Christian Church from ‘Turkish rule. ie : 

These thoughts have occupied the Emperor since the beginning of his 
clorious reign, and now the time has arrived for His Imperial Majesty to 
exeente his long settled plan, notwithstanding the interference of the other 
powerless States of unbelieving Europe. ; ; 

We are with God, God 15 with ws, and victory 18 On CUE side. 

His Majesty the Emperor desires you, M. le Baron, to reproach the 

suvards severely, and the other high Wallachian functionaries, for their disloyal 
conduct towards aur troops. 

The time will come when these refractory Wallachtans, who have excited 
Ilis Majesty's indignation in the highest degree, will bitterly atone for their 
disloyalty. Only act severely, M. le Baron, the more severely the better against 
these lawless Wallachians; this ve the desire of the Emperor.

was indisposed to converse OF the last communications from St. Petersburgh or 
Vienna, and [was unable to learn from him anything which could throw a light 
an the intentions of Austria or Prussia. 

He said that he had expected by this time to have received from Count 
Buol an indication of the wishes of the Austrian Government, but that nothing 
had vet reached him. 

‘TL usked his Excellency if it were trae, os | had been told, that he objected 
to the communication to the Conterence of Count Nesselrade’s despatch to 
Prince Gortehakolt? He replied that personally he wished the Conference to 
take cognizance of it, but that he did not know whether he should be able to

cppored io the communication of account of the discussions that must elisue, 
for he felt that Baron Bourqueney, Upon this occasion as Upon previous ones,

would take the lead, and that he would probably make proposals which it might 
he inconvenient to adopt. 

I endeavoured to show to Baron Manteuffel the il effect that would be 
caused if the. Representative of Prussia did not attend the Conference, and that 
‘1 would be immediately ‘inferred that the policy of the King was changed, anc 
that His Majesty wanted to he freed from his engagements. “He replied, that as 
far as he was concerned he was most desirous that the Austrian and Prugsian 
sovernments should be fully agreed and act together, and that he hoped it 
would still be so, but that until he heard further from Vienna he could not say 
what Prussia would do, 

It appears to me from what his Excellency said, and from what I have heard 
from other quarters, that we are on the eve of a serious Crisis ; that the King is 
not disposed to go the lengths desired by Count Buol; that His Majesty fears 
another step might involve him more deeply ; and that as he°is resolved, if 
possible, not to epart from his peace poliey, His Majesty will, if pressed, retire 
altogether from the Vienna Conference and from the connection with the Western 
Powers, though he will not on that account consider himsel! released from his 
engagements with Austria. 

These I believe to be the opinions held by the Prussian Government at 
this moment, and if they were to separate from the Conference, there 18 no 
doubt that such defection would be viewed with the highest satisfaction at 
St. Petersburgh. 

Prussia desires neutrality more than ever, and will, T apprehend, take any 
step likely to msure her not being called on to adopt active measures against 
Russia: at the same time T cannot helieve that she will willingly separate from 
Austria, but will use her best endeavours to induce Austria so to modify her 
policy that the two Governments. may continue to: act together on the fastern 
question. 1 understand ‘ndeed that the Prussian Government is most anxious 
to correct impressions that have gone abroad as to a difference of opinion 
existing between the two Governments, and that an ‘natruction has been sent to 
M. de Bismark, at Frankfort, to declare that the policy of Austria and Prussia 
continue unchanged. 

The communication of the Treaty of the 20th of April to the Diet will 
probably be made very shortly, Darmstadt has sent in its adhesion to it, and 
Wurtemburg stands now alone in her opposition £0 the measure; but it is 
believed that when the time comes she will also yield, and accede to the ‘Treaty.

(Na, 272, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, Jnly 15, 1854, 

COUNT BUOL having requested Haron Bourqueney and myself to 
call upon him together on the 13th, he went ‘nto further explanations of his 
views as to the present position af the relutions of Austria with Russia and with 
the allies, than he had done the previous day. Tt appeared to Baron Bourqueney 
and myself that the first impression of Count Buol, regarding the answer from 
St, Petersburgh, was more favourable than his present one. This arises from his 
sense of the difficulties which will attend the negotiation which may tow be 
undertaken as to the guarantees which the Governments of England and France 
will ask for, which are the abdieation of all the exceptional positions which, for 
years be have been held by Russia in the East ; and this Count Buol feels, as 
does the Emperor, that Russia, under present circumstances, cannot accept, 

Count Buol says: England and France may refuse to negotiate, and we 
shall still be bound to carry out our engagements. We feel that we shall have 
great embarrassments and dificulties with Prussia and Germany, but we shall 
act: we call upon you, however, to consider our position, and, hy moderation of 
language, to spare US 0S far as you are able from these difficulties, and to seek to 
lessen, if you cannot avert them. Now, it is not probable that any Government 
will brusquement reject 8 proposition of peace. You may indicate, therefore, 
the guarantees which you consider us necessary, and without which a peace 
would not now be necepted ; but you may do this in the most courteous form. 
All the discussions as to these points must necessarily take a certain time, during 
which your operations will not stop either by sca or land, and Austria, during 
that time, wil be engaged in completing her most extensive military preparations, 
and will weigh upon, and influence all, the plans and operations of the Russians. 
If Russia, on being acquainted with all the guarantees you require, rejects 
them, we (Austria), according to the engagements by which we are bound, must 
enter Moldavia, to carry out our demand for evacuation; and, if resisted, we do 
not disguise that it is, for us, War. So, in the two cases, by agreeing to the 
proposal to enter ‘nto the Conference for the purpose of discussing the Russian 
answer, you neither have diminished the chance of the successful conduct 
of the war and of the operations you have determined upon, nor of obtaining 
a peace such as you desire. |

(No. 275. Confidential.) 

My Lord, Vienna, July 18, 1854. 
IN a conversation which took place yesterday with Count Buol, relative to 

the mode of convoking the Conference, he held to j 


a language too im yortant not to be faithfully reported to your Lordship. It is 
the most decided indication we have yet received of the serious intention of the 


avon Bourqueney and myself 


343 


Austrian Government, under the circumstances contemplated, to take an active 
and decisive part towards obtaining the general objects of the alliance. 

Count Buol stated in this conversation, that he raised no objections 
generally to the ‘conditions which you specify as desirable to be obtained in your 
Lordship’s despatch No. 298 of the 7th instant. 

If you transmit these conditions, as the hasis upon which you will consent 
to negotiate, in your Lordship’s reply to the Russian note, which will be 


communicated to you through the Conference, Count Buol will forward them to 


‘St Petersburgh; and, in case of their rejection, Count Esterhazy will be directed 


to require, in accordance with the demand already addressed to the Russian 
Cabinet, the order for the evacuation of the Principalities. If this be not 
complied: with, he will be instructed, after a short delay, to announce: to Count 
Nesselrode the decision of his Government that he should quit St. Petersburgh, 
after which the Austrian army will receive orders to enter the Principalities, with 
the view of obtaining their evacuation by the Russian armies. Count Buol 
looks upon this decision as leading at once to the commencement of hostilities, 
unless the Russian Government should conform to the requisition they will have 
received. He conceives, therefore, that in three weeks the Austrian army may De 
required to act, and he appeals to the English and French Governments to direct 
their forces to be ready to cooperate with those of Austria, in the operations 
which they will then be called upon to undertake. 

Count Buol stated that he had reecived a telegraphic message from 
Belgrade, announcing the arrival there of despatches from Constantinople, 
which reported the nomination of Dervish Pasha as the Commissioner Extra- 
ordinary of the Porte for the Principalities, and the intention of the Porte to 
replace there the Government of the Hospodars. . 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

Sir A. Malet to the Earl of Clurendon—( Received July 22.) 
(No. 69.) 
My Lord, Frankfort, July 21, 1854. 

THE long-deferred communication of the Austro-Prussian ‘Treaty was 
made by the Plenipotentiaries of the two States to the Diet in the sitting of 
yesterday, 

A Commission was named to prepare the reply, consisting of the Repre- 
seu of Austria, Prussia, Bavaria, Hanover, Saxony (Royal), and Mecklen- 

ure. 

It is expected that an extraordinary sitting will be convoked on Monday to 
receive the report which will be presented by M, de Schrenk, the Plenipotentiary 
of Bavaria. : 

The only positive declaration of non-aecession made yesterday was from 
Denmark, and it was accompanied by such expressions of warm. approval of the 
principles on which the two Powers have acted, as very much to weaken its 
appearance of dissent. 

Wurtemburg made a rather equivocs! declaration. to the effect that her 
adhesion might have been secured under certain conditions, but it is not thought 
that she will venture to record decided dissent on the Protocol. 

The objectionable pretensions of the Bamberg Conference will, I am 
positively assured, be altogether got rid of. 

As | hepe to obtain all particulars of the report of the Commission, | need 
not at present detain your Lordship further in the matter, 

| I have, Ke. 
(Signed) A. MALET.

The Barl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No. 248,) 
My Lord, . Foreign Office, July 22, L854. 

HER Majesty's Government have attentively considered the answer of the 
Russian Government to the demands of Austria, and can arrive at no other 
conclusion than that it is evasive and altogether eludes those demands, 

Austria required of Russia to evacuate both the Principalities within a short 
space of time, und not to make that evacuation, which was essential to the 
interests of the whole of Germany, dependent on conditions with which Austria 
had not the means of complying: ‘The Russian answer fixes no time for the 
evacuation o€ the Principalities ; it demands an armistice as the indispensable 
condition of withdrawing behind the Pruth, aud requires from Austria the very 
concessions on the part of the belligerent Powers which Austria declared before- 
hand her inability to procure. 

Russia affects to adhere to the Protocol of April 9, but she always proclaimed 
her intention to uphold the integrity and independence of the Ottoman Empire, 
even while occupying by force a large portion of the Sultan's territory ; and the 
manner in whieh she now alludes to the protection of the Christian subjects 
of the Porte by no means indicates that she has abandoned her original 
pretensions, or that she views the question in the sane light as the Powers who 

signed the Protocol of Ap 


ee) die ee ol a 


vil 9; and Count Negselrode passes by in silence the 
47 


sara 


S46 


most important point in that Protocol, viz., the pledge of the Four Powers to 
connect the Ottoman Empire with the general equilibriam of Europe. There is 
nothing in Count Nesselrode’s despatch to lead to a belief that Russia will lend 
herself to any such arrangement, but without which, according to the opinion 
of the Austrian Government, no peace can be solid or lasting. 

The answer then of Russia appears to be derogatory to the dignity and 
interests of the two German Courts which addressed these demands to Russia, 
and to contain nothing which merits the favourable consideration of England 
and France. 

We have every reason to believe that Count Buol concurs with Her 
Majesty’s Government, and that of the Emperor of the French, in considering as 
bases of peace— 

1. A new organisation of the Prineipalities, calculated to substitute the 
Protectorate of Europe for the influence that has so long been abused in those 
provinces. 

®, A revision of the Treaty of 1841, and the limitation of the naval power 
of Russia in the Black Sea. 

® ‘The freedom of the navigation of the Danube under the guarantee of the 
Great Powers of Europe. 

4. The abolition of the Protectorate claimed by Russia oyer the Greek 
subjects of the Porte, and plucing the different Christian communities in the 
Ottoman Empire under the safeguard of the Christian Powers, with due respect 
to the independence und sovereign rights of the Sultan. 

The Austrian Government is aware that England and France, without 
precluding themselves from making other demands, adhere to the above 
stipulations as the indispensable bases of peace ; and Count Buol will doubtless 
admit that, no overture with respect to an armistice or a Congress can be 
seriously entertained unless accompanied by the full and unreserved assent of 
Russia to the conditions already agreed upon between the maritime Powers and 
Austrin. 

In the meanwhile the season for ‘operations 1s wearing away, and Her 
Majesty's Government deeply regret this prolonged indecision on the part of 
Austria, She has hitherto, as | have observed in my despatch No, 247 of this 
day's date, declined to make known her intentions, or to concert her military 
movements with the allies, upon the ground that her geographical position con- 


stituted an important distinction between her and the Western Powers; that if 


she had declared war at the same time as England and France, she would on 
the very next day have come into collision with Russia, single handed, and 
before her own preparations were completed, and that she must therefore wait 
until the allied forces were in a position, such as the Balkan, which would 
enable her to reckon upon their cooperation, 

Her Majesty's Government did not altogether agree in these views, for by 
so doing, they would have admitted that the well-organized army of Austria 
was inferior to, or had anything to fear from any force that Russia could bring 
against it; but it was for Austrin to determine upon the moment when she 
thought it expedient to take the field. The allied forees, however, have for 
some time pust been at Varna. ‘The effect of their arrival there must have 
operated in raising the siege of Silistria, and there can be no doubt that if the 
Russians had had the Turks in their front, the allied forees on one flank, and 
the Austrian army on the other, they would have been destroyed, or compelled 
to make a precipitate retreat, and a great step would thus have been made 
towards the reestablishment of peace. 

Ingland and France have given abundant proof of their desire to. act 
cordially with Austria in defence of principles that are eommon to the three 
Powers, and for objects which may be said to affeet Austria more immediately than 
they do the Western Powers; but England and France having at vast expense 
and inconvenience been forced into this war, are determined that it shall be pro- 
secuted with unabating vigour; their honour is engaged im not laying down 
their arms until a just and honourable peace is secured; but ther military 
operations cannot be made subordinate to indecision which they are unable to 
control, and the duration of the war, as well as the conditions of peace, must 
depend on whether England and France are to net alone or in conjunction with 
Austria. 1 am, &e. 

(Signed) CLARENDON.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland, 
(No. 249.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, July 22, 1854. 

I HAVE to acknowledge the receipt this day of your Lordship’s telegraphic 
despatch, by which Her Majesty's Government learn that Prussia has declined 
to attend the Conference which Count Buol proposed to summon for the 
purpose of communicating the answer to the demands addressed by Austria to 
the Cabinet of St, Petersburgh, and that it will in consequence be transmitted 
by Count Buol to Count Colloredo for the information of [ler Majesty's 
Government, 

Her Majesty's Government, however, being already 1m possession of thits 
answer, and having taken it into mature consideration, | shall no longer 
delay communicating to your Lordship the views which they entertain with 
respect to it. 

lt is unnecessary to dwell at any length upon the arguments by which 
Count Nesselrode endeavours to throw upon the Western Powers the responsi- 
bility of the war which Russia alone has provoked. Count Nesselrode objects 
to the form of the summons addressed to Russia by England and France, and 
maintains that this summons, rendered imperative by the acts of Russia, was 
the true cause of war; but he takes no account of the long series of negotiations 
during the past year, nor of the repeated warnings which were given to Russia 
by France and England, and le chooses to forget that it was the invasion of the 
Principalities by Russian troops which first disturbed the peace of Europe, and 
which has rendered abortive every effort for its restoration. The despatches of 
Count Buol to Count Esterhazy, to which Count Nesselrode’s despatch is an 
answer, points ont clearly upon whom the responsibility falls of the present state 
of things; and in the Protocol of the 9th of April the four Powers have solemnly 
recorded their opinion, that the summons addressed to Russia by England and 
France was founded in justice. 

The opinion of Europe has been pronounced im favour of the course 
pursued by England and France, and it is needless therefore that they should 
defend themselves against the accusations of Russia, 1 proceed to examine the 
other points contained in the Russian answer. 

In the first place, if the demands of Austria, supported by Prussia, are 
considered in a purely German sense, it is impossible that the answer of the 
Russian Cabinet can be considered satisfactory by the two German Powers. 
The main points put forward in Count Buol’s despateh to Count Esterhazy 
were; 

L. The necessity of a speedy evacuation of the Danubian Prineipalities ; 

9. ‘The impossibilities of making this evacuation, required by the essential 
interests of Germany, dependent upon conditions which it was out of the power 
of Austria to ensure. 

But Russia fixes no limit whatever to the occupation of the Principalitics, 
and she looks upon an armistice us a previous condition sine qud non of the 
withdrawal of her armies beyond the Prath. 

The injury then which, in the opinion of Austria and Prussia, the Russian 
occupation infligts upon the Germanic Confederation continues unabated ; nay 
more, it is aggravated by the refusal of Russia to attend to the just demands of 
the two German Powers. 

Count Nesselrode professes, it is true, to adhere to the principles laid down 
in the Protecol of the 9th of April, but this declaration is worth little as long 
us the Russian troops remain on ‘Turkish soil, 

Tn fact, the evacuation of the Principalities is essential to the integrity of 
the Ottoman Empire, and their occupation is in itself a flagrant breach of the 
public law of Europe. The erisis which disturbs the peace of the world had its 
origin in the passage of the Pruth, and it is impossible to acimit the pretensions 
of Russia to make the reparation which she owes for an act unanimously 
condemned, tepenilene upon the exigencies of a position which she has volun- 
turily created for herself. 

Nor can England and France consent to an armistice upon the vague 


a4é 


assurances given by Count Nesselrode of the pacific disposition of the Russian 
Government. After making such great efforts and sacrifices, and engaged as 
they are in a cause so just, the allied Powers will not stop in their course 
without the certainty that they will not again be ealled upon, after a short 
‘aterval, to reeommence the wer, The particular conditions of peace must 
depend upon too many contingencies for it to be possible to Tay them down 
definitively at the present moment. Her Majesty s Government have, however, 
no hesitation in stating the guarantees which, in their opinion and m that of 
the French Government, are essential to secure the tranquillity of Europe from 
future disturbance. ‘These guarantees are naturally suggested by the dangers to 
uard against which they are required, 

Thus, Russia has taken advantage of the exclusive right which she had 
acquired by Treaty, to watch over the relations of Wallachia and Moldavia with 
the Suzerain Power, to enter those provinces as if they were part of her own 
territory. 

Again, the privileged position of Russia ‘1 the Black Sea has enabled her 
to establish in those waters a naval power which, in the absence of any counter: 
balancing power, 15 a standing menace to the Ottoman Empire. 

The uncontrolled possession by Russia of the principal mouth of the 
Danube has created obstacles to the navigation of that great river which 
seriously affect the general commerce of Europe. 

Finally, the stipulations of the ‘Treaty of Kutchuk-Kainardji, relative to 
the protection af the Christians, have become, by a wrongtul interpretation, the 
principal cause of the present strugele. 

Upon all these points the status quo ante bellum must undergo important 
modifications. 

Her Majesty's Government cannot doubt that the Austrian Government 
will admit that these views. are in accordance with the principles laid down in 
the Protocol of April 9, and that ‘i would be difficult to restrict within more 
moderate bounds the inquiry which, by that Protocol, the four Powers engaged 
themselves to make In common, 85 to the means best caleuluted to maintain the 
Ottoman Empire, by attaching ‘eto the general balance of Europe. But it is 
remarkable that, to this passage in the Protocol of the 9th of April, the only 
passage of capital imporuines, implying, as it does, the necessity of a European 
revision of the ancient relations of Russia with ‘Turkey, Count Nesselrode care- 
fully avoids making the slightest allusion. 

In fact, the profession of the Russian Cabinet, that it adheres to the prin- 
ciples laid down by the Conference at Vienna, eontains nothing which is of a 
satisfactory nature, 

Her Majesty's Government are at a loss to understand the meaning of 
Count Nesselrode’s declaration, that the integrity of the Ottoman Empire will 
not be menaced by Russia so long as that integrity is respected by the Powers 
who new occupy the territory and waters of the Sultan, What comparison can 
he drawn between the invaders and the defenders of the ‘Parkish territory ? 
What analogy can exist between the presence of the allied troops at the 
invitation of the Parte, under the authority of a diplomatic Convention, and the 
forvible invasion af the Ottoman territory by the Russian armies ! 

It ig unnecessary to say anything further as to the conditions which are 
attached by Russia to the evacuation of the Principalitics, and | come now to 
that paragraph in Count Nesselrode’s despatch which relates to the situation of 
the Christian subjects of the Sultan. 

It amounts to nothing less than this: that the Russian Cabinet includes 
amongst the ancient privileges which are to be preserved to the Greek Church, 
the entire rights which flow ftom the Protectorate, civil as well as religious, 
claimed by Russia; but it eannot for a moment be supposed that the system 
catablished hy such w Protectorate, even eit were based upon a European 
eyorantee, could be compatible with the independence and sovereign rights of 
the Porte. Fler Majesty's Government is very far from saying that Europe can 
he indifferent to the amelioration of the condition of the Christians in Turkey ; 
on the contrary, they think that Europe ought to take an active interest in the 
welfare of the Rayal populations, and ought to come to an understanding as to 
the best mode of taking advantage of the generous intentions of the Sultan 
towards his Christian subjects, but, at the same time they are firmly convinced 
that the reforms which are necded in the government of the various Christian 


349 


commiunities in the Ottoman Empire can only be effectually and beneficially 
earried out by the Porte taking the initiative with regard to them, and that if 
such reforms are to be promoted by any foreign influence, it can only be by 
means of friendly counsel and advice, and not by an interference grounded upon 
Treaty engagements into whieh no State could enter without abdicating its 
independence. 

In fine, it appears to Her Majesty’s Government that the respective 
situations of the different Powers are in no way whatever changed, they are 
only more clearly marked out, by the answer of the Russian Cabinet. England 
and France must therefore continue in the attitude of belligerents ; on the other 
hand, ag the Principalities have not been evacuated, Austria and Prussia will, 
no doubt, consider that the obligation of the ‘Treaty of the 20th of April, 
strenethened, so far as ‘Austria is concerned, by her separate engagement with 
the Porte, subsist in all their force, and that the time has now arrived for their 
fulfilment. 

1 have thus fully explained to you the views of Her Majesty's Government, 
which are entirely shared by the Government of the Emperor of the Freneh, 
with whom Her Majesty’s. Government has been in constant communication 
upon this subject, and 1 have to instruct your Lordship to deliver a copy of 
this despatch to Count Buol. 


Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon, —(Recewed July 23 


(No. 413.) 
My Lord, Berlin, July 21, 1854 

1 HAVE seen Baron Manteutfel to-day, and found his Excellency as little 
disposed as at any of my late interviews, to enter into confidential conversation 
respecting the intention of the Prussian Government with regard to the last 
communication from St, Petersburgh. I inquired whether he had sent instruc: 
tions to Count Alvensleben to attend the Conference which 1 understood Count 
Buol wished to assemble, to take cognizance of the despatch addressed by 
Count Nesselrade to Prince Gortchakoff on the 44th of June. He replied that 
he had not done so, and on my asking what objection there could be to # 
conference of this nature, which after all, was a mere matter of form, he gave 
me to understand that there was as much hesitation on the subject at Vienna 
is here, but he would not enter into details as to the reasons which prevailed 
with the two Cabinets; and on my urging him further, on the plea that Count 
Buol had at all events origmally proposed the Conference, and that but for the 
‘wterference of the Prussian Government the communication would have long 
since taken place, he observed that 1 was not correctly informed when I believed 
that the difficulty rested solely with Berlin, for that Austria was far from being 
anxious to press for the ‘mmediate ussembling of the Conference. 

After exchanging these observations with his Excellency, 1 told him that I 
felt it my duty to call his attention to the impression whieh the late conduct of 
the Prussian Government had produced in England : that we had hoped to have 
found it acting in conformity with the engagements contracted in the Protocols 
of Conferences signed at Vienna, but that there were now evident symptoms of a 
desire, not only to thwart our policy in the Eastern question, but_to encourage 
Austria to take a less active part than she wished to do; that Prussia was no 
longer pursuing even a system of neutrality, for her acts were, diplomatically 
eae tack hostile to us, and that he must not be surprised if Her Majesty's 

fovernment felt that they had good reason to complain of euch conduct, 
Baron Manteuffel attempted to explain, that these proceedings were solely 
dictated by the King’s desire for the restoration of peace, and that there was 
nothing hostile in his intentions towards England; when L observed that much, 
as Her Mujesty’s Government desired peace, and I believed they desired tt as 
unilently as the Prussian Government, it was useless to entertain the idea that 
we should be blinded by such flimsy Prepares as those contained in Count

Nesselrode’s despatch ; that England was prepared to carry on the war with 
vizour, and would not stop until she saw an opening for negotiating an honour- 
able and durable peace, and that in my opinion it would be wise for Prussia to 
desist from attempting to force upon the consideration of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, any proposals that did not hold forth a prospect of being favourably 
received; that we had not embarked in the war lightly, and that although we 
had been deceived in our expectations, that Prussia would have seen her interest 
in joining with us, and thus prevent the extension of the field of hostilities, that 
Prussia must not suppose, because she seemed more inclined to espouse the 
cause of Russian aggression, rather than the just one which we were supporting, 
that her defection would induce the least relaxation in our preparations ; on the 
contrary, the conduct of Prossia might oblige us to increase them, and would 
force us to consider the necessity of adopting some new mcasurts to meet the 
apparent desertion of a Power that we had heretofore looked on as an ally. 
Baron Manteufiel persisted in the assurances that all that Prussia wished 
for was peace, and that the attainment of that point was the abject of her 


policy. 

Her Majesty's Government will be better able to judge than 1 can be, of 
the probable results of the efforts which have been made by Count Alvensleben 
and Colonel Manteuffel at Vienna, to prevent the assembling of the Conference, 
but I am credibly informed that Colonel Manteuffel had obtained an audience 
of the Emperor Francis Joseph, and that he had succeeded in obtaining the 
assurance from His Imperial Majesty, that he would endeavour to meet the 
desire of the King of Prussia on the subject, and [ may add that the general 
impression amongst persons here, usually well informed, is that the Prussian 
arguments will prevail. 

It is not unworthy of remark, that at a moment like the present one, 
Count ‘Thun has taken leave of Baron Manteuffel for some weeks, and that the 
Austrian Mission is now in charge of Count Crivelli, the first secretary.

the Conference of Count Nesselrode’s despatch of the 17th ultimo. In deference, 
however, to the wishes of Prussia, Count Buol had sent that despatch to London 
and Paris, instead of submitting it fo the Conference. In the opinion of the 
‘Austrian Government, it was unsatisfactory, and Austria would be obliged to 
enter the Principalities. He trusted that, under these circumstances, Prussin 
would act up to the engagements which she had contracted, and immediately 
begin her armaments, ; 

Prussia, the despatch adds, had returned an evasive answer, stating that 
she must know the opinion produced in London and Paris by Count Nesselrode's 
despatch, before she could reply to Count Buol’s communication. 

After giving me this intelligence, M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that he was 
about to send to Berlin copies of the despatches which he liad lately addressed 
ta M. de Bourqueney upon the subject of Count Nesselrode’s despatch, in 
concert with y 
communicated to M. de Manteuflel; and that be did not doubt that your

Government to know the opinion of the two Western Powers.

Count Brandenburgh, the Prussian Chargé d’Atfaires (Count Hatsfeldt having 
taken a few weeks’ leave of absence!, he told that gentleman that he must

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received July 25.)

My Lord, Paris, July 24, 1854. 

THE despatch concerted with Her Majesty’s Government as that which 
should be sent to Vienna in answer to the confidential communication of Count 
Nesselrode’s despatch of the 17th instant to the Cabinets of London and Paris, 
was forwarded to M. de Bourquency yesterday. It was accompanied by another 
despatch in which M. Drouyn de Lhuys gave M. de Bourqueney clearly to 
Sap ear that the French Government did not intend to enter into any 
diseussion of the contents of the Russian despatch, but to consider Count 
Nesselrode’s proposals, if they could be called such, as inadmissible, At the 
same time it is laid down that, such being the case, it is absolutely necessary 
that the allies should know the intentions of the Austrian Government, and 
whether the latter is willing, by joming the Convention of London or of Con- 
stantinople, or by replacing them by some equally binding instrament, to 
cooperate actively against Russia. 

The allies would not have advanced to Varna, it is said, without the 
confident expectation of being aided by the Austrian troops. Public fecling m 
England and France will not brook any further inactivity in the allied camps, 
but the two Governments must know, and have a right to inquire into the degree 
of cooperation which they are to receive from Austria, as the plan of the 
campaign must in a measure depend upon the movements of the Austrian 
armies. 

I have, &e.
