Communication made to the Diet by the Representatives of Austria and Prussia. 
(Translation.) 


Austria AND Prussts.—The Envoys have been charged with the following 
communication :— . 

In their declaration of the 24th of May of this year, the Courts of Austria 
and Prussia have laid before their confederates their position 1n the present 
Suropean difficulties, and added the expression of a wish, that by means of a 
constitutional declaration of will on the part of the Diet, a solid guarantee might 
he obtained for the agreement of the united Governments of Germany, amidst 
the dangers of the state of the world, 

The Dict has by its resolution of the above-mentioned day, declared that it 
acknowledges the agreement of the two Powers to be the real foundation for the 
union of Germany, and for the preservation of common German interests. It 
has acknowledged it as requisite that the resolution of the members af the 
Dict vigorously and faithfully to cooperate, should obtain a suitable expression 
through the legal organ of the Confederation. 

The more sincerely the Governments of Austria and Prussia rejoiced in this 
declaration, so much the greater will be the satisfaction in finding themselves 
now in the position to be able to lay befere this assembly an agreement 
euaranteed in the appointed form of a Treaty, and comprising the whole range 
of German interests. 

The Enyoys have the honour herewith to transmit the authentic text of the 
Treaty concluded at Berlin on April 20th of this year, and since ratified by 
both parties, between His Imperial Majesty the Emperor of Austria and His 
Majesty the King of Prussia, respecting the establishment of an offensive and 
defensive alliance, as well as an Additional Article belonging to it and forming an 
integral part of the same, and to invite the German Diet in the name of their 
‘Ilustrious monarchs to accede to this ‘Treaty. 

They are commissioned to accompany this document with the following 
remarks and further communications :— 

“Austria and Prussia, in the negotiations which have led to the conclusion 
af the alliance, have followed out the leading idea, not only to strengthen the 
bonds of friendship and federal alliance which already exist between them, but 
also to procure for themselves still more extended pledges for the security of 
their States, and also for the common protection of the united interests of 
Germany. The provisions of the Treaty realize this elevated solidarity, inasmuch 
as they bind the Contracting Parties, for the continuance of the present war, to a 
common defence against every foreign attack on any part of their united 
possessions, and expressly extend this union to the case of one of the partict- 
pators being obliged, for the protection of German interests, to take more active 
Wieasures. 

These obligations, when the Gonfederation unitedly gives its adhesion to 
this alliance, will be extended according to ‘Treaty to the whole compuss of the 
German territory of the Confederation, and to the non-German possessions of 
Avstria and Prussia, Germany will then, by virtue of the provisions of the 
alliaee, without devinting from the fundamental character of its Constitution, 
with a view to its preservation and defence, be able to fulfil its task with 
mereased energy, of protecting, us @ closely united integral Power, the common 
German interest, and at the sume time of cooperating for the maintenance of 
the European balance of power, on which the safety of all States rests. 

The principles which the chief instrument of the ‘Treaty of the 20th of 
April establishes have, ‘1 the Additional Article, supplementary to Article I] of 
thie same, found w special application to the state of difficulties in the Enst, ancl 
the Envoys have the commission to lay before the Diet, ut the same time, 
copies of those instructions which the Courts of Vienna and Berlin, in execulion 
of the provision of this ‘Additional Article, have addressed to their Missions at 
the Court of Tussia. 

The Government of Germany will certainly know how to appreciate the 
forethought which induced the Sovereigns of Austria and Prussia to determine 
that a further extension of warlike operations on the part of Russia on the right 


350 


bank of the Danube, as well as the continuance of the occupation of Moldavia 
and Wallachia for an indefinite time, werk incompatible with the great interests 
entrusted to their care. But also their Germanic confederates will not refuse 
acknowledgment and approbation of the spirit of moderation and love af peace, 
which the two Powers have not disowned in any of their proceedings, ‘The 
restoration of a permanent peace remains the object of the wishes and the 
efforts of both Cabinets; and they cling firmly to the hope, that His Majesty 
the Emperor of Russia will give heed to the language of his old allies, which 
springs from a deep sense of duty, and thus carry out the wish of a peace- 
able settlement, 1 order that in consequence of this changed position of Russia, 
and of the necessary practical ‘nfluence of the same on those of the remaining 
belligerent Powers, the way for an understanding may be again 0 ned; and 
that, obtained in the interest of Germany, be also made useful for the peace of 
urope. 

The Cabinets of Vienna and Berlin are submitting, in this moment, the 
answer of Russia to the most conscientious examination, and they will consider 
“as their duty to communicate this answer to the Dict, as soon a8 it shall have 
acceded to the alliance, and to enter ‘ato confidential relations with tt there- 
upon in the spirit of the Treaty. ‘They will also take care to ensure to the Diet 
its due influence in all further negotiations concerning it, as participator in the 
alliance; and as far as it depends upon the question of the form of its represen- 
tation not to be separated from considerations of expediency, they will at present 
hold to the principle of the XLIXth Article of the Vienna Final Acts, and, at 
any rate, in the eventuality there pointed out, will see to the complete carrying 
out of this provision of the Laws of the Confederation, 

The Govermnents of Austria and Prussia draw, from their confidence in 
the judgment and common sense of the Governments of Germany, the consoling 
conviction, that as regards the objects and the duties which are provided for the 
Germanic Confederation in the face of the events of the pee time, a genuine 
union of feeling and fellowship reigns among its members, The resolution 
whieh the two Courts now look for, will make the united moral and material 
power of the great German Contederation serviceable for these objects and 
duties, and assure to this powerful confederacy, under ull cireumstances, its due 
influenee ; so that Germany, DY the Divine help, will rise unshaken out of the 
most serious of political difficulties that have betallen Europe since the founda- 
fion of the German Confederation.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Reeeived July 31.) 
(No. 286.) 
My Lord, Vienna, July 26, 1854. 

THE decision of the Austrian Government to occupy the Principality ot 
Wallachia, which was reported to be on the point of being evacuated by the 
Russian armies, referred to in your Lordship's despateh No. 247 of the 22nd 
instant, was taken during the period of suspense as to the reply which the 
Russian Government would return to the requisition of Austria to withdraw 
from both the Principalities. The Austrian Government, while waiting for that 
answer, could not by any act of hostility enter upon a course of action opposed 
to the means she had in the first instance adopted to endeavour to obtain that 
withdrawal and which were still in the course of being carried out. — But during 
the period occupied by this proceeding, the evacuation of one of the Principalities 
appearing to be about to take place, the Austrian Government believed that they 
should obtain an important advantage to the allied eause by at ance oceupying 
that Principality, by reestablishing the former Govermnent, by preventing the 


| 


reoceupation of the country by the Russian troops, and by thus arriving 
immediately (whatever might be the answer to the Austrian requisition) at the 
permanent removal from one Principality of a Russian vossllane 

The Austrian Government, being at that time precluded from taking a 
hostile part, believed that they were doing good service by rendering sale from 
future occupation a portion of that territory, the liberation of which it was the 
eeneral interest to obtain, | : 

Count Buol believed that the allied and Turkish forces were assembled itt 
Bulgaria, not merely for the rchef of Silistria, but tor the expulsion of the 
Russian invaders from the Principalities, and although he was engaged and 
determined to obtain this object by peacable representations, if that was possible, 
but if not, by foree of arms, he was not aware that the allied ani Turkish 
urmies intended to subordinate their-action to the longer process which, under 
the difficult circumstances of her position, Austrian had felt herself obliged to 
adopt. It was under this erroneous impression that she declared that her 
oecupation of the evacuated portion of the Principalities should not in any 
way interfere with the advance of the allied armies, and, although she 
expressed her belief that they would so advance, she in no way found 
fault with their not doing it; on the contrary, she would now regret that 
those armics should expose themselves to an operation against the great foree of 
the Russian armies now assembled near Bucharest, until, if the Government of 
St. Petersburgh should still refuse the evacuation, Austria should be able to take 
part in that operation. | | wi eae 

The Austrian Government never contemplated the possibility of its being 
supposed that she could have exercised any armed mediation. — Her object. by 
entering the evacuated portion of Wallachia was to place herself in an advanced 
position, from which to occupy at a later period the remainder of the Princi- 
valities, either by the consent of Russia, or by the more active employment 0! 
er troops. . rare 

The Austrian Government never regarded the evacuation of one of the 
Principalities as in any way a compliance with the demand they had addressed 
to St, Petersburgh; and should it have been so interpreted by that Cabinet, 
their demand would in no way have been swayed or restricted by such an 
insinuation. : 

Count Buol is entirely alive to the obligations taken by the Protocol of the 
9th April, for the attainment of the evacuation of the lrincipalities, as well as 


afl 


to those taken by the Treaty with Prussia, by the note to the Diet, and by the 
Treaty with the Porte; and he steadily maintams the declaration made to your 
Lordship by Count Colloredo, that his Government would procure that evacua- 
tion “de gré ou de force.” His expectation that the allied armies would follow 
the retreating Russian armies, was founded in the belief that they would profit 
by a movement which, at the time, was reported as one of great precipitation, 
and which would have advanced the general cause for which the allies were 
united; but he in no way intended, by the expression of that expectation, to 
impose upon them a task the fair share in which (when the moment for action 
had arrived) his Government was prepared and willing to undertake. 

The present inaction of Austria is imposed on her by the lapse of time 
whith was necessary to enable her to communicate the Russian reply to the 
Western Powers, in compliance with the consent they had expressed to receive 
it for consideration; and this inaction will be brought to an end when she has 
transmitted their answers to St. Petersburgh, unless the Russian Government 
should at once comply with her reiterated demand for the evacuation of the 
Prineipalities, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

The Eorl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 
(No. 205.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, July 31, 1854. 

ON the 27th instant Count Bernstorlf read to mea despatch to himself from 
Baron Manteuffel, another from Baron Manteuffel to Baron Werther, and a 
third from Count Nesselrode to Baron Budberg. 

In the first despatch Baron Manteuffel states, with reference to the Russian 
answer to the demands made by Austria, that Russia having announced her 
readiness to negotiate, or to agree to an armistice, had entirely abandoned the 
exceptional character she had hitherto given to her occupation of the Prin- 
cipalities, which she now engages to evacuate upon certain military securities 
being guaranteed to her, | 

The King of Prussia, Baron Manteutffel adds, entirely approves of this 
condition, which he considers to be dictated by prudence and military honour, 
and His Majesty, in making himself the medium of communicating the overture 
of Russia, hopes that they will be impartially exammed by Her Majesty's 
Government, in order that the objects which it ts sought to attain by the war 
may be clearly made known, 

Baron Manteuffel declares that there can be no doubt of the sincerity of 
the intentions of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh to accede to the Protocol of 
April 9 

In writing to the Prussian Minister at St. Petersburgh, Baron Manteuffel 
says, that the King fully recognises the moderate and conciliatory spirit which 
dictated the Russian answer to Austria, and His Mujesty engages to renew his 
efforts at Vienna, London, and Paris to arrive ata peaceful solution. 

Baron Manteuffel further says, that this task would be impossible i full 
reliance were not placed on the wisdom and good faith of the Emperor Nicholas, 
and that His Imperial Majesty would enable the German Powers to feel that 
their interests were safe, as the defence of those interests was the object of the 
engagements entered into, whether with themselves or with the Cabinets of 
Paris and London. 

Count Nesselrode’s despatch to Baron Budberg is an abridgement of the 
one he has addressed to Prince Gortchakoff, He states that the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh, although not agrecing entirely in the opinions of Austria 
respecting the occupation of the Principalities, yet taking into consideration the 
particular interests of Austria and of Germany on the Danube, and the nature 
of the engagements contracted by the Courts of Vienna and Berlin with the 
Western Powers by the Protocol of A pril O, Russia is willing to retire from the 
Principalities upon certain securities, and to negotiate for peace on the basis of 
the three principal points of the Protocol, or, at least, to prepare the way for 
negotiation by concluding an armistice. In this way, Count Nesselrode says, 
the means will at once be offered to Austria and Prussia to fulfil their obligations 
towards the belligerent. Powers, 

1 thanked Count Bernstoril for these communications, and again assured 
him that Hor Majesty's Government was fully alive to the pacilic mtentions of 
the King, and that as the Russian answer had been transmitted to us irom 
Vienna it had been duly examined, and that the opinion formed of it here and 
at Paris differed entirely from that which was conveyed in Baron Manteutfel’s 
despatch, That opinion, T said, had been transmitted to Vienna, and your 
Lordship had been instructed to communicate the substance of it to Baron 
Manteutlel, 

1 added that war had altogether changed the position in which England 
und Fruce stood, when, in conjunction with Austria and Prussia, they recon 
mended to the Emperor of Russia the terms of peace, ahke honourable and 
advantageous to Russia, offered by the Porte; and that we could now accept 
of no medivtion, nor, under present cireumstances, be parties to any negotiation, 
direct or indirect, with the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. 

Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

hands a letter from the King of Prussia to Her Majesty, expressed a doubt as to 
whether he had said what I reported to your Lordship, respecting the reasons 
whieh had induced the King to forbid ihe attendance of his Minister at the 

Conference, and upon which matter it appears by your No. 425 that M. Balan 
spoke to your Lordship. 

LT reminded Count Bernstorff of what had passed between us, and told hin 
that 1 adhered verbatim to the statement made in my despatch No. 196 to 
your Lordship. 

In the course of conversation Count Bernstorft remarked, that Prussta had 
no intention of rendering service to Russian; and | answered that the 
intentions of the Prussian Government could be known only to themselves, but 
that the fact of great and continuous services being rendered to Russia by 
Prussia was beyond all doubt; and I thought, moreover, that if tt had suited 
the interests of Prussia, or that the Prussian people would have consented 
openly to take part with Russia in the war, it would have been a great advantage 
to the Western Powers: we should then have had an avowed enemy with whom 
we should have known how to deal, but that now we had an enemy under the 
guise of an ally, who was inflicting upon us all the injury in his power, hy 
paralyzing the action of Austria when she was prepared to identify her poliew 
with that of England and France. 

The Cabinet of Berlin, however, I said, might be assured, that we were 
under no delusion with respect to its proceedings, and that they would not be 
easily forgotten. 

Count Bernstorff having stated that the Prussian Minister would now be 


ava 


allowed to attend the Conference at Vienna, I said it was too late; that if the 
Russian answer, immediately on ‘ts arrival at Vienna, had been communicated 
to the Conference, the proceeding would have been regular and in accordance 
with the course previously pusued; but the King of Prussia had thought proper 
to depart from that course, and the opinions of England and France had been 
asked and given upon Count Nesselrode’s despatch, and now, after a lapse of 
three weeks, to assemble the Conference to take this despatch into consideration 
would, In addition to other objections, be attended with a degree of ridicule to 
which the Governments of England and France were not inclined to expose 
themselves. | a 
Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

My bord; Stockholm, July 24, 1854, 

IN my despatch No, 187 of the 2st instant I had the honour of informing 
your Lordship that the Commandant Blanchard had returned to this city from 
Paris. He was furnished with a private letter from M. Drouyn de Lhuys to the 
French Minister, and brought also a most satisfactory report of some verbal 
assurances relating to Sweden, whieh had been given him by the Emperor of 
Austria, by whom he was received twice during his visit to Vienna. ‘The letter 
from M, Drouyn de Lhuys instructed M. Lobstein to obtain an audience of the 
King for M. Blanchard, who was authorized to tell His Majesty that the condi- 
tions required by Sweden were agreed to (admises) in London and Paris, and 
consequently to urge the King to declare, without delay, against Russia. | 
2 esterday evening the French Minister and M. Blanchard were received at 
the Palace of Haga by the King, and remained in conference with His Majesty 
for nearly two hours. M. Blanchard proceeded, without delay, ta lay before the 
King a report of his interviews with the Emperor of Austria, regarding which | 
am only able to state generally to your Lordship that assurances most satis- 
factory to Sweden, in the event of her declaring war against Russia, with the 
ultimate view of reacquiring possession of Finland, were given verbally by Mis 
Imperial Majesty. M. Blanchard then communicated the substance of M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys’ letter, which I have mentioned above, to the King, who replied that 
he was “ conyaineu et rassuré” by the report of the Emperor's language, Still 
he, as a Constitutional Sovereign, must necessarily require more, or, in other 
words, the approval in writing on the part of Austria of the Treaty for an 
offensive and defensive alliance between England, Franee, and Sweden. After 
some discussion, during which M. Blanchard was the principal speaker, the King 
agreed to enter into official negotiations without delay, and to proceed at once 
to prepare troops (préparer des soldats) ; but His Majesty added that, before the 
7th (the day upon which the steamer suils for Lubeck), he would himself draw 
up astatement of his views and conditions, which le should request M. Blanchard 
to carry to Paris in person. 

M. Blanchard said that he should be only able to do so if His Majesty's 


‘statement was such as would meet the views of the French Government, and so 


justify his (M. Blanchard’s} return to Paris, which was contrary to his orders. 

_. Thave above given your Lordship a summary of the result arrived at, not 
without some hesitation on the part of the King; but it seems that when once 
thus much was obtained from His Majesty, the whole question was very freely 
discussed, The King stated that he should be able to bring into the field a 
force consisting of 70,000 men, 4 line-of-battle ships, 2 frigates, 10 steamers, and 
200 gunboats. ‘The ships of the line would not, His Majesty said, be required, 
perhaps, with so lange a fleet in the Baltic, but they would, at all events, be 
useful for transporting the troops. In addition to this, I will venture to remind 
your Lordship that a Swedish Aa of the line carrying from 74 to 80 guns, does 
not draw more than 23 feet of water. | 

The subsidies which would be required for the above force would be 


of 


3,300,000 rix-dollars banco (about 275,0001.) a-mouth, and with regard to this 
the King spoke very decidedly. Less was out of the question ; and His Majesty 
proceeded to point out the cheapness of a Swedish soldier, and the cconomy it 
would be for England and France to employ 4 Swedish army. ‘To this may be 
added the consideration of the climate in the north, as regards which neither 
English nor French can be put in comparison with the Swedes. And Tam 
informed by M. Blanchard that the King did not appear to shrink from the idea 
of a winter campaign. 

The great difficulty in His Majesty's mind appeared to be to find a pretext 
for breaking with Russia, but that would be overcome if something was done by 
the fleet, and the expeditionary corps from France, which we presume is now 
onits way to the Baltic. The King said that some decisive blow (un fait d’armes), 
such as the taking of the Aland Islands, would so rouse the enthusiasm of the 
Swedish people, that he would be justified in saying to the Emperor of Russia 
that he was no longer able to maintain his neutrality. 

Although the arrival of Her Majesty's Minister at this Court, Mr. Magemis, 
may be expected here on the S7th instant, I think it right to lay betore your 
Lordship the substanee of what T have been able to learn from M. Lobstein and 
M. Blanchard.

My Lord, . Munich, July 29, 1854, 

THE uncertainty which has, until lately, prevailed at all the smaller Courts, 
and the reserve niaintained towards them by the two great German Cabinets, 
relative to the answer returned by that of St. Petersburgh to the summons fo 
evacuate the Danubian Principalities, addressed to it by Austria on the Srd of 
Tune, has occasioned a tolerable amount of dissatisfaction, and has given rise, I 
understand, to many complaints of the intentional slight thus put upon them, 
This silence, however, seems to me to be completely j ustified by motives ot prudence, 
and, in fact, to have been the natural consequence of the insight afforded into 
the views and designs of all those States which were represented at the Bamberg 
Confercnees } even without any reference to the part which I still believe them 
to be Si kode of playing in the present political crisis, if they think they can do so 
with safety to themselves; whilst, on the other hand, the unnecessary delays 
whieh they have thought proper to interpose in signifying their accession to the 
‘Treaty of Berl'n could TE fuil to weaken, to a great extent, that confidence 
of which their ready acquiescence in. the policy of the two great Federal Powers 
was one of the first conditions, That object is now happily attained, and 
protestations of their devotion to the common cause of German interests are 
not wanting; but yet an attentive observer can scarcely avoid remarking certain 
lurking Russian tendencies among the many petty Sovereigns of Germany, 
which indicate that, in spite of the reverses inflicted on the Emperor, their faith 
in his omnipotence is us yet but little shaken. 

Towards fostering this blind reliance on the Conservative power of thei 
Imperial Master are directed all the efforts of Russian diplomacy, which is 
unremitting in its endeavours to produce, on their part, a coolness and suspicion 
towards their more powerful neighbours, with the ill-concealed design of creating 
disunion and embarrassment between them, suflicient ta incupucitate Austria 
from taking any effective steps for curbing the aggressive inclinations of Russia 
in the direction of the East. 

The Bamberg Conferences went far to enlighten Europe on these points, but 
they were inopportune, inasmuch as they exhibited to the world the want of 
unanimity subsisting within the bosom of the Confederation, which each 
Government feels, but which they are all so unwilling to admit; and, in this 
respect, the result of that meeting may not be altogether without importance, 
when the great question at issuc Bhad Suare further developed itself. ‘The 

5D 


378 


submission of the smaller Governments to the will of their two more powerful 
confsderates, has, forthe moment, caved them from the danger to which their 
own imprudence had exposed them, but should they hereafter give any indi- 
cations of too great a readiness to listen to the attractive suggestions of Russia, 
and attempt to commit any fresh act of folly likely to thwart or compromise 
the united action of Germany, they would then, in all probability, meet with 
that reward which they would then so richly merit, and for which they would 
not have long to wait, if a sincere and cordial understanding were once established 
between Austria and Prussia. ' 
‘The knowledge, however, that this is next to unattainable, even as regards 
what are commonly termed German interests, forms the basis of the hopes and 
operations of the Russian Cabinet, and it is remarkable that the smaller Courts 
owe the first communication of the Emperor's reply to the summons ol 
the Austrian Government of the 3rd of June to the Russian Agents avere- 
dited to them. Such, at any rate, was the course adopted here, and the

the Bavarian Minister for Foreign Affairs was, 1 am told, acecompanied by a 
most urgent appeal to the Government to join with Prussia ith counteracting the 
projects bearing a character so hostile to Russia, which the Austrian Cabinet 
is supposed to be about to pursue, Phe tone of this despatch, which M. von 
der Plordten read to me at a late interview, and with which your Lordship 15 of 
course acquainted, presents a singular contrast to the haughty language hitherto 
held towards the European Powers, and almost supplicates for permission to 
withdraw, without further saerifice, from the embarrassing position im which the

results leave but little room for conjecture, since the determination: of Austria to 
insist upon her demands for the speedy evacuation of the Prineipalities, is, to 
all appearance, daily becoming more fixed, and her preparations for the 
approaching ¢risis mare matured, ; 
‘The Russian Cabinet, however, amidst the host of untoward events which 
have accumulated upon it of late, seems averse [0 throw away even a chance, 
and encouraged no doubt by the sentiments exhibited at Bamberg, which 


unquestionably predominate in the higher regions here, recently made a last 


effort to detach the Bavarian Government from the policy of Austria. 

Your Lordship is aware that a similar course was pursucd im respect to 
most of the other small Courts of Germany which took part 1n the Conferences ; 
and that autograph letters from the Emperor to the respective Sovereigns were 
dispatched in all directions, ; | 

Colonel Isakoft, one of His Imperial Majesty's wides-de-camp, was the 
bearer of that addressed to the King of Buvaria, and his arrival here some 
three weeks ago, and his reception at the Royal country residence at Hohen: 
schwangau, where the King was then residing, created no sul sensation IN the 
capital. Every one was naturally wnxious to ascertain what wis going On, and 
what could have occasioned a mission of this deserption ; and my Austrian 
colleague in particular appeared desirous to get at the bottom of what bore 
every mark of a new intrigue against the policy pursued by his Cabinet, ce 

For same time nothing upon which any reliance could he placed transpired ; 
but trusting to information derived from two different sources, both usually well 
acquainted with what is passing within the precincts of the Court, I think I may 
venture to state, that the journey of Colonel Isakotl, who after a short absence 
at Stuttgurdt reappeared here a few days ago, and received a Bavarian decor 
tion, had for its object to express to the King the great gratification experienced 
by the Emperor at the friendly dispositions manifested at the Bamberg meeting, 
and to sound the Bavarian Cabinet in respect to its future policy, with a view 
to discovering whether there was any chance of persuading it to act with Prussia 
in arresting the course about to be entered upon by Austria, Fy! 

Colonel. Isakolf was, Tam told, also charged to convey to the King the 
strongest assurances of the s smpathy felt by the Emperor tor the humiliation 
and sufferings of the King of Greece, and to express His Imperial Majesty's 
sincere regret at his inability to assist him at the present moment. 

Now, notwithstanding the exposure ot the Emperor's intentions 1 regard 
to the restriction of the Kingdom of Greece within its actual limits, made in the 


avg 


secret and confidential correspondence laid before Parliament, I can scarcely 
hesitate to own an apprehension that these shallow attempts at cajolery may 
produce some effect in quarters so predisposed in favour of the Court from 
whence they come, 

M. von der Pfordten had several interviews with Colonel Isakoff, sometimes 
in the presence of my Russian colleague, and sometimes alone, and | have no 
doubt that at them all these matters were thoroughly canvassed, 1 am unable 
to state what passed in reference to the interests of the Bavarian dynasty in 
Greece, but I have reason to believe that on the other point, M, von der 
Pfordten, whilst avawing his entire disapproval of the policy of the Cabmet of 
Vienna on the Eastern question, added that Bavaria would, whatever happened, 
be compelled to follow Austria. He was at some pams, I understand, to 
impress upon the mind of Colonel Isakoff the prodigious weight which 70,000,000 
United Germans would be able to throw into the scale on either side, and he is 
not altogether without hope that this consideration may have some influence on 
the further conduct of the Emperor, 

His Excellency is completely satisfied with the moderate language in which 
the Russian reply to the Vienna summons is drawn up, and he considers that 
the readiness to subscribe to the Protocol of Vienna announced in it, is evidence 
of pacific intentions on the part of Russia, and offers a fiir basis for the renewal 
of negotiations, and particularly for the immediate conclusion of an armistice, 

Without wishing to commence any discussion on the merits or demerits of 
the composition before us, I replied that [ viewed it in somewhat a different light. 
It insinuated, I said, throughout, that Russia was the aggrieved party, and tliat 
the others were the aggressors, It sought to justify the protracted occupation 
of a large portion of the Turkish territory on the ground of the necessity for 
keeping a military position, Why, I asked, if the Emperor were so pacifically 
disposed, did he not take up his military positions within his own dominions? 
Then, | observed, if | understood the concluding paragraph rightly, Count 
Nesselrode afleeted to consider that the Vienna Protocol established the prin- 
ciple of an European Protectorate over the Christian subjects of the Porte, 
which he perfectly well knew was never contemplated in the Russian sense, 

| was unwilling, I said, to prejudge the answer which would be returned to 
the communication of this despatch by Her Majesty's Government, but I 
thought I might safely hazard a conjecture that it would not meet with the 
approbation that he seemed to consider due to it. 

Now the practical consequences of all these divergencies of opinions and 
views, inay, | conceive, be summed up in a very few words. If Austria and 
Prussia are really of one mind, and determined to act with energy, of which | 
may he permitted to entertain doubts, the smaller States must necessarily march 
march with them. Should Prussia refuse to participate in any hostile demou- 
stration against Russia, and in general evince a desire to bold back, the latter 
will redouble her efforts to secure the support of the smaller Governments, in 
the hope of thus being able to cripple the action of the disposable forces of 
Austria, in which, notwithstanding M. von der Pfordten’s asseverations, she is 
even liere not unlikely to be partially successful. But this pressure will, in my 
opinion, be the more stringently applied at the moment when the Russian forces 
shal have either voluntarily withdrawn or been driven from the Prineipalities ; 
the evacuation of which most of the German Governments regard as the sole 
object of the war, in as far, at least, as they are called upon to take part in it 
in defence of German interests, 

In the event, however, of a reluctance to advance on the part of Prussia, 
or more properly speaking on the part of the King, another question of no small 
importance to the interna welfare of Germany would be at once raised, with ull 
its concomitant dangers; for | cannot for a moment suppose that public opinion 
would suffer Austria to support single-handed the chances of a war, avowedly 
undertaken for the protection of German interests, with the sanction of the 
Sovereign who appears now so anxious to escape from the responsibility he 
incurred by the signature of the Protocols of Vienna.

My Lord, Theramia, July 24, 1854. 

THE Prussian Envoy at Constantinople, whether by order of his Court or 
not | am ignorant, intimated lately, in confidence, to Reshid Pasha that the Porte 
would, in his opinion, act wisely in not allowing the Austrians to effect an 
exelusive occupation of the Principalities, and advised, as the better course, that 
a portion of the Turkish army, even in conjunction with British and French 
troops, should be sent into Wallachia at the same time. His impression, 
according to the message conveyed secretly to me, appeared to be that the object 
of the Court of Vienna was to take the place of the Russians, and to assume, 10 
some degree, the character of protectors.

My Lord, Berlin, August 4, 1854. 

WITH reference ta my despatch No. 421 of the 25th ultimo, in which | 
informed your Lordship of my having, in the absence of Baron Manteutfel, com- 
municated to the Acting Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, the 
substance of your Loridship’s despatches to the Earl of Westmorland, Nos. 247, 
248, and 249 of the 22nd ultimo, on the policy of the Western Powers towards 
Russia, I have thought it advisable to refer to this communication at an interview 
whieh | have had with the Minister President, since his return from the country. 

L recapitulated, shortly, the four points upon which Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment were agreed with Austria, as the bases upon which a peace with Russia 
might be negotiated : 

1. A new organization of the Principalities calculated to substitute the 
protectorate of Europe for the influence so long abused in these provinces. 

9. A revision of the Treaty of 1541, and the limitation of the naval power 
of Russia in the Black Sea. 

5. Freedom of the navigation of the Danube under the guarantee of the 
Great Powers of Europe. 

4. The abolition of Protectorate claimed by Russia over Greek subjects of 
the Porte, and placing the diferent Christian communities in the Ottoman 
Empire under the safeguard of the Christian’ Powers, with due respect to the 
independence and sovereign rights of the Sultan; and 1 told his Excellency 
that he would at once comprehend that with these opinions Her Majesty"s 
Government must consider the Russian answer addresed to Prince Gortchakotf 
as unworthy of serious consideration. 

Baron Manteuffel replied that he nevertheless thought there were points 
upon which Her Majesty’s Government might have conselited tognegotiate, and 
that it was not advisable to threw over the Russian propositions altogether, 
L then said that your Lordship’s answer was. already at Vien; and that, in 
the present temper of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, it was useless to think 
of negotiating with it; and that Her Majesty's Government would not be 
parties to any more negotiation, direct. or indirect, with the Imperial Govern- 
ment; that our answer was in Count Buol’s hands, who might, on his own 
responsibility, do what he pleased with it, but that he was not nuthorized to 
communicate it to St. Petersburgh. 

Baron Manteuffel appeared deeply to regret these decisions of Tler Majesty's 
Government, feeling, probably, that an end would thus be put to the efforts of 
mediation which the King o Prussia was so desirous to continue, and that His 
Majesty's policy would soon be foreed into another direction.

My Lord, Berlin, August 4. 1854. 
1 CALLED to-day on Baron Manteuffel, and asked him if he had received 


from Count Bernstoff the reports of two interviews which he had lately had with 
your Lordship. 


a 


His Excellency replied that they had reached him, but as he showed no 
disposition to converse respecting these reports, L read to him the latter part 
of your Lordship’s despatch No. 208 of the 3lst ultimo, and the whole of 
your No. 208 of the Ist mstant, in the hope of extracting some remarks 
from him. 

His Excellency attempted to defend the King from Russian predilections, 
and endeavoured to show that though Prussia was disposed to go with ua to 
a certain extent, we expected more from her than she was at present disposed 
to give, and that she wished, and had all along wished, to keep out of war ; that 
we desired her to unite her policy with ours, which she hesitated doing, because 
we wished to push matters further than she was prepared for. 

Baron Manteuffel spoke upon the subject of the Vienna Conference, and 
of Count Alvensleben being authorised to attend it, and evidently seemed 
desirous that the Prussian Plenipotentiary should be a party to any meetings 
that might take place at Vienna; upon which T drew his Exeellency’s attention 
to the latter part of your Lordship's despatch No. 208,10 which you state that 
it was now too late, and that it would be casting ridicule on the British Govern- 
ment to attend a Conference for the purpose of communicating to it a Russian 
despatch which we considered unworthy of our consideration, and which, in 
fact, was already replied to by a communication to the Cabinet of Vienna. 
That we did not want a Conference, but an explanation of the future intentions 
of Prussia, in order that we might make our arrangements accordingly, for we 
could no longer submit to render our plans subordinate to the vacillation of 
other countries. 

Baron Manteuffel was silent, and evidently felt unable to give any opinion 
of the King's intentions at this moment. 

1 understand that Count Esterhazy has male communications of importance 
to Baron Manteuffel, and has pressed the Prussian Government to arm without 
loss of time, and that the more decided language of the Austrian Legation since 
Count Esterhazy's arrival at Berlin, has taken them by surprise, and may be 
productive of good results. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

containing the guarantees. With respect lo the Convention, he represented that

soon occur which night render necessary an act of a similar nature, 

The Austrian Government will immediately order the oceupation of the

YOUR Lordship will have been informed by the Farl of Westmorland that 
the Austrian Government is willing to proceed at once to exchange the 
notes proposed by the French Government and alluded to in my despateh 
No. 987 of the 27th ultimo, but that the Emperor objects to signing the Treaty 
alluded to in the same despateh, until another overture has been made to St. 
Petersburgh, In M. de Bourqueney’s statement it 1s said that if after eight days 
the Russian Government does not accept the Austrian proposals, Count Ester- 
hazy is to leave St. Petersburgh, and that the Emperor of Austria then engages 
to sanction the signature af the Treaty, In the communication, however. which 
\i. de Hibner made to M. Drouyn de Lhuys on this matter, he only went so far 
as to say that his Imperial Master reserved to himsclf to order the signature 
when the refusal of Russia should be announced. Your Lordship will have 
loarnt, likewise, that M. de Bourqueney refused to accept the exchange of notes 
only, and that his example was followed by Lord Westmorland. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys approved the proceedings of M. de Bourqueney, who 
hoped by this refusal to mduce the Austrian Government to sign the two 
instruments at the same time, and he stated as much to M.de Hitbner, observing 
on the inconsistency of three Powers specifying the terms on which peace could 
he made, before any engagement wis signed which made them joint belligerents. 
Nevertheless, his Excellency is so much alive to the advantages to the alliances 
which he conceives must result from the exchange of notes, that, having 
ascertaincd that Lord Westmorland was to follow the instructions sent to the 
French Minister im this matter, he has authorised M, de Bourqueney to exchange 
the notes without signing the Treaty. Indeed, he observes that the signature of 
the Treaty is for the moment impossible, as Her Majesty's Government have 
riised objections, which ure yet under discussion.

THE Prussian Chareé d’Affaires made this morning to M. Dronyn de

All that the Prossian Government desired was to come to some wnderstinding

and the adhesion of the Germanic Diet to the ‘Treaty signed between Prussin

soon as the conditions on which the belligerent Powers would make peace, were 
made known to them in writing, to take them into their consideration. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied at once to Count Brandenburgh, that when 
a Conference had been summoned by Count Buol, the day and hour fixed, and 
when the Plenipotentiaries of Great Britain and France, on presenting themselves, 
were informed that the Conference could not take place, beciuse the Prussian

380) 


the part of Prussis to continue the Conferences, particularly as elzht days 
elapsed without any change. ‘n the intentions of her Representative heme 
announced; that to say the least of it, there was a want of courtesy in this 
proceeding to whieb the French Government would not again expose their 
Representative, and that finding that 4 union of the four Powers had been thus

ather Powers, and he added that Count Brandenburgh showed considerable
